They are not the critics predestined to bring me out, and *develop* my morals:﻿—that is the secret. By and by the *North American Quarterly Humdrum* will make them ashamed of their stupidity. In the meantime, by way of staying execution﻿—by way of mitigating the accusations against me﻿—I offer the sad history appended﻿—a history about whose obvious moral there can be no question whatever, since he who runs may read it in the large capitals which form the title of the tale. I should have credit for this arrangement﻿—a far wiser one than that of La Fontaine and others, who reserve the impression to be conveyed until the last moment, and thus sneak it in at the fag end of their fables.

===Chinese===

所以，几个无知之徒加给我的罪名——说我从不曾写过一篇寓意故事，或者说明白些，一篇有寓意的故事——是全无根据的。他们不是命中注定要把我阐发出来、*发扬*我的寓意的那班批评家：——秘密就在这里。早晚《北美季刊温吞》会叫他们为自己的愚蠢害臊。眼下，作为缓刑之计——作为减轻对我的控告——我献上后面这篇凄惨的史实：它的寓意明摆着，绝无争辩的余地，因为跑着的人也能从标题那几个大号字母里把它读出来。这个安排，我该得几分功劳——比拉封丹那班人高明得多，他们把要传达的教训拖到最后一刻，鬼鬼祟祟塞在寓言的屁股后头。

===Original===

*Defuncti injuriâ ne afficiantur* was a law of the twelve tables, and *De mortuis nil nisi bonum* is an excellent injunction﻿—even if the dead in question be nothing but dead small beer. It is not my design, therefore, to vituperate my deceased friend, Toby Dammit. He was a sad dog, it is true, and a dog’s death it was that he died; but he himself was not to blame for his vices. They grew out of a personal defect in his mother. She did her best in the way of flogging him while an infant﻿—for duties to her well-regulated mind were always pleasures, and babies, like tough steaks, or the modern Greek olive trees, are invariably the better for beating﻿—but, poor woman! she had the misfortune to be left-handed, and a child flogged left-handedly had better be left unflogged. The world revolves from right to left. It will not do to whip a baby from left to right. If each blow in the proper direction drives an evil propensity out, it follows that every thump in an opposite one knocks its quota of wickedness in. I was often present at Toby’s chastisements, and, even by the way in which he kicked, I could perceive that he was getting worse and worse every day. At last I saw, through the tears in my eyes, that there was no hope of the villain at all, and one day when he had been cuffed until he grew so black in the face that one might have mistaken him for a little African, and no effect had been produced beyond that of making him wriggle himself into a fit, I could stand it no longer, but went down upon my knees forthwith, and, uplifting my voice, made prophecy of his ruin.

The fact is that his precocity in vice was awful. At five months of age he used to get into such passions that he was unable to articulate. At six months, I caught him gnawing a pack of cards. At seven months he was in the constant habit of catching and kissing the female babies. At eight months he peremptorily refused to put his signature to the Temperance pledge. Thus he went on increasing in iniquity, month after month, until, at the close of the first year, he not only insisted upon wearing *moustaches*, but had contracted a propensity for cursing and swearing, and for backing his assertions by bets.

===Chinese===

《十二铜表法》里有一条：*死者不得受辱*；*死者唯善可言*也是一句极好的箴言——哪怕死者不过是一杯走了气的淡啤酒。所以，谩骂我亡友托比·达米特，不是我的用意。他是个坏小子，不假；他的死，也是一条狗的死法；可他的恶习，他自己并没有罪。那是从他母亲身上的一处缺陷里长出来的。他襁褓之中，她尽力抽打过他——于她那颗规行矩歩的心，本分向来就是快乐；而婴儿，同老牛肉、同现代的希腊橄榄树一样，挨打只有好处——可是，可怜的女人！她不走运，是个左撇子；而左撇子抽大的孩子，还不如不抽。世界自右向左转。从左往右抽婴儿，万万使不得。顺着正方向的一鞭，赶一分恶性出去；那么反方向的一记，就必敲一分恶行进来。托比受刑的时候我常在场；单看他乱踢的那副样子，我也能看出他一天坏似一天。到末了，我含着一泡眼泪看出，这小恶棍全无指望了。有一天他又挨了一顿耳刮子，脸上打得乌青，人家险些把他当成个小黑奴，而除了抽得他扭出一场抽风，全无别的效验——我再也看不下去，当即跪倒在地，扬声预言了他的毁灭。

实情是，他为恶的早熟骇人。五个月上，他就常发脾气发到说不出话。六个月，我抓住他啃一副纸牌。七个月，他养成 habit，专逮女婴来亲。八个月，他断然拒绝在戒酒公约上签名。就这样，他一月恶似一月，到周岁末尾，不但非要留*小胡子*不可，还养成了赌咒发誓的习气，以及拿打赌给自己话作保的习气。

===Original===

Through this latter most ungentlemanly practice, the ruin which I had predicted to Toby Dammit overtook him at last. The fashion had “grown with his growth and strengthened with his strength,” so that, when he came to be a man, he could scarcely utter a sentence without interlarding it with a proposition to gamble. Not that he actually *laid* wagers﻿—no. I will do my friend the justice to say that he would as soon have laid eggs. With him the thing was a mere formula﻿—nothing more. His expressions on this head had no meaning attached to them whatever. They were simple if not altogether innocent expletives﻿—imaginative phrases wherewith to round off a sentence. When he said “I’ll bet you so-and-so,” nobody ever thought of taking him up; but still I could not help thinking it my duty to put him down. The habit was an immoral one, and so I told him. It was a vulgar one﻿—this I begged him to believe. It was discountenanced by society﻿—here I said nothing but the truth. It was forbidden by act of Congress﻿—here I had not the slightest intention of telling a lie. I remonstrated﻿—but to no purpose. I demonstrated﻿—in vain. I entreated﻿—he smiled. I implored﻿—he laughed. I preached﻿—he sneered. I threatened﻿—he swore. I kicked him﻿—he called for the police. I pulled his nose﻿—he blew it, and offered to bet the Devil his head that I would not venture to try that experiment again.

Poverty was another vice which the peculiar physical deficiency of Dammit’s mother had entailed upon her son. He was detestably poor, and this was the reason, no doubt, that his expletive expressions about betting, seldom took a pecuniary turn. I will not be bound to say that I ever heard him make use of such a figure of speech as “I’ll bet you a dollar.” It was usually “I’ll bet you what you please,” or “I’ll bet you what you dare,” or “I’ll bet you a trifle,” or else, more significantly still, “*I’ll bet the Devil my head.*”

===Chinese===

正是这后一种最不绅士的习气，终于给托比·达米特招来了我预言过的毁灭。这毛病「随他的成长而成长，随他的强健而强健」，到成人时，他几乎说不出一句话，不夹上一句赌注的。倒不是他当真*下*注——不。我这位朋友得说句公道话：他下注同母鸡下蛋一样难得。在他，这不过一个套语——仅此而已。他这方面的话，一概没有意义。那是单纯的、不说全然无辜也算无邪的感叹词——把一句话收拢收拢的想象性词藻。他说「我同你赌个什么什么」，从没有人想到接茬；可我仍不免觉得，把他这毛病压下去是我的本分。这习气不道德——我这样告诉他。这习气下流——这一层我求他相信。上流社会不齿它——这里我句句是实。国会有法案禁止它——这里我丝毫没有撒谎的打算。我劝——无效。我论证——徒劳。我恳求——他微笑。我哀告——他大笑。我说教——他讥讽。我威胁——他咒骂。我踢他——他喊警察。我拉他的鼻子——他擤了擤，提出拿他的脑袋同魔鬼打赌，赌我不敢再试一回那个实验。

贫穷是达米特之母那处特殊的身体缺陷遗传给儿子的另一宗恶。他穷得可憎；毫无疑问，这就是他赌咒的口头禅难得拐到钱上的缘故。我不敢说我听他用过「我同你赌一块钱」这样的说法。往常总是「我同你赌你随便什么」，或「我同你赌你敢什么」，或「我同你赌个小意思」，再不然，意味更深长地，「*我拿我的脑袋同魔鬼赌。*」

===Original===

This latter form seemed to please him best;﻿—perhaps because it involved the least risk; for Dammit had become excessively parsimonious. Had anyone taken him up, his head was small, and thus his loss would have been small too. But these are my own reflections and I am by no means sure that I am right in attributing them to him. At all events the phrase in question grew daily in favor, notwithstanding the gross impropriety of a man betting his brains like banknotes﻿—but this was a point which my friend’s perversity of disposition would not permit him to comprehend. In the end, he abandoned all other forms of wager, and gave himself up to “*I’ll bet the Devil my head*,” with a pertinacity and exclusiveness of devotion that displeased not less than it surprised me. I am always displeased by circumstances for which I cannot account. Mysteries force a man to think, and so injure his health. The truth is, there was something in *the air* with which Mr. Dammit was wont to give utterance to his offensive expression﻿—something in his *manner* of enunciation﻿—which at first interested, and afterwards made me very uneasy﻿—something which, for want of a more definite term at present, I must be permitted to call *queer*; but which Mr. Coleridge would have called mystical, Mr. Kant pantheistical, Mr. Carlyle twistical, and Mr. Emerson hyperquizzitistical. I began not to like it at all. Mr. Dammits soul was in a perilous state. I resolved to bring all my eloquence into play to save it. I vowed to serve him as St. Patrick, in the Irish chronicle, is said to have served the toad﻿—that is to say, “awaken him to a sense of his situation.” I addressed myself to the task forthwith. Once more I betook myself to remonstrance. Again I collected my energies for a final attempt at expostulation.

===Chinese===

这最后一种句式似乎最合他的胃口；——也许因为风险最小；因为达米特已变得抠门透顶。真有人接了，他的脑袋也小，损失也就小。不过这些是我自己的揣度，把它们派给他头上，对不对，我全无把握。无论如何，这句话一天比一天得宠，尽管拿自己的脑子当钞票押，粗俗失礼之至——可这一层，我朋友的拗性不容他领会。到末了，他把别的赌式一概舍弃，专心致志于「我拿脑袋同魔鬼赌」，那份执拗与专一，令我惊讶，也令我大为不快。凡是我不明所以的事，我一概不快。神秘逼人思考，有损健康。实情是，达米特先生惯于吐出那句浑话时，*空气*里有一样什么——他*吐字*的腔调里有一样什么——起初叫我感兴趣，随后叫我极不自在——一样什么，眼下找不到更确切的词，只好容我叫它*怪*；可柯尔律治先生会叫它神秘，康德先生会叫它泛神，卡莱尔先生会叫它拧巴，爱默生先生会叫它超诘屈。我开始一点也不喜欢它了。达米特先生的灵魂岌岌可危。我决计施展出我全部的辩才去救它。我许愿要像爱尔兰编年史里的圣帕特里克侍候蟾蜍那样侍候他——也就是说，「唤醒他，让他明白自己的处境」。我立刻着手办这件大事。我再一次诉诸规劝。我重又鼓起全副力气，作最后一次诤谏。

===Original===

When I had made an end of my lecture, Mr. Dammit indulged himself in some very equivocal behavior. For some moments he remained silent, merely looking me inquisitively in the face. But presently he threw his head to one side, and elevated his eyebrows to a great extent. Then he spread out the palms of his hands and shrugged up his shoulders. Then he winked with the right eye. Then he repeated the operation with the left. Then he shut them both up very tight. Then he opened them both so very wide that I became seriously alarmed for the consequences. Then, applying his thumb to his nose, he thought proper to make an indescribable movement with the rest of his fingers. Finally, setting his arms akimbo, he condescended to reply.

I can call to mind only the heads of his discourse. He would be obliged to me if I would hold my tongue. He wished none of my advice. He despised all my insinuations. He was old enough to take care of himself. Did I still think him baby Dammit? Did I mean to say anything against his character? Did I intend to insult him? Was I a fool? Was my maternal parent aware, in a word, of my absence from the domiciliary residence? He would put this latter question to me as to a man of veracity, and he would bind himself to abide by my reply. Once more he would demand explicitly if my mother knew that I was out. My confusion, he said, betrayed me, and he would be willing to bet the Devil his head that she did not.

Mr. Dammit did not pause for my rejoinder. Turning upon his heel, he left my presence with undignified precipitation. It was well for him that he did so. My feelings had been wounded. Even my anger had been aroused. For once I would have taken him up upon his insulting wager. I would have won for the Arch-Enemy Mr. Dammit’s little head﻿—for the fact is, my mamma *was* very well aware of my merely temporary absence from home.

===Chinese===

我的训话收了尾，达米特先生便纵情做出一套含意暧昧的举动。有几秒钟，他一言不发，只把脸探究地望着我。随后他把头一歪，眉毛高高挑起。然后他摊开双掌，耸起双肩。然后他眨了眨右眼。然后他用左眼重复了一遍这套动作。然后他把两只眼睛紧紧闭上。然后又把两只眼睛睁得老大老圆，叫我当真为后果担忧。然后他把大拇指按上鼻尖，其余四指得体地做出一番难以形容的运动。末了，他双手叉腰，纡尊降贵地作答。

他的演说，我记得起的只有几个要点。我肯闭上嘴，他就承我的情。我的忠告他一律不要。我的一切影射他一律唾弃。他年纪不小了，自己管得了自己。我还当他是娃娃达米特么？我是想说他人品有亏么？我是有意侮辱他么？我是傻子么？一句话，我的生身母亲知不知道我没在家里待着？这后一问，他要当作问一个老实人那样问我，并且自愿受我的回答约束。他要再明白地问一遍：我妈知不知道我出来了。他说，我的慌乱出卖了我；他愿意拿脑袋同魔鬼打赌——我妈不知道。

达米特先生没有停下来听我回嘴。他脚跟一转，带着有失体面的仓促，从我面前走了。他这样倒好。我的感情受了伤。连我的怒气都被激起来了。这一回，我本要接下他那句侮辱性的赌注的。我会替那位大仇敌赢下达米特先生的小脑袋——因为实情是，我妈*非常*清楚我只是暂时不在家。

===Original===

But *Khoda shefa midêhed*﻿—Heaven gives relief﻿—as the Mussulmans say when you tread upon their toes. It was in pursuance of my duty that I had been insulted, and I bore the insult like a man. It now seemed to me, however, that I had done all that could be required of me, in the case of this miserable individual, and I resolved to trouble him no longer with my counsel, but to leave him to his conscience and himself. But although I forebore to intrude with my advice, I could not bring myself to give up his society altogether. I even went so far as to humor some of his less reprehensible propensities; and there were times when I found myself lauding his wicked jokes, as epicures do mustard, with tears in my eyes:﻿—so profoundly did it grieve me to hear his evil talk.

===Chinese===

可是，*霍达·谢法·米德赫德*——上天解救——你踩了穆斯林的脚趾时，他们这样说。我受辱是为了尽本分，我便像条汉子般受了。不过在我看来，对这个可怜虫，我已尽了人家能要求于我的一切；我决意不再拿我的忠告去烦他，由他跟着他自己的良心去吧。可我虽忍住不再进忠言，却狠不下心同他绝交。我甚至迁就他几样较不可鄙的癖性；有几回，我发现自己竟夸起他那些缺德的俏皮话来——像美食家夸芥末那样，眼里含着泪：——听他说浑话，我实在伤心到这步田地。

===Original===

One fine day, having strolled out together, arm in arm, our route led us in the direction of a river. There was a bridge, and we resolved to cross it. It was roofed over, by way of protection from the weather, and the archway, having but few windows, was thus very uncomfortably dark. As we entered the passage, the contrast between the external glare and the interior gloom struck heavily upon my spirits. Not so upon those of the unhappy Dammit, who offered to bet the Devil his head that I was hipped. He seemed to be in an unusual good humor. He was excessively lively﻿—so much so that I entertained I know not what of uneasy suspicion. It is not impossible that he was affected with the transcendentals. I am not well enough versed, however, in the diagnosis of this disease to speak with decision upon the point; and unhappily there were none of my friends of the *Dial* present. I suggest the idea, nevertheless, because of a certain species of austere Merry-Andrewism which seemed to beset my poor friend, and caused him to make quite a tomfool of himself. Nothing would serve him but wriggling and skipping about under and over everything that came in his way; now shouting out, and now lisping out, all manner of odd little and big words, yet preserving the gravest face in the world all the time. I really could not make up my mind whether to kick or to pity him. At length, having passed nearly across the bridge, we approached the termination of the footway, when our progress was impeded by a turnstile of some height. Through this I made my way quietly, pushing it around as usual. But this turn would not serve the turn of Mr. Dammit. He insisted upon leaping the stile, and said he could cut a pigeon-wing over it in the air. Now this, conscientiously speaking, I did not think he could do. The best pigeon-winger over all kinds of style was my friend Mr. Carlyle, and as I knew *he* could not do it, I would not believe that it could be done by Toby Dammit. I therefore told him, in so many words, that he was a braggadocio, and could not do what he said. For this I had reason to be sorry afterward;﻿—for he straightway offered to *bet the Devil his head* that he could.

===Chinese===

一个晴朗的日子，我们挽着胳膊一同散步，一路走到了河边。有一座桥，我们决意过桥去。桥上有顶，为的是避风雨；桥洞里窗子又少，因此黑得极不舒服。一走进廊道，外间的亮同里面的暗一对照，重重压在我的心绪上。不幸的达米特却不然，他提出拿脑袋同魔鬼打赌，赌我情绪低落。他像是心情好得出奇。他快活得过了头——过头到叫我生出某种不安的疑心。他染上的，未必不是超验病。不过这病的症候，我不够娴熟，不敢断言；不巧我的《日晷》诸友又都不在场。我提这个话，是因为我那可怜的朋友周身笼着一种严其肃其的小丑气，叫他把自己弄成了十足的活宝。什么都不依他，除非钻来蹦去，从挡他道的一切东西底下钻过、上面跳过；一会儿喊出、一会儿咬着舌念出各种稀奇古怪的大词小词，脸上却始终绷着天下最庄重的表情。我真拿不定主意，该踢他，还是该怜他。好容易快到桥那头，走近人行道的尽头，路被一道相当高的回转栅拦住了。我安安静静地照例一推，从栅门里走了过去。可这一转，服侍不了达米特先生的转。他非要跳过栅栏不可，还说能凌空在它上面剪一个鸽翅。凭良心说，这我不信他能做得到。遍历各种栅栏的头号鸽翅好手，是我朋友卡莱尔先生；我知道*他*尚且做不得，便不肯相信托比·达米特做得了。于是我直截了当告诉他：他是个牛皮匠，他说的事他办不到。这话我后来有理由懊悔；——因为他立刻提出*拿脑袋同魔鬼打赌*，赌他办得到。

===Original===

I was about to reply, notwithstanding my previous resolutions, with some remonstrance against his impiety, when I heard, close at my elbow, a slight cough, which sounded very much like the ejaculation “*ahem!*” I started, and looked about me in surprise. My glance at length fell into a nook of the frame﻿—work of the bridge, and upon the figure of a little lame old gentleman of venerable aspect. Nothing could be more reverend than his whole appearance; for he not only had on a full suit of black, but his shirt was perfectly clean and the collar turned very neatly down over a white cravat, while his hair was parted in front like a girl’s. His hands were clasped pensively together over his stomach, and his two eyes were carefully rolled up into the top of his head.

Upon observing him more closely, I perceived that he wore a black silk apron over his small-clothes; and this was a thing which I thought very odd. Before I had time to make any remark, however, upon so singular a circumstance, he interrupted me with a second “*ahem!*”

To this observation I was not immediately prepared to reply. The fact is, remarks of this laconic nature are nearly unanswerable. I have known a *Quarterly Review* nonplussed by the word “*Fudge!*” I am not ashamed to say, therefore, that I turned to Mr. Dammit for assistance.

“Dammit,” said I, “what are you about? don’t you hear?﻿—the gentleman says ‘*ahem!*’ ” I looked sternly at my friend while I thus addressed him; for, to say the truth, I felt particularly puzzled, and when a man is particularly puzzled he must knit his brows and look savage, or else he is pretty sure to look like a fool.

“Dammit,” observed I﻿—although this sounded very much like an oath, than which nothing was further from my thoughts﻿—“Dammit,” I suggested﻿—“the gentleman says ‘ahem!’ ”

I do not attempt to defend my remark on the score of profundity; I did not think it profound myself; but I have noticed that the effect of our speeches is not always proportionate with their importance in our own eyes; and if I had shot Mr. D. through and through with a Paixhan bomb, or knocked him in the head with the *Poets and Poetry of America*, he could hardly have been more discomfited than when I addressed him with those simple words: “Dammit, what are you about?﻿—don’t you hear?﻿—the gentleman says ‘*ahem!*’ ”

===Chinese===

我不顾先前的决心，正要回敬几句，谏一谏他的渎神，忽然听见肘边一声轻咳，很有些像「*啊咳！*」的惊叹。我一惊，诧异地四下张望。末了，我的目光落进桥架的一个角落，落在一位跛脚小老头的身影上，一派可敬的仪表。再没有比他通身的模样更可敬的了：他不只穿着一身黑，衬衫还雪白，领子端端正正翻下来，压着一条白领结；头发像姑娘那样从正中间分开。他的手若有所思地交叠在肚腹上，两只眼睛小心翼翼地翻上去，只留眼白。

再一细看，我发觉他马裤外头还系着一条黑绸围裙；这东西我觉得很怪。可我还没来得及就这桩奇事开口，他又一声「*啊咳！*」把我拦住了。

对这句话，我一时不及应对。实情是，这类言简意赅的话，几乎无法回。我就见过《评论季刊》被一个「*呸！*」字问得张口结舌。所以我不惭愧地说，我转向达米特先生求援。

「达米特，」我说，「你要干什么？没听见么？——这位先生说『*啊咳！*』」我这样说他时，狠狠盯着我的朋友；因为说实在的，我窘极了；而人一窘，就得皱起眉毛、摆出凶相，不然准像个傻子。

「达米特，」我说——这话听去很有点像骂人，而我心里实在离骂人十万八千里——「达米特，」我提点他——「这位先生说『啊咳！』」

我不为这话的深度辩护；我自己也不觉得它深；可我注意到，我们言语的效力，并不总同它们在我们自己眼里的分量相称。倘若我用一门佩克桑炮把达先生打个对穿，或者拿《美国的诗人与诗》敲他的脑袋，也未必能叫他比方才更狼狈——我只用了这几个简单的字：「达米特，你要干什么？——没听见么？——这位先生说『*啊咳！*』」

===Original===

“You don’t say so?” gasped he at length, after turning more colors than a pirate runs up, one after the other, when chased by a man-of-war. “Are you quite sure he said *that*? Well, at all events I am in for it now, and may as well put a bold face upon the matter. Here goes, then﻿—*ahem!*”

At this the little old gentleman seemed pleased﻿—God only knows why. He left his station at the nook of the bridge, limped forward with a gracious air, took Dammit by the hand and shook it cordially, looking all the while straight up in his face with an air of the most unadulterated benignity which it is possible for the mind of man to imagine.

“I am quite sure you will win it, Dammit,” said he, with the frankest of all smiles, “but we are obliged to have a trial, you know, for the sake of mere form.”

“Ahem!” replied my friend, taking off his coat, with a deep sigh, tying a pocket-handkerchief around his waist, and producing an unaccountable alteration in his countenance by twisting up his eyes and bringing down the corners of his mouth﻿—“ahem!” And “ahem!” said he again, after a pause; and not another word more than “ahem!” did I ever know him to say after that. “Aha!” thought I, without expressing myself aloud﻿—“this is quite a remarkable silence on the part of Toby Dammit, and is no doubt a consequence of his verbosity upon a previous occasion. One extreme induces another. I wonder if he has forgotten the many unanswerable questions which he propounded to me so fluently on the day when I gave him my last lecture? At all events, he is cured of the transcendentals.”

“Ahem!” here replied Toby, just as if he had been reading my thoughts, and looking like a very old sheep in a revery.

===Chinese===

「不会吧？」他喘着气说，脸色接连变换，比战舰追赶下的海盗升旗还多。「你敢肯定他说的是*那个*？好吧，反正我已上了船，索性放硬正着脸面对。那就来吧——*啊咳！*」

听了这话，小老头像是很高兴——天知道为什么。他离开桥角那一站，和霭地一瘸一拐走上前来，握住达米特的手，热忱地摇着，两眼自始至终直望上他的脸，那副再纯粹不过的慈祥，人心所能想见的无过于此。

「我笃定你赢，达米特，」他说，带着世上最坦率的笑，「不过咱们总得试一回，你知道，不过走个形式。」

「啊咳！」我的朋友答道，深深叹了一口气，脱下外衣，往腰上束了一条手帕，又把眼睛拧上去、嘴角拉下来，脸上的模样登时改了个不可名状——「啊咳！」停了片刻，他又「啊咳！」了一声；此后我认得的达米特，除了「啊咳！」再没说过半个字。「啊哈，」我心想，没有出声——「托比·达米特这般沉默，实在少见，必是上回他滔滔不绝的报应。一极端招致另一极端。不知他还记不记得，我最后一次训他那天，他口若悬河地向我提出的那些无法回答的问题？无论如何，他的超验病是治好了。」

「啊咳！」托比在这里应了一声，正像他读出了我的心思，那神气像一头出神的老公羊。

===Original===

The old gentleman now took him by the arm, and led him more into the shade of the bridge﻿—a few paces back from the turnstile. “My good fellow,” said he, “I make it a point of conscience to allow you this much run. Wait here, till I take my place by the stile, so that I may see whether you go over it handsomely, and transcendentally, and don’t omit any flourishes of the pigeon-wing. A mere form, you know. I will say ‘one, two, three, and away.’ Mind you, start at the word ‘away.’ ” Here he took his position by the stile, paused a moment as if in profound reflection, then *looked up* and, I thought, smiled very slightly, then tightened the strings of his apron, then took a long look at Dammit, and finally gave the word as agreed upon﻿—

*One﻿—two﻿—three﻿—and﻿—away!*

Punctually at the word “away,” my poor friend set off in a strong gallop. The stile was not very high, like Mr. Lord’s﻿—nor yet very low, like that of Mr. Lord’s reviewers, but upon the whole I made sure that he would clear it. And then what if he did not?﻿—ah, that was the question﻿—what if he did not? “What right,” said I, “had the old gentleman to make any other gentleman jump? The little old dot-and-carry-one! who is *he*? If he asks me to jump, I won’t do it, that’s flat, and I don’t care who *the devil he is*.” The bridge, as I say, was arched and covered in, in a very ridiculous manner, and there was a most uncomfortable echo about it at all times﻿—an echo which I never before so particularly observed as when I uttered the four last words of my remark.

===Chinese===

老头儿如今挽起他的胳膊，领他退到桥影更深处——离回转栅几步远。「我的好朋友，」他说，「我凭良心，许你这点助跑。在这里等着，我到栅栏边就位，好看你跳得漂亮不漂亮、超验不超验，鸽翅的花样一式也别漏。不过走个形式，你知道。我喊『一，二，三，跑』。记住，喊到『跑』字才起跳。」说着他在栅栏旁就了位，停了片刻，仿佛沉入深思，然后*抬眼望了望*，我想，极淡地笑了一笑，然后紧了紧围裙的带子，然后把达米特长长端详了一遍，末了照约定的喊出了口令——

*一——二——三——跑！*

「跑」字刚落，我可怜的朋友便撒腿飞奔。那栅栏不很高，不像洛德先生的那座；也不很低，不像洛德先生的批评家们的那座；但总的来说，我确信他跳得过去。可他要是跳不过去呢？——啊，问题在这里——他要是跳不过去呢？「这老头，」我说，「凭什么叫另一位先生跳？这瘸一拐的小东西！他是*谁*？他要叫我跳，我就不跳，明摆着，我才不管他*是哪个鬼*。」那桥，如我所说，罩着可笑的拱顶，四下向来有一股极不舒服的回声——这回声，我从前从不曾像说出最后那四个字时这般清楚地察觉。

===Original===

But what I said, or what I thought, or what I heard, occupied only an instant. In less than five seconds from his starting, my poor Toby had taken the leap. I saw him run nimbly, and spring grandly from the floor of the bridge, cutting the most awful flourishes with his legs as he went up. I saw him high in the air, pigeon-winging it to admiration just over the top of the stile; and of course I thought it an unusually singular thing that he did not *continue* to go over. But the whole leap was the affair of a moment, and, before I had a chance to make any profound reflections, down came Mr. Dammit on the flat of his back, on the same side of the stile from which he had started. At the same instant I saw the old gentleman limping off at the top of his speed, having caught and wrapt up in his apron something that fell heavily into it from the darkness of the arch just over the turnstile. At all this I was much astonished; but I had no leisure to think, for Dammit lay particularly still, and I concluded that his feelings had been hurt, and that he stood in need of my assistance. I hurried up to him and found that he had received what might be termed a serious injury. The truth is, he had been deprived of his head, which after a close search I could not find anywhere; so I determined to take him home and send for the homoeopathists. In the meantime a thought struck me, and I threw open an adjacent window of the bridge, when the sad truth flashed upon me at once. About five feet just above the top of the turnstile, and crossing the arch of the footpath so as to constitute a brace, there extended a flat iron bar, lying with its breadth horizontally, and forming one of a series that served to strengthen the structure throughout its extent. With the edge of this brace it appeared evident that the neck of my unfortunate friend had come precisely in contact.

===Chinese===

可我说的、想的、听见的，统共不过一瞬。起跑不出五秒，我可怜的托比已经腾身而起。我见他轻捷地奔跑，从桥面上壮美地一蹬，两腿朝天剪出最骇人的花样。我见他高高在空，正在栅栏顶上出神入化地剪着鸽翅；他竟没有*继续*翻过去，这自然使我觉得异乎寻常。可整个一跳不过一瞬间的事，我还来不及作任何深沉的思索，达米特先生已仰面朝天，摔回了他起跳那一边的地上。同一瞬，我看见那老头儿一瘸一拐、撒腿飞逃，围裙里兜住一样东西——那东西从回转栅正上方的黑暗里沉沉落进他的围裙，他裹起来就跑。这一切叫我大为惊愕；可我没工夫细想，因为达米特躺得格外安静，我断定他的感情受了伤，需要我帮忙。我赶上前去，发现他受了可以称为重伤的伤。实情是，他的脑袋没有了；我细细搜寻，哪里也寻不见；于是我决计把他抬回家，去请顺势疗法医师。这当口，一个念头闪过，我推开桥上一扇邻窗，凄惨的真相登时照在我脸上：回转栅顶上方约五英尺处，横着一条扁铁，跨过人行道的拱，起着斜撑的作用，宽面水平安放，是通桥身全长一系列加固铁条中的一条。我那不幸的朋友的脖颈，看来正是恰恰撞上了这条铁撑的棱。

===Original===

He did not long survive his terrible loss. The homoeopathists did not give him little enough physic, and what little they did give him he hesitated to take. So in the end he grew worse, and at length died, a lesson to all riotous livers. I bedewed his grave with my tears, worked a *bar* sinister on his family escutcheon, and, for the general expenses of his funeral, sent in my very moderate bill to the transcendentalists. The scoundrels refused to pay it, so I had Mr. Dammit dug up at once, and sold him for dog’s meat.

===Chinese===

遭了这场可怕的损失，他没能活多久。顺势疗法医师们给他的药，还不够少；给的那一点点，他又迟疑不肯吃。于是他每况愈下，末了死了——给一切浪荡子留一个教训。我用眼泪浇了他的坟，在他家的纹章上添了一道*斜杠*，又把他丧葬的杂费，开了一张极克己的账单，送给超验主义者们。那班恶棍拒付；我当即把达米特先生掘出来，卖了狗肉钱。

## Eleonora / 埃莉奥诺拉
===Original===

Sub conservatione formæ specificæ salva anima.

> Raymond Lully

I am come of a race noted for vigor of fancy and ardor of passion. Men have called me mad; but the question is not yet settled, whether madness is or is not the loftiest intelligence﻿—whether much that is glorious﻿—whether all that is profound﻿—does not spring from disease of thought﻿—from *moods* of mind exalted at the expense of the general intellect. They who dream by day are cognizant of many things which escape those who dream only by night. In their gray visions they obtain glimpses of eternity, and thrill, in awakening, to find that they have been upon the verge of the great secret. In snatches, they learn something of the wisdom which is of good, and more of the mere knowledge which is of evil. They penetrate, however, rudderless or compassless into the vast ocean of the “light ineffable,” and again, like the adventures of the Nubian geographer, “*agressi sunt mare tenebrarum, quid in eo esset exploraturi*.”

We will say, then, that I am mad. I grant, at least, that there are two distinct conditions of my mental existence﻿—the condition of a lucid reason, not to be disputed, and belonging to the memory of events forming the first epoch of my life﻿—and a condition of shadow and doubt, appertaining to the present, and to the recollection of what constitutes the second great era of my being. Therefore, what I shall tell of the earlier period, believe; and to what I may relate of the later time, give only such credit as may seem due, or doubt it altogether, or, if doubt it ye cannot, then play unto its riddle the Oedipus.

===Chinese===

形有所存，魂乃得全。

——雷蒙·吕利（Raymond Lully）

我出身于一个以想象之劲、情热之烈著称的种族。人们说我疯；可疯癫究竟是不是最高的智慧——一切辉煌的、一切深刻的，是否都不出于思想的疾病、不出于以总体理智为代价而高涨的心境——这问题还没有定论。白日做梦的人，知晓许多只在夜间做梦的人所无从知晓的事。在他们灰蒙的幻象里，他们得以窥见永恒；醒来时战栗不已，发見自己方才正站在那大秘密的边缘上。他们一段一段地，学到一点属善的智慧，学到更多的属恶的知识。然而他们无舵无针，一头扎进那「不可言传之光」的汪洋，又像那位努比亚地理学家的历险——「agressi sunt mare tenebrarum, quid in eo esset exploraturi」（他们闯入黑暗之海，要去探明海中何物）。

那么，就算我疯罢。我至少承认，我的心智存在有两种分明的状态——一种清明理智的状态，无可争辩，属于我人生第一个纪元的记忆——一种阴影与疑惑的状态，属于现在，属于构成我第二个大纪元的回忆。所以，我讲早年的事，你们只管信；我讲晚近的事，你们看着给几分信用，或者干脆疑它，倘若疑它不动，那就替它的谜语做一回俄狄浦斯。

===Original===

She whom I loved in youth, and of whom I now pen calmly and distinctly these remembrances, was the sole daughter of the only sister of my mother long departed. Eleonora was the name of my cousin. We had always dwelled together, beneath a tropical sun, in the Valley of the Many-Colored Grass. No unguided footstep ever came upon that vale; for it lay away up among a range of giant hills that hung beetling around about it, shutting out the sunlight from its sweetest recesses. No path was trodden in its vicinity; and, to reach our happy home, there was need of putting back, with force, the foliage of many thousands of forest trees, and of crushing to death the glories of many millions of fragrant flowers. Thus it was that we lived all alone, knowing nothing of the world without the valley﻿—I, and my cousin, and her mother.

From the dim regions beyond the mountains at the upper end of our encircled domain, there crept out a narrow and deep river, brighter than all save the eyes of Eleonora; and, winding stealthily about in mazy courses, it passed away, at length, through a shadowy gorge, among hills still dimmer than those whence it had issued. We called it the “River of Silence”; for there seemed to be a hushing influence in its flow. No murmur arose from its bed, and so gently it wandered along, that the pearly pebbles upon which we loved to gaze, far down within its bosom, stirred not at all, but lay in a motionless content, each in its own old station, shining on gloriously forever.

The margin of the river, and of the many dazzling rivulets that glided through devious ways into its channel, as well as the spaces that extended from the margins away down into the depths of the streams until they reached the bed of pebbles at the bottom﻿—these spots, not less than the whole surface of the valley, from the river to the mountains that girdled it in, were carpeted all by a soft green grass, thick, short, perfectly even, and vanilla-perfumed, but so besprinkled throughout with the yellow buttercup, the white daisy, the purple violet, and the ruby-red asphodel, that its exceeding beauty spoke to our hearts in loud tones, of the love and of the glory of God.

===Chinese===

她是我年轻时所爱，如今我平心静气、清清楚楚写下这些回忆的那个人，是我早已亡故的母亲唯一的姐妹的独女。埃莉奥诺拉是我表妹的名字。我们一向同住，在一轮热带的太阳底下，住在五色草山谷里。从没有一只无引路的脚步踏上过那座山谷；因为它深藏在一片巍峨的群山之间，山岭嶙峋地环抱着它，把日光挡在它最甜美的隐處之外。左近没有一条踩出的路；要走到我们幸福的家，须用力拨开千千万万株林木的枝叶，踩死千千万万朵香花的荣华。我们就这样独自生活，对山谷之外的世界一无所知——我、我的表妹，和她的母亲。

从我们这片环山之地的上端、群山那边昏暗的地界里，流出一条窄而深的河，比一切都亮，只除却埃莉奥诺拉的眼睛；它曲曲折折地悄然绕行，末了穿过一道阴影的峡谷，在比它发源的那些山更昏暗的群山间消失。我们叫它「静默之河」；因为它的流动仿佛有一种叫万物噤声的力量。河床上不起一丝汩汩；它流得那样轻，连我们爱凝望的、河心深处那些珍珠似的卵石，也毫不动摇，一动不动地心满意足，各自守着各自的旧位置，永远光荣地亮着。

河的两岸，还有那些闪闪发光、蜿蜒入河的许多细流的两岸，以及从两岸一直伸到水底卵石床的那些水底空处——这些地方，连同山谷从河到环抱它的群山的整个地面，都铺着一片柔软的绿草，厚、短、匀净，带着香草的气息，又遍地洒满了金黄的毛茛、白色的雏菊、紫色的堇花和红宝石色的日光兰，它那绝色高声向我们心里诉说著上帝的爱与荣光。

===Original===

And, here and there, in groves about this grass, like wildernesses of dreams, sprang up fantastic trees, whose tall slender stems stood not upright, but slanted gracefully toward the light that peered at noonday into the centre of the valley. Their mark was speckled with the vivid alternate splendor of ebony and silver, and was smoother than all save the cheeks of Eleonora; so that, but for the brilliant green of the huge leaves that spread from their summits in long, tremulous lines, dallying with the Zephyrs, one might have fancied them giant serpents of Syria doing homage to their sovereign the Sun.

===Chinese===

而在这些草的四围，一片片树丛，像梦的荒野，长出一株株奇树：高挑細細的干并不直立，而是曼妙地斜向着正午照进谷心的光明。树干上斑斑驳驳，乌木与白银的亮色交相辉映，平滑得胜过一切，只除却埃莉奥诺拉的面頬；要不是树顶上那巨大的绿叶，长长的、颤巍巍的一行行垂散开来，同西风纠缠嬉戏，人真会把它们当作叙利亚的巨蟒，正向它们的君主太阳朝拜。

===Original===

Hand in hand about this valley, for fifteen years, roamed I with Eleonora before Love entered within our hearts. It was one evening at the close of the third lustrum of her life, and of the fourth of my own, that we sat, locked in each other’s embrace, beneath the serpent-like trees, and looked down within the water of the River of Silence at our images therein. We spoke no words during the rest of that sweet day, and our words even upon the morrow were tremulous and few. We had drawn the God Eros from that wave, and now we felt that he had enkindled within us the fiery souls of our forefathers. The passions which had for centuries distinguished our race, came thronging with the fancies for which they had been equally noted, and together breathed a delirious bliss over the Valley of the Many-Colored Grass. A change fell upon all things. Strange, brilliant flowers, star-shaped, burn out upon the trees where no flowers had been known before. The tints of the green carpet deepened; and when, one by one, the white daisies shrank away, there sprang up in place of them, ten by ten of the ruby-red asphodel. And life arose in our paths; for the tall flamingo, hitherto unseen, with all gay glowing birds, flaunted his scarlet plumage before us. The golden and silver fish haunted the river, out of the bosom of which issued, little by little, a murmur that swelled, at length, into a lulling melody more divine than that of the harp of Aeolus﻿—sweeter than all save the voice of Eleonora. And now, too, a voluminous cloud, which we had long watched in the regions of Hesper, floated out thence, all gorgeous in crimson and gold, and settling in peace above us, sank, day by day, lower and lower, until its edges rested upon the tops of the mountains, turning all their dimness into magnificence, and shutting us up, as if forever, within a magic prison-house of grandeur and of glory.

The loveliness of Eleonora was that of the Seraphim; but she was a maiden artless and innocent as the brief life she had led among the flowers. No guile disguised the fervor of love which animated her heart, and she examined with me its inmost recesses as we walked together in the Valley of the Many-Colored Grass, and discoursed of the mighty changes which had lately taken place therein.

===Chinese===

十五年里，我和埃莉奥诺拉手携手在这山谷里漫游，后来爱情进了我们的心。那是在她一生的第三个五年、我的第四个五年将尽的一个傍晚，我们在那蛇一般的树下相拥而坐，望着静默之河水里我们两人的倒影。那甜美的一日剩下的时光，我们一句话也没有说；到第二天，我们的话也是颤巍巍的、寥寥无几。我们从那道水波里钓起了厄洛斯神，如今我们觉得，他在我们心里点燃了我们祖辈火热的魂。几世纪来为我们种族增色的那些情热，携着同样为我们种族增色的幻想，一齐湧来，在五色草山谷上空呵出一阵迷醉的极乐。万物都起了变化。奇异的、亮丽的花，星形的，在从未开过花的树上绽放出来。绿毯的色泽深了；白色的雏菊一朵一朵退去，原地上十朵十朵地，冒出红宝石色的日光兰。生命在我们路上升起；因为高高的火烈鸟带着一群光彩灼灼的鸟儿，先前从未见过，如今在我们面前炫它猩红的羽衣。金的鱼、银的鱼游进了河里；河心渐渐汩汩地起了一阵低语，终至涨成一支比埃俄罗斯的竖琴更神妙的催睡的旋律——比一切都甜，只除却埃莉奥诺拉的声音。这时，我们久已在赫斯珀的天界里守望的那一大朵云，也从那里漂了出来，遍体绯红与金黄，华丽之至，安然停在我们头顶，一日低似一日，直到它的边搭上山巅，把满山的昏暗尽数化作壮丽，把我们封在一座宏伟与荣光的魔宫里，仿佛直到永远。

埃莉奥诺拉的美，是炽天使的美；可她是一个质朴无邪的少女，同她在花丛里度过的短暂生涯一样无邪。没有一点矫饰掩藏她心中燃烧的爱的热，她同我一起探究它最深的隐处，那时我们一同在五色草山谷里漫步，谈论山谷里近来发生的那些巨大变化。

===Original===

At length, having spoken one day, in tears, of the last sad change which must befall Humanity, she thenceforward dwelt only upon this one sorrowful theme, interweaving it into all our converse, as, in the songs of the bard of Schiraz, the same images are found occurring, again and again, in every impressive variation of phrase.

===Chinese===

末了，有一天，她噙着泪讲起人类在劫难逃的最后一次悲哀的变化；从此她只萦怀于这唯一的哀思，把它织进我们全部的谈话，正如设拉子的诗人所唱的，同一批意象，在每一番动人的措辞变化里，一次又一次地重现。

===Original===

She had seen that the finger of Death was upon her bosom﻿—that, like the ephemeron, she had been made perfect in loveliness only to die; but the terrors of the grave to her lay solely in a consideration which she revealed to me, one evening at twilight, by the banks of the River of Silence. She grieved to think that, having entombed her in the Valley of the Many-Colored Grass, I would quit forever its happy recesses, transferring the love which now was so passionately her own to some maiden of the outer and everyday world. And, then and there, I threw myself hurriedly at the feet of Eleonora, and offered up a vow, to herself and to Heaven, that I would never bind myself in marriage to any daughter of Earth﻿—that I would in no manner prove recreant to her dear memory, or to the memory of the devout affection with which she had blessed me. And I called the Mighty Ruler of the Universe to witness the pious solemnity of my vow. And the curse which I invoked of *Him* and of her, a saint in Helusion should I prove traitorous to that promise, involved a penalty the exceeding great horror of which will not permit me to make record of it here. And the bright eyes of Eleonora grew brighter at my words; and she sighed as if a deadly burden had been taken from her breast; and she trembled and very bitterly wept; but she made acceptance of the vow, (for what was she but a child?) and it made easy to her the bed of her death. And she said to me, not many days afterward, tranquilly dying, that, because of what I had done for the comfort of her spirit she would watch over me in that spirit when departed, and, if so it were permitted her return to me visibly in the watches of the night; but, if this thing were, indeed, beyond the power of the souls in Paradise, that she would, at least, give me frequent indications of her presence, sighing upon me in the evening winds, or filling the air which I breathed with perfume from the censers of the angels. And, with these words upon her lips, she yielded up her innocent life, putting an end to the first epoch of my own.

===Chinese===

她看出死亡的手指已经按上她的胸膛——看出她像蜉蝣一样，生得这样完美可爱，只为死去；可坟墓之可怖，在她只在一个念头，一天黄昏，她在静默之河边把它吐露给了我。她悲伤地想：他们把她埋进五色草山谷之后，我会永远离开这幸福的隐处，把如今这样热烈地只属于她的爱，转付给外面那个庸碌尘世的什么少女。于是，当时当地，我扑倒在埃莉奥诺拉脚前，对她、也对上天立誓：我永不与尘世的任何女儿结缡——我永不负她对我们的甜蜜记忆，永不负她祝福我时那一片虔诚的爱。我请宇宙的大主宰见证我誓约的度敬庄严。而且，倘若我背弃这誓言，我请他、也请她——她已是极乐仙境里的圣女——降下的那个诅咒，其可怖之甚，使我不能在此记它一笔。我这些话叫埃莉奥诺拉明亮的眼睛更亮了；她叹了一口气，仿佛胸口卸下了一副致命的重担；她发抖，簌簌地流汨；可她受了这一誓（她还不过是个孩子呢），她的死榻由此安帖了。不多几天后，她安然长逝，对我说：因为我为她灵魂的安宁做了这一切，她去后必在灵里守护我；倘若许可，她会在守夜的时辰里显形回到我身边；倘若这事真超出了乐园里众魂的力所能及，她至少会频频向我显示她的同在——在晚风里对我叹息，或用天使香炉里的芬芳，注满我呼吸的空气。这几句话还留在唇边，她便交出了她无邪的生命，也结束了我自己的第一个纪元。

===Original===

Thus far I have faithfully said. But as I pass the barrier in Time’s path, formed by the death of my beloved, and proceed with the second era of my existence, I feel that a shadow gathers over my brain, and I mistrust the perfect sanity of the record. But let me on.﻿—Years dragged themselves along heavily, and still I dwelled within the Valley of the Many-Colored Grass; but a second change had come upon all things. The star-shaped flowers shrank into the stems of the trees, and appeared no more. The tints of the green carpet faded; and, one by one, the ruby-red asphodels withered away; and there sprang up, in place of them, ten by ten, dark, eye-like violets, that writhed uneasily and were ever encumbered with dew. And Life departed from our paths; for the tall flamingo flaunted no longer his scarlet plumage before us, but flew sadly from the vale into the hills, with all the gay glowing birds that had arrived in his company. And the golden and silver fish swam down through the gorge at the lower end of our domain and bedecked the sweet river never again. And the lulling melody that had been softer than the wind-harp of Aeolus, and more divine than all save the voice of Eleonora, it died little by little away, in murmurs growing lower and lower, until the stream returned, at length, utterly, into the solemnity of its original silence. And then, lastly, the voluminous cloud uprose, and, abandoning the tops of the mountains to the dimness of old, fell back into the regions of Hesper, and took away all its manifold golden and gorgeous glories from the Valley of the Many-Colored Grass.

Yet the promises of Eleonora were not forgotten; for I heard the sounds of the swinging of the censers of the angels; and streams of a holy perfume floated ever and ever about the valley; and at lone hours, when my heart beat heavily, the winds that bathed my brow came unto me laden with soft sighs; and indistinct murmurs filled often the night air, and once﻿—oh, but once only! I was awakened from a slumber, like the slumber of death, by the pressing of spiritual lips upon my own.

But the void within my heart refused, even thus, to be filled. I longed for the love which had before filled it to overflowing. At length the valley *pained* me through its memories of Eleonora, and I left it forever for the vanities and the turbulent triumphs of the world.

---

===Chinese===

至此，我讲述得忠实。可当我跨过时间之路上那道由爱人之死筑成的关隘，进入我存在的第二个纪元时，我感到一片阴影聚上我的头脑，我开始怀疑这记述是否完全清明。可让我讲下去罢。——年月沉重地拖看自己爬行，我还住在五色草山谷里；可万物又起了第二番变化。星形的花缩回了树干，不再出现。绿毯的色泽褪了；红宝石色的日光兰一朵一朵枯萎，原地上十朵十朵地，冒出深色的、眼睛似的堇花，不安地扭动，永远坠着露水。生命离开了我们的路；因为高高的火烈鸟不再在我们面前炫它猩红的羽衣，只带着同来的那一群光彩灼灼的鸟儿，悲慘地飞出山谷，进了山。金的鱼、银的鱼顺水游下我们这片地下端的峡谷，从此不再装点这条可爱的河。那支比埃俄罗斯的风弦琴更温柔、比一切都神妙、只除却埃莉奥诺拉声音的催睡旋律，也一丝一丝地息了，低而又低，直到河水终于完全回到它起初那种庄严的寂静。最后，那朵大云升了起来，把山巅还给旧日的昏暗，退回赫斯珀的天界去了，把它万千金红的荣华，从五色草山谷里一并带走。

然而埃莉奥诺拉的许诺没有被忘记；因为我听见天使香炉摇荡的声音；一脉一脉圣洁的芬芳，永远在山谷里浮动；在寂寞的时辰，我的心跳沉重，吹拂我額头的风里，满载着柔软的叹息；夜气里常常充满模糊的低语；还有一次——啊，只一次！一双灵唇印上我的唇，把我从一场死亡似的沉睡中唤醒。

可我心里的空，即使这样，也填不满。我渴望那先前把它注得满满的爱。末了，山谷因它对埃莉奥诺拉的记忆而叫我痛楚，我便永远离开了它，投身于尘世的虚荣与喧嚣的荣华。

---

===Original===

I found myself within a strange city, where all things might have served to blot from recollection the sweet dreams I had dreamed so long in the Valley of the Many-Colored Grass. The pomps and pageantries of a stately court, and the mad clangor of arms, and the radiant loveliness of women, bewildered and intoxicated my brain. But as yet my soul had proved true to its vows, and the indications of the presence of Eleonora were still given me in the silent hours of the night. Suddenly these manifestations they ceased, and the world grew dark before mine eyes, and I stood aghast at the burning thoughts which possessed, at the terrible temptations which beset me; for there came from some far, far distant and unknown land, into the gay court of the king I served, a maiden to whose beauty my whole recreant heart yielded at once﻿—at whose footstool I bowed down without a struggle, in the most ardent, in the most abject worship of love. What, indeed, was my passion for the young girl of the valley in comparison with the fervor, and the delirium, and the spirit-lifting ecstasy of adoration with which I poured out my whole soul in tears at the feet of the ethereal Ermengarde?﻿—Oh, bright was the seraph Ermengarde! and in that knowledge I had room for none other. Oh, divine was the angel Ermengarde! and as I looked down into the depths of her memorial eyes, I thought only of them﻿—and *of her*.

I wedded﻿—nor dreaded the curse I had invoked; and its bitterness was not visited upon me. And once﻿—but once again in the silence of the night; there came through my lattice the soft sighs which had forsaken me; and they modelled themselves into familiar and sweet voice, saying:

“Sleep in peace! for the Spirit of Love reigneth and ruleth, and, in taking to thy passionate heart her who is Ermengarde, thou art absolved, for reasons which shall be made known to thee in Heaven, of thy vows unto Eleonora.”

===Chinese===

我发觉自己身处一座陌生的城，那里的一切，原都可以把我久居五色草山谷里所做的甜梦，从记忆中抹去。庄严宫廷的华彩与仪仗，兵戈的疯狂铿锵，女子的煊艳姿容，迷乱了我的头脑，使我陶醉。可我的魂至今还忠于它的誓约；埃莉奥诺拉显示同在的征兆，也还在夜的静时里降临于我。忽然，这些显示停止了，世界在我眼前暗了下去，我惊懼地站着，看占据我的思想何等灼热，看围困我的诱惑何等可怕；因为从我事奉的国王那豪华的宫廷里，从一片遥远遥远、不知名的土地上，来了一位少女，她的美，叫我那负心的心当场降伏——我在她的脚凳前下拜，全不挣扎，怀着最炽热、最卑微的爱之崇拜。真的，比起我在飘逸的埃尔门加德脚下流泪倾尽整个灵魂时那种狂热的、迷醉的、摄人心神的崇拜，我对山谷里那位少女的激情又算得了什么？——啊，埃尔门加德这炽天使何等明亮！有了这份明知，我心里便容不下第二个。啊，埃尔门加德这天使何等神圣！当我俯望她那双纪念之眼的深处时，我心里只有它们——只有她。

我成婚了——并不畏惧我曾自招的诅咒；诅咒的苦味也没有临到我身上。而有一次——只有一次，在夜的寂静里，那早已离弃我的轻柔叹息，穿过我的窗棂而来；它们凝成一个熟悉的、甜蜜的声音，说道：

「安睡罢！因为爱之灵临世而治；你把埃尔门加德娶进你炽热的心，便算无罪了——其中缘由，天国自会晓你——你对埃莉奥诺拉的誓言，就此豁免。」

## Three Sundays in a Week / 一周三个星期日
===Original===

“You hardheaded, dunder-headed, obstinate, rusty, crusty, musty, fusty, old savage!” said I, in fancy, one afternoon, to my grand uncle Rumgudgeon﻿—shaking my fist at him in imagination.

Only in imagination. The fact is, some trivial discrepancy *did* exist, just then, between what I said and what I had not the courage to say﻿—between what I did and what I had half a mind to do.

The old porpoise, as I opened the drawing-room door, was sitting with his feet upon the mantelpiece, and a bumper of port in his paw, making strenuous efforts to accomplish the ditty.

Remplis ton verre vide!

Vide ton verre plein!

“My *dear* uncle,” said I, closing the door gently, and approaching him with the blandest of smiles, “you are always so *very* kind and considerate, and have evinced your benevolence in so many﻿—so *very* many ways﻿—that﻿—that I feel I have only to suggest this little point to you once more to make sure of your full acquiescence.”

“Hem!” said he, “good boy! go on!”

“I am sure, my dearest uncle [you confounded old rascal!], that you have no design really, seriously, to oppose my union with Kate. This is merely a joke of yours, I know﻿—ha! ha! ha!﻿—how *very* pleasant you are at times.”

“Ha! ha! ha!” said he, “curse you! yes!”

“To be sure﻿—of course! I *knew* you were jesting. Now, uncle, all that Kate and myself wish at present, is that you would oblige us with your advice as﻿—as regards the *time*﻿—*you* know, uncle﻿—in short, when will it be most convenient for yourself, that the wedding shall﻿—shall﻿—come off, you know?”

“Come off, you scoundrel!﻿—what do you mean by that?﻿—Better wait till it goes on.”

“Ha! ha! ha!﻿—he! he! he!﻿—hi! hi! hi!﻿—ho! ho! ho!﻿—hu! hu! hu!﻿—oh, that’s good!﻿—oh, that’s capital﻿—*such* a wit! But all we want just *now*, you know, uncle, is that you would indicate the time precisely.”

“Ah!﻿—precisely?”

“Yes, uncle﻿—that is, if it would be quite agreeable to yourself.”

“Wouldn’t it answer, Bobby, if I were to leave it at random﻿—some time within a year or so, for example?﻿—*must* I say precisely?”

“*If* you please, uncle﻿—precisely.”

“Well, then, Bobby, my boy﻿—you’re a fine fellow, aren’t you?﻿—since you *will* have the exact time I’ll﻿—why I’ll oblige you for once.”

“Dear uncle!”

===Chinese===

「你这死脑筋、蠢脑袋、顽固、生锈、硬壳、发霉、陈腐的老野蛮！」一天下午，我在心里冲着我的叔公拉姆加奇恩（Rumgudgeon）说——在想象里朝他挥着拳头。

只在想象里。实情是，那时我说的同我没勇气说的之间——我做的同我有半分心思要做的之间——*的确*存在一点小小的出入。

我推开客厅门时，那老海豚正双脚架在壁炉架上，爪子里端着满满一杯波尔图酒，拼着老命要唱完那支小调：

斟满你空的杯！

倒空你满的杯！

「我*亲爱的*叔公，」我说，轻轻掩上门，带着最甜的笑容走近他，「您一向*极其*仁厚体贴，已经在这样多——这样*许许多多*的方面显出您的善心——所以——所以我觉得，这一点小事，只消我再向您提一回，就必定得到您全心全意的允准。」

「哼！」他说，「好孩子！讲下去！」

「我确信，我最亲爱的叔公[你这老混账！]，您并不是真心实意要阻挠我和凯特的婚事。这不过是您的一个玩笑，我知道——哈！哈！哈！——您有时候*多么*风趣。」

「哈！哈！哈！」他说，「咒你的！没错！」

「可不是——当然！我*就知道*您在打趣。现在，叔公，凯特和我眼下只求您行个方便，给我们一点指教——关于*日子*——您知道的，叔公——一句话，婚礼在哪天——哪天——办起来，您自己最方便？」

「办起来，你这无赖！——你这是什么意思？——最好等它办不起来再说。」

「哈！哈！哈！——嘿！嘿！嘿！——嗨！嗨！嗨！——嗬！嗬！嗬！——呼！呼！呼！——哦，真妙！——哦，好极了——*这样*的妙人！可我们眼下要的，您知道，叔公，就是您把日子确切地指明。」

「啊！——确切？」

「是的，叔公——就是说，倘若这完全合您的心意。」

「博比，随便定一个日子不行吗——比如一年之内？——*非得*我说确切？」

「*请*您，叔公——确切。」

「好吧，博比，好孩子——你是个好家伙，是不是？——既然你*非要*确切的日子，我——那我就依你一回。」

「亲爱的叔公！

===Original===

“Hush, sir!” [drowning my voice]﻿—“I’ll oblige you for once. You shall have my consent﻿—and the *plum*, we mus’n’t forget the plum﻿—let me see! when shall it be? Today’s Sunday﻿—isn’t it? Well, then, you shall be married precisely﻿—*precisely*, now mind!﻿—*when three Sundays come together in a week*! Do you hear me, sir! *What* are you gaping at? I say, you shall have Kate and her plum when three Sundays come together in a week﻿—but not *till* then﻿—you young scapegrace﻿—not *till* then, if I die for it. You know me﻿—*I’m a man of my word*﻿—now be off!” Here he swallowed his bumper of port, while I rushed from the room in despair.

A very “fine old English gentleman,” was my granduncle Rumgudgeon, but unlike him of the song, he had his weak points. He was a little, pursy, pompous, passionate semicircular somebody, with a red nose, a thick skull, a long purse, and a strong sense of his own consequence. With the best heart in the world, he contrived, through a predominant whim of *contradiction*, to earn for himself, among those who only knew him superficially, the character of a curmudgeon. Like many excellent people, he seemed possessed with a spirit of *tantalization*, which might easily, at a casual glance, have been mistaken for malevolence. To every request, a positive “No!” was his immediate answer; but in the end﻿—in the long, long end﻿—there were exceedingly few requests which he refused. Against all attacks upon his purse he made the most sturdy defence; but the amount extorted from him, at last, was generally in direct ratio with the length of the siege and the stubbornness of the resistance. In charity no one gave more liberally or with a worse grace.

===Chinese===

「别吵，先生！」[压过我的声音]——「我依你一回。你将得到我的允准——还有那份*嫁妆*，我们别忘了嫁妆——让我想想！哪一天呢？今天是星期日——是不是？好，那你们就结婚，确切地——*确切地*，记住！——*等一个星期里凑上三个星期日*！听见没有，先生！你张着嘴愣什么？我说，等一个星期里凑上三个星期日，凯特和她的嫁妆都归你——但不到那时不成——你这小混球——不到那时不成，我拼了命也不成。你了解我——*我说话算话*——现在滚吧！」说着他咕咚咽下那杯波尔图，我绝望地冲出屋子。

一位极好的「英国老绅士」，是我的叔公拉姆加奇恩；但同歌里那一位不一样，他有他的弱点。他是个矮小、气促、神气活现、火性子的半圆形人物，红鼻子，硬脑壳，长钱袋，一股强烈的自以为了不起。心肠本是世上最好的，他却借一种占上风的*抬杠*怪癖，在只认识他皮相的人中间，给自己挣来一个吝啬鬼的名声。像许多极好的人一样，他似乎被一种*逗弄*的精神附了体，乍看之下，很容易被误认作恶意。对每一个请求，他的立即回答是斩钉截铁的「不！」；但到末了——到那长长的、长长的末了——他拒绝的请求屈指可数。对他的钱袋的任何进攻，他都抵抗得最顽强；但最终从他那里敲出的数目，一般同围攻的长短、抵抗的顽固成正比。行善没人比他更大方，也没人比他脸色更坏。

===Original===

For the fine arts, and especially for the belles-lettres, he entertained a profound contempt. With this he had been inspired by Casimir Perier, whose pert little query “À quoi un poète est il bon?” he was in the habit of quoting, with a very droll pronunciation, as the ne plus ultra of logical wit. Thus my own inkling for the Muses had excited his entire displeasure. He assured me one day, when I asked him for a new copy of Horace, that the translation of “*Poeta nascitur non fit*” was “a nasty poet for nothing fit”﻿—a remark which I took in high dudgeon. His repugnance to “the humanities” had, also, much increased of late, by an accidental bias in favor of what he supposed to be natural science. Somebody had accosted him in the street, mistaking him for no less a personage than Doctor Dubble L. Dee, the lecturer upon quack physics. This set him off at a tangent; and just at the epoch of this story﻿—for story it is getting to be after all﻿—my granduncle Rumgudgeon was accessible and pacific only upon points which happened to chime in with the caprioles of the hobby he was riding. For the rest, he laughed with his arms and legs, and his politics were stubborn and easily understood. He thought, with Horsley, that “the people have nothing to do with the laws but to obey them.”

===Chinese===

对美术，尤其对文学，他抱着深切的轻蔑。这轻蔑是卡西米尔·佩里埃（Casimir Perier）传给他的；那人的冒失小问句「诗人有什么用？」（À quoi un poète est il bon?）他惯常用一种极滑稽的发音引用，当作逻辑机智的极致。因此我自己对缪斯的癖好，早惹起他整个的不快。一天我向他要一部新的《贺拉斯》，他向我担保：「*Poeta nascitur non fit*」的翻译是「一个下流的诗人，白白废物一个」——这话叫我大为恼火。近来他对「人文之学」的反感又大大增加了，起因是偶然偏向了他以为的自然科学。有人在街上招呼他，把他错认作达布尔·L·迪博士——那位讲庸医物理学的名人。这一下叫他岔了道；就在本篇故事的纪元——毕竟它渐渐要成一篇故事了——我的叔公拉姆加奇恩，只在恰好合于他正在骑的木马的腾跃的那些问题上，才通融与平和。其余的时候，他连胳膊带腿地笑，他的政治顽固而易懂。他同霍斯利一个鼻孔出气，认为「老百姓同法律没有关系，只消服从」。

===Original===

I had lived with the old gentleman all my life. My parents, in dying, had bequeathed me to him as a rich legacy. I believe the old villain loved me as his own child﻿—nearly if not quite as well as he loved Kate﻿—but it was a dog’s existence that he led me, after all. From my first year until my fifth, he obliged me with very regular floggings. From five to fifteen, he threatened me, hourly, with the House of Correction. From fifteen to twenty, not a day passed in which he did not promise to cut me off with a shilling. I was a sad dog, it is true﻿—but then it was a part of my nature﻿—a point of my faith. In Kate, however, I had a firm friend, and I knew it. She was a good girl, and told me very sweetly that I might have her (plum and all) whenever I could badger my granduncle Rumgudgeon, into the necessary consent. Poor girl!﻿—she was barely fifteen, and without this consent, her little amount in the funds was not come-at-able until five immeasurable summers had “dragged their slow length along.” What, then, to do? At fifteen, or even at twenty-one (for I had now passed my fifth olympiad) five years in prospect are very much the same as five hundred. In vain we besieged the old gentleman with importunities. Here was a pièce de résistance (as Messieurs Ude and Careme would say) which suited his perverse fancy to a T. It would have stiffed the indignation of Job himself, to see how much like an old mouser he behaved to us two poor wretched little mice. In his heart he wished for nothing more ardently than our union. He had made up his mind to this all along. In fact, he would have given ten thousand pounds from his own pocket (Kate’s plum was *her own*) if he could have invented anything like an excuse for complying with our very natural wishes. But then we had been so imprudent as to broach the subject *ourselves*. Not to oppose it under such circumstances, I sincerely believe, was not in his power.

I have said already that he had his weak points; but in speaking of these, I must not be understood as referring to his obstinacy: which was one of his strong points﻿—“*assurement ce n’était pas sa foible.*” When I mention his weakness I have allusion to a *bizarre* old-womanish superstition which beset him. He was great in dreams, portents, et id genus omne of rigmarole. He was excessively punctilious, too, upon small points of honor, and, after his own fashion, was a man of his word, beyond doubt. This was, in fact, one of his hobbies. The *spirit* of his vows he made no scruple of setting at naught, but the *letter* was a bond inviolable. Now it was this latter peculiarity in his disposition, of which Kate’s ingenuity enabled us one fine day, not long after our interview in the dining-room, to take a very unexpected advantage, and, having thus, in the fashion of all modern bards and orators, exhausted in prolegomena, all the time at my command, and nearly all the room at my disposal, I will sum up in a few words what constitutes the whole pith of the story.

It happened then﻿—so the Fates ordered it﻿—that among the naval acquaintances of my betrothed, were two gentlemen who had just set foot upon the shores of England, after a year’s absence, each, in foreign travel. For about half an hour the conversation ran upon ordinary topics, but at last, we contrived, quite naturally, to give it the following turn:

Capt. Pratt

“Well I have been absent just one year.﻿—Just one year today, as I live﻿—let me see! yes!﻿—this is October the tenth. You remember, Mr. Rumgudgeon, I called, this day year to bid you goodbye. Smitherton

“Yes! just one year to a fraction. You will remember, Mr. Rumgudgeon, that I called with Capt. Pratol on this very day, last year, to pay my parting respects.”

事情是这样——命运这样安排——我未婚妻的海军相识里有两位绅士，各在外洋航行一年之后，刚刚踏上英国的海岸。我同我的表妹商量好了，趁十月十日星期日下午——客厅里那场刻骨的决定残酷挫败我们的希望之后刚三个星期——拉上这两位先生去拜访拉姆加奇恩叔公。约莫半小时里，谈话在寻常题目上运转；但终于我们设法把它自然而然地引上下面这条道：

普拉特上尉

## The Oval Portrait / 椭圆形画像
===Original===

The château into which my valet had ventured to make forcible entrance, rather than permit me, in my desperately wounded condition, to pass a night in the open air, was one of those piles of commingled gloom and grandeur which have so long frowned among the Appennines, not less in fact than in the fancy of Mrs. Radcliffe. To all appearance it had been temporarily and very lately abandoned. We established ourselves in one of the smallest and least sumptuously furnished apartments. It lay in a remote turret of the building. Its decorations were rich, yet tattered and antique. Its walls were hung with tapestry and bedecked with manifold and multiform armorial trophies, together with an unusually great number of very spirited modern paintings in frames of rich golden arabesque. In these paintings, which depended from the walls not only in their main surfaces, but in very many nooks which the bizarre architecture of the château rendered necessary﻿—in these paintings my incipient delirium, perhaps, had caused me to take deep interest; so that I bade Pedro to close the heavy shutters of the room﻿—since it was already night﻿—to light the tongues of a tall candelabrum which stood by the head of my bed, and to throw open far and wide the fringed curtains of black velvet which enveloped the bed itself. I wished all this done that I might resign myself, if not to sleep, at least alternately to the contemplation of these pictures, and the perusal of a small volume which had been found upon the pillow, and which purported to criticise and describe them.

Long, long I read﻿—and devoutly, devotedly I gazed. Rapidly and gloriously the hours flew by and the deep midnight came. The position of the candelabrum displeased me, and outreaching my hand with difficulty, rather than disturb my slumbering valet, I placed it so as to throw its rays more fully upon the book.

===Chinese===

我的仆人宁可强行闯入，也不肯让我这伤重垂危的人在露天过夜——闯进的这座古堡，是那种阴郁与壮丽混杂的一大堆建筑：它们久已在亚平宁山脉间皱着眉头，实际如此，在拉德克利夫夫人（Mrs. Radcliffe）的想象里也如此。看上去，它是不久前才临时废弃的。我们把家安在最小、陈设最不豪华的一间屋子里。屋子在楼上一个偏远的角塔里。陈设华丽，却破旧而古老。墙上挂着花毯，缀满形形色色的纹章战利品，连同极多的、生气勃勃的近代绘画，装在富丽的金阿拉伯花式框子里。这些画不只挂在墙面，也挂满了古怪的建筑格局逼出来的许多角落——我的初起的谵妄，也许使我对这些画发生了深厚的兴趣；于是我吩咐佩德罗（Pedro）把房间的沉重百叶关死——天已经黑了——点起床头那只大烛台的烛舌，把裹着床的黑丝绒流苏帐幔大大敞开。我要这一切照办，好让我把自己交出去——纵不入梦，至少轮流着观照这些画，并读一本小册子：它是在枕上找到的，自称是对这些画的评述与描写。

我读了很久很久——虔诚地、痴迷地凝望。时光又快又壮丽地飞逝，深夜来临。烛台的位置不合我的意，我费力地把手伸过去——不愿惊动我酣睡的仆人——把它摆成使光线更充分地照在书上。

===Original===

But the action produced an effect altogether unanticipated. The rays of the numerous candles (for there were many) now fell within a niche of the room which had hitherto been thrown into deep shade by one of the bedposts. I thus saw in vivid light a picture all unnoticed before. It was the portrait of a young girl just ripening into womanhood. I glanced at the painting hurriedly, and then closed my eyes. Why I did this was not at first apparent even to my own perception. But while my lids remained thus shut, I ran over in my mind my reason for so shutting them. It was an impulsive movement to gain time for thought﻿—to make sure that my vision had not deceived me﻿—to calm and subdue my fancy for a more sober and more certain gaze. In a very few moments I again looked fixedly at the painting.

That I now saw aright I could not and would not doubt; for the first flashing of the candles upon that canvas had seemed to dissipate the dreamy stupor which was stealing over my senses, and to startle me at once into waking life.

===Chinese===

然而这一动作产生了全然未料的效果。许多支蜡烛（确实很多）的光此刻落进屋里的一个壁龛，它先前一直被一根床柱投在深深的暗影里。于是我在鲜明的光里看见一幅先前全然未察的画。那是一个少女刚刚熟透为妇人的画像。我匆匆瞥了一眼那画，随即闭上了眼睛。我为什么这样，起初连我自己也不明白。但眼睑这样闭着时，我在心里把这样闭它们的理由过了一遍。这是一个冲动的动作，为思考赢得时间——证实我的视觉不曾欺骗我——镇定并压伏我的幻想，以便一次更清醒、更确实的凝视。极短的几刻之后，我又定定地看那画。

我此刻看得不错，我不能也不会怀疑；因为烛光在那画布上的第一闪，仿佛已驱散那正偷袭我感官的梦似的昏沉，把我一下惊进醒着的人生。

===Original===

The portrait, I have already said, was that of a young girl. It was a mere head and shoulders, done in what is technically termed a vignette manner; much in the style of the favorite heads of Sully. The arms, the bosom, and even the ends of the radiant hair melted imperceptibly into the vague yet deep shadow which formed the background of the whole. The frame was oval, richly gilded and filigreed in Moresque. As a thing of art nothing could be more admirable than the painting itself. But it could have been neither the execution of the work, nor the immortal beauty of the countenance, which had so suddenly and so vehemently moved me. Least of all, could it have been that my fancy, shaken from its half slumber, had mistaken the head for that of a living person. I saw at once that the peculiarities of the design, of the vignetting, and of the frame, must have instantly dispelled such idea﻿—must have prevented even its momentary entertainment. Thinking earnestly upon these points, I remained, for an hour perhaps, half sitting, half reclining, with my vision riveted upon the portrait. At length, satisfied with the true secret of its effect, I fell back within the bed. I had found the spell of the picture in an absolute *life-likeliness* of expression, which, at first startling, finally confounded, subdued, and appalled me. With deep and reverent awe I replaced the candelabrum in its former position. The cause of my deep agitation being thus shut from view, I sought eagerly the volume which discussed the paintings and their histories. Turning to the number which designated the oval portrait, I there read the vague and quaint words which follow:

===Chinese===

那画像，我已经说过，是一个少女的。它只是头与肩，以技术上称作晕影的画法绘成，大有萨利（Sully）所爱画的那种头像的风致。手臂、胸脯，甚至那飞扬的秀发的末梢，都不知不觉融进那构成全画背景的朦胧然而深沉的阴影里。框子是椭圆的，镀金富丽，又饰以摩尔式的金银丝。作为一件艺术品，画本身再没有什么更可叹赏。然而如此突然、如此强烈地感动我的，既不可能是画的笔法，也不可能是那面容的不朽的美。更不可能是：我的幻想从半睡里震醒，错把那颗头当作活人。我立刻明白：那设计的特质、那晕影的画法、那框子的样式，必定立刻驱散这样的念头——必定不许它哪怕片刻被当作一回事。认真想着这几点，我半坐半靠，或许停了一个小时，目光钉在画像上。终于，对它的效果的真正秘密心满意足，我倒回床上。我已找到这幅画的魔咒，在它表情里一种绝对的*活灵活现*——它起初吓我一跳，终于把我搅乱，压伏，骇住。我怀着深深的、虔诚的敬畏，把烛台放回原处。我深切的激动的根由既已遮出视野，我便急切去寻那本讨论这些画及它们的历史的小册子。翻到标着这椭圆画像的那一节，我读到下面这些隐约而古旧的话：

===Original===

“She was a maiden of rarest beauty, and not more lovely than full of glee. And evil was the hour when she saw, and loved, and wedded the painter. He, passionate, studious, austere, and having already a bride in his Art; she a maiden of rarest beauty, and not more lovely than full of glee; all light and smiles, and frolicsome as the young fawn; loving and cherishing all things; hating only the Art which was her rival; dreading only the pallet and brushes and other untoward instruments which deprived her of the countenance of her lover. It was thus a terrible thing for this lady to hear the painter speak of his desire to portray even his young bride. But she was humble and obedient, and sat meekly for many weeks in the dark, high turret-chamber where the light dripped upon the pale canvas only from overhead. But he, the painter, took glory in his work, which went on from hour to hour, and from day to day. And he was a passionate, and wild, and moody man, who became lost in reveries; so that he *would* not see that the light which fell so ghastly in that lone turret withered the health and the spirits of his bride, who pined visibly to all but him. Yet she smiled on and still on, uncomplainingly, because she saw that the painter (who had high renown) took a fervid and burning pleasure in his task, and wrought day and night to depict her who so loved him, yet who grew daily more dispirited and weak. And in sooth some who beheld the portrait spoke of its resemblance in low words, as of a mighty marvel, and a proof not less of the power of the painter than of his deep love for her whom he depicted so surpassingly well. But at length, as the labor drew nearer to its conclusion, there were admitted none into the turret; for the painter had grown wild with the ardor of his work, and turned his eyes from canvas merely, even to regard the countenance of his wife. And he would not see that the tints which he spread upon the canvas were drawn from the cheeks of her who sat beside him. And when many weeks had passed, and but little remained to do, save one brush upon the mouth and one tint upon the eye, the spirit of the lady again flickered up as the flame within the socket of the lamp.

===Chinese===

「她是一位艳绝人寰的少女，可爱不下于快活。她看见画家、爱画家、嫁画家，那一刻钟是凶刻。他热情、勤学、冷峻，早已在艺术里有了新娘；她艳绝人寰，可爱不下于快活；一身光华与笑意，像小鹿般嬉戏；爱抚珍重万物；只恨那与她的爱相抗的艺术；只怕调色板、画笔和其他夺走她情人面目的作梗的器械。因此，听画家说要画他的新婚妻子，对这位太太是可怕的事。但她谦卑柔顺，便乖乖地在那黑暗的高角塔楼里坐了许多星期的模型；那楼里的光只从顶上滴到惨白的画布上。可他，那画家，以他的工作为荣，那工作一时一刻、一天一天地做下去。他是一个热情、狂野、喜怒无常的人，渐渐迷失在遐想里；于是他*不肯*看见：落在这孤塔里的那道惨惨的光，正在枯萎他的新娘的健康与精神——她消瘦下去，人人看在眼里，唯独他不见。可她仍旧笑，还是笑，毫无怨言，因为她看见画家（他名声极高）在他的工作里有一种炽热燃烧的快乐，日夜操劳，画着那如此爱他的她——而她一天比一天更消沉、更孱弱。的确，有些见过画像的人低声说起它的逼真，当作一件大奇观，既证明画家的功力，也证明他对被他画得这样出神入化的她的深爱。但终于，工作临近完成，角塔里不许任何人进来；因为画家被工作的狂热迷了心窍，他的眼睛从画布上挪开，只是为了看他妻子的面容。他不肯看见：他涂在画布上的那些颜色，是从坐在他身旁的她的面颊上取来的。许多星期过去，剩下的只有一点：嘴唇上添一笔，眼睛上点一色。这时，那位太太的精神又闪出火苗，像灯盏窝里的火。

===Original===

And then the brush was given, and then the tint was placed; and, for one moment, the painter stood entranced before the work which he had wrought; but in the next, while he yet gazed, he grew tremulous and very pallid, and aghast, and crying with a loud voice, ‘This is indeed *Life* itself!’ turned suddenly to regard his beloved:﻿—*She was dead!*”

===Chinese===

于是画笔递了过去，颜色点上了；有一刻，画家站在他造成的工作前，神魂颠倒；但下一刻，他还在凝视，便发起抖来，脸色极白，骇然失色，高声喊道，「这确是*生命*本身！」随即猛然转身去看他的爱人：——*她已经死了！*」

## The Masque of the Red Death / 红死魔的假面舞会
===Original===

The “Red Death” had long devastated the country. No pestilence had ever been so fatal, or so hideous. Blood was its Avatar and its seal﻿—the redness and the horror of blood. There were sharp pains, and sudden dizziness, and then profuse bleeding at the pores, with dissolution. The scarlet stains upon the body and especially upon the face of the victim, were the pest ban which shut him out from the aid and from the sympathy of his fellow-men. And the whole seizure, progress and termination of the disease, were the incidents of half an hour.

But the Prince Prospero was happy and dauntless and sagacious. When his dominions were half depopulated, he summoned to his presence a thousand hale and lighthearted friends from among the knights and dames of his court, and with these retired to the deep seclusion of one of his castellated abbeys. This was an extensive and magnificent structure, the creation of the prince’s own eccentric yet august taste. A strong and lofty wall girdled it in. This wall had gates of iron. The courtiers, having entered, brought furnaces and massy hammers and welded the bolts. They resolved to leave means neither of ingress or egress to the sudden impulses of despair or of frenzy from within. The abbey was amply provisioned. With such precautions the courtiers might bid defiance to contagion. The external world could take care of itself. In the meantime it was folly to grieve, or to think. The prince had provided all the appliances of pleasure. There were buffoons, there were improvisatori, there were ballet-dancers, there were musicians, there was Beauty, there was wine. All these and security were within. Without was the “Red Death.”

It was toward the close of the fifth or sixth month of his seclusion, and while the pestilence raged most furiously abroad, that the Prince Prospero entertained his thousand friends at a masked ball of the most unusual magnificence.

===Chinese===

「红死魔」（the Red Death）摧残国土久矣。从来没有一种瘟疫这样致命，这样骇人。血是它的阿凡达与印玺——血的红，血的恐怖。剧痛袭来，接着是一阵突如其来的眩晕，然后毛孔大量渗血，随即消陨。被害人身上，尤其脸上，那些猩红的斑点，便是逐他出境的疫符：从此得不到同类的救助与同情。而这病的侵袭、进程与终结，统共是半个钟头内的事。

普洛斯佩罗亲王（Prince Prospero）却快乐、无畏、精明。他的国土死去一半时，他从宫廷的骑士与贵妇中召来一千名健壮快活的友人，同他们一起退进他一座设堡的修道院的深隐之处。那是一座宏大壮丽的构筑，亲王自己那古怪然而威严的趣味的手笔。一圈高大坚固的墙把它围住。墙上是铁门。朝臣们进了门，便搬来熔炉和沉重的铁锤，把门闩焊死。他们决意不留一丝进出的门路，来应付从内里突然袭来的绝望或疯狂的冲动。修道院里储粮充足。有这样周全的防备，朝臣们尽可向疫气挑战。外面的世界尽可自谋生路。与此同时，悲伤或思考都是蠢事。亲王已备齐一切享乐的器械。有丑角，有即兴诗人，有芭蕾舞者，有乐师，有美，有酒。这一切连同安全都在墙内。墙外是「红死魔」。

在隐居的第五或第六个月将尽、瘟疫在外面肆虐最烈的时候，普洛斯佩罗亲王设了一场极尽奇丽的假面舞会，款待他的一千个朋友。

===Original===

It was a voluptuous scene, that masquerade. But first let me tell of the rooms in which it was held. There were seven﻿—an imperial suite. In many palaces, however, such suites form a long and straight vista, while the folding doors slide back nearly to the walls on either hand, so that the view of the whole extent is scarcely impeded. Here the case was very different; as might have been expected from the duke’s love of the *bizarre*. The apartments were so irregularly disposed that the vision embraced but little more than one at a time. There was a sharp turn at every twenty or thirty yards, and at each turn a novel effect. To the right and left, in the middle of each wall, a tall and narrow Gothic window looked out upon a closed corridor which pursued the windings of the suite. These windows were of stained glass whose color varied in accordance with the prevailing hue of the decorations of the chamber into which it opened. That at the eastern extremity was hung, for example, in blue﻿—and vividly blue were its windows. The second chamber was purple in its ornaments and tapestries, and here the panes were purple. The third was green throughout, and so were the casements. The fourth was furnished and lighted with orange﻿—the fifth with white﻿—the sixth with violet. The seventh apartment was closely shrouded in black velvet tapestries that hung all over the ceiling and down the walls, falling in heavy folds upon a carpet of the same material and hue. But in this chamber only, the color of the windows failed to correspond with the decorations. The panes here were scarlet﻿—a deep blood color. Now in no one of the seven apartments was there any lamp or candelabrum, amid the profusion of golden ornaments that lay scattered to and fro or depended from the roof. There was no light of any kind emanating from lamp or candle within the suite of chambers. But in the corridors that followed the suite, there stood, opposite to each window, a heavy tripod, bearing a brazier of fire that projected its rays through the tinted glass and so glaringly illumined the room. And thus were produced a multitude of gaudy and fantastic appearances.

===Chinese===

那假面舞会是一场穷奢极欲的景象。但先容我讲讲举行它的那几间屋子。共七间——一列帝王气派的套房。然而在许多宫殿里，这样的套房是一条又长又直的纵深，折叠门几乎推到两边的墙上，全局的视野几乎不受阻拦。这里的情形却大不相同——这本在意料之中，凭公爵对*古怪*的癖好。屋子的布置极不规整，视野一次只能收进一间多一点。每二三十码便是一道急转，每一转便是一种新奇的效果。左右两面，在每面墙的中央，一扇高而窄的哥特窗，望着一条封闭的走廊，那走廊沿着套房的曲折蜿蜒。窗是彩色的玻璃，颜色随它开向的那间屋子里占上风的陈设之色而变。东端那间，例如，悬着蓝色——它的窗也是鲜明的蓝。第二间屋的陈设与挂毯是紫色的，这里的窗玻璃便是紫色。第三间通体是绿的，窗槅也是。第四间以橙色陈设并照明——第五间白色——第六间紫色。第七间罩在黑丝绒的挂毯里，从天花板直垂到墙，成沉沉的褶裥落在一块同样料子同样颜色的地毯上。但唯独这间屋子，窗的颜色不与陈设相应。这里的玻璃是猩红——深深的血色。而在七间屋里，任何一间都没有灯或烛台，虽然金饰四处散布或从屋顶垂下，灿然满目。这套房间里没有一点从灯或烛里发出的光。但顺着套房的走廊里，每扇窗的对面立着一只沉重的三脚架，架上承着一只火盆，把光芒投过有色玻璃，把屋子照得炫目。于是便生出无数俗艳而幻怪的景象。

===Original===

But in the western or black chamber the effect of the firelight that streamed upon the dark hangings through the blood-tinted panes, was ghastly in the extreme, and produced so wild a look upon the countenances of those who entered, that there were few of the company bold enough to set foot within its precincts at all.

It was in this apartment, also, that there stood against the western wall, a gigantic clock of ebony. Its pendulum swung to and fro with a dull, heavy, monotonous clang; and when the minute-hand made the circuit of the face, and the hour was to be stricken, there came from the brazen lungs of the clock a sound which was clear and loud and deep and exceedingly musical, but of so peculiar a note and emphasis that, at each lapse of an hour, the musicians of the orchestra were constrained to pause, momentarily, in their performance, to hearken to the sound; and thus the waltzers perforce ceased their evolutions; and there was a brief disconcert of the whole gay company; and, while the chimes of the clock yet rang, it was observed that the giddiest grew pale, and the more aged and sedate passed their hands over their brows as if in confused reverie or meditation. But when the echoes had fully ceased, a light laughter at once pervaded the assembly; the musicians looked at each other and smiled as if at their own nervousness and folly, and made whispering vows, each to the other, that the next chiming of the clock should produce in them no similar emotion; and then, after the lapse of sixty minutes (which embrace three thousand and six hundred seconds of the Time that flies), there came yet another chiming of the clock, and then were the same disconcert and tremulousness and meditation as before.

But, in spite of these things, it was a gay and magnificent revel. The tastes of the duke were peculiar. He had a fine eye for colors and effects. He disregarded the decora of mere fashion. His plans were bold and fiery, and his conceptions glowed with barbaric lustre. There are some who would have thought him mad. His followers felt that he was not. It was necessary to hear and see and touch him to be *sure* that he was not.

===Chinese===

但在西面那间黑屋，火光透过血色的窗玻璃打在暗色的帷幔上，效果骇人到极点，给进来的人的脸上都镀上一层狂野，以至于满座宾客没有几个胆子大得敢踏进它的地界。

也是在这间屋里，靠着西墙立着一座黑檀的巨钟。它的钟摆来来回回地摆，声调沉闷、滞重、单调；当分针在钟面上走完一圈、报时的时刻一到，钟的黄铜肺腑里便发出一种声音，清晰，响亮，深沉，极富乐感，然而音色与重音如此奇特，以至每逢一点钟过去，乐队的乐师便不得不在演奏里停一瞬，听那声音；于是旋转的舞者也不得不停下他们的回旋；整个欢快的满座宾客起一阵短促的慌乱；而钟声还在响时，便可以看出最轻狂的人脸色发白，年长而稳重些的把手按上额头，仿佛在纷乱的遐想或沉思里。但回声一停，一阵轻笑立刻弥漫全场；乐师们你看看我，我看看你，笑了，仿佛笑自己的紧张与愚蠢，又互相低声发誓：下一次钟响，绝不再起同样的心绪；然后，过了六十分钟（其中包着飞逝的时间的三千六百秒），钟又敲响，于是又是同样的慌乱、颤抖与沉思。

但尽管有这一切，那是一场欢快而豪华的狂欢。公爵的趣味奇特。他对于色彩与效果，眼光极精。他无视时尚的那些陈规。他的设计大胆而炽烈，他的构想闪着野蛮的光辉。有些人会当他疯了。他的追随者觉得他没有。要*确证*他没有，须得听他、看他、摸他。

===Original===

He had directed, in great part, the moveable embellishments of the seven chambers, upon occasion of this great fête; and it was his own guiding taste which had given character to the masqueraders. Be sure they were grotesque. There were much glare and glitter and piquancy and phantasm﻿—much of what has been since seen in *Hernani*. There were arabesque figures with unsuited limbs and appointments. There were delirious fancies such as the madman fashions. There was much of the beautiful, much of the wanton, much of the bizarre, something of the terrible, and not a little of that which might have excited disgust. To and fro in the seven chambers there stalked, in fact, a multitude of dreams. And these﻿—the dreams﻿—writhed in and about, taking hue from the rooms, and causing the wild music of the orchestra to seem as the echo of their steps. And, anon, there strikes the ebony clock which stands in the hall of the velvet. And then, for a moment, all is still, and all is silent save the voice of the clock. The dreams are stiff-frozen as they stand. But the echoes of the chime die away﻿—they have endured but an instant﻿—and a light, half-subdued laughter floats after them as they depart. And now again the music swells, and the dreams live, and writhe to and fro more merrily than ever, taking hue from the many-tinted windows through which stream the rays from the tripods. But to the chamber which lies most westwardly of the seven, there are now none of the maskers who venture; for the night is waning away; and there flows a ruddier light through the blood-colored panes; and the blackness of the sable drapery appals; and to him whose foot falls upon the sable carpet, there comes from the near clock of ebony a muffled peal more solemnly emphatic than any which reaches *their* ears who indulge in the more remote gaieties of the other apartments.

===Chinese===

为着这场大宴，七间屋的活动装饰大部分由他亲自指点；给化装者定下格调的，也是他自己那主导的趣味。无疑他们怪诞。处处是闪耀、辉煌、辛辣、幻影——许多此后在《埃尔纳尼》（Hernani）里见过的东西。有四肢与配备不称的阿拉伯花式的形影。有狂人编织的那类谵妄的幻想。美的很多，妖冶的很多，古怪的很多，可怕的一些，而足以令人作呕的也不少。实际上，在七间屋里荡来荡去的，是一大群梦。而这些——这些梦——在屋里屋外扭动，从屋子借得颜色，把乐队的狂野的音乐，弄成仿佛他们脚步的回声。而俄顷，绒厅里那座黑檀钟又敲了。于是，有一瞬，一切都停，一切都静，只剩钟的声音。梦们僵着，冻着，站在那里。但钟声的回声渐渐熄灭——它们只延了一瞬——一串轻轻压住的笑，跟着它们飘散。此刻音乐又涌起，梦们复活了，比先前更欢畅地扭来扭去，从三脚架的光线流过的那些五彩的窗上借得颜色。但七间屋里最西边的那间，此刻没有化装者敢去；因为夜在流逝；血色的玻璃里淌进更红的光；黑檀帷幔的黑压得人惊惶；谁的脚一踏上那黑檀的地毯，近旁的黑檀钟便向他发出一声闷沉的轰响，比那在其余几间屋的较远的欢愉里、落进*他们*耳朵的任何一响，都更庄严，更沉重。

===Original===

But these other apartments were densely crowded, and in them beat feverishly the heart of life. And the revel went whirlingly on, until at length there commenced the sounding of midnight upon the clock. And then the music ceased, as I have told; and the evolutions of the waltzers were quieted; and there was an uneasy cessation of all things as before. But now there were twelve strokes to be sounded by the bell of the clock; and thus it happened, perhaps, that more of thought crept, with more of time, into the meditations of the thoughtful among those who revelled. And thus, too, it happened, perhaps, that before the last echoes of the last chime had utterly sunk into silence, there were many individuals in the crowd who had found leisure to become aware of the presence of a masked figure which had arrested the attention of no single individual before. And the rumor of this new presence having spread itself whisperingly around, there arose at length from the whole company a buzz, or murmur, expressive of disapprobation and surprise﻿—then, finally, of terror, of horror, and of disgust.

In an assembly of phantasms such as I have painted, it may well be supposed that no ordinary appearance could have excited such sensation. In truth the masquerade license of the night was nearly unlimited; but the figure in question had out-Heroded Herod, and gone beyond the bounds of even the prince’s indefinite decorum. There are chords in the hearts of the most reckless which cannot be touched without emotion. Even with the utterly lost, to whom life and death are equally jests, there are matters of which no jest can be made. The whole company, indeed, seemed now deeply to feel that in the costume and bearing of the stranger neither wit nor propriety existed. The figure was tall and gaunt, and shrouded from head to foot in the habiliments of the grave. The mask which concealed the visage was made so nearly to resemble the countenance of a stiffened corpse that the closest scrutiny must have had difficulty in detecting the cheat. And yet all this might have been endured, if not approved, by the mad revellers around. But the mummer had gone so far as to assume the type of the Red Death. His vesture was dabbled in *blood*﻿—and his broad brow, with all the features of the face, was besprinkled with the scarlet horror.

===Chinese===

但其余几间屋子挤得密密层层，生命的心在那里发烧般跳动。狂欢旋转着继续，直到午夜开始敲响。于是音乐停了，如我已经讲过；舞者的回旋静了；万物起一阵同先前一样的不安的停顿。但这一回，钟的铃要敲十二下；也许因此，更多的时间带来更多的思绪，爬进狂欢者中间那些善思者的冥想。也许因此，在最后一响的最后回声全然沉入寂静之前，人群里已有许多人得着闲空，察觉一个假面身影的存在——先前它不曾引起任何一个人的注意。这新来的存在的谣言低语着散开，终于从整个人群中升起一片嗡嗡，或曰喃喃，表示不满与惊异——最后，是恐怖，惊骇，与嫌恶。

在我描绘的这样一个幻影的集会里，无妨设想，寻常的模样激不起这样的感觉。的确，那一夜化装的自由几乎无限；但所说的这个身影比希律还希律，越过了甚至亲王的无限礼法。在最莽撞的人的心里，也有几根弦，非动之以情碰不得。即便那些彻底沦丧的人，视生与死为同等的笑柄，也有一些事情开不得玩笑。全场此刻似乎深深感到：在那陌生人的装束与举止里，机趣与得体都不存在。那身影高而枯瘦，从头到脚裹在坟墓的衣衾里。遮住面目的面具做得几乎酷肖一具僵直的尸体的面容，最细的审视也难找出假来。然而这一切，纵不获赞许，也可以被四周疯狂的狂欢者们忍受。但那化装的人竟走得那样远，竟装成红死魔的形貌。他的衣衾溅满*血*——他宽阔的前额，连同脸上的五官，都洒满那猩红的恐怖。

===Original===

When the eyes of Prince Prospero fell upon this spectral image (which with a slow and solemn movement, as if more fully to sustain its role, stalked to and fro among the waltzers) he was seen to be convulsed, in the first moment with a strong shudder either of terror or distaste; but, in the next, his brow reddened with rage.

“Who dares?” he demanded hoarsely of the courtiers who stood near him﻿—“who dares insult us with this blasphemous mockery? Seize him and unmask him﻿—that we may know whom we have to hang at sunrise, from the battlements!”

It was in the eastern or blue chamber in which stood the Prince Prospero as he uttered these words. They rang throughout the seven rooms loudly and clearly﻿—for the prince was a bold and robust man, and the music had become hushed at the waving of his hand.

===Chinese===

普洛斯佩罗亲王的眼睛落在这个幽灵似的形象上（它正以一种缓慢而庄严的移动，仿佛要把它的角色撑得更足，在舞者之间荡来荡去），人们看见他先是浑身痉挛，第一刻起了一阵强烈的战栗，不知是恐怖还是嫌恶；但下一刻，他的额头因暴怒涨红了。

「谁敢？」他嘶哑地向站在近旁的朝臣们喝问——「谁敢用这渎神的滑稽来侮辱我们？抓住他，揭下他的面具——好叫我们知道日出时该把谁吊上城垛！」

普洛斯佩罗亲王说这些话时，站在东面那间蓝屋里。这些话响亮而清晰地响遍七间屋——因为亲王是个大胆而健壮的人，音乐已在他一挥手间静了下来。

===Original===

It was in the blue room where stood the prince, with a group of pale courtiers by his side. At first, as he spoke, there was a slight rushing movement of this group in the direction of the intruder, who at the moment was also near at hand, and now, with deliberate and stately step, made closer approach to the speaker. But from a certain nameless awe with which the mad assumptions of the mummer had inspired the whole party, there were found none who put forth hand to seize him; so that, unimpeded, he passed within a yard of the prince’s person; and, while the vast assembly, as if with one impulse, shrank from the centres of the rooms to the walls, he made his way uninterruptedly, but with the same solemn and measured step which had distinguished him from the first, through the blue chamber to the purple﻿—through the purple to the green﻿—through the green to the orange﻿—through this again to the white﻿—and even thence to the violet, ere a decided movement had been made to arrest him. It was then, however, that the Prince Prospero, maddening with rage and the shame of his own momentary cowardice, rushed hurriedly through the six chambers, while none followed him on account of a deadly terror that had seized upon all. He bore aloft a drawn dagger, and had approached, in rapid impetuosity, to within three or four feet of the retreating figure, when the latter, having attained the extremity of the velvet apartment, turned suddenly and confronted his pursuer. There was a sharp cry﻿—and the dagger dropped gleaming upon the sable carpet, upon which, instantly afterwards, fell prostrate in death the Prince Prospero. Then, summoning the wild courage of despair, a throng of the revellers at once threw themselves into the black apartment, and, seizing the mummer, whose tall figure stood erect and motionless within the shadow of the ebony clock, gasped in unutterable horror at finding the grave-cerements and corpse-like mask which they handled with so violent a rudeness, untenanted by any tangible form.

===Chinese===
