背心，刀，钱夹，弹丸，都是他自己放在被发现的地方的，为的是向彭尼菲瑟先生报仇。那染血的领巾与衬衫的被发现，也是他安排的。

到那令人血液倒流的供述之末，那有罪的可怜虫的字句迟疑了，空了。记录终于倾吐干净时，他立起身，从桌边踉跄后退，跌倒——*死了*。

---

借以榨出这场来得恰逢其时的供状的手段，虽然有效，实在简单。古德费洛先生那过分的坦率早叫我厌恶，早从起初便激起我的疑心。彭尼菲瑟先生打他的时候我在场；那时他脸上涌起的恶魔似的表情，虽只一瞬，向我担保：他那句报复的话，倘若办得到，会被一丝不苟地履行。这样我便有预备，用一种同拉特尔伯勒的好居民们截然不同的眼光去看「老查利」的种种运作。我一眼看出：一切定罪的发现，直接或间接，都出自他本人。但那桩分明叫我睁开眼睛看清案子的真态的事实，是那颗弹丸——*被*古德费洛先生在马的尸身里*发现*的那颗。*我*不曾忘记——虽然拉特尔伯勒人*忘了*——马身上有一个弹丸穿入的孔，还有另一个它*穿出*的孔。它既已穿出，却又在牲口身体里被找到，我分明看出：它必定是发现它的人放进去的。那件血衬衫和领巾证实了弹丸提示的念头；因为一经查验，那血证明确是上好的红葡萄酒，并非别的。当我想到这些，又想到古德费洛先生晚近的慷慨与花销的增加，我便怀了一种疑心；正因为把它整个藏在自己心里，它才分毫不减其强。

这期间我办了一次严格的私下的搜寻，寻找沙特尔沃西先生的尸体；并且出于充分的理由，专往同古德费洛先生领着众人去的方向尽可能分歧的地方去搜。结果是：过了几天，我碰上一口老旧的干井，井口几乎叫荆棘遮没了；就在井底，我找到了我寻的东西。

===Original===

Now it so happened that I had overheard the colloquy between the two cronies, when Mr. Goodfellow had contrived to cajole his host into the promise of a box of Châteaux-Margaux. Upon this hint I acted. I procured a stiff piece of whalebone, thrust it down the throat of the corpse, and deposited the latter in an old wine box﻿—taking care so to double the body up as to double the whalebone with it. In this manner I had to press forcibly upon the lid to keep it down while I secured it with nails; and I anticipated, of course, that as soon as these latter were removed, the top would fly *off* and the body *up*.

Having thus arranged the box, I marked, numbered, and addressed it as already told; and then writing a letter in the name of the wine merchants with whom Mr. Shuttleworthy dealt, I gave instructions to my servant to wheel the box to Mr. Goodfellow’s door, in a barrow, at a given signal from myself. For the words which I intended the corpse to speak, I confidently depended upon my ventriloquial abilities; for their effect, I counted upon the conscience of the murderous wretch.

I believe there is nothing more to be explained. Mr. Pennifeather was released upon the spot, inherited the fortune of his uncle, profited by the lessons of experience, turned over a new leaf, and led happily ever afterward a new life.

===Chinese===

凑巧的是，那两位老友的对话我曾在场偷听：古德费洛先生设计哄得他的东道主许下一箱玛歌的事。我便照这一提示行动。我弄来一根挺硬的鲸须，捅进尸体的喉咙，把尸体放进一只旧酒箱——小心地把尸身折起来，把鲸须也一并折起。这样我压住盖子才钉得上钉子；我自然预先料到：钉子一拔，顶盖便会*飞*起来，尸身便会*坐*起来。

箱子这样布置停当，我便照已经讲过的那样标了号、写了地址；然后以沙特尔沃西先生往来的那家酒商的名义写了一封信，吩咐我的仆人听我的信号，用独轮车把箱子推到古德费洛先生的门口。至于我打算叫尸体说的那些话，我满心倚仗我的腹语的本领；至于它们的效果，我指望那杀人凶手的良心。

我相信再没有什么可解释的了。彭尼菲瑟先生当场获释，继承了舅舅的产业，受了经验的教训，翻开新的一页，此后快快活活地过着一种新的人生。

## The Literary Life of Thingum Bob, Esq. / 廷根·鲍勃先生的文学生涯
===Original===

Late Editor of the *Goosetherumfoodle*

By Himself

I am now growing in years, and﻿—since I understand that Shakespeare and Mr. Emmons are deceased﻿—it is not impossible that I may even die. It has occurred to me, therefore, that I may as well retire from the field of Letters and repose upon my laurels. But I am ambitious of signalizing my abdication of the literary sceptre by some important bequest to posterity; and, perhaps, I cannot do a better thing than just pen for it an account of my earlier career. My name, indeed, has been so long and so constantly before the public eye, that I am not only willing to admit the naturalness of the interest which it has everywhere excited, but ready to satisfy the extreme curiosity which it has inspired. In fact, it is no more than the duty of him who achieves greatness to leave behind him, in his ascent, such landmarks as may guide others to be great. I propose, therefore, in the present paper (which I had some idea of calling “Memoranda to serve for the Literary History of America”) to give a detail of those important, yet feeble and tottering first steps, by which, at length, I attained the high road to the pinnacle of human renown.

Of one’s *very* remote ancestors it is superfluous to say much. My father, Thomas Bob, Esq., stood for many years at the summit of his profession, which was that of a merchant-barber, in the city of Smug. His warehouse was the resort of all the principal people of the place, and especially of the editorial corps﻿—a body which inspires all about it with profound veneration and awe. For my own part, I regarded them as gods, and drank in with avidity the rich wit and wisdom which continuously flowed from their august mouths during the process of what is styled “lather.” My first moment of positive inspiration must be dated from that ever-memorable epoch, when the brilliant conductor of the *Gad-Fly*, in the intervals of the important process just mentioned, recited aloud, before a conclave of our apprentices, an inimitable poem in honor of the “Only Genuine Oil-of-Bob,” (so called from its talented inventor, my father), and for which effusion the editor of the *Fly* was remunerated with a regal liberality by the firm of Thomas Bob & Company, merchant-barbers.

===Chinese===

《鹅噜噜福多》前主编

本人自述

我如今渐渐上了年纪——既然我懂得莎士比亚与埃蒙斯先生都已过世，我甚至死掉也不是不可能。因此我想到，我不如从文坛引退，在桂冠上安卧。但我野心勃勃，要以一项重要的遗产留给后世，来为我文学权杖的禅让增光；而我所能做的最好的事，也许不过是给它写下一篇我早年生涯的记述。我的名字，实在说，久已持续地摆在公众眼前，我不但愿意承认它四处激起的兴趣之自然，而且乐于满足它所激起的无穷好奇。实在，凡成就了伟大的人，其义务便是在上升的路上留下路标，指引别人走向伟大。因此我打算在这篇文字里（我原有一些念头想把它叫作《供美国文学史用的备忘录》）细述那些重要然而羸弱蹒跚的最初脚步，靠了它们，我终于踏上通往人类名誉顶峰的大道。

关于一个人的*极*远的祖先，多说便是画蛇添足。我的父亲托马斯·鲍勃（Thomas Bob）先生，多年立于他那一行的顶峰：那是斯马格城里一名理发的商人。他的铺子是全城头面人物的聚会所，尤其是编辑队伍——一个使它四邻满怀崇敬与敬畏的群体。就我自己而言，我视他们为神明，贪婪地啜饮那源源不断的丰饶的机智与智慧：在所谓「打肥皂」的过程里，从他们庄严的嘴里滔滔流出。我第一个确实的灵感之顷，必须记在那令人永志不忘的时代：才华横溢的《牛虻》（Gad-Fly）主编，在那要紧工序的间隙里，在我们学徒的评议会面前，朗声背诵了一首无与伦比的诗，题赠「鲍勃纯真油」（以其天才的发明者、我的父亲得名）；那家公司托马斯·鲍勃父子理发商人行，以王侯般的慷慨报酬了《牛虻》的主编这篇创作。

===Original===

The genius of the stanzas to the “Oil-of-Bob” first breathed into me, I say, the divine afflatus. I resolved at once to become a great man, and to commence by becoming a great poet. That very evening I fell upon my knees at the feet of my father.

“Father,” I said, “pardon me!﻿—but I have a soul above lather. It is my firm intention to cut the shop. I would be an editor﻿—I would be a poet﻿—I would pen stanzas to the ‘Oil-of-Bob.’ Pardon me and aid me to be great!”

“My dear Thingum,” replied my father, (I had been christened Thingum after a wealthy relative so surnamed,) “My dear Thingum,” he said, raising me from my knees by the ears﻿—“Thingum, my boy, you’re a trump, and take after your father in having a soul. You have an immense head, too, and it must hold a great many brains. This I have long seen, and therefore had thoughts of making you a lawyer. The business, however, has grown ungenteel, and that of a politician don’t pay. Upon the whole you judge wisely;﻿—the trade of editor is best:﻿—and if you can be a poet at the same time﻿—as most of the editors are, by the by﻿—why you will kill two birds with one stone. To encourage you in the beginning of things, I will allow you a garret; pen, ink, and paper; a rhyming dictionary; and a copy of the *Gad-Fly*. I suppose you would scarcely demand any more.”

“I would be an ungrateful villain if I did,” I replied with enthusiasm. “Your generosity is boundless. I will repay it by making you the father of a genius.”

Thus ended my conference with the best of men, and immediately upon its termination, I betook myself with zeal to my poetical labors; as upon these, chiefly, I founded my hopes of ultimate elevation to the editorial chair.

===Chinese===

那几节「鲍勃纯真油」的诗的天才，我说，最先朝我呼出了神的气息。我立刻立志要做一个大人物，先从做一个大诗人着手。就在当天晚上，我跪倒在父亲的脚下。

「父亲，」我说，「饶恕我！——但我的灵魂高出肥皂沫之上。我拿定主意不干铺子了。我要做编辑——我要做诗人——我要为『鲍勃纯真油』写诗。饶恕我，扶助我成个伟人吧！」

「我亲爱的廷根，」我的父亲答道（我受洗时便跟着一位姓这个姓的有钱的亲戚，得了廷根这个名字）——「我亲爱的廷根，」他说着揪住我的耳朵把我从跪处提起来，「廷根，我的孩子，你是块好料，有灵魂这一点像你父亲。你的脑袋也大，里面必定装着许多脑子。这一点我早看见了，因此想过叫你去做律师。然而这一行变得不体面了，政客的营生又不赚钱。总的说你判断得聪明；——编辑这一行最好：——倘若你还能同时做个诗人——顺便说，编辑们多半是诗人——那你便一石二鸟。为了在你起头的时候鼓励你，我允许你一间阁楼；笔，墨水，纸；一部押韵词典；一份《牛虻》。我想你不会再要求更多了。」

「倘若要求，我便是个忘恩的恶棍了，」我热烈地答道。「您的慷慨无边无际。我要用它报答您：叫您做一个天才的父亲。」

同这位最好的人的谈话就此结束；谈话一完，我便热心地投身诗艺的劳作；因为主要在它上面，我建立着我终将升入编辑宝座的希望。

===Original===

In my first attempts at composition I found the stanzas to “The Oil-of-Bob” rather a drawback than otherwise. Their splendor more dazzled than enlightened me. The contemplation of their excellence tended, naturally, to discourage me by comparison with my own abortions; so that for a long time I labored in vain. At length there came into my head one of those exquisitely original ideas which now and then *will* permeate the brain of a man of genius. It was this:﻿—or, rather, thus was it carried into execution. From the rubbish of an old bookstall, in a very remote corner of the town, I got together several antique and altogether unknown or forgotten volumes. The bookseller sold them to me for a song. From one of these, which purported to be a translation of one Dante’s *Inferno*, I copied with remarkable neatness a long passage about a man named Ugolino, who had a parcel of brats. From another which contained a good many old plays by some person whose name I forget, I extracted in the same manner, and with the same care, a great number of lines about “angels” and “ministers saying grace,” and “goblins damned,” and more besides of that sort. From a third, which was the composition of some blind man or other, either a Greek or a Choctaw﻿—I cannot be at the pains of remembering every trifle exactly﻿—I took about fifty verses beginning with “Achilles’ wrath,” and “grease,” and something else. From a fourth, which I recollect was also the work of a blind man, I selected a page or two all about “hail” and “holy light”; and although a blind man has no business to write about light, still the verses were sufficiently good in their way.

Having made fair copies of these poems, I signed every one of them “Oppodeldoc” (a fine sonorous name), and, doing each up nicely in a separate envelope, I despatched one to each of the four principal magazines, with a request for speedy insertion and prompt pay. The result of this well conceived plan, however, (the success of which would have saved me much trouble in after life,) served to convince me that some editors are not to be bamboozled, and gave the coup de grâce (as they say in France) to my nascent hopes (as they say in the city of the transcendentals).

===Chinese===

在我最初的写作尝试里，我发现「鲍勃纯真油」那几节诗与其说是助力，不如说是累赘。它们的光辉照耀我多于启发我。细想它们的卓越，自然会同我自己的流产之作比较，使我泄气；于是我长久徒劳。终于一个极其独创的念头钻进我的脑袋——这类念头时不时*总要*渗进天才人物的脑子。念头是这样的：——或者说，这样实行出来的。从城边极偏僻的一个角落里的一个旧书摊的破烂里，我凑集了几本古老的、全然无名或被遗忘的卷册。书商贱价卖给我。其中一本，自称是但丁《地狱篇》的译本，我从里面用惊人的工整抄下长长的一段，讲一个名叫乌戈利诺的人，养了一大群小崽子。另一本收着许多旧戏，作者的名字我忘了，我用同样的方式、同样的仔细，从里面摘出许许多多关于「天使」与「蒙恩的侍者」的诗句，关于「被打入地狱的鬼魂」的诗句，还有那一类的旁的。第三本是某一个盲人的著作，要么是希腊人，要么是乔克托人——每一件小事情我都懒得记得十分确切——我取了约莫五十行，开头是「阿喀琉斯的怒气」，「油脂」，以及别的什么。第四本，我记得也是一位盲人的手笔，我选了一两页，全是讲「光」与「圣光」的；虽然盲人没有资格写光，那些诗行倒也自有可观之处。

把这些诗誊清之后，我在每一首上署名「奥波德多克」（一个响当当的名字），把每首分别用信封好好封起，寄给四家最主要的杂志各一份，请求尽快刊载、立刻付酬。然而这个构想完美的计划的结果（它的成功原会在往后的生涯里省去我许多麻烦），使我确信：有些编辑不是可以蒙哄的，并给我初生的希望（如他们那超越之城的居民所说）送来一刀（如法国人所说）。

===Original===

The fact is, that each and every one of the magazines in question, gave Mr. “Oppodeldoc” a complete using up, in the “Monthly Notices to Correspondents.” The *Hum-Drum* gave him a dressing after this fashion:

“ ‘Oppodeldoc’ (whoever he is) has sent us a long tirade concerning a bedlamite whom he styles ‘Ugolino,’ who had a great many children that should have been all whipped and sent to bed without their suppers. The whole affair is exceedingly tame﻿—not to say *flat*. ‘Oppodeldoc’ (whoever he is) is entirely devoid of imagination﻿—and imagination, in our humble opinion, is not only the soul of **Poesy**, but also its very heart. ‘Oppodeldoc’ (whoever he is) has the audacity to demand of us, for his twattle, a ‘speedy insertion and prompt pay.’ We neither insert nor purchase any stuff of the sort. There can be no doubt, however, that he would meet with a ready sale for all the balderdash he can scribble, at the office of either the *Rowdy-Dow*, the *Lollipop*, or the *Goosetherumfoodle*.”

All this, it must be acknowledged, was very severe upon “Oppodeldoc”﻿—but the unkindest cut was putting the word **Poesy** in small caps. In those five preeminent letters what a world of bitterness is there not involved!

But “Oppodeldoc” was punished with equal severity in the *Rowdy-Dow*, which spoke thus:

“We have received a most singular and insolent communication from a person (whoever he is) signing himself ‘Oppodeldoc’﻿—thus desecrating the greatness of the illustrious Roman Emperor so named. Accompanying the letter of ‘Oppodeldoc’ (whoever he is) we find sundry lines of most disgusting and unmeaning rant about ‘angels and ministers of grace’﻿—rant such as no madman short of a Nat Lee, or an ‘Oppodeldoc,’ could possibly perpetrate. And for this trash of trash, we are modestly requested to ‘pay promptly.’ No sir﻿—no! We pay for nothing of *that* sort. Apply to the *Hum-Drum*, the *Lollipop*, or the *Goosetherumfoodle*. These *periodicals* will undoubtedly accept any literary offal you may send them﻿—and as undoubtedly *promise* to pay for it.”

This was bitter indeed upon poor “Oppodeldoc”; but, in this instance, the weight of the satire falls upon the *Hum-Drum*, the *Lollipop*, and the *Goosetherumfoodle*, who are pungently styled “*periodicals*”﻿—in Italics, too﻿—a thing that must have cut them to the heart.

===Chinese===

实情是，所涉的每一家杂志，都不折不扣地在「每月致通讯者启事」栏里把「奥波德多克」先生收拾了一通。《沉闷刊》（Hum-Drum）这样给他上刑：

「『奥波德多克』（不知他是谁）寄来一篇长论，讲一个疯子，他称之为『乌戈利诺』，养了一大群孩子，这群孩子本该个个挨一顿鞭子，不给晚饭打发上床。整桩事情平淡之极——不必说*乏味*。『奥波德多克』（不知他是谁）全然没有想象力——而想象力，照我们浅见，不但**诗**的灵魂是它，诗的心也是它。『奥波德多克』（不知他是谁）竟敢为他的呓语向我们讨一个『尽快刊载、立刻付酬』。这类货色我们既不刊载也不收购。然而毫无疑问：他所能涂抹的一切胡话，在《闹哄哄》《棒棒糖》或《鹅噜噜福多》任何一家的办事处里都会立刻销出去。」

这一切必须承认对「奥波德多克」够狠的——但最狠的一刀是把**诗**那个词排成了小型大写。那五个卓越的字母里头，包藏着多少刻毒啊！

但「奥波德多克」在《闹哄哄》（Rowdy-Dow）里受到同样严厉的惩罚，那份报纸这样说：

「我们收到一个署名『奥波德多克』的人（不知他是谁）的一封最古怪、最无礼的来信——这样亵渎那位有名的罗马皇帝的大名。伴随『奥波德多克』（不知他是谁）的来信，我们发现有若干行最可厌、最无意义的胡话，讲『天使和蒙恩的侍者』——除非是纳特·李、或一个『奥波德多克』那样的疯子，谁也胡诌不出这样的东西。而为了这废物里的废物，我们竟被谦逊地请求『立刻付酬』。不行，先生——不行！*那样的*东西我们一个钱也不付。请去找《沉闷刊》《棒棒糖》或《鹅噜噜福多》。这些*期刊*无疑肯收下你寄去的任何文学的渣滓——也同样无疑地*许诺*为它付钱。」

这于可怜的「奥波德多克」实在苦涩；但在这里，讽刺的分量落在《沉闷刊》《棒棒糖》与《鹅噜噜福多》头上：他们被尖刻地称作「*期刊*」——还是斜体——这一下必得叫他们痛彻心扉。

===Original===

Scarcely less savage was the *Lollipop*, which thus discoursed:

“Some *individual*, who rejoices in the appellation ‘Oppodeldoc,’ (to what low uses are the names of the illustrious dead too often applied!) has enclosed us some fifty or sixty *verses* commencing after this fashion:

Achilles’ wrath, to Greece the direful spring

Of woes unnumbered, etc., etc., etc., etc.

“ ‘Oppodeldoc’ (whoever he is) is respectfully informed that there is not a printer’s devil in our office who is not in the daily habit of composing better *lines*. Those of ‘Oppodeldoc’ will not *scan*. ‘Oppodeldoc’ should learn to *count*. But why he should have conceived the idea that *we*, (of all others, *we*!) would disgrace our pages with his ineffable nonsense, is utterly beyond comprehension. Why, the absurd twattle is scarcely good enough for the *Hum-Drum*, the *Rowdy-Dow*, the *Goosetherumfoodle*﻿—things that are in the practice of publishing ‘Mother Goose’s Melodies’ as original lyrics. And ‘Oppodeldoc’ (whoever he is) has even the assurance to demand *pay* for this drivel. Does ‘Oppodeldoc’ (whoever he is) know﻿—is he aware that we could not be paid to insert it?”

As I perused this I felt myself growing gradually smaller and smaller, and when I came to the point at which the editor sneered at the poem as “verses” there was little more than an ounce of me left. As for “Oppodeldoc,” I began to experience *compassion* for the poor fellow. But the *Goosetherumfoodle* showed, if possible, less mercy than the *Lollipop*. It was the *Goosetherumfoodle* that said:

“A wretched poetaster, who signs himself ‘Oppodeldoc,’ is silly enough to fancy that *we* will print and *pay for* a medley of incoherent and ungrammatical bombast which he has transmitted to us, and which commences with the following most *intelligible* line:

‘Hail, Holy Light! Offspring of Heaven, first born.’

===Chinese===

《棒棒糖》（Lollipop）的凶残也差不了多少，它这样训话：

「某一个*人物*，高兴顶着『奥波德多克』的称呼（不朽的亡者的名字被派上低贱的用场，何其多也！）寄给我们五六十行*诗句*，开头是这样：

阿喀琉斯的怒气，那一发灾祸的引信，

给希腊带来无穷的苦难，等等，等等，等等，等等。

「谨向『奥波德多克』（不知他是谁）恭谨致知：本办事处里没有一个印刷小厮，不曾天天写出更好的*诗行*。『奥波德多克』的诗行*合不上格律*。『奥波德多克』该学学*数数*。可是他怎么会设想*我们*（在所有的人里头，偏是*我们*！）肯把他的无法形容的胡话登在我们版上玷污篇幅，实在超乎理解。怎么，那荒唐的呓语几乎不够格给《沉闷刊》《闹哄哄》《鹅噜噜福多》——那些惯于把『鹅妈妈歌谣』当原创抒情诗发表的货色。而『奥波德多克』（不知他是谁）竟有脸为这涎水讨*报酬*。『奥波德多克』（不知他是谁）可知道——他可明白，我们倒贴钱也不肯登它吗？」

读到这里我觉得自己渐渐地越缩越小，当我读到编辑讥那诗不过是「诗句」的地方，我身上剩不下比一盎司更多的东西了。至于「奥波德多克」，我开始对那可怜的家伙生出*怜悯*。然而《鹅噜噜福多》（Goosetherumfoodle）显出的仁慈，倘若可能，比《棒棒糖》更少。说这话的正是《鹅噜噜福多》：

「一个可怜的小诗人，署名『奥波德多克』，蠢到设想*我们*会刊登并且*付钱*买一锅语无伦次、文理不通的大话；那锅东西是他寄给我们的，开头是这样一行最*可懂*的句子：

『光，神圣的光！上天的后嗣，初生的长子。』

===Original===

“We say, ‘most *intelligible*.’ ‘Oppodeldoc’ (whoever he is) will be kind enough to tell us, perhaps, how ‘*hail*’ can be ‘*holy light*’ We always regarded it as *frozen rain*. Will he inform us, also, how frozen rain can be, at one and the same time, both ‘holy light,’ (whatever that is) and an ‘offspring?’﻿—which latter term (if we understand anything about English) is only employed, with propriety, in reference to small babies of about six weeks old. But it is preposterous to descant upon such absurdity﻿—although ‘Oppodeldoc’ (whoever he is) has the unparalleled effrontery to suppose that we will not only ‘insert’ his ignorant ravings, but (absolutely) *pay for them*!

“Now this is fine﻿—it is rich!﻿—and we have half a mind to punish this young scribbler for his egotism, by really publishing his effusion, *verbatim et literatim*, as he has written it. We could inflict no punishment so severe, and we *would* inflict it, but for the boredom which we should cause our readers in so doing.

“Let ‘Oppodeldoc’ (whoever he is) send any future *composition* of like character to the *Hum-Drum*, the *Lollipop*, or the *Rowdy-Dow*, *They* will ‘insert’ it. *They* ‘insert’ every month just such stuff. Send it to them. **We** are not to be insulted with impunity.”

This made an end of me; and as for the *Hum-Drum*, the *Rowdy-Dow*, and the *Lollipop*, I never could comprehend how they survived it. The putting *them* in the smallest possible *minion*, (that was the rub﻿—thereby insinuating their lowness﻿—their baseness,) while **we** stood looking down upon them in gigantic capitals!﻿—oh it was *too* bitter!﻿—it was wormwood﻿—it was gall. Had I been either of these periodicals I would have spared no pains to have the *Goosetherumfoodle* prosecuted. It might have been done under the Act for the “Prevention of Cruelty to Animals.” As for Oppodeldoc (whoever he was) I had by this time lost all patience with the fellow, and sympathized with him no longer. He was a fool, beyond doubt, (whoever he was,) and got not a kick more than he deserved.

===Chinese===

「我们说『最*可懂*』。『奥波德多克』（不知他是谁）也许肯费神告诉我们，『光』怎么可以是『神圣的光』。我们一向把它当作*冻雨*。他也肯告诉我们吗，冻雨怎么能在同一时刻既是『神圣的光』（不管那是什么），又是『后嗣』？——后一个词（倘若我们对英语还懂得一点），只在恰当的场合用来指六个星期大的小娃娃。但在这类荒唐事上浪费口舌是可笑的——虽然『奥波德多克』（不知他是谁）有着无与伦比的厚脸皮，设想我们不但会『刊登』他无知的呓语，而且（竟然）会*为它付钱*！

「此刻这可妙了——这可真阔了！——我们颇有一半的心思要惩罚这位小涂抹家，罚他的自大：当真把他的大作*一字一句、原原本本*照他所写的发表出来。我们施不出比这更重的刑罚，我们*会*施行的，只因那样做会使我们的读者厌倦，才罢手。

「让『奥波德多克』（不知他是谁）把将来类似性质的*作品*寄给《沉闷刊》《棒棒糖》或《闹哄哄》去。*他们*会『刊登』它。*他们*每月刊登的正是这样的货色。寄给他们去。**我们**这里，侮辱是要付出代价的。」

这一下结束了我的性命；至于《沉闷刊》《闹哄哄》《棒棒糖》，我至今不懂他们怎么活了下来。把*他们*排在最小可能的小型字里（那才是要害——借此暗示他们的低贱——他们的卑污），而**我们**以巨人的大写俯临他们！——哦，那*太*苦了！——那是苦艾——那是胆汁。我倘若是他们中的任何一家，必不辞劳苦把《鹅噜噜福多》告到官里。那原是可以依着「防止虐待动物法」办的。至于奥波德多克（不知他是谁），我此刻对那家伙已失尽耐心，不再同情他了。他是傻瓜无疑（不知他是谁），一脚也不曾多挨。

===Original===

The result of my experiment with the old books, convinced me, in the first place, that “honesty is the best policy,” and, in the second, that if I could not write better than Mr. Dante, and the two blind men, and the rest of the old set, it would, at least, be a difficult matter to write worse. I took heart, therefore, and determined to prosecute the “entirely original” (as they say on the covers of the magazines), at whatever cost of study and pains. I again placed before my eyes, as a model, the brilliant stanzas on “The Oil-of-Bob” by the editor of the *Gad-Fly*, and resolved to construct an ode on the same sublime theme, in rivalry of what had already been done.

With my first verse I had no material difficulty. It ran thus:

“To pen an Ode upon the ‘Oil-of-Bob.’ ”

Having carefully looked out, however, all the legitimate rhymes to “Bob,” I found it impossible to proceed. In this dilemma I had recourse to paternal aid; and, after some hours of mature thought, my father and myself thus constructed the poem:

“To pen an Ode upon the ‘Oil-of-Bob’

Is all sorts of a job.

> (Signed) Snob.

To be sure, this composition was of no very great length﻿—but I “have yet to learn” as they say in the *Edinburgh Review*, that the mere extent of a literary work has anything to do with its merit. As for the Quarterly cant about “sustained effort,” it is impossible to see the sense of it. Upon the whole, therefore, I was satisfied with the success of my maiden attempt, and now the only question regarded the disposal I should make of it. My father suggested that I should send it to the *Gad-Fly*﻿—but there were two reasons which operated to prevent me from so doing. I dreaded the jealousy of the editor﻿—and I had ascertained that he did not pay for original contributions. I therefore, after due deliberation, consigned the article to the more dignified pages of the *Lollipop*, and awaited the event in anxiety, but with resignation.

In the very next published number I had the proud satisfaction of seeing my poem printed at length, as the leading article, with the following significant words, prefixed in italics and between brackets:

===Chinese===

我用旧书做的那场试验的结果，首先叫我确信「诚实是上策」，其次叫我确信：倘若我写不赢但丁先生和两位盲人，以及其余的老古董们，那么至少，要写得更糟也是难事。于是我鼓起勇气，决意贯彻「全然独创」（照杂志封皮的说法），不惜任何研究与苦心。我重新把《牛虻》主编那几节灿烂的「鲍勃纯真油」的诗摆在眼前作范本，决意就同一庄严的主题造一首颂歌，同既成的作品一较短长。

第一行诗我没有多大的困难。它是这样：

「为『鲍勃纯真油』写一首颂歌。」

然而我把「鲍勃」的一切合辙的韵仔细查遍之后，发觉没法进行下去。在这个两难里我求了父亲的援手；经过几个钟头的深思，我的父亲和我这样把诗造了出来：

为「鲍勃纯真油」写一首颂歌

是样样齐全的活儿。

——（署名）斯诺布

诚然这篇作品篇幅不算很长——但我「尚待领会」，照《爱丁堡评论》的说法：一篇作品的单纯篇幅同它的功绩有什么相干。至于《季刊》那种关于「持续用力」的行话，看不出它的道理。总之，我对处女作的成果满意，此刻唯一的问题只在把它怎样处置。我父亲提议寄给《牛虻》——但有两层缘由拦住我。我怕编辑的嫉妒——而且我查明他不付原创稿酬。因此经过深思，我把稿件交给《棒棒糖》那更尊贵的版面，在焦灼里、然而顺从地等着结果。

紧接着出版的一期里，我便得到骄傲的满足，看见我的诗作为头条全文印出，前面用斜体、加括号添着这几句意味深长的话：

===Original===

[We call the attention of our readers to the subjoined admirable stanza on “The Oil of Bob.” We need say nothing of their sublimity, or their pathos:﻿—it is impossible to peruse them without tears. Those who have been nauseated with a sad dose on the same august topic from the goose quill of the editor of the *Gad-Fly* will do well to compare the two compositions.

P.S.﻿—We are consumed with anxiety to probe the mystery which envelops the evident pseudonym “Snob.” May we hope for a personal interview?]

===Chinese===

[我们请读者注意下面这几节关于「鲍勃纯真油」的可叹赏的诗。它们的崇高，它们的哀婉，无须我们说什么：——读它而不落泪，是不可能的。那些曾被《牛虻》主编的鹅毛笔在同一庄严题目上灌下苦药的人们，把两篇作品比一比，是有益的。

又及——我们急不可耐，想探一探裹着显然的假名「斯诺布」的那个谜。我们可敢指望一次亲面的会谈吗？]

All this was scarcely more than justice, but it was, I confess, rather more than I had expected:﻿—I acknowledged this, be it observed, to the everlasting disgrace of my country and of mankind. I lost no time, however, in calling upon the editor of the *Lollipop*, and had the good fortune to find this gentleman at home. He saluted me with an air of profound respect, slightly blended with a fatherly and patronizing admiration, wrought in him, no doubt, by my appearance of extreme youth and inexperience. Begging me to be seated, he entered at once upon the subject of my poem;﻿—but modesty will ever forbid me to repeat the thousand compliments which he lavished upon me. The eulogies of Mr. Crab (such was the editor’s name) were, however, by no means fulsomely indiscriminate. He analyzed my composition with much freedom and great ability﻿—not hesitating to point out a few trivial defects﻿—a circumstance which elevated him highly in my esteem. The *Gad-Fly* was, of course, brought upon the tapis, and I hope never to be subjected to a criticism so searching, or to rebukes so withering, as were bestowed by Mr. Crab upon that unhappy effusion. I had been accustomed to regard the editor of the *Gad-Fly* as something superhuman; but Mr. Crab soon disabused me of that idea. He set the literary as well as the personal character of the Fly (so Mr. C. satirically designated the rival editor), in its true light. He, the Fly, was very little better than he should be. He had written infamous things. He was a penny-a-liner, and a buffoon. He was a villain. He had composed a tragedy which set the whole country in a guffaw, and a farce which deluged the universe in tears. Besides all this, he had the impudence to pen what he meant for a lampoon upon himself (Mr. Crab), and the temerity to style him “an ass.” Should I at any time wish to express my opinion of Mr. Fry, the pages of the *Lollipop*, Mr. Crab assured me, were at my unlimited disposal. In the meantime, as it was very certain that I would be attacked in the *Fly* for my attempt at composing a rival poem on the “Oil-of-Bob,” he (Mr. Crab) would take it upon himself to attend, pointedly, to my private and personal interests. If I were not made a man of at once, it should not be the fault of himself (Mr. Crab).

===Chinese===

这一切不过略微超出了公道，但我承认，超出了我的预料：——请注意，我这样承认，是我国家与人类的万古之耻。然而我毫不迟延地去拜访《棒棒糖》的主编，侥幸发现这位先生在家。他以深恭的仪态向我致意，微微掺着一种父辈的、提携的赏识，无疑是被我那极其年轻、极其无经验的外表引出来的。他请我坐下，立刻进入我的诗的题目；——但廉耻永远不许我复述他倾洒在我身上的千百句恭维。然而克拉布（Crab）先生（主编便姓这个）的颂词绝不是滥而不分的。他以充分的自由、极大的本领分析我的作品——毫不迟疑地指出几处小小的瑕疵——这情形使他在我心目中身价大涨。《牛虻》自然被摆上台面，我但愿自己永不再受那样一种搜根究底的批评、那样一种摧肝裂胆的申斥，如克拉布先生加在那不幸的作品上的。我向来把《牛虻》的主编看作近乎超人；克拉布先生不久便替我破除了那个念头。他把《牛虻》（克拉布先生这样讽刺地称呼那位对手的编辑）的文学品格与人身品格放回它的真光里。那位牛虻，比他应有的样子好不了多少。他写过臭名昭著的东西。他是按字拿钱的雇佣文人，是一个小丑。他是个恶棍。他编过一出悲剧，叫全国哄笑；一出闹剧，叫宇宙流泪。此外，他竟有脸写下他打算当作对克拉布先生（他）的讽刺诗的东西，竟敢狂妄到叫他（克拉布先生）「一头驴」。我倘若任何时候想对弗赖先生表示意见，《棒棒糖》的版面，克拉布先生向我担保，由我无限支配。与此同时，既然十分确定我会因试着写「鲍勃纯真油》的竞歌而在《牛虻》上受攻，他（克拉布先生）要自任一件事：把我的私人的、切身利害照管得妥妥帖帖。倘若我不立刻被捧成个人物，那决不怪他（克拉布先生）。

===Original===

Mr. Crab having now paused in his discourse, (the latter portion of which I found it impossible to comprehend), I ventured to suggest something about the remuneration which I had been taught to expect for my poem, by an announcement on the cover of the *Lollipop*, declaring that it (the *Lollipop*) “insisted upon being permitted to pay exorbitant prices for all accepted contributions﻿—frequently expending more money for a single brief poem than the whole annual cost of the *Hum-Drum*, the *Rowdy-Dow*, and the *Goosetherumfoodle* combined.”

As I mentioned the word “remuneration,” Mr. Crab first opened his eyes, and then his mouth, to quite a remarkable extent; causing his personal appearance to resemble that of a highly-agitated elderly duck in the act of quacking; and in this condition he remained (ever and anon pressing his hands tightly to his forehead, as if in a state of desperate bewilderment) until I had nearly made an end of what I had to say.

Upon my conclusion, he sank back into his seat, as if much overcome, letting his arms fall lifelessly by his side, but keeping his mouth still rigorously open, after the fashion of the duck. While I remained in speechless astonishment at behavior so alarming, he suddenly leaped to his feet and made a rush at the bell-rope; but just as he reached this, he appeared to have altered his intention, whatever it was, for he dived under a table and immediately reappeared with a cudgel. This he was in the act of uplifting (for what purpose I am at a loss to imagine), when, all at once, there came a benign smile over his features, and he sank placidly back in his chair.

“Mr. Bob,” he said (for I had sent up my card before ascending myself), “Mr. Bob, you are a young man, I presume﻿—*very*?”

I assented; adding that I had not yet concluded my third lustrum.

===Chinese===

克拉布先生此刻的谈话停了停（后半段我实在无从领会），我冒昧提了一句我曾从《棒棒糖》的封面启事里学会指望的那种稿酬——那启事声明该刊（*棒棒糖*）「坚持要被允许为一切采用的投稿支付高昂的稿酬——常常为一首短诗花的钱，比《沉闷刊》《闹哄哄》《鹅噜噜福多》三家的全年开销加在一起还多」。

我一提「稿酬」两个字，克拉布先生先睁大了眼睛，然后张大了嘴，张到相当可观的程度；使他个人的外观活像一只激动极了的老公鸭正在嘎嘎叫；他就留在这个状态里（不时把两只手紧紧按住额头，仿佛陷入绝望的纷乱），直到我差不多说完我要说的话。

我住口时，他瘫回座位，仿佛被压垮了，两条胳膊没精打采地垂在身侧，嘴却照那鸭子的样式仍旧死死张着。我正对着这样吓人的举止惊愕得说不出话，他骤然跳起，朝拉铃的绳猛扑过去；但他刚到绳边，仿佛改了主意——不论那主意是什么——因为他钻到一张桌子底下，立刻带着一根棍子重新出现。他正把这根棍子举起来（要做什么我无从想象），忽然间，一缕慈祥的微笑漫过他的五官，他便安安稳稳瘫回椅子里。

「鲍勃先生，」他说（因为我上楼之前先把名片送了上去），「鲍勃先生，我想您是年轻人——*非常*年轻吧？」

我承认；并补说我还不曾过完我的第三个五年。

===Original===

“Ah!” he replied, “very good! I see how it is﻿—say no more! Touching this matter of compensation, what you observe is very just: in fact it is excessively so. But ah﻿—ah﻿—the *first* contribution﻿—the *first*, I say﻿—it is never the magazine custom to pay for﻿—you comprehend, eh? The truth is, we are usually the *recipients* in such case.” [Mr. Crab smiled blandly as he emphasized the word “recipients.”] “For the most part, we are *paid* for the insertion of a maiden attempt﻿—especially in verse. In the second place, Mr. Bob, the magazine rule is never to disburse what we term in France the *argent comptant*﻿—I have no doubt you understand. In a quarter or two after publication of the article﻿—or in a year or two﻿—we make no objection to giving our note at nine months; provided always that we can so arrange our affairs as to be quite certain of a ‘burst up’ in six. I really *do* hope, Mr. Bob, that you will look upon this explanation as satisfactory.” Here Mr. Crab concluded, and the tears stood in his eyes.

Grieved to the soul at having been, however innocently, the cause of pain to so eminent and so sensitive a man, I hastened to apologize, and to reassure him, by expressing my perfect coincidence with his views, as well as my entire appreciation of the delicacy of his position. Having done all this in a neat speech, I took leave.

One fine morning, very shortly afterwards, “I awoke and found myself famous.” The extent of my renown will be best estimated by reference to the editorial opinions of the day. These opinions, it will be seen, were embodied in critical notices of the number of the *Lollipop* containing my poem, and are perfectly satisfactory, conclusive and clear with the exception, perhaps, of the hieroglyphical marks, “Sep. 15﻿—1 t.” appended to each of the critiques.

The *Owl*, a journal of profound sagacity, and well known for the deliberate gravity of its literary decisions﻿—the *Owl*, I say, spoke as follows:

===Chinese===

「啊！」他答道，「好极了！我明白是怎么回事了——不必多说！关于报酬这件事，你观察得很对：实在对得过分了。可是啊——啊——*第一*件投稿——第一件，我说——按杂志的惯例是从来不付酬的——你懂吗，嗯？实情是，这样的案子里，我们通常是*受酬*的一方。」[克拉布先生加重说出「受酬」两个字时，温和地微笑。]「大体上，一篇处女作——尤其是诗——的刊载，是我们*收*钱的。其次，鲍勃先生，杂志的规矩是从不支付我们在法国所谓*现银*的东西——毫无疑问你懂得。文章刊出之后一两个季度——或一两年——我们不妨出具九个月期的期票，始终以我们能把事务安排到确知六个月内「散伙」为条件。鲍勃先生，我实在*指望*你把这番解释当作满意的。」克拉布先生说到这里收了口，眼里噙着泪。

我虽全然无辜，却做了叫这样一位杰出而敏感的人痛苦的原因，我心里难过极了，连忙道歉，安抚他，表示我同他的见解完全一致，对他地位的细微处抱有全然的体谅。这一切在一篇干净利落的小演说里办完，我便告退。

不久之后一个晴朗的早晨，「我一觉醒来，发现自己已经名满天下」。我的声名的广被，只须查一查当时的各家编辑意见便最好地估定。这些意见，人们看得见，都载在对载有我的诗的那一期《棒棒糖》的批评短评里，都完全满意、结论性、明白晓畅，或许除开每一篇批评后头附着的那些象形文字的标记，「九月十五——一行」。

《猫头鹰》，一份见识深远的报纸，以它文学判词的从容庄重知名——我说的是《猫头鹰》——这样讲：

===Original===

“*The Lollipop*! The October number of this delicious magazine surpasses its predecessors, and sets competition at defiance. In the beauty of its typography and paper﻿—in the number and excellence of its steel plates﻿—as well as in the literary merit of its contributions﻿—the *Lollipop* compares with its slow-paced rivals as Hyperion with a Satyr. The *Hum-Drum*, the *Rowdy-Dow*, and the *Goosetherumfoodle*, excel, it is true, in braggadocio, but, in all other points, give us the *Lollipop*! How this celebrated journal can sustain its evidently tremendous expenses, is more than we can understand. To be sure, it has a circulation of 100,000, and its subscription-list has increased one-fourth during the last month; but, on the other hand, the sums it disburses constantly for contributions are inconceivable. It is reported that Mr. Slyass received no less than thirty-seven and a half cents for his inimitable paper on ‘Pigs.’ With Mr. **Crab**, as editor, and with such names upon the list of contributors as **Snob** and Slyass, there can be no such word as ‘fail’ for the *Lollipop*. Go and subscribe. Sep. 15﻿—1 t.”

I must say that I was gratified with this high-toned notice from a paper so respectable as the *Owl*. The placing my name﻿—that is to say, my nom de guerre﻿—in priority of station to that of the great Slyass, was a compliment as happy as I felt it to be deserved.

My attention was next arrested by these paragraphs in the *Toad*﻿—a print highly distinguished for its uprightness, and independence﻿—for its entire freedom from sycophancy and subservience to the givers of dinners:

“The *Lollipop* for October is out in advance of all its contemporaries, and infinitely surpasses them, of course, in the splendor of its embellishments, as well as in the richness of its literary contents. The *Hum-Drum*, the *Rowdy-Dow*, and the *Goosetherumfoodle* excel, we admit, in braggadocio, but, in all other points, give us the *Lollipop*. How this celebrated magazine can sustain its evidently tremendous expenses, is more than we can understand. To be sure, it has a circulation of 200,000, and its subscription list has increased one-third during the last fortnight, but on the other hand, the sums it disburses, monthly, for contributions, are fearfully great. We learn that Mr. Mumblethumb received no less than fifty cents for his late ‘Monody in a Mud-Puddle.’

===Chinese===

「*《棒棒糖》*！这份甜美的杂志的十月号胜过它的前辈们，把竞争一脚踢开。在排印与纸张之美里——在钢版画的数目与精彩里——正如在投稿的文学功绩里——《棒棒糖》同它的慢吞吞的对手们相比，如许珀里翁之于萨堤尔。《沉闷刊》《闹哄哄》《鹅噜噜福多》在说大话上确有可观，但在其余一切方面，请给我们《棒棒糖》！这份著名的报纸怎样撑住它分明庞大的开销，我们无从理解。诚然，它销数十万份，它的订户单上月增了四分之一；但另一方面，它为投稿经常付出的款项不可想象。据说斯莱阿斯先生为他的论『猪』的绝妙文章，拿到足足三十七美分半。有**克拉布**先生做编辑，投稿名单上又有**斯诺布**与斯莱阿斯这样的名字，《棒棒糖》字典里便没有『失败』这两个字。快去订吧。九月十五——一行。」

我得说，我从一份像《猫头鹰》这样可敬的报纸的这一高格调的短评里得到满足。把我的名字——就是说，我的战名——排在那伟大的斯莱阿斯的席位之前，是一种同我自觉应得恰相称的恭维。

我的注意接着被《蟾蜍》里的这些段落捉住——那家报纸以它的正直与独立著称——以它对宴请者全无谄媚与依从著称：

「十月号的《棒棒糖》抢在所有同辈前头，自然无限地胜过它们，无论在插图的富丽上，还是在文字内容的丰厚上。《沉闷刊》《闹哄哄》《鹅噜噜福多》在说大话上确有可观，我们承认，但在其余一切方面，请给我们《棒棒糖》！这份著名的杂志怎样撑住它分明庞大的开销，我们无从理解。诚然，它销数二十万份，它的订户单近两周增了三分之一；但另一方面，它每月为投稿付出的款项吓人地大。我们得知，姆布尔姆桑先生为他新近的『泥潭悼歌』，拿到足足五十美分。

===Original===

“Among the original contributors to the present number we notice (besides the eminent editor, Mr. **Crab**), such men as **Snob**, Slyass, and Mumblethumb. Apart from the editorial matter, the most valuable paper, nevertheless, is, we think, a poetical gem by Snob, on the ‘Oil-of-Bob’﻿—but our readers must not suppose from the title of this incomparable bijou, that it bears any similitude to some balderdash on the same subject by a certain contemptible individual whose name is unmentionable to ears polite. The *present* poem ‘On the Oil-of-Bob,’ has excited universal anxiety and curiosity in respect to the owner of the evident pseudonym, ‘Snob’﻿—a curiosity which, happily, we have it in our power to satisfy. ‘Snob’ is the nom de plume of Mr. Thingum Bob, of this city﻿—a relative of the great Mr. Thingum (after whom he is named), and otherwise connected with the most illustrious families of the State. His father, Thomas Bob, Esq., is an opulent merchant in Smug. Sep. 15﻿—1 t.”

This generous approbation touched me to the heart﻿—the more especially as it emanated from a source so avowedly﻿—so proverbially pure as the *Toad*. The word “balderdash,” as applied to the “Oil-of-Bob” of the *Fly*, I considered singularly pungent and appropriate. The words “gem” and “bijou,” however, used in reference to my composition, struck me as being, in some degree, feeble, and seemed to me to be deficient in force. They were not sufficiently *prononcés* (as we have it in France).

I had hardly finished reading the *Toad*, when a friend placed in my hands a copy of the *Mole*, a daily, enjoying high reputation for the keenness of its perception about matters in general, and for the open, honest, aboveground style of its editorials. The *Mole* spoke of the *Lollipop* as follows:

===Chinese===

「本期原创的撰稿人里，我们注意到（除杰出的主编**克拉布**先生之外）**斯诺布**、斯莱阿斯、姆布尔姆桑这样的人物。除编辑部文字之外，最有价值的一篇，我们想，当推斯诺布论『鲍勃纯真油』的那颗诗的明珠——但我们的读者切不可因这件无与伦比的小珍宝的题目，便以为它同某个不值一提的家伙在同一题目上的一派胡话有任何相似之处；那家伙的名字，在斯文的耳朵里提不得。*眼前*这首『论鲍勃纯真油』，已就在那显然的假名『斯诺布』的主人身上激起普遍的焦灼与好奇——一种我们有幸有权满足的好奇。『斯诺布』是本市廷根·鲍勃（Thingum Bob）先生的笔名——他是伟大的廷根先生（他便以此得名）的亲属，此外还同本州最煊赫的几家门第攀着亲。他的父亲托马斯·鲍勃先生是斯马格城一位富商。九月十五——一行。」

这样慷慨的褒奖摸着我的心——尤其因为它的源头是《蟾蜍》那样*公认地*、*出名地*纯净的报纸。「胡话」两个字，用在《牛虻》的「鲍勃纯真油」上，我觉得尖利而贴切得出奇。但「明珠」「小珍宝」这样几个字，用在我的作品上，我觉得在某种程度上乏力，在我看似乎缺些劲道。它们不够*分明*（照我们法国人的说法）。

我几乎还没有读完《蟾蜍》，一位朋友把一份《鼹鼠》放进我手里——一份日报，以它对一般事物知觉的敏锐、以它社论那公开、诚实、摆在地面上的风格享有盛名。《鼹鼠》这样讲《棒棒糖》：

===Original===

“We have just received the *Lollipop* for October, and must say that never before have we perused any single number of any periodical which afforded us a felicity so supreme. We speak advisedly. The *Hum-Drum*, the *Rowdy-Dow* and the *Goosetherumfoodle* must look well to their laurels. These prints, no doubt, surpass everything in loudness of pretension, but, in all other points, give us the *Lollipop*! How this celebrated magazine can sustain its evidently tremendous expenses, is more than we can comprehend. To be sure, it has a circulation of 300,000 and its subscription-list has increased one half within the last week, but then the sum it disburses, monthly, for contributions, is astoundingly enormous. We have it upon good authority, that Mr. Fatquack received no less than sixty-two cents and a half for his late domestic nouvelette, the ‘Dish-Clout.’

“The contributors to the number before us are Mr. **Crab** (the eminent editor), **Snob**, Mumblethumb, Fatquack, and others; but, after the inimitable compositions of the editor himself, we prefer a diamond-like effusion from the pen of a rising poet who writes over the signature ‘Snob’﻿—a nom de guerre which we predict will one day extinguish the radiance of ‘Boz.’ ‘Snob,’ we learn, is a Mr. Thingum Bob, Esq., sole heir of a wealthy merchant of this city, Thomas Bob, Esq., and a near relative of the distinguished Mr. Thingum. The title of Mr. B.’s admirable poem is the ‘Oil-of-Bob’﻿—a somewhat unfortunate name, by the by, as some contemptible vagabond connected with the penny press has already disgusted the town with a great deal of drivel upon the same topic. There will be no danger, however, of confounding the compositions. Sep. 15﻿—1 t.”

The generous approbation of so clear-sighted a journal as the *Mole* penetrated my soul with delight. The only objection which occurred to me was, that the terms “contemptible vagabond” might have been better written “odious and *contemptible* wretch, villain and *vagabond*.” This would have sounded more gracefully, I think. “Diamond-like,” also, was scarcely, it will be admitted, of sufficient intensity to express what the *Mole* evidently *thought* of the brilliancy of the “Oil-of-Bob.”

===Chinese===

「我们刚收到十月的《棒棒糖》，必须说，从来没有任何期刊的任何一期，给过我们这样至上的欢愉。我们是斟酌了说的。《沉闷刊》《闹哄哄》《鹅噜噜福多》必须好好看住它们的桂冠。这些报纸无疑在虚声恫吓上胜过一切，但在其余一切方面，请给我们《棒棒糖》！这份著名的杂志怎样撑住它分明庞大的开销，我们无从理解。诚然，它销数三十万份，它的订户单上星期增了二分之一；但另一方面，它每月为投稿付出的款项大得惊人。我们有可靠的权威得知，法特夸克先生为他新近的家庭小品《洗碗布》，拿到足足六十二美分半。

「本期撰稿的有**克拉布**先生（杰出的主编）、**斯诺布**、姆布尔姆桑、法特夸克诸位，以及其他；但在这位主编本人的绝妙篇章之后，我们宁取一支新起诗人的笔下面一颗钻石似的华章，那位诗人署名『斯诺布』——一个我们预言有朝一日将扑灭『博兹』的光辉的战名。『斯诺布』，我们得知，是廷根·鲍勃先生，本市富商托马斯·鲍勃先生的独子，杰出的廷根先生的近亲。鲍勃先生那篇可叹赏的诗的题目是『鲍勃纯真油』——顺便说，这名字有点不幸，因为某个同廉价报纸有牵连的、不值一提的流浪汉，已经在同一题目上用一大堆涎水叫全城倒了胃口。然而把两篇作品认混的危险是不会有的。九月十五——一行。」

《鼹鼠》这样一份目光如炬的报纸的慷慨褒奖，把欢喜灌进我的灵魂。我唯一想到的异议是：「不值一提的流浪汉」几个字，最好写作「可憎而*不值一提*的坏蛋，恶棍兼*流浪汉*」。我想这样听起来更文雅些。「钻石似的」，大家也会承认，仍嫌不够强烈，表达不出《鼹鼠》分明*觉得*的「鲍勃纯真油」的光辉。

===Original===

On the same afternoon in which I saw these notices in the *Owl*, the *Toad*, and the *Mole* I happened to meet with a copy of the *Daddy-Long-Legs*, a periodical proverbial for the extreme extent of its understanding. And it was the *Daddy-Long-Legs* which spoke thus:

“The *Lollipop*!! This gorgeous magazine is already before the public for October. The question of preeminence is forever put to rest, and hereafter it will be excessively preposterous in the *Hum-Drum*, the *Rowdy-Dow*, or the *Goosetherumfoodle*, to make any farther spasmodic attempts at competition. These journals may excel the *Lollipop* in outcry, but, in all other points, give us the *Lollipop*! How this celebrated magazine can sustain its evidently tremendous expenses, is past comprehension. To be sure it has a circulation of precisely half a million, and its subscription-list has increased seventy-five percent, within the last couple of days; but then the sums it disburses, monthly, for contributions, are scarcely credible; we are cognizant of the fact, that Mademoiselle Cribalittle received no less than eighty-seven cents and a half for her late valuable Revolutionary tale, entitled ‘The York-Town Katy-Did, and the Bunker-Hill Katy-Didn’t.’

“The most able papers in the present number, are, of course, those furnished by the editor (the eminent Mr. **Crab**), but there are numerous magnificent contributions from such names as **Snob**, Mademoiselle Cribalittle, Slyass, Mrs. Fibalittle, Mumblethumb, Mrs. Squibalittle, and last, though not least, Fatquack. The world may well be challenged to produce so rich a galaxy of genius.

「《棒棒糖》！！这份华美的杂志的十月号已在公众面前。独尊的问题永远安歇了，此后《沉闷刊》《闹哄哄》《鹅噜噜福多》还要作任何进一步的痉挛式的竞争尝试，便荒谬透顶了。这些报纸的叫喊或可胜过《棒棒糖》，但在其余一切方面，请给我们《棒棒糖》！这份著名的杂志怎样撑住它分明庞大的开销，非理解所能及。诚然，它销数整整五十万份，它的订户单上两天里增了百分之七十五；但另一方面，它每月为投稿付出的款项几乎叫人不能相信；我们确知这件事：克里巴莉特小姐为她新近那篇极有价值的革命故事《约克城的卡蒂蒂，与邦克山的卡蒂没》，拿到足足八十七美分半。

「本期最出色的篇章，自然要数主编（杰出的**克拉布**先生）供的那几篇，但还有**斯诺布**、克里巴莉特小姐、斯莱阿斯、法巴莉特太太、姆布尔姆桑、斯奎巴莉特太太，以及最后虽非最次的法特夸克诸位名字底下的许多宏伟的投稿。世界尽可以被人挑战：拿出这样一片天才的辉煌的星群来。

===Original===

“The poem over the signature ‘**Snob**’ is, we find, attracting universal commendation, and, we are constrained to say, deserves, if possible, even more applause than it has received. The ‘Oil-of-Bob’ is the title of this masterpiece of eloquence and art. One or two of our readers *may* have a *very* faint, although sufficiently disgusting recollection of a poem (?) similarly entitled, the perpetration of a miserable penny-a-liner, mendicant, and cutthroat, connected in the capacity of scullion, we believe, with one of the indecent prints about the purlieus of the city; we beg them, for God’s sake, not to confound the compositions. The author of *the* ‘Oil-of-Bob’ is, we hear, **Thingum Bob**, Esq., a gentleman of high genius, and a scholar. ‘Snob’ is merely a nom-de-guerre. Sep. 15﻿—1 t.”

I could scarcely restrain my indignation while I perused the concluding portions of this diatribe. It was clear to me that the yea-nay manner﻿—not to say the gentleness﻿—the positive forbearance with which the *Daddy-Long-Legs* spoke of that pig, the editor of the *Gad-Fly*﻿—it was evident to me, I say, that this gentleness of speech could proceed from nothing else than a partiality for the *Fly*﻿—whom it was clearly the intention of the *Daddy-Long-Legs* to elevate into reputation at my expense. Anyone, indeed, might perceive, with half an eye, that, had the real design of the *Daddy* been what it wished to appear, it (the *Daddy*) might have expressed itself in terms more direct, more pungent, and altogether more to the purpose. The words “penny-a-liner,” “mendicant,” “scullion,” and “cutthroat,” were epithets so intentionally inexpressive and equivocal, as to be worse than nothing when applied to the author of the very worst stanzas ever penned by one of the human race. We all know what is meant by “damning with faint praise,” and, on the other hand, who could fail seeing through the covert purpose of the *Daddy*﻿—that of glorifying with feeble abuse?

===Chinese===

「署名『**斯诺布**』的诗，我们发现，正博得普遍的赞许，我们不得不说，倘若可能，它所应得的赞美还多于它已经得到的。『鲍勃纯真油』是这篇雄辩与艺术的杰作的题目。我们的一两位读者*也许*对一个同题的诗（？）存着*很*淡薄、然而足够令人作呕的追忆，那诗的作者是一个可怜的按字拿钱的雇佣文人，乞丐兼刽子手，我们相信，在城里边儿某家不体面的报纸上充当烧火小厮的角色；我们奉劝他们，看在上帝的份上，千万别把两篇作品认混。*真正的*『鲍勃纯真油』的作者，我们听说，是**廷根·鲍勃**先生，一位高天才的绅士，一位学者。『斯诺布』不过是一个战名。九月十五——一行。」

我读着这篇漫骂的收尾的几段，几乎按捺不住我的愤怒。分明得很，那种含含糊糊的腔调——不说那温和——那种正面的节制，《长脚爷叔》谈论那头猪、《牛虻》的主编时的腔调——分明得很，我说，这样的温言只可能出自对《牛虻》的偏爱——而《长脚爷叔》分明打算靠牺牲我把《牛虻》捧进名誉里。的确，谁只消半只眼便能看出：倘若《长脚爷叔》的真意当真便是它想要装出的那个样子，它（《长脚爷叔》）尽可以用更直接、更尖利、总之更切题的词句说话。「按字拿钱的雇佣文人」「乞丐」「烧火小厮」「刽子手」，这些字眼那样存心地含糊、模棱，用在这人类笔下写出的最坏的诗节的作者身上，比什么都不如。我们都知道「以微薄的赞美行诛心之实」是什么意思；另一方面，谁又能看不穿《长脚爷叔》的隐秘的用意——以微弱的骂来捧场？

===Original===

What the *Daddy* chose to say of the *Fly*, however, was no business of mine. What it said of myself *was*. After the noble manner in which the *Owl*, the *Toad*, the *Mole*, had expressed themselves in respect to my ability, it was rather too much to be coolly spoken of by a thing like the *Daddy-Long-Legs*, as merely “a gentleman of high genius and a scholar.” Gentleman indeed! I made up my mind at once, either to get a written apology from the *Daddy-Long-Legs*, or to call it out.

Full of this purpose, I looked about me to find a friend whom I could entrust with a message to his *Daddy*ship, and as the editor of the *Lollipop* had given me marked tokens of regard, I at length concluded to seek assistance upon the present occasion.

I have never yet been able to account, in a manner satisfactory to my own understanding, for the *very* peculiar countenance and demeanor with which Mr. Crab listened to me, as I unfolded to him my design. He again went through the scene of the bell-rope and cudgel, and did not omit the duck. At one period I thought he really intended to quack. His fit, nevertheless, finally subsided as before, and he began to act and speak in a rational way. He declined bearing the cartel, however, and in fact, dissuaded me from sending it at all; but was candid enough to admit that the *Daddy-Long-Legs* had been disgracefully in the wrong﻿—more especially in what related to the epithets “gentleman and scholar.”

Towards the end of this interview with Mr. Crab, who really appeared to take a paternal interest in my welfare, he suggested to me that I might turn an honest penny, and, at the same time, advance my reputation, by occasionally playing Thomas Hawk for the *Lollipop*.

I begged Mr. Crab to inform me who was Mr. Thomas Hawk, and how it was expected that I should play him.

Here Mr. Crab again “made great eyes” (as we say in Germany), but at length, recovering himself from a profound attack of astonishment, he assured me that he employed the words “Thomas Hawk” to avoid the colloquialism, Tommy, which was low﻿—but that the true idea was Tommy Hawk﻿—or tomahawk﻿—and that by “playing tomahawk” he referred to scalping, browbeating and otherwise using up the herd of poor-devil authors.

===Chinese===

《长脚爷叔》对《牛虻》拣了什么话讲，原不干我的事。它讲到我自己的，*就*干我的事。《猫头鹰》《蟾蜍》《鼹鼠》都曾以那样高贵的腔调谈论我的才能之后，被一件像《长脚爷叔》这样的东西冷冷地说成不过「一位高天才的绅士、一位学者」，这未免太过分了。绅士，好一个绅士！我立刻拿定主意：要么从《长脚爷叔》讨一封书面道歉，要么约它决斗。

满怀这个目的，我四下张望，要寻一位可以信托他给*长脚爷叔*阁下递信的朋友；《棒棒糖》的主编既已给我显著的青睐的凭证，我终于决定就眼前的场合向他求援。

我至今不能以使我自己的理解满意的方式，说明克拉布先生听我陈述我的设计时的那种*非常*奇特的面目与举止。他又把拉铃的绳和棍子那一幕重演了一遍，那鸭子也没有省去。有一个时期我以为他当真要嘎嘎叫了。然而他的发作终于照老样子平息下去，他开始以一种理性的方式行动与说话。然而他拒绝担任递送战书，实在，还劝我干脆不送；但他坦白到足以承认：《长脚爷叔》错得可耻——尤其在「绅士与学者」那两个称号上错得可耻。

同克拉布先生这次会谈将终时，他当真显出一种父辈般的对我福祉的关怀，他向我提议：我可以偶尔为《棒棒糖》客串一把托马斯·霍克，既挣一个诚实的便士，又同时推进我的声名。

我求克拉布先生见告：托马斯·霍克先生是谁，又怎么能指望我去扮演他。

这里克拉布先生又「睁大了眼睛」（照我们德国人的说法），但终于从一场深沉的惊异的袭击里恢复过来，向我担保：他用「托马斯·霍克」这几个字，为的是避免「汤米」那个口语，那太低贱了——但真意是汤米·霍克——或战斧——而所谓「扮战斧」，他指的是剥头皮，威吓，以及把那一群穷苦的作者用干用尽。

===Original===

I assured my patron that, if this was all, I was perfectly resigned to the task of playing Thomas Hawk. Hereupon Mr. Crab desired me to use up the editor of the *Gad-Fly* forthwith, in the fiercest style within the scope of my ability, and as a specimen of my powers. This I did, upon the spot, in a review of the original “Oil-of-Bob,” occupying thirty-six pages of the *Lollipop*. I found playing Thomas Hawk, indeed, a far less onerous occupation than poetizing; for I went upon *system* altogether, and thus it was easy to do the thing thoroughly and well. My practice was this. I bought auction copies (cheap) of *Lord Brougham’s Speeches*, *Cobbett’s Complete Works*, the *New Slang-Syllabus*, the *Whole Art of Snubbing*, *Prentice’s Billingsgate* (folio edition), and *Lewis G. Clarke on Tongue*. These works I cut up thoroughly with a currycomb, and then, throwing the shreds into a sieve, sifted out carefully all that might be thought decent (a mere trifle); reserving the hard phrases, which I threw into a large tin pepper-castor with longitudinal holes, so that an entire sentence could get through without material injury. The mixture was then ready for use. When called upon to play Thomas Hawk, I anointed a sheet of foolscap with the white of a gander’s egg; then, shredding the thing to be reviewed as I had previously shredded the books﻿—only with more care, so as to get every word separate﻿—I threw the latter shreds in with the former, screwed on the lid of the castor, gave it a shake, and so dusted out the mixture upon the egged foolscap; where it stuck. The effect was beautiful to behold. It was captivating. Indeed, the reviews I brought to pass by this simple expedient have never been approached, and were the wonder of the world. At first, through bashfulness﻿—the result of inexperience﻿—I was a little put out by a certain inconsistency﻿—a certain air of the *bizarre* (as we say in France), worn by the composition as a whole. All the phrases did not *fit* (as we say in the Anglo-Saxon). Many were quite awry. Some, even, were upside-down; and there were none of them which were not, in some measure, injured in regard to effect, by this latter species of accident, when it occurred﻿—with the exception of Mr.

===Chinese===

我向我恩主担保：倘若不过如此，我便完全安心接受扮演托马斯·霍克的任务。于是克拉布先生嘱我立刻把《牛虻》的编辑用尽用绝，用我能力所及的最凶的笔调，作一个我的手段的样本。我当场照办，写了一篇评《牛虻》原版「鲍勃纯真油」的文字，占《棒棒糖》三十六页。我发现扮演托马斯·霍克实在远比写诗轻松；因为我完全依*体系*行事，于是把事情办得彻底而好便容易了。我的做法是这样。我在拍卖行廉价买得*布鲁厄姆勋爵演说集*、*科贝特全集*、*新俚语 syllabus*、*排挤全书*、*普伦蒂斯的伦敦粗话*（对开本）、*刘易斯·G·克拉克论舌头*。我用马梳把这些书梳个彻底，然后，把碎屑倒进一只筛子，细心筛出一切或许可算体面的东西（不过一点点），把硬话留下，倒进一只带纵孔的大锡胡椒罐，叫整句整句能毫发无伤地漏出来。混合物于是备好待用。凡有人来叫我扮托马斯·霍克，我便用一只雄鹅的蛋清把一张大页纸涂满；然后把要评的东西照先前剁书那样剁碎——只是更加小心，以便每个词都分开——把后一种碎屑倒进前一种，拧紧罐盖，一摇，便把混合物抖在蛋清的大页纸上；它便粘住了。那效果美得叫人屏息。它叫人心醉。实在，我用这简单的手段制造出来的批评，从来不曾有人企及，是世上的奇迹。起初，由于羞怯——无经验所致——我有点被某种不一致搅扰——被整体整体构图穿着的那种*古怪*的气派（照我们法国人的说法）搅扰。各短句并不*合身*（照我们盎格鲁撒克逊人的说法）。许多歪得厉害。有的甚至头脚倒置；而它们没有一句不多少被这类意外伤了效果，一旦发生——唯刘易斯·克拉克先生的段落除外，那些段落那样遒劲，浑身上下那样结实，似乎任何极端的姿势都不特别叫它们狼狈，正着倒着都一样快活、一样叫人满意。

===Original===

Lewis Clarke’s paragraphs, which were so vigorous, and altogether stout, that they seemed not particularly disconcerted by any extreme of position, but looked equally happy and satisfactory, whether on their heads, or on their heels.

What became of the editor of the *Gad-Fly*, after the publication of my criticism on his “Oil-of-Bob,” it is somewhat difficult to determine. The most reasonable conclusion is, that he wept himself to death. At all events he disappeared instantaneously from the face of the earth, and no man has seen even the ghost of him since.

This matter having been properly accomplished, and the Furies appeased, I grew at once into high favor with Mr. Crab. He took me into his confidence, gave me a permanent situation as Thomas Hawk of the *Lollipop*, and, as for the present, he could afford me no salary, allowed me to profit, at discretion, by his advice.

“My dear Thingum,” said he to me one day after dinner, “I respect your abilities and love you as a son. You shall be my heir. When I die I will bequeath you the *Lollipop*. In the meantime I will make a man of you﻿—I *will*﻿—provided always that you follow my counsel. The first thing to do is to get rid of the old bore.”

“Boar?” said I inquiringly﻿—“pig, eh?﻿—*aper*? (as we say in Latin)﻿—who?﻿—where?”

“Your father,” said he.

“Precisely,” I replied﻿—“pig.”

“You have your fortune to make, Thingum,” resumed Mr. Crab, “and that governor of yours is a millstone about your neck. We must cut him at once.” [Here I took out my knife.] “We must cut him,” continued Mr. Crab, “decidedly and forever. He won’t do﻿—he *won’t*. Upon second thoughts, you had better kick him, or cane him, or something of that kind.”

“What do you say,” I suggested modestly, “to my kicking him in the first instance, caning him afterwards, and winding up by tweaking his nose?”

Mr. Crab looked at me musingly for some moments, and then answered:

===Chinese===

《牛虻》的主编在我的批评发表之后变成了什么，颇难断定。最合理的结论是：他把自己哭死了。无论如何，他霎时间从地面上消失，从此连他的鬼影也没有人见过。

这件事既已办得妥妥帖帖，复仇女神也安抚停当，我立刻在克拉布先生那里大红大紫。他把心腹事托给我，给了我《棒棒糖》托马斯·霍克的永久职位，至于眼下他供不起薪水，便允许我随意地靠他的指教发财。

「我亲爱的廷根，」一天饭后他对我说，「我敬重你的才能，爱你如子。你将是我的继承人。我死时，我要把《棒棒糖》遗赠给你。与此同时我要把你造就成个人物——我*一定*——始终以你听从我的指点为条件。头一件事是同那个老讨厌鬼一刀两断。」

「公猪？」我探询地说——「猪，是吗？——*公猪*？（照我们拉丁人的说法）——谁？——哪里？」

「你的父亲，」他说。

「正是，」我答——「猪。」

「你的前程要靠你自己去挣，廷根，」克拉布先生接着说，「你那位老爷子是你脖子上的一块磨石。我们必须立刻同他割断。」[这里我掏出刀子。]「我们必须同他割断，」克拉布先生继续说，「断然地，永远地。他不行——他*不行*。再想想，你顶好踢他一顿，或者拿藤条抽他一顿，或者诸如此类的什么。」

「依你看，」我谦逊地建议，「我先踢他，然后拿藤条抽他，最后拧他的鼻子收场，怎么样？」

克拉布先生沉吟着看了我片刻，然后答道：

===Original===

“I think, Mr. Bob, that what you propose would answer sufficiently well﻿—indeed remarkably well﻿—that is to say, as far as it went﻿—but barbers are exceedingly hard to cut, and I think, upon the whole, that, having performed upon Thomas Bob the operations you suggest, it would be advisable to blacken, with your fists, both his eyes, very carefully and thoroughly, to prevent his ever seeing you again in fashionable promenades. After doing this, I really do not perceive that you can do any more. However﻿—it might be just as well to roll him once or twice in the gutter, and then put him in charge of the police. Any time the next morning you can call at the watch-house and swear an assault.”

I was much affected by the kindness of feeling towards me personally, which was evinced in this excellent advice of Mr. Crab, and I did not fail to profit by it forthwith. The result was, that I got rid of the old bore, and began to feel a little independent and gentleman-like. The want of money, however, was, for a few weeks, a source of some discomfort; but at length, by carefully putting to use my two eyes, and observing how matters went just in front of my nose, I perceived how the thing was to be brought about. I say “thing”﻿—be it observed﻿—for they tell me the Latin for it is *rem*. By the way, talking of Latin, can anyone tell me the meaning of *quocunque*﻿—or what is the meaning of *modo*?

===Chinese===

「我看，鲍勃先生，你提议的办法尽够用了——实在出色地够用——就是说，就它所及的范围而言——但理发匠是极难割断的，我想，总的说，你把对托马斯·鲍勃的那些手术做完之后，最好再用你的拳头把他的两只眼睛仔细而彻底地打青，免得他日后在时新的散步场上再看见你。做了这个，我实在看不出你还能做什么了。不过——把他往阴沟里滚一两回，然后把警察叫来交给他，倒也一样不妨。第二天任何时候你可以到拘留所去，起誓告他打人。」

克拉布先生这一极好的忠告里对我个人的那种体恤的情意，深深打动了我，我立刻照单全收。结果是：我甩掉了那个老讨厌鬼，开始觉得有一点独立，有一点绅士气派了。然而有几个星期，缺钱是一层不便的苦楚；但终于，靠细心使用我的两只眼睛，观察我鼻子尖前头事情怎样走动，我看出了这件事怎样才办得成。我说「这件事」——请注意——因为他们告诉我它的拉丁文是*rem*。顺便说一句，提起拉丁文，谁能告诉我*quocunque*是什么意思——或者*modo*是什么意思？

===Original===

My plan was exceedingly simple. I bought, for a song, a sixteenth of the *Snapping-Turtle*:﻿—that was all. The thing was *done*, and I put money in my purse. There were some trivial arrangements afterwards, to be sure; but these formed no portion of the plan. They were a consequence﻿—a result. For example, I bought pen, ink, and paper, and put them into furious activity. Having thus completed a magazine article, I gave it, for appellation, “**Fol Lol**, by the Author of ‘**The Oil-of-Bob**,’ ” and enveloped it to the *Goosetherumfoodle*. That journal, however, having pronounced it “twattle” in the “Monthly Notices to Correspondents,” I reheaded the paper “ ‘Hey-Diddle-Diddle,’ by **Thingum Bob**, Esq., Author of the Ode on ‘The Oil-of-Bob,’ *and* Editor of the *Snapping-Turtle*.” With this amendment, I re-enclosed it to the *Goosetherumfoodle*, and, while I awaited a reply, published daily, in the *Turtle*, six columns of what may be termed philosophical and analytical investigation of the literary merits of the *Goosetherumfoodle*, as well as of the personal character of the editor of the *Goosetherumfoodle*. At the end of a week the *Goosetherumfoodle* discovered that it had, by some odd mistake, “confounded a stupid article, headed ‘Hey-Diddle-Diddle’ and composed by some unknown ignoramus, with a gem of resplendent lustre similarly entitled, the work of Thingum Bob, Esq., the celebrated author of ‘The Oil-of-Bob.’ ” The *Goosetherumfoodle* deeply “regretted this very natural accident,” and promised, moreover, an insertion of the *genuine* “Hey-Diddle-Diddle” in the very next number of the magazine.

===Chinese===

我的计划简单到极点。我贱价买下《咬人龟》的十六分之一：——如此而已。事情*成了*，我荷包里有了钱。当然，随后还有几桩琐碎的布置；但这些不构成计划的一部分。它们是后果——是结果。比方说，我买来笔，墨水，纸，叫它们疯狂地动起来。这样完成了一篇杂志文章之后，我给它取名叫「**乐乐**，『**鲍勃纯真油**』的作者作」，寄给《鹅噜噜福多》。然而那份报纸在「每月致通讯者启事」里把它判作「呓语」，我便把文章改题「『嘀嗒嘀咚』，**廷根·鲍勃**先生作，『鲍勃纯真油』颂歌的作者，*兼*《咬人龟》主编」。改过之后，我重新寄给《鹅噜噜福多》，一面等回信，一面每天在《龟》上登六栏不妨称作哲学的与分析的研究的文字，研究《鹅噜噜福多》的文学功绩，以及《鹅噜噜福多》主编的人身品格。一星期之末，《鹅噜噜福多》发现它出于某种古怪的差错，「把一篇题为『嘀嗒嘀咚』、出自某个无名蠢材之手的愚蠢文章，同一篇题名相类、光彩夺目的明珠混作了一谈，那明珠是『鲍勃纯真油』的名作者廷根·鲍勃先生的大作」。《鹅噜噜福多》深「憾于这桩极自然的意外」，并且许诺：*真正的*「嘀嗒嘀咚」将在杂志的下一期里刊出。

===Original===

The fact is, I *thought*﻿—I *really* thought﻿—I thought at the time﻿—I thought *then*﻿—and have no reason for thinking otherwise *now*﻿—that the *Goosetherumfoodle* *did* make a mistake. With the best intentions in the world, I never knew anything that made as many singular mistakes as the *Goosetherumfoodle*. From that day I took a liking to the *Goosetherumfoodle*, and the result was I soon saw into the very depths of its literary merits, and did not fail to expatiate upon them, in the *Turtle*, whenever a fitting opportunity occurred. And it is to be regarded as a very peculiar coincidence﻿—as one of those positively *remarkable* coincidences which set a man to serious thinking﻿—that just such a total revolution of opinion﻿—just such entire *bouleversement* (as we say in French)﻿—just such thorough topsiturviness (if I may be permitted to employ a rather forcible term of the Choctaws), as happened, pro and con, between myself on the one part, and the *Goosetherumfoodle* on the other, did actually again happen, in a brief period afterwards, and with precisely similar circumstances, in the case of myself and the *Rowdy-Dow*, and in the case of myself and the *Hum-Drum*.

Thus it was that, by a masterstroke of genius, I at length consummated my triumphs by “putting money in my purse,” and thus may be said really and fairly to have commenced that brilliant and eventful career which rendered me illustrious, and which now enables me to say, with Chateaubriand, “I have made history”﻿—“*J’ai fait l’histoire.*”

I have indeed “made history.” From the bright epoch which I now record, my actions﻿—my works﻿—are the property of mankind. They are familiar to the world. It is, then, needless for me to detail how, soaring rapidly, I fell heir to the *Lollipop*﻿—how I merged this journal in the *Hum-Drum*﻿—how again I made purchase of the *Rowdy-Dow*, thus combining the three periodicals﻿—how, lastly, I effected a bargain for the sole remaining rival, and united all the literature of the country in one magnificent magazine, known everywhere as the

*Rowdy-Dow*, *Lollipop*, *Hum-Drum*,

and

*Goosetherumfoodle*.

===Chinese===

实情是，我*以为*——我*当真以为*——我当时以为——我*那时*以为——如今*没有*理由作别种想法——《鹅噜噜福多》*当真*出了一个错。怀着世上最善良的用意，我不知道还有什么东西像《鹅噜噜福多》那样出那么许多奇特的错。从那一天起我喜欢上了《鹅噜噜福多》，结果是：我很快看进它的文学功绩的最深的底，每逢合适的时机便在《龟》上把它们铺陈一番。而这必须被看作一个极特殊的巧合——一种真正*显著*的巧合，叫人认真动起脑筋——恰是这样的意见的全盘翻转，恰是这样整个的*颠倒乾坤*（照我们法国人的说法），恰是这样彻底的天翻地覆（倘若容我用乔克托人的一个相当有力的词），一面是我，另一面是《鹅噜噜福多》，实际地在往后很短的时期里又发生了一遍，带着恰相类似的情形，在我同《闹哄哄》之间，在我同《沉闷刊》之间。

就这样，凭天才的一记妙手，我终于以「荷包里装进了钱」完成了我的凯旋，这样才算当真、才算公平地开始了那辉煌而多事的生涯：它使我名扬四海，如今使我得以同夏多布里昂一起说：「我创造了历史」——「*我创造了历史*。」

我的确「创造了历史」。从我所记的这个光辉的时代起，我的行动——我的作品——便是人类的产业了。它们为世人所熟知。于是无须我细说：我怎样疾飞，继承了《棒棒糖》——怎样把这份报纸并进《沉闷刊》——怎样又买下《闹哄哄》，把三份期刊合在一起——怎样最后同仅存的那一个对手做成买卖，把全国的文学统一在一份宏伟的杂志里，举世知名，叫做

《闹哄哄》《棒棒糖》《沉闷刊》，

与

《鹅噜噜福多》。

===Original===

Yes; I have made history. My fame is universal. It extends to the uttermost ends of the earth. You cannot take up a common newspaper in which you shall not see some allusion to the immortal **Thingum Bob**. It is Mr. Thingum Bob said so, and Mr. Thingum Bob wrote this, and Mr. Thingum Bob did that. But I am meek and expire with an humble heart. After all, what is it?﻿—this indescribable something which men will persist in terming “genius?” I agree with Buffon﻿—with Hogarth﻿—it is but *diligence* after all.

Look at *me*!﻿—how I labored﻿—how I toiled﻿—how I wrote! Ye Gods, did I *not* write? I knew not the word “ease.” By day I adhered to my desk, and at night, a pale student, I consumed the midnight oil. You should have seen me﻿—you *should*. I leaned to the right. I leaned to the left. I sat forward. I sat backward. I sat upon end. I sat *tete baissée* (as they have it in the Kickapoo), bowing my head close to the alabaster page. And, through all, I﻿—*wrote*. Through joy and through sorrow, I﻿—*wrote*. Through hunger and through thirst, I﻿—*wrote*. Through good report and through ill report, I﻿—*wrote*. Through sunshine and through moonshine, I﻿—*wrote. What* I wrote it is unnecessary to say. The *style*!﻿—that was the thing. I caught it from Fatquack﻿—whizz!﻿—fizz!﻿—and I am giving you a specimen of it now.

===Chinese===

对；我创造了历史。我的名声遍宇宙。它伸到地球的最尽头。你拿起一张寻常的报纸，里头不会有哪一张不见不朽的**廷根·鲍勃**的一点踪影。这是廷根·鲍勃先生这样说，廷根·鲍勃先生这样写，廷根·鲍勃先生这样做。可我谦逊，怀着卑微的心咽了气。归根结底，这算什么呢？——这人们坚持要称作「天才」的无从描述的东西？我赞同布丰，赞同荷加斯——归根结底它不过是*勤勉*。

看*我*吧！——我怎样劳作——怎样苦干——怎样写！诸神在上，我难道*没有*写吗？我不知「安逸」这个词。白天我守在书桌边，夜里，一个苍白的学生，我燃着午夜的灯油。你们真该看见我——你们*真该*。我朝右倾。我朝左倾。我朝前坐。我朝后坐。我端坐。我*埋头*坐着（照奇克托人的说法），把头低得贴着那雪花石膏般的纸页。而贯穿这一切，我——*写*。历欢与悲，我——*写*。历饥与渴，我——*写*。历誉与毁，我——*写*。历日与月，我——*写。写的*是什么不必说。*文体*！——那才是关键。我从法特夸克那里学来的——嗖！——嘶！——此刻我正在给你们看它的样品。

## The Purloined Letter / 失窃的信
===Original===

Nil sapientiæ odiosius acumine nimio.

> Seneca

At Paris, just after dark one gusty evening in the autumn of 18﻿—, I was enjoying the twofold luxury of meditation and a meerschaum, in company with my friend C. Auguste Dupin, in his little back library, or book-closet, *au troisième, No. 33, Rue Dunôt, Faubourg St. Germain*. For one hour at least we had maintained a profound silence; while each, to any casual observer, might have seemed intently and exclusively occupied with the curling eddies of smoke that oppressed the atmosphere of the chamber. For myself, however, I was mentally discussing certain topics which had formed matter for conversation between us at an earlier period of the evening; I mean the affair of the Rue Morgue, and the mystery attending the murder of Marie Rogêt. I looked upon it, therefore, as something of a coincidence, when the door of our apartment was thrown open and admitted our old acquaintance, Monsieur G﻿—﻿—, the Prefect of the Parisian police.

We gave him a hearty welcome; for there was nearly half as much of the entertaining as of the contemptible about the man, and we had not seen him for several years. We had been sitting in the dark, and Dupin now arose for the purpose of lighting a lamp, but sat down again, without doing so, upon G.’s saying that he had called to consult us, or rather to ask the opinion of my friend, about some official business which had occasioned a great deal of trouble.

“If it is any point requiring reflection,” observed Dupin, as he forebore to enkindle the wick, “we shall examine it to better purpose in the dark.”

“That is another of your odd notions,” said the Prefect, who had a fashion of calling everything “odd” that was beyond his comprehension, and thus lived amid an absolute legion of “oddities.”

“Very true,” said Dupin, as he supplied his visitor with a pipe, and rolled towards him a comfortable chair.

“And what is the difficulty now?” I asked. “Nothing more in the assassination way, I hope?”

“Oh no; nothing of that nature. The fact is, the business is *very* simple indeed, and I make no doubt that we can manage it sufficiently well ourselves; but then I thought Dupin would like to hear the details of it, because it is so excessively *odd*.”

“Simple and odd,” said Dupin.

===Chinese===

智者最厌过分机巧。

——塞内加（Seneca）

巴黎（Paris），18——年秋天一个刮风的日子，天刚擦黑，我正同我的朋友C·奥古斯特·杜宾（C. Auguste Dupin）一起，享受着冥想与海泡石烟斗的双重奢侈；地点在他小小的后藏书室，或曰书橱间，*三楼，圣日耳曼郊区迪诺街三十三号*。至少有一个钟头，我们保持着深沉的沉默；在随便哪个偶然过路的旁观者眼里，两人各自都像一心一意、别无旁骛，只管盯着满屋逼人的空气里盘旋打转的烟涡。不过就我自己而言，心里讨论着的，是当晚早些时候我们谈过的话题；我是说莫尔格街（Rue Morgue）事件，以及萦绕着玛丽·罗热（Marie Rogêt）被杀之谜的种种。因此，当我们的房门蓦地敞开，放进我们的老相识、巴黎警察总监G——先生时，我把这当作多少算是一种巧合。

我们热诚地接待了他；因为这个人身上可鄙的成分虽有，可观的成分却几乎也有一半，何况我们已有几年不见。我们原本坐在黑暗里，杜宾这时起身要掌灯，但听说G——是为着一件惹出许多麻烦的公事来向我们讨教，或者不如说来征求我朋友的意见，便又坐下了，没有点灯。

「倘若是个要动脑筋的问题，」杜宾说，忍住没去点灯芯，「我们在黑暗里会把它琢磨得更透。」

「这又是你的怪念头之一，」总监说。他有一种习气：凡超出他理解的东西一概唤作「怪」，于是活在一支不折不扣的「怪事」大军之中。

「对得很，」杜宾说，一面把一只烟斗递给客人，又把一把舒服的椅子推到他跟前。

「这会儿的难处又是什么？」我问。「但愿不是又出了暗杀一路的事？」

「哦不；不是那一类的事。实情是，这件公事实在*很*简单，我们自己也满可以办得够好，这一点我毫不怀疑；不过我想，杜宾愿意听听它的细情，因为它实在*太*怪了。」

「又简单，又怪，」杜宾说。

===Original===

“Why, yes; and not exactly that, either. The fact is, we have all been a good deal puzzled because the affair *is* so simple, and yet baffles us altogether.”

“Perhaps it is the very simplicity of the thing which puts you at fault,” said my friend.

“What nonsense you *do* talk!” replied the Prefect, laughing heartily.

“Perhaps the mystery is a little *too* plain,” said Dupin.

“Oh, good heavens! who ever heard of such an idea?”

“A little *too* self-evident.”

“Ha! ha! ha﻿—ha! ha! ha!﻿—ho! ho! ho!” roared our visitor, profoundly amused, “oh, Dupin, you will be the death of me yet!”

“And what, after all, *is* the matter on hand?” I asked.

“Why, I will tell you,” replied the Prefect, as he gave a long, steady and contemplative puff, and settled himself in his chair. “I will tell you in a few words; but, before I begin, let me caution you that this is an affair demanding the greatest secrecy, and that I should most probably lose the position I now hold, were it known that I confided it to anyone.”

“Proceed,” said I.

“Or not,” said Dupin.

“Well, then; I have received personal information, from a very high quarter, that a certain document of the last importance has been purloined from the royal apartments. The individual who purloined it is known; this beyond a doubt; he was seen to take it. It is known, also, that it still remains in his possession.”

“How is this known?” asked Dupin.

“It is clearly inferred,” replied the Prefect, “from the nature of the document, and from the nonappearance of certain results which would at once arise from its passing out of the robber’s possession; that is to say, from his employing it as he must design in the end to employ it.”

“Be a little more explicit,” I said.

“Well, I may venture so far as to say that the paper gives its holder a certain power in a certain quarter where such power is immensely valuable.” The Prefect was fond of the cant of diplomacy.

“Still I do not quite understand,” said Dupin.

“No? Well; the disclosure of the document to a third person, who shall be nameless, would bring in question the honor of a personage of most exalted station; and this fact gives the holder of the document an ascendancy over the illustrious personage whose honor and peace are so jeopardized.”

===Chinese===

「哎，对；可也并不全是这样。实情是，我们全给弄得够糊涂的，因为这桩事情*是*那样简单，却又把我们全然难住。」

「也许恰恰是这桩事情的简单本身，叫你们栽了跟头，」我的朋友说。

「你这话讲得*多么*没道理！」总监答，畅快地大笑。

「也许这桩谜案有点*太*明白了，」杜宾说。

「哦，老天！谁听过这样的想法？」

「有点*太*不言自明了。」

「哈！哈！哈——哈！哈！哈！——呵！呵！呵！」我们的客人吼着，深深被逗乐了，「哦，杜宾，你迟早要把我的命笑掉！」

「那么，眼下手头的事究竟*是*什么？」我问。

「呃，我来告诉你，」总监答，长长地、稳稳地、若有所思地喷了一口烟，在椅子里坐定。「几句话就告诉你；不过，开讲之前，容我叮嘱一句：这是一桩要求极端机密的事，倘若走漏我已把它托付给什么人，我十有八九要丢掉如今的位子。」

「讲吧，」我说。

「不讲也罢，」杜宾说。

「好吧，那么；我从极高的方面得到了第一手的消息：某份头等要紧的文件，已从王室内室里被窃走。窃取它的人，是知道的；这一点千真万确；有人看见他拿了去。同样知道的还有：它至今仍在他的占有之中。」

「这怎么会知道？」杜宾问。

「这明白地是推出来的，」总监答，「从文件的性质，也从某些结果之未见出现——它一旦脱出窃贼的占有，那些结果立刻就会跟着来；就是说，从他把它派上用场——他终究必定要派它用场——这一点上推出来的。」

「说得再明白一点，」我说。

「呃，我不妨冒昧说到这个地步：这纸在某个地方给它持有人一种权柄，而在那个地方，这种权柄价值无穷。」总监爱讲外交行话。

「我还是不大明白，」杜宾说。

「不明白？好吧；把这份文件向第三者——此人无须具名——一泄露，便要叫一位地位极其尊崇的人物的名誉成了问题；这一事实，便叫文件的持有人，对那位名誉与安宁陷于如此危殆的显赫人物，占了上风。」

===Original===

“But this ascendancy,” I interposed, “would depend upon the robber’s knowledge of the loser’s knowledge of the robber. Who would dare﻿—”

“The thief,” said G., “is the Minister D﻿—﻿—, who dares all things, those unbecoming as well as those becoming a man. The method of the theft was not less ingenious than bold. The document in question﻿—a letter, to be frank﻿—had been received by the personage robbed while alone in the royal boudoir. During its perusal she was suddenly interrupted by the entrance of the other exalted personage from whom especially it was her wish to conceal it. After a hurried and vain endeavor to thrust it in a drawer, she was forced to place it, open as it was, upon a table. The address, however, was uppermost, and, the contents thus unexposed, the letter escaped notice. At this juncture enters the Minister D﻿—﻿—. His lynx eye immediately perceives the paper, recognises the handwriting of the address, observes the confusion of the personage addressed, and fathoms her secret. After some business transactions, hurried through in his ordinary manner, he produces a letter somewhat similar to the one in question, opens it, pretends to read it, and then places it in close juxtaposition to the other. Again he converses, for some fifteen minutes, upon the public affairs. At length, in taking leave, he takes also from the table the letter to which he had no claim. Its rightful owner saw, but, of course, dared not call attention to the act, in the presence of the third personage who stood at her elbow. The minister decamped; leaving his own letter﻿—one of no importance﻿—upon the table.”

“Here, then,” said Dupin to me, “you have precisely what you demand to make the ascendancy complete﻿—the robber’s knowledge of the loser’s knowledge of the robber.”

“Yes,” replied the Prefect; “and the power thus attained has, for some months past, been wielded, for political purposes, to a very dangerous extent. The personage robbed is more thoroughly convinced, every day, of the necessity of reclaiming her letter. But this, of course, cannot be done openly. In fine, driven to despair, she has committed the matter to me.”

“Than whom,” said Dupin, amid a perfect whirlwind of smoke, “no more sagacious agent could, I suppose, be desired, or even imagined.”

===Chinese===

「可是这种上风，」我插话，「要看窃贼知道失主知道窃贼而定。谁敢——」

「那贼，」G——说，「就是D——部长，一个什么都敢做的人，男人做得的、做不得的，他都敢做。行窃的手法，胆大之外，机巧也不在胆大之下。那份文件——说白了，是一封信——是失窃的那位大人物独在王室闺阁里时收到的。她正读到一半，忽然被另一位尊贵人物的进来打断，而她偏偏最想把信瞒住的正是这位。她匆匆忙忙想把它塞进抽屉，白费了力气，只得把摊开着的信放在一张桌上。好在信封的地址面朝上，内容便没有露出，那封信才逃过了注意。正在这时，D——部长进来了。他那双山猫似的眼睛立刻看出那张纸，认出地址上的笔迹，看出收信人的慌乱，看透她的秘密。他照他素常的样子匆匆办了几桩公务的交割，随后拿出一封信来，同那封要紧的信有点相像，拆开，装作读它，然后把它紧挨着另一封摆下。他又谈了大约一刻钟的公务。到告辞的时候，他也顺手从桌上拿走了那封他无权染指的信。信的合法主人看见了，但自然不敢唤起对这一举动的注意，因为第三位大人物正站在她身边。部长溜之大吉；把他自己那封信——一封无关紧要的信——留在桌上。」

「那么，」杜宾对我说，「这里你恰恰有了你要的、使这种上风十足完备的东西——窃贼知道失主知道窃贼。」

「对，」总监答；「这样得来的权柄，近几个月来，为着政治的目的，已被运用到极危险的地步。失窃的那位大人物一天比一天更深地确信，必须收回她的信。可这当然不能公开做。末了，逼到绝望的地步，她把这事托给了我。」

「据我看，」杜宾说，全身裹在一阵烟的旋风里，「再想不出、甚至再想象不出比这位大人更精明的经办人了。」

===Original===

“You flatter me,” replied the Prefect; “but it is possible that some such opinion may have been entertained.”

“It is clear,” said I, “as you observe, that the letter is still in possession of the minister; since it is this possession, and not any employment of the letter, which bestows the power. With the employment the power departs.”

“True,” said G.; “and upon this conviction I proceeded. My first care was to make thorough search of the minister’s hotel; and here my chief embarrassment lay in the necessity of searching without his knowledge. Beyond all things, I have been warned of the danger which would result from giving him reason to suspect our design.”

“But,” said I, “you are quite au fait in these investigations. The Parisian police have done this thing often before.”

“Oh, yes; and for this reason I did not despair. The habits of the minister gave me, too, a great advantage. He is frequently absent from home all night. His servants are by no means numerous. They sleep at a distance from their master’s apartment, and, being chiefly Neapolitans, are readily made drunk. I have keys, as you know, with which I can open any chamber or cabinet in Paris. For three months a night has not passed, during the greater part of which I have not been engaged, personally, in ransacking the D﻿—﻿— Hotel. My honor is interested, and, to mention a great secret, the reward is enormous. So I did not abandon the search until I had become fully satisfied that the thief is a more astute man than myself. I fancy that I have investigated every nook and corner of the premises in which it is possible that the paper can be concealed.”

“But is it not possible,” I suggested, “that although the letter may be in possession of the minister, as it unquestionably is, he may have concealed it elsewhere than upon his own premises?”

“This is barely possible,” said Dupin. “The present peculiar condition of affairs at court, and especially of those intrigues in which D﻿—﻿— is known to be involved, would render the instant availability of the document﻿—its susceptibility of being produced at a moment’s notice﻿—a point of nearly equal importance with its possession.”

“Its susceptibility of being produced?” said I.

“That is to say, of being destroyed,” said Dupin.

===Chinese===

「你这是恭维我，」总监答；「不过也许人家心里真存过几分这样的看法。」

「清楚的是，」我说，「如你所见，信还在部长手里；因为正是这一种占有——而不是对信的任何运用——授予了权柄。运用一起，权柄就去了。」

「正是，」G——说；「我就凭这个信念着手。我的第一件要务，是把部长的府邸彻底搜一遍；而这里我最大的难处，在于必须背着主人搜。我预先得到的告诫，头一件事就是：让他有理由怀疑我们的企图，会造成何等的危险。」

「可是，」我说，「这类侦查你们的门道熟得很。巴黎警察从前办过多少回。」

「哦，是的；就为这个我不曾绝望。部长的习惯也给了我一个大便利。他常常整夜不在家。他的仆役并不算多。他们睡的地方离主人的居室远，又大半是那不勒斯人，灌醉不难。我有钥匙，你知道，巴黎随便哪间屋子哪口柜子都开得开。三个月来，没有一个夜晚的大部分时间，我不亲自在翻检D——府邸。我的名誉系于此，而且，说句天大的机密，赏格又大得惊人。所以我并不放弃搜查，直到我十足满意为止：那贼是个比我精明的人。我想，那宅子里每一处可能藏得下这张纸的旮旯角落，我都查过了。」

「可是有没有可能，」我提出来，「信虽然在部长手里——这是确凿无疑的——他却把它藏在自家宅子以外的地方？」

「这可能性极小，」杜宾说。「宫廷时下特殊的局面，尤其是D——人所共知卷在内的那些阴谋，会使这份文件的须臾可得——一唤即可取出——成为几乎同占有它一样要紧的一点。」

「须臾可得？」我说。

「就是说，随时可以毁掉，」杜宾说。

===Original===

“True,” I observed; “the paper is clearly then upon the premises. As for its being upon the person of the minister, we may consider that as out of the question.”

“Entirely,” said the Prefect. “He has been twice waylaid, as if by footpads, and his person rigorously searched under my own inspection.”

“You might have spared yourself this trouble,” said Dupin. “D﻿—﻿—, I presume, is not altogether a fool, and, if not, must have anticipated these waylayings, as a matter of course.”

“Not *altogether* a fool,” said G., “but then he’s a poet, which I take to be only one remove from a fool.”

“True,” said Dupin, after a long and thoughtful whiff from his meerschaum, “although I have been guilty of certain doggrel myself.”

“Suppose you detail,” said I, “the particulars of your search.”

“Why the fact is, we took our time, and we searched *everywhere*. I have had long experience in these affairs. I took the entire building, room by room; devoting the nights of a whole week to each. We examined, first, the furniture of each apartment. We opened every possible drawer; and I presume you know that, to a properly trained police agent, such a thing as a secret drawer is impossible. Any man is a dolt who permits a ‘*secret*’ drawer to escape him in a search of this kind. The thing is *so* plain. There is a certain amount of bulk﻿—of space﻿—to be accounted for in every cabinet. Then we have accurate rules. The fiftieth part of a line could not escape us. After the cabinets we took the chairs. The cushions we probed with the fine long needles you have seen me employ. From the tables we removed the tops.”

“Why so?”

“Sometimes the top of a table, or other similarly arranged piece of furniture, is removed by the person wishing to conceal an article; then the leg is excavated, the article deposited within the cavity, and the top replaced. The bottoms and tops of bedposts are employed in the same way.”

“But could not the cavity be detected by sounding?” I asked.

“By no means, if, when the article is deposited, a sufficient wadding of cotton be placed around it. Besides, in our case, we were obliged to proceed without noise.”

===Chinese===

「不错，」我说；「这么说来，纸分明就在宅子里。至于它贴在部长身上，那可以认为根本不在话下。」

「全然不在话下，」总监说。「他两次被人半路拦劫，像是路劫的强盗干的，我亲自监看之下，把他本人从里到外搜了个严实。」

「这一番麻烦你原可以省掉，」杜宾说。「D——，我想，总不是个十足的傻瓜；既然不是，这些拦劫他自然早就料到。」

「*不是十足*的傻瓜，」G——说，「可他是个诗人，依我看，这离傻瓜不过隔着一层。」

「不错，」杜宾说，从海泡石烟斗里长长地、沉思地吸了一口，「虽然我自己也犯过写打油诗的罪。」

「你且说说，」我说，「你搜查的详情。」

「呃，实情是，我们不慌不忙，*处处*都搜了。这类事情我经验久得很。整座宅子我一间一间地来；每间屋子整整花上一个星期的夜晚。我们先查每间屋子的家具。凡是抽屉，我们一只不剩全打开；我想你知道，对一个训练有素的警探来说，什么暗屉是绝不可能的事。谁要是让一个「*暗*屉在这类搜查里逃过手去，谁就是蠢货。事情*太*明白了。每口柜子里总有一定数量的体积——空间——要交代得清。再说我们有一套精确的规程。一线的五十分之一也逃不过我们。柜子查完，接着查椅子。坐垫用你见我使过的那种细长针探过。桌面统统卸了下来。」

「为什么卸？」

「有时人想把一件东西藏起来，便卸掉桌面，或是别的同类构造的家具；把桌腿掏空，东西放进空腔，再把桌面装回去。床柱的底和顶也照这个法子用。」

「可是那空腔敲一敲不就听出来了？」我问。

「决计听不出，只要放东西进去的时候，拿足够的棉花垫衬在四围。再说，我们那几回，是不得不悄悄进行的。」

===Original===

“But you could not have removed﻿—you could not have taken to pieces *all* articles of furniture in which it would have been possible to make a deposit in the manner you mention. A letter may be compressed into a thin spiral roll, not differing much in shape or bulk from a large knitting-needle, and in this form it might be inserted into the rung of a chair, for example. You did not take to pieces all the chairs?”

“Certainly not; but we did better﻿—we examined the rungs of every chair in the hotel, and, indeed the jointings of every description of furniture, by the aid of a most powerful microscope. Had there been any traces of recent disturbance we should not have failed to detect it instantly. A single grain of gimlet-dust, for example, would have been as obvious as an apple. Any disorder in the glueing﻿—any unusual gaping in the joints﻿—would have sufficed to insure detection.”

“I presume you looked to the mirrors, between the boards and the plates, and you probed the beds and the bedclothes, as well as the curtains and carpets.”

“That of course; and when we had absolutely completed every particle of the furniture in this way, then we examined the house itself. We divided its entire surface into compartments, which we numbered, so that none might be missed; then we scrutinized each individual square inch throughout the premises, including the two houses immediately adjoining, with the microscope, as before.”

“The two houses adjoining!” I exclaimed; “you must have had a great deal of trouble.”

“We had; but the reward offered is prodigious!”

“You include the *grounds* about the houses?”

“All the grounds are paved with brick. They gave us comparatively little trouble. We examined the moss between the bricks, and found it undisturbed.”

“You looked among D﻿—﻿—’s papers, of course, and into the books of the library?”

===Chinese===

「可是你不可能卸——不可能把*所有*可能照你说的法子藏进东西的家具统统拆开。一封信可以压成一卷细长的螺旋卷，样子和体积同一条粗毛线针相差无几；这么着，比方说，就可以插进椅子的一根横档里去。你没有把所有的椅子都拆开吧？」

「当然没有；可是我们干得更好——凭一架极有威力的显微镜，我们把宅子里每一把椅子的横档都验看过了，实在说，每一种家具的接榫也都验看过了。只要有一丝近期动过的痕迹，我们当场就会查觉，绝无失误。比方一粒钻锥的木屑，也会显眼得像一只苹果。胶合上有一点乱——接榫上有一点不合常的裂缝——就足以保证查出来。」

「我想，镜子你查过，木板与镜面之间；床、被褥、帘幕和地毯你也探过。」

「那自然；等我们用这个法子把家具的每一星末屑都十足查完，我们就查房子本身。我们把它的整个表面分成一格一格，编上号，免得漏掉一格；然后把宅子内外每一平方寸，连同紧邻的两座房子，都照方才那样用显微镜细察了一遍。」

「连紧邻的两座房子！」我叫起来；「你的麻烦一定小不了。」

「小不了；可悬赏是大得惊人的！」

「房子四周的*场地*也在内？」

「场地全铺着砖。相对说来给我们添的麻烦少。砖缝里的苔藓我们验过，没有动过的痕迹。」

「D——的文件你当然查过，藏书的书也查过？」

===Original===

“Certainly; we opened every package and parcel; we not only opened every book, but we turned over every leaf in each volume, not contenting ourselves with a mere shake, according to the fashion of some of our police officers. We also measured the thickness of every book-cover, with the most accurate admeasurement, and applied to each the most jealous scrutiny of the microscope. Had any of the bindings been recently meddled with, it would have been utterly impossible that the fact should have escaped observation. Some five or six volumes, just from the hands of the binder, we carefully probed, longitudinally, with the needles.”

“You explored the floors beneath the carpets?”

“Beyond doubt. We removed every carpet, and examined the boards with the microscope.”

“And the paper on the walls?”

“Yes.”

“You looked into the cellars?”

“We did.”

“Then,” I said, “you have been making a miscalculation, and the letter is *not* upon the premises, as you suppose.”

“I fear you are right there,” said the Prefect. “And now, Dupin, what would you advise me to do?”

“To make a thorough research of the premises.”

“That is absolutely needless,” replied G﻿—﻿—. “I am not more sure that I breathe than I am that the letter is not at the Hotel.”

“I have no better advice to give you,” said Dupin. “You have, of course, an accurate description of the letter?”

“Oh yes!”﻿—And here the Prefect, producing a memorandum-book, proceeded to read aloud a minute account of the internal, and especially of the external appearance of the missing document. Soon after finishing the perusal of this description, he took his departure, more entirely depressed in spirits than I had ever known the good gentleman before.
