## The Imp of the Perverse / 乖戾之魔
===Original===

In the consideration of the faculties and impulses﻿—of the *prima mobilia* of the human soul, the phrenologists have failed to make room for a propensity which, although obviously existing as a radical, primitive, irreducible sentiment, has been equally overlooked by all the moralists who have preceded them. In the pure arrogance of the reason, we have all overlooked it. We have suffered its existence to escape our senses, solely through want of belief﻿—of faith;﻿—whether it be faith in Revelation, or faith in the Kabbala. The idea of it has never occurred to us, simply because of its supererogation. We saw no need of the impulse﻿—for the propensity. We could not perceive its necessity. We could not understand, that is to say, we could not have understood, had the notion of this *primum mobile* ever obtruded itself;﻿—we could not have understood in what manner it might be made to further the objects of humanity, either temporal or eternal. It cannot be denied that phrenology and, in great measure, all metaphysicianism have been concocted *a priori*. The intellectual or logical man, rather than the understanding or observant man, set himself to imagine designs﻿—to dictate purposes to God. Having thus fathomed, to his satisfaction, the intentions of Jehovah, out of these intentions he built his innumerable systems of mind. In the matter of phrenology, for example, we first determined, naturally enough, that it was the design of the Deity that man should eat. We then assigned to man an organ of alimentiveness, and this organ is the scourge with which the Deity compels man, will-I nill-I, into eating. Secondly, having settled it to be God’s will that man should continue his species, we discovered an organ of amativeness, forthwith. And so with combativeness, with ideality, with causality, with constructiveness﻿—so, in short, with every organ, whether representing a propensity, a moral sentiment, or a faculty of the pure intellect. And in these arrangements of the principia of human action, the Spurzheimites, whether right or wrong, in part, or upon the whole, have but followed, in principle, the footsteps of their predecessors; deducing and establishing everything from the preconceived destiny of man, and upon the ground of the objects of his Creator.

===Chinese===

在考察诸官能与诸冲动——人类灵魂的*原始动力*（prima mobilia）——的时候，颅相学家们没有为一种癖性留出位置；这种癖性虽然显然作为一种根本的、原初的、不可还原的情感而存在，也同样被他们之前的所有道德学家所忽略。在纯粹理性的傲慢里，我们大家都把它忽略了。我们任它的存在逃过我们的感官，仅仅由于缺乏信仰——缺乏信；——无论是对启示的信，还是对喀巴拉的信。它的观念从不曾临到我们，仅仅因为它纯属多余。我们看不出需要这冲动——需要这癖性。我们看不出它的必要。我们不能理解——就是说，倘若这个*原初动力*（primum mobile）的观念曾经硬挤进来，我们也不能理解——我们不能理解它可以怎样用来推进人类的目的，无论尘世的还是永恒的。不可否认，颅相学，以及在极大程度上，一切形而上学，都是*先验地*（a priori）编造出来的。是理智的、逻辑的人，而不是理解的、观察的人，自己动手去想象设计——去对上帝口授目的。就这样把自己满意的耶和华的意图探明之后，他从这些意图里建造了他那数不清的心灵体系。比方说，在颅相学的事情上，我们自然先断定：神的用意是要人吃。于是我们给人派了一个饮食欲的器官，这器官便是神用来强迫人吃饭的鞭子，愿也罢不愿也罢。其次，既已断定上帝的旨意是要人延续他的种，我们随即又发现了一个情爱的器官。好斗的器官、理想的器官、因果的器官、构造的器官，也都如此——总之，每一个器官都如此，无论它代表一种癖性、一种道德情感，还是纯粹智性的官能。而在人类行动原理的这些安排里，施普尔茨海姆派（Spurzheimites），无论对错，是部分还是全体，在原则上不过踏着他们前人的足迹；从人预先注定的命运、从他造物主的目的出发，推出并确立一切。

===Original===

It would have been wiser, it would have been safer, to classify (if classify we must) upon the basis of what man usually or occasionally did, and was always occasionally doing, rather than upon the basis of what we took it for granted the Deity intended him to do. If we cannot comprehend God in his visible works, how then in his inconceivable thoughts, that call the works into being? If we cannot understand him in his objective creatures, how then in his substantive moods and phases of creation?

Induction, *a posteriori*, would have brought phrenology to admit, as an innate and primitive principle of human action, a paradoxical something, which we may call *perverseness*, for want of a more characteristic term. In the sense I intend, it is, in fact, a *mobile* without motive, a motive not *motivirt*. Through its promptings we act without comprehensible object; or, if this shall be understood as a contradiction in terms, we may so far modify the proposition as to say, that through its promptings we act, for the reason that we should *not*. In theory, no reason can be more unreasonable, but, in fact, there is none more strong. With certain minds, under certain conditions, it becomes absolutely irresistible. I am not more certain that I breathe, than that the assurance of the wrong or error of any action is often the one unconquerable *force* which impels us, and alone impels us to its prosecution. Nor will this overwhelming tendency to do wrong for the wrong’s sake, admit of analysis, or resolution into ulterior elements. It is a radical, a primitive impulse﻿—elementary. It will be said, I am aware, that when we persist in acts because we feel we should *not* persist in them, our conduct is but a modification of that which ordinarily springs from the *combativeness* of phrenology. But a glance will show the fallacy of this idea. The phrenological combativeness has for its essence, the necessity of self-defence. It is our safeguard against injury. Its principle regards our well-being; and thus the desire to be well is excited simultaneously with its development. It follows, that the desire to be well must be excited simultaneously with any principle which shall be merely a modification of combativeness, but in the case of that something which I term *perverseness*, the desire to be well is not only not aroused, but a strongly antagonistical sentiment exists.

===Chinese===

假如分类（倘若我们必须分类）以人通常或偶尔做了什么、并且始终偶尔在做着什么为根据，而不以我们想当然认作神要他做什么为根据，那会更聪明，也更稳妥。倘若我们无法在神可见的作为里理解他，又怎能在他那唤出这些作为的不可思议的思想里理解他？倘若我们无法在他客观的造物里理解他，又怎能在他创造的主导的情绪与阶段里理解他？

归纳，*后验地*（a posteriori），原会把颅相学引到承认一种自相矛盾的什么，作为人类行动先天的、原初的原则；我们可以把它唤作*乖戾*（perverseness），因为找不到更有特色的字眼。照我打算的意思，它实在是一种没有动机的动力，一个不曾*被动机化*（motivirt）的动机。在它的怂恿下，我们行动，没有可解的对象；或者，倘若这会被当作词语里的矛盾，我们不妨把这个命题这样修改一下说：在它的怂恿下，我们行动，正因为按理我们*不该*行动。理论上，没有比这更不合理的理由；可事实上，没有比这更强的理由。在一定的头脑里，在一定的情况下，它变得绝对不可抗拒。我呼吸的把握有多大，这一点就有多大：任何行为的错或不对的确证，往往正是那唯一不可征服的*力*，催逼我们、也唯独它催逼我们，去把那行为做到底。而这种为错而错的压倒一切的倾向，也不容分析，不容分解成更后面的元素。它是一个根本的、原初的冲动——初元的。我知道，有人会说：当我们坚持去做，恰恰因为觉得我们*不该*坚持去做，我们的行为不过是颅相学所谓*好斗性*寻常来源的一种变形罢了。可是看一眼就会显出这观念的谬误。颅相学的好斗性，本质在自卫的必要。它是我们抵挡伤害的保障。它的原则关切我们的康健；于是求康健的欲望同它的发展一同被唤起。既然如此，任何一个仅仅是好斗性之变形的原则，也必同时唤起求康健的欲望；可是在我称作*乖戾*的那个什么身上，求康健的欲望不但不兴起，反而存在一种强烈对抗的情绪。

===Original===

An appeal to one’s own heart is, after all, the best reply to the sophistry just noticed. No one who trustingly consults and thoroughly questions his own soul, will be disposed to deny the entire radicalness of the propensity in question. It is not more incomprehensible than distinctive. There lives no man who at some period has not been tormented, for example, by an earnest desire to tantalize a listener by circumlocution. The speaker is aware that he displeases; he has every intention to please; he is usually curt, precise, and clear; the most laconic and luminous language is struggling for utterance upon his tongue; it is only with difficulty that he restrains himself from giving it flow; he dreads and deprecates the anger of him whom he addresses; yet, the thought strikes him, that by certain involutions and parentheses this anger may be engendered. That single thought is enough. The impulse increases to a wish, the wish to a desire, the desire to an uncontrollable longing, and the longing (to the deep regret and mortification of the speaker, and in defiance of all consequences) is indulged.

===Chinese===

向自己的心讨教，终究是对方才那种诡辩的最好回答。谁若信实地省察、彻底地拷问自己的灵魂，谁就不至于否认所说癖性十足的根本性。它并不比它的独特更难懂。没有哪个人，在某一个时期，不曾被一种恳切的欲望折磨过，比方说，想用绕弯子的话去撩拨一个听众。说话的人知道他讨人嫌；他满心要讨人好；他通常简短、精确、清楚；最简洁而明亮的语言正在他舌尖上挣着要出口；他勉强自己，才拦住它不流出来；他畏惧他面对的人的恼怒，也恳求那恼怒别来；可是，一个念头击中他：借着某种迂回与插语，这恼怒是生得出来的。那一个念头就够了。冲动涨成心愿，心愿涨成欲望，欲望涨成不可控制的渴念，而那渴念（说话的人深深懊悔、深深屈辱，也不顾一切后果）纵容了。

===Original===

We have a task before us which must be speedily performed. We know that it will be ruinous to make delay. The most important crisis of our life calls, trumpet-tongued, for immediate energy and action. We glow, we are consumed with eagerness to commence the work, with the anticipation of whose glorious result our whole souls are on fire. It must, it shall be undertaken today, and yet we put it off until tomorrow; and why? There is no answer, except that we feel *perverse*, using the word with no comprehension of the principle. Tomorrow arrives, and with it a more impatient anxiety to do our duty, but with this very increase of anxiety arrives, also, a nameless, a positively fearful, because unfathomable, craving for delay. This craving gathers strength as the moments fly. The last hour for action is at hand. We tremble with the violence of the conflict within us﻿—of the definite with the indefinite﻿—of the substance with the shadow. But, if the contest have proceeded thus far, it is the shadow which prevails﻿—we struggle in vain. The clock strikes, and is the knell of our welfare. At the same time, it is the chanticleer-note to the ghost that has so long overawed us. It flies﻿—it disappears﻿—we are free. The old energy returns. We will labor *now*. Alas, it is *too late*!

===Chinese===

我们面前摆着一件事，必须赶紧办。我们知道，拖延会招致毁灭。我们一生最重要的关头，喇叭似的大声喊着，要即刻的精力与行动。我们燃烧，我们给急切的焦灼烧尽，要动手做那件工作；预想着它辉煌的结果，我们整个灵魂都在火里。它必须、它应当今天就着手，然而我们把它推到明天；为什么？没有回答，除了我们觉得*乖戾*，用这个词时全然不懂它的原则。明天来了，随着它来的是更急迫的焦虑，要尽我们的本分；可是随着这焦虑的增长，一同来的，还有一种无名的、实实在在可怖的——因为深不可测——渴求拖延的欲念。这欲念随着时刻飞逝聚起力气。行动的最后时刻到了。我们由于内心冲突的激烈而发抖——有定者的冲突与无定者——实体与影子的冲突。可是，倘若争斗已进行到这里，占胜的是影子——我们徒然挣扎。钟敲了，那是我们福祉的丧钟。同时，那又是给久久威慑着我们的那个幽灵听的雄鸡之鸣。它飞了——它消失了——我们自由了。旧日的精力回来了。我们要*现在*干活了。唉，已经*太迟*了！

===Original===

We stand upon the brink of a precipice. We peer into the abyss﻿—we grow sick and dizzy. Our first impulse is to shrink from the danger. Unaccountably we remain. By slow degrees our sickness and dizziness and horror become merged in a cloud of unnamable feeling. By gradations, still more imperceptible, this cloud assumes shape, as did the vapor from the bottle out of which arose the genius in the Arabian Nights. But out of this *our* cloud upon the precipice’s edge, there grows into palpability, a shape, far more terrible than any genius or any demon of a tale, and yet it is but a thought, although a fearful one, and one which chills the very marrow of our bones with the fierceness of the delight of its horror. It is merely the idea of what would be our sensations during the sweeping precipitancy of a fall from such a height. And this fall﻿—this rushing annihilation﻿—for the very reason that it involves that one most ghastly and loathsome of all the most ghastly and loathsome images of death and suffering which have ever presented themselves to our imagination﻿—for this very cause do we now the most vividly desire it. And because our reason violently deters us from the brink, *therefore* do we the most impetuously approach it. There is no passion in nature so demoniacally impatient, as that of him who, shuddering upon the edge of a precipice, thus meditates a plunge. To indulge, for a moment, in any attempt at *thought*, is to be inevitably lost; for reflection but urges us to forbear, and *therefore* it is, I say, that we *cannot*. If there be no friendly arm to check us, or if we fail in a sudden effort to prostrate ourselves backward from the abyss, we plunge, and are destroyed.

Examine these similar actions as we will, we shall find them resulting solely from the spirit of the *Perverse*. We perpetrate them because we feel that we should *not*. Beyond or behind this there is no intelligible principle; and we might, indeed, deem this perverseness a direct instigation of the Archfiend, were it not occasionally known to operate in furtherance of good.

===Chinese===

我们站在悬崖的边上。我们朝深渊里窥——我们变得恶心、眩晕。我们的第一个冲动是避开危险。莫名其妙地，我们留在原地。一寸一寸地，我们的恶心、眩晕和恐怖融进一团无名的感觉之云。一步一步，更难觉察地，这云显出形状，正如《一千零一夜》里从瓶中升起巨灵的那道烟气。可是，就在这团*我们*在悬崖边上的云里，长成一个可以触知的形状，比任何故事里的巨灵或恶魔都可怕得多的形状；然而它不过是一个念头，虽然是一个可怖的念头，一个用它那恐怖之欣喜的猛烈，把我们骨髓都冻僵的念头。那不过是这样一个念头：从这样的高度跌落下去，在那直坠的急势里，我们的感觉会是什么。而这一跌——这奔涌的毁灭——恰恰因为它牵涉那幅死亡与苦难的一切最狰狞、最可憎的意象中最狰狞、最可憎的一幅——恰恰为这个缘故，我们此刻最鲜明地渴望它。又因为我们的理智猛烈地拦我们离开崖边，*所以*我们最急不可耐地凑近它。天性里没有一种激情，比这更恶魔似地按捺不住：人在悬崖边上发着抖，这样筹划一跃。哪怕片刻纵容自己去*思想*，也必然全完；因为反省只会催我们止步，而我说的正是：*所以*我们*不能*止步。倘若没有一只友善的手臂拦住我们，或者倘若我们猛然向后仰倒、逃出深渊的努力落了空，我们便跳下去，毁灭了。

我们随我们高兴细察这些相似的行为吧，我们会发现它们单单出自*乖戾*（Perverse）之灵。我们干出它们，因为觉得我们*不该*。在这之外或背后，没有可解的原则；而我们确实不妨把这种乖戾认作大恶魔的直接唆使，倘若它不曾偶尔被知会在行善里起作用。

===Original===

I have said thus much, that in some measure I may answer your question﻿—that I may explain to you why I am here﻿—that I may assign to you something that shall have at least the faint aspect of a cause for my wearing these fetters, and for my tenanting this cell of the condemned. Had I not been thus prolix, you might either have misunderstood me altogether, or, with the rabble, have fancied me mad. As it is, you will easily perceive that I am one of the many uncounted victims of the Imp of the Perverse.

It is impossible that any deed could have been wrought with a more thorough deliberation. For weeks, for months, I pondered upon the means of the murder. I rejected a thousand schemes, because their accomplishment involved a *chance* of detection. At length, in reading some French memoirs, I found an account of a nearly fatal illness that occurred to Madame Pilau, through the agency of a candle accidentally poisoned. The idea struck my fancy at once. I knew my victim’s habit of reading in bed. I knew, too, that his apartment was narrow and ill-ventilated. But I need not vex you with impertinent details. I need not describe the easy artifices by which I substituted, in his bedroom candle-stand, a wax-light of my own making for the one which I there found. The next morning he was discovered dead in his bed, and the coroner’s verdict was﻿—“Death by the visitation of God.”

===Chinese===

我讲这许多，是要在几分之内答覆你的问题——向你解释我为什么在这里——给你指派一点东西，至少勉强像一个原因的影子：为我戴着这副镣铐、住着这间死囚的牢房。我若不是这样冗长，你也许全然误解我，或者，同那群氓一道，把我当作疯子。如今这样，你便容易看出：我是乖戾之魔（the Imp of the Perverse）许多不曾入册的牺牲者中间的一个。

任何行为都不可能以更彻底的深思熟虑做成。几个星期，几个月，我琢磨着那桩凶杀的手段。我驳回了一千个方案，因为它们的成就牵涉到被发觉的*机会*。终于，在读到几部法国回忆录时，我看见一篇记载，说的是皮洛夫人（Madame Pilau）一场几乎致命的病，起于一支偶然下了毒的蜡烛。这主意立刻击中我的兴味。我知道我的牺牲者有就着床头读书的习惯。我也知道他的屋子狭窄，通风不好。可是我不必拿不得体的细节来搅扰你。我不必描述那些轻巧的手段，凭它们我把卧房烛台上我找到的那一支，换成了我自己制造的一支。第二天早上，他被发现死在床上；验尸官的判词是——「死于天谴。」

===Original===

Having inherited his estate, all went well with me for years. The idea of detection never once entered my brain. Of the remains of the fatal taper I had myself carefully disposed. I had left no shadow of a clue by which it would be possible to convict, or even to suspect me of the crime. It is inconceivable how rich a sentiment of satisfaction arose in my bosom as I reflected upon my absolute security. For a very long period of time I was accustomed to revel in this sentiment. It afforded me more real delight than all the mere worldly advantages accruing from my sin. But there arrived at length an epoch, from which the pleasurable feeling grew, by scarcely perceptible gradations, into a haunting and harassing thought. It harassed because it haunted. I could scarcely get rid of it for an instant. It is quite a common thing to be thus annoyed with the ringing in our ears, or rather in our memories, of the burden of some ordinary song, or some unimpressive snatches from an opera. Nor will we be the less tormented if the song in itself be good, or the opera air meritorious. In this manner, at last, I would perpetually catch myself pondering upon my security, and repeating, in a low undertone, the phrase, “I am safe.”

One day, whilst sauntering along the streets, I arrested myself in the act of murmuring, half aloud, these customary syllables. In a fit of petulance, I remodelled them thus: “I am safe﻿—I am safe﻿—yes﻿—if I be not fool enough to make open confession!”

No sooner had I spoken these words, than I felt an icy chill creep to my heart. I had had some experience in these fits of perversity (whose nature I have been at some trouble to explain), and I remembered well that in no instance I had successfully resisted their attacks. And now my own casual self-suggestion that I might possibly be fool enough to confess the murder of which I had been guilty, confronted me, as if the very ghost of him whom I had murdered﻿—and beckoned me on to death.

===Chinese===

继承了他的产业之后，多年我诸事顺遂。被发觉的念头一次也不曾进过我的脑子。那截致命蜡烛的残余，我亲手小心处理掉了。我没有留下一丝线索的影子，凭它可以定罪，或哪怕疑心我犯这罪。我想到我的绝对安全时，胸中涌起一种满足之情，富得难以想象。很长一段时期，我惯于在这种情绪里狂欢。它给我的实在的快意，比我的罪从尘世上带来的种种便宜加在一起还多。可是终于到了一个时候，那快活的感受，凭着几乎觉察不到的阶梯，长成一个萦回不去、搅扰不休的念头。它搅扰，因为它萦回。我几乎一时一刻也摆脱不了它。像这样，叫一支寻常的歌的叠句——或者不如说，叫我们记忆里的一支歌的叠句——或一部歌剧里几段不惹眼的调子，在耳朵里鸣响不休，搅扰我们，本是极平常的事。哪怕那歌本身好，那歌剧的调子有功德，我们也不会少受一点折磨。这样，到末了，我会永远抓着自己正在思量我的安全，用低低的调子反复念着那句话：「我是安全的。」

一天，沿着街道闲步，我抓住自己正半出声地咕哝这几个惯常的音节。一阵烦躁之中，我把它们改成了这样：「我是安全的——我是安全的——不错——只要我不傻到公开招认！」

这些话刚一出口，我便觉得一股冰冷的寒意爬上心头。这种乖戾的发作（它的性质我已费了不少口舌解释过），我是有过一些经验的；我记得清清楚楚：没有哪一回我成功抵挡过它们的进攻。此刻，我自己这随口的自我暗示——我也许傻到足以招认我所犯的那桩凶杀——当面对峙着我，仿佛我被杀的那人的真魂——招引着我走向死亡。

===Original===

At first, I made an effort to shake off this nightmare of the soul. I walked vigorously﻿—faster﻿—still faster﻿—at length I ran. I felt a maddening desire to shriek aloud. Every succeeding wave of thought overwhelmed me with new terror, for, alas! I well, too well understood that to *think*, in my situation, was to be lost. I still quickened my pace. I bounded like a madman through the crowded thoroughfares. At length, the populace took the alarm, and pursued me. I felt *then* the consummation of my fate. Could I have torn out my tongue, I would have done it, but a rough voice resounded in my ears﻿—a rougher grasp seized me by the shoulder. I turned﻿—I gasped for breath. For a moment I experienced all the pangs of suffocation; I became blind, and deaf, and giddy; and then some invisible fiend, I thought, struck me with his broad palm upon the back. The long imprisoned secret burst forth from my soul.

They say that I spoke with a distinct enunciation, but with marked emphasis and passionate hurry, as if in dread of interruption before concluding the brief but pregnant sentences that consigned me to the hangman and to hell.

Having related all that was necessary for the fullest judicial conviction, I fell prostrate in a swoon.

But why shall I say more? Today I wear these chains, and am *here*! Tomorrow I shall be fetterless!﻿—*but where*?

===Chinese===

起初，我极力甩脱这灵魂的梦魇。我健步地走——更快——还要快——末了跑了起来。我感到一种发疯的欲望，要高声尖叫。每一阵接踵而来的思想之浪，都拿新的恐怖把我淹没；因为唉！我明白得太清楚了：在我这样的处境里，*去想*，便是全完。我仍然加快脚步。我像个疯子一样，在拥挤的大街上连蹦带跳。末了，民众警觉起来，追起我来。*这时*我感到了我命运的圆满。我若能把自己的舌头撕出来，我会撕的；可是一个粗厉的声音在我耳边响——一只更粗厉的手一把攥住我的肩。我转过身——我喘不上气。一时间，我尝尽窒息的一切苦痛；我瞎了，聋了，眩晕了；随后，我想，是什么看不见的恶灵，拿他宽阔的手掌，照我背上猛击一记。那久囚的秘密，从我灵魂里迸了出来。

他们说，我说得吐字分明，但带着显著的强调和热烈匆忙，仿佛唯恐那几句简短而孕育着一切的句子没说完就被打断；就是那几句，把我交给了绞刑手，交给了地狱。

把定罪所需的一切都供述完毕之后，我昏厥着扑倒了。

可是我还有什么可说的呢？今天我戴着这些锁链，*在这里*！明天我将没有镣铐！——*可是在哪里*？

## The System of Doctor Tarr and Professor Fether / 塔尔医生与费瑟教授的疗法
===Original===

During the autumn of 18﻿—, while on a tour through the extreme southern provinces of France, my route led me within a few miles of a certain *Maison de Santé* or private madhouse, about which I had heard much, in Paris, from my medical friends. As I had never visited a place of the kind, I thought the opportunity too good to be lost; and so proposed to my travelling companion (a gentleman with whom I had made casual acquaintance a few days before), that we should turn aside, for an hour or so, and look through the establishment. To this he objected﻿—pleading haste in the first place, and, in the second, a very usual horror at the sight of a lunatic. He begged me, however, not to let any mere courtesy towards himself interfere with the gratification of my curiosity, and said that he would ride on leisurely, so that I might overtake him during the day, or, at all events, during the next. As he bade me goodbye, I bethought me that there might be some difficulty in obtaining access to the premises, and mentioned my fears on this point. He replied that, in fact, unless I had personal knowledge of the superintendent, Monsieur Maillard, or some credential in the way of a letter, a difficulty might be found to exist, as the regulations of these private madhouses were more rigid than the public hospital laws. For himself, he added, he had, some years since, made the acquaintance of Maillard, and would so far assist me as to ride up to the door and introduce me; although his feelings on the subject of lunacy would not permit of his entering the house.

I thanked him, and, turning from the main road, we entered a grass-grown bypath, which, in half an hour, nearly lost itself in a dense forest, clothing the base of a mountain. Through this dank and gloomy wood we rode some two miles, when the *Maison de Santé* came in view. It was a fantastic château, much dilapidated, and indeed scarcely tenantable through age and neglect. Its aspect inspired me with absolute dread, and, checking my horse, I half resolved to turn back. I soon, however, grew ashamed of my weakness, and proceeded.

===Chinese===

18——年秋天，我游历法兰西极南诸省，路线把我带到了一所*Maison de Santé*（私立疯人院）几英里之内；这地方我早有耳闻，在巴黎（Paris），从我的医生朋友们那里。我从来没有参观过这一类的场所，觉得这机会失掉太可惜，于是向我的旅伴（一位几天前偶然结识的绅士）提议：我们不妨拐过去，花个把钟头，看看这所机构。对此他反对——先说赶路，其次说见了疯人他有一股寻常人都有的恐惧。然而他求我千万别因为对他客气一点，就妨碍我好奇心的满足；他说他愿意慢慢骑，白天里、至少第二天，我总能追上他。同我道别的时候，我想起进这宅子也许会碰上难处，就把这层顾虑说了。他答道，实情是，除非我同主管马亚尔先生（Monsieur Maillard）有私交，或有书信一类的凭证，难处是会有的，因为这些私立疯人院的规矩比公立医院的法令严得多。至于他自己，他添上一句，几年前他同马亚尔认识，愿意尽力帮我：骑到门前，替我引见；不过一提疯癫这个话题，他的情绪便不许他走进这屋子里去。

我谢了他，我们离开大路，拐进一条蔓草丛生的小径；半点钟后，小径几乎隐没在一片浓密的林子里，这林子罩着一座山的山脚。我们在这潮湿阴森的林子里骑了两英里光景，*Maison de Santé* 便在眼前了。那是一座光怪陆离的城堡，荒废得很，实在说，因年久失修，几乎住不得人了。它的样子叫我生出十足的恐惧；我勒住马，几乎要打退堂鼓。可是我随即为自己的怯弱害臊，往前去了。

===Original===

As we rode up to the gateway, I perceived it slightly open, and the visage of a man peering through. In an instant afterward, this man came forth, accosted my companion by name, shook him cordially by the hand, and begged him to alight. It was Monsieur Maillard himself. He was a portly, fine-looking gentleman of the old school, with a polished manner, and a certain air of gravity, dignity, and authority which was very impressive.

My friend, having presented me, mentioned my desire to inspect the establishment, and received Monsieur Maillard’s assurance that he would show me all attention, now took leave, and I saw him no more.

When he had gone, the superintendent ushered me into a small and exceedingly neat parlor, containing, among other indications of refined taste, many books, drawings, pots of flowers, and musical instruments. A cheerful fire blazed upon the hearth. At a piano, singing an aria from Bellini, sat a young and very beautiful woman, who, at my entrance, paused in her song, and received me with graceful courtesy. Her voice was low, and her whole manner subdued. I thought, too, that I perceived the traces of sorrow in her countenance, which was excessively, although to my taste, not unpleasingly, pale. She was attired in deep mourning, and excited in my bosom a feeling of mingled respect, interest, and admiration.

I had heard, at Paris, that the institution of Monsieur Maillard was managed upon what is vulgarly termed the “system of soothing”﻿—that all punishments were avoided﻿—that even confinement was seldom resorted to﻿—that the patients, while secretly watched, were left much apparent liberty, and that most of them were permitted to roam about the house and grounds in the ordinary apparel of persons in right mind.

===Chinese===

我们骑到门前，我看见大门微微开着，一张脸从缝里朝外张望。转眼之间，那人走了出来，喊出我旅伴的名字，热诚地同他握手，请他下马。正是马亚尔先生本人。他是旧派人物里那种体面端方的绅士，丰腴轩昂，举止文雅，带着一股庄重、尊贵与威严的气派，令人印象深刻。

我的朋友把我介绍过，说了我想参观这所机构的心愿，得了马亚尔先生尽力照拂的许诺，便告辞而去；此后我再没有见到他。

他走后，主管把我引进一间小巧而极整洁的客厅；里头，除了别的雅致的趣味，还有许多书、素描、盆花和乐器。炉火烧得欢畅。一架钢琴前，坐着一位年轻而极美的女子，正唱着贝利尼（Bellini）的一支咏叹调；我一进来，她停了歌，落落大方地接待我。她的嗓音低柔，整个人神态温婉。我还以为在她脸上看出了悲哀的痕迹；那脸色苍白之极，虽然照我的口味，并不难看。她一身重孝，在我胸中激起一种交织着敬意、关切与赞叹的情感。

我在巴黎听说，马亚尔先生的机构，管理上用的是俗话所称的「安抚体系」——一切惩罚都避免——连拘禁也少用——病人受着暗中监视，表面上却有颇多的自由，而且多数病人获准穿着神志正常之人的寻常衣裳，在宅子和园子里随意走动。

===Original===

Keeping these impressions in view, I was cautious in what I said before the young lady; for I could not be sure that she was sane; and, in fact, there was a certain restless brilliancy about her eyes which half led me to imagine she was not. I confined my remarks, therefore, to general topics, and to such as I thought would not be displeasing or exciting even to a lunatic. She replied in a perfectly rational manner to all that I said; and even her original observations were marked with the soundest good sense, but a long acquaintance with the metaphysics of mania, had taught me to put no faith in such evidence of sanity, and I continued to practise, throughout the interview, the caution with which I commenced it.

Presently a smart footman in livery brought in a tray with fruit, wine, and other refreshments, of which I partook, the lady soon afterward leaving the room. As she departed I turned my eyes in an inquiring manner toward my host.

“No,” he said, “oh, no﻿—a member of my family﻿—my niece, and a most accomplished woman.”

“I beg a thousand pardons for the suspicion,” I replied, “but of course you will know how to excuse me. The excellent administration of your affairs here is well understood in Paris, and I thought it just possible, you know﻿—”

“Yes, yes﻿—say no more﻿—or rather it is myself who should thank you for the commendable prudence you have displayed. We seldom find so much of forethought in young men; and, more than once, some unhappy contretemps has occurred in consequence of thoughtlessness on the part of our visitors. While my former system was in operation, and my patients were permitted the privilege of roaming to and fro at will, they were often aroused to a dangerous frenzy by injudicious persons who called to inspect the house. Hence I was obliged to enforce a rigid system of exclusion; and none obtained access to the premises upon whose discretion I could not rely.”

“While your *former* system was in operation!” I said, repeating his words﻿—“do I understand you, then, to say that the ‘soothing system’ of which I have heard so much is no longer in force?”

“It is now,” he replied, “several weeks since we have concluded to renounce it forever.”

“Indeed! you astonish me!”

===Chinese===

记着这些印象，我在那位年轻女士面前说话很小心；因为我无法断定她神志健全；实在说，她眼睛里有一种躁动不安的亮光，倒教我半信她不健全。于是我把话题限于一般的事情，限于我以为连疯子听了也不恼不激的事情。她对我说的每一句话，都以全然理性的方式作答；甚至她主动的议论，也带着顶健全的常识；可是同躁狂症的形而上学长久打交道，早已教会我不把这类健全的凭据放在眼里，于是整场晤面，我始终守着我开始时的小心。

不久，一个穿号衣的伶俐男仆端进一只托盘，盛着水果、葡萄酒和别的点心；我吃了些，那位女士随即离屋。她出去时，我探询似地朝主人望过去。

「不，」他说，「哦，不——是我家里的人——我的侄女，一位极有教养的女子。」

「为这点疑心，我求千金宽恕，」我答，「不过您当然明白该怎么原谅我。您这里的事务管理得好，巴黎是尽人皆知的；我不过觉得，您知道，多少也有可能——」

「好了，好了——不必说了——或者说，该道谢的倒是我，谢您这份可嘉的谨慎。年轻人有这样深谋远虑的少见；我们的客人欠思量，已经不止一次惹出些不愉快的岔子。从前我的旧体系行用的时候，病人享有随意走动的特权，常有欠斟酌的人来参观宅子，把他们激成危险的狂怒。因此我不得不立起一套严格的闭门规矩；凡是我不敢信赖其分寸的人，一律进不了这道门。」

「您的*旧*体系行用的时候！」我说，把他的话重了一遍——「那么，我听得这样多的那套『安抚体系』，照您的意思，已经不再行用了？」

「如今，」他答，「已经几个星期，我们决意永远把它抛弃了。」

「真的！您叫我吃惊！」

===Original===

“We found it, sir,” he said, with a sigh, “absolutely necessary to return to the old usages. The *danger* of the soothing system was, at all times, appalling; and its advantages have been much overrated. I believe, sir, that in this house it has been given a fair trial, if ever in any. We did everything that rational humanity could suggest. I am sorry that you could not have paid us a visit at an earlier period, that you might have judged for yourself. But I presume you are conversant with the soothing practice﻿—with its details.”

“Not altogether. What I have heard has been at third or fourth hand.”

“I may state the system, then, in general terms, as one in which the patients were *menagés*﻿—humored. We contradicted no fancies which entered the brains of the mad. On the contrary, we not only indulged but encouraged them; and many of our most permanent cures have been thus effected. There is no argument which so touches the feeble reason of the madman as the *reductio ad absurdum*. We have had men, for example, who fancied themselves chickens. The cure was, to insist upon the thing as a fact﻿—to accuse the patient of stupidity in not sufficiently perceiving it to be a fact﻿—and thus to refuse him any other diet for a week than that which properly appertains to a chicken. In this manner a little corn and gravel were made to perform wonders.”

“But was this species of acquiescence all?”

“By no means. We put much faith in amusements of a simple kind, such as music, dancing, gymnastic exercises generally, cards, certain classes of books, and so forth. We affected to treat each individual as if for some ordinary physical disorder; and the word ‘lunacy’ was never employed. A great point was to set each lunatic to guard the actions of all the others. To repose confidence in the understanding or discretion of a madman, is to gain him body and soul. In this way we were enabled to dispense with an expensive body of keepers.”

“And you had no punishments of any kind?”

“None.”

“And you never confined your patients?”

“Very rarely. Now and then, the malady of some individual growing to a crisis, or taking a sudden turn of fury, we conveyed him to a secret cell, lest his disorder should infect the rest, and there kept him until we could dismiss him to his friends﻿—for with the raging maniac we have nothing to do. He is usually removed to the public hospitals.”

===Chinese===

「我们发觉，先生，」他叹口气说，「回到旧章程是绝对必要的。安抚体系的*危险*，任何时候都是骇人的；它的好处又被大大高估了。我相信，先生，倘若别处也试过它，那这里给它的是一场公平的试验。凡是理性的人道所能想到的，我们都做了。可惜您不能早些来看我们，好叫您亲自判断。不过我想您对安抚的做法——对它的细节——是熟悉的。」

「并不全熟。我听来的，都是三手四手的。」

「那么，这体系我可以大略说给您听：病人受到*将就*（menagés）——被迁就。凡是钻进疯人脑袋的妄想，我们从不驳斥。恰恰相反，我们不但纵容，而且鼓励；我们许多最持久的治愈，便是这样奏效的。没有任何论证，像*归谬法*（reductio ad absurdum）那样打动疯人那点微弱的理智。比方说，我们有几位病人自以为是鸡。治法便是把这件事当作事实来坚持——责备病人愚笨，竟看不透这是事实——于是整整一个星期，只给他鸡该吃的东西作口粮。这样，一点儿谷子加沙砾，就创造了奇迹。」

「可是这种迁就就是全部么？」

「决不是。我们极信简单一类娱乐的功用，比如音乐、跳舞、一般的体操、纸牌、某几类书，等等。我们装作把每个人当作寻常的躯体失调来治疗；『疯癫』这个词从不出口。一件要紧的事，是叫每个疯人看守所有其余疯人的行动。把理解与分寸托付给一个疯人，就是赢得了他整个人，身与魂。这样，我们便省下一班子昂贵的看守人。」

「那么你们没有任何惩罚？」

「没有。」

「你们也从不拘禁病人？」

「极少。偶尔，某个人的病长到了关口，或突然发起怒来，我们便把他送进一间秘密的斗室，免得他的病传染别人，关到我们能够打发他回朋友家去为止——因为发作的狂人我们不管。他通常被移送到公立医院去。」

===Original===

“And you have now changed all this﻿—and you think for the better?”

“Decidedly. The system had its disadvantages, and even its dangers. It is now, happily, exploded throughout all the *Maisons de Santé* of France.”

“I am very much surprised,” I said, “at what you tell me; for I made sure that, at this moment, no other method of treatment for mania existed in any portion of the country.”

“You are young yet, my friend,” replied my host, “but the time will arrive when you will learn to judge for yourself of what is going on in the world, without trusting to the gossip of others. Believe nothing you hear, and only one half that you see. Now about our *Maisons de Santé*, it is clear that some ignoramus has misled you. After dinner, however, when you have sufficiently recovered from the fatigue of your ride, I will be happy to take you over the house, and introduce to you a system which, in my opinion, and in that of everyone who has witnessed its operation, is incomparably the most effectual as yet devised.”

“Your own?” I inquired﻿—“one of your own invention?”

“I am proud,” he replied, “to acknowledge that it is﻿—at least in some measure.”

In this manner I conversed with Monsieur Maillard for an hour or two, during which he showed me the gardens and conservatories of the place.

“I cannot let you see my patients,” he said, “just at present. To a sensitive mind there is always more or less of the shocking in such exhibitions; and I do not wish to spoil your appetite for dinner. We will dine. I can give you some veal à la Menehoult, with cauliflowers in velouté sauce﻿—after that a glass of Clos de Vougeôt﻿—then your nerves will be sufficiently steadied.”

===Chinese===

「如今这一切都变了——您认为变得更好了？」

「一定。那体系有它的弊病，甚至有它的危险。如今，幸好，法兰西所有的*Maison de Santé*里都把它废除了。」

「您告诉我的话，」我说，「叫我非常惊讶；因为我原来拿得准：眼下这个国家任何地方，都不存在别的治疯法了。」

「你还年轻呢，我的朋友，」主人答，「总有一天你会学会靠自己去判断世上进行的事，不靠别人的闲话。听来的话一句也别信，看见的只信一半。至于我们的*Maison de Santé*，分明是哪个无知之徒把你引岔了。不过饭后，等你骑马的劳乏歇够了，我乐于领你看看这宅子，给你介绍一套体系；照我的意见，也照一切亲见它运行的人的意见，它是迄今想出的诸法里无比最见效的。」

「您自己的？」我问——「您自己发明的？」

「我很自豪地承认，」他答，「正是——至少几分之内是。」

我同马亚尔先生就这样谈了一两个钟头，其间他领我看了这地方的园圃与温室。

「我不能让你看我的病人，」他说，「眼下不能。对一颗敏感的心，这样的展示总有些可骇之处；我不想败坏你的饭量。我们要吃饭了。我能给你来一道门乌尔式（à la Menehoult）小牛肉，配白汁（velouté）花椰菜——之后一杯伏旧园（Clos de Vougeôt）酒——那时你的神经就定得住了。」

===Original===

At six, dinner was announced; and my host conducted me into a large salle à manger, where a very numerous company were assembled﻿—twenty-five or thirty in all. They were, apparently, people of rank﻿—certainly of high breeding﻿—although their habiliments, I thought, were extravagantly rich, partaking somewhat too much of the ostentatious finery of the *vieille cour*. I noticed that at least two thirds of these guests were ladies; and some of the latter were by no means accoutred in what a Parisian would consider good taste at the present day. Many females, for example, whose age could not have been less than seventy were bedecked with a profusion of jewelry, such as rings, bracelets, and earrings, and wore their bosoms and arms shamefully bare. I observed, too, that very few of the dresses were well made﻿—or, at least, that very few of them fitted the wearers. In looking about, I discovered the interesting girl to whom Monsieur Maillard had presented me in the little parlor; but my surprise was great to see her wearing a hoop and farthingale, with high-heeled shoes, and a dirty cap of Brussels lace, so much too large for her that it gave her face a ridiculously diminutive expression. When I had first seen her, she was attired, most becomingly, in deep mourning. There was an air of oddity, in short, about the dress of the whole party, which, at first, caused me to recur to my original idea of the “soothing system,” and to fancy that Monsieur Maillard had been willing to deceive me until after dinner, that I might experience no uncomfortable feelings during the repast, at finding myself dining with lunatics; but I remembered having been informed, in Paris, that the southern provincialists were a peculiarly eccentric people, with a vast number of antiquated notions; and then, too, upon conversing with several members of the company, my apprehensions were immediately and fully dispelled.

===Chinese===

六点钟，饭宣告开了；主人领我走进一间大餐厅（salle à manger），那里已聚着极多的人——总共二十五到三十位。他们显然是有身分的人——教养也无疑极高——虽然他们的衣饰，我看着，奢华得过分，太沾着*旧宫廷*（vieille cour）那种炫耀的浮华。我注意到，宾客至少三分之二是女客；其中一些人的装束，照如今一个巴黎人的眼光，决说不上雅。比方说，好些年纪决不下于七十的妇人，遍身珠光宝气——戒指、手镯、耳环——胸口和臂膀裸露得可羞。我还看出，衣裳很少是做得好的——或者至少，很少合身。四下张望时，我认出了马亚尔先生在小客厅里介绍给我的那位有趣的姑娘；可是看到她竟穿着裙箍和法伦吉尔撑裙（farthingale），踩着高跟鞋，头上歪着一顶布鲁塞尔花边的脏帽子——帽子对她来说大得过分，把她的脸衬得小得可笑——我的惊讶大极了。我头一回见她时，她穿着合身之极的重孝。总之，满座衣冠都带着一股古怪之气，起初竟使我回到我「安抚体系」那个老念头上去，揣想马亚尔先生是有意哄我到饭后再说，好叫我在席间不生一点不舒服的感觉，不至于发觉自己同疯人同桌；可是我记起，在巴黎听说，南方省里的人本是一伙特别的怪物，怀着大批老掉牙的观念；接着又同席上几个人交谈了几句，我的疑虑立刻全消了。

===Original===

The dining-room itself, although perhaps sufficiently comfortable and of good dimensions, had nothing too much of elegance about it. For example, the floor was uncarpeted; in France, however, a carpet is frequently dispensed with. The windows, too, were without curtains; the shutters, being shut, were securely fastened with iron bars, applied diagonally, after the fashion of our ordinary shop-shutters. The apartment, I observed, formed, in itself, a wing of the château, and thus the windows were on three sides of the parallelogram, the door being at the other. There were no less than ten windows in all.

The table was superbly set out. It was loaded with plate, and more than loaded with delicacies. The profusion was absolutely barbaric. There were meats enough to have feasted the Anakim. Never, in all my life, had I witnessed so lavish, so wasteful an expenditure of the good things of life. There seemed very little taste, however, in the arrangements; and my eyes, accustomed to quiet lights, were sadly offended by the prodigious glare of a multitude of wax candles, which, in silver candelabra, were deposited upon the table, and all about the room, wherever it was possible to find a place. There were several active servants in attendance; and, upon a large table, at the farther end of the apartment, were seated seven or eight people with fiddles, fifes, trombones, and a drum. These fellows annoyed me very much, at intervals, during the repast, by an infinite variety of noises, which were intended for music, and which appeared to afford much entertainment to all present, with the exception of myself.

Upon the whole, I could not help thinking that there was much of the bizarre about everything I saw﻿—but then the world is made up of all kinds of persons, with all modes of thought, and all sorts of conventional customs. I had travelled, too, so much, as to be quite an adept at the nil admirari; so I took my seat very coolly at the right hand of my host, and, having an excellent appetite, did justice to the good cheer set before me.

===Chinese===

餐厅本身虽然够舒适，间量也大，谈不上太多的雅致。比方说，地上没有地毯；不过在法兰西，地毯常是省去的。窗户也没有帘子；百叶窗关着，拿铁条斜斜地别住，钉得牢牢的，跟我们寻常店铺的窗板一个样式。我注意到这间屋子自成城堡的一翼，窗便开在平行四边形的三个方面，门开在另一面。窗户足足有十扇。

桌子摆得豪华。银器压着桌面，美味压得过了头。丰盈绝对野蛮。肉多到够亚衲族人（Anakim）摆一席盛宴。平生我不曾见过把生活的好东西这样挥霍、这样糟蹋。可是布置里似乎很少品味；我的眼睛惯于安静的光，给一大堆白蜡烛炫目的光刺得难过；那些蜡烛插在银烛台上，桌上、屋里，凡能寻出个地方的地方都摆着。伺候的仆人倒有几个手脚麻利；屋子那头一张大桌旁，坐着七八个人，带着提琴、笛子、长号和一面鼓。这一伙人在席间时不时拿无数种吵闹折磨我——他们管那吵闹叫音乐——那吵闹在满座看来，除了我之外，倒似乎都有趣得很。

总之，我不能不想到，我看见的一切处处透着怪诞——可是世界本由各式各样的人组成，怀着各式各样的心思，守着各式各样的习俗。我也旅行得太多，早精于*nil admirari*（万事不惊）之道；于是我极其冷静地在主人右手坐下，胃口极好，把面前的佳肴吃了个尽兴。

===Original===

The conversation, in the meantime, was spirited and general. The ladies, as usual, talked a great deal. I soon found that nearly all the company were well educated; and my host was a world of good-humored anecdote in himself. He seemed quite willing to speak of his position as superintendent of a *Maison de Santé*; and, indeed, the topic of lunacy was, much to my surprise, a favorite one with all present. A great many amusing stories were told, having reference to the *whims* of the patients.

“We had a fellow here once,” said a fat little gentleman, who sat at my right﻿—“a fellow that fancied himself a teapot; and by the way, is it not especially singular how often this particular crotchet has entered the brain of the lunatic? There is scarcely an insane asylum in France which cannot supply a human teapot. *Our* gentleman was a Britannia-ware teapot, and was careful to polish himself every morning with buckskin and whiting.”

“And then,” said a tall man just opposite, “we had here, not long ago, a person who had taken it into his head that he was a donkey﻿—which allegorically speaking, you will say, was quite true. He was a troublesome patient; and we had much ado to keep him within bounds. For a long time he would eat nothing but thistles; but of this idea we soon cured him by insisting upon his eating nothing else. Then he was perpetually kicking out his heels﻿—so﻿—so﻿—”

“Mr. De Kock! I will thank you to behave yourself!” here interrupted an old lady, who sat next to the speaker. “Please keep your feet to yourself! You have spoiled my brocade! Is it necessary, pray, to illustrate a remark in so practical a style? Our friend here can surely comprehend you without all this. Upon my word, you are nearly as great a donkey as the poor unfortunate imagined himself. Your acting is very natural, as I live.”

“*Mille pardons!* Ma’m’selle!” replied Monsieur De Kock, thus addressed﻿—“a thousand pardons! I had no intention of offending. Ma’m’selle Laplace﻿—Monsieur De Kock will do himself the honor of taking wine with you.”

Here Monsieur De Kock bowed low, kissed his hand with much ceremony, and took wine with Ma’m’selle Laplace.

“Allow me, *mon ami*,” now said Monsieur Maillard, addressing myself, “allow me to send you a morsel of this veal à la St. Menhoult﻿—you will find it particularly fine.”

===Chinese===

谈话，这工夫，是热闹的、四座的。太太们照例说得很多。我很快发觉，几乎满座都受过好的教育；我主人本人便是一世界的风趣谈资。他很乐意谈他*Maison de Santé*主管的地位；而且疯癫这个话题，出乎我意料，是满座人人的心爱题目。讲了许许多多有趣的故事，都关涉病人的*怪念头*。

「我们这里从前有过一个家伙，」我右边坐着的胖胖的小绅士说——「一个自以为是茶壶的家伙；顺带说一句，这种*褊狭的*怪念头多么常钻进疯人的脑袋，难道不特别稀奇么？法兰西几乎没有一座疯人院拿不出一只人做的茶壶。*我们*的这位先生是不列颠锡器的茶壶，每天早上拿麂皮和白垩粉小心地擦亮自己。」

「还有呢，」对面一个高个子说，「不久之前，我们这里还有一个人，他认定自己是一头驴——打比方说，你要讲，这话倒是千真万确。他是个难弄的病人；我们费了好大的劲才把他圈在界限之内。很长一段时间他只肯吃蓟草；这个念头我们很快治好了，办法是坚持只许他吃蓟草。然后他永远在往后踢他的蹄子——这样——这样——」

「德科克先生（Monsieur De Kock）！劳您驾放规矩些！」这里一位老太太插进来，坐在说话人旁边。「请把您的脚管在您自己脚下！您把我的锦缎毁了！请问，有必要拿这样实际的样子来演一个比喻么？我们这位朋友自然听得懂您，用不着这些。说老实话，您几乎同那可怜的不幸人想象自己是的一头驴一样地是头驴。您演得真自然，一点不假。」

「*万分抱歉*（Mille pardons）！小姐！」德科克先生这样被称呼了，便答——「一千个抱歉！我没有得罪的意思。拉普拉斯小姐（Ma'm'selle Laplace）——德科克先生有幸同您共饮一杯。」

这里德科克先生深深一躬，极尽礼数地飞了一个吻，同拉普拉斯小姐共了酒。

「容我，*我的朋友*（mon ami），」这时马亚尔先生朝我说，「容我给您送一小块这圣门乌尔式（à la St. Menhoult）小牛肉——您会觉得它特别精美。」

===Original===

At this instant three sturdy waiters had just succeeded in depositing safely upon the table an enormous dish, or trencher, containing what I supposed to be the “*monstrum, horrendum, informe, ingens, cui lumen ademptum*.” A closer scrutiny assured me, however, that it was only a small calf roasted whole, and set upon its knees, with an apple in its mouth, as is the English fashion of dressing a hare.

“Thank you, no,” I replied; “to say the truth, I am not particularly partial to veal à la St.﻿—what is it?﻿—for I do not find that it altogether agrees with me. I will change my plate, however, and try some of the rabbit.”

There were several side-dishes on the table, containing what appeared to be the ordinary French rabbit﻿—a very delicious *morceau*, which I can recommend.

“Pierre,” cried the host, “change this gentleman’s plate, and give him a side-piece of this rabbit *au-chat*.”

“This what?” said I.

“This rabbit *au-chat*.”

“Why, thank you﻿—upon second thoughts, no. I will just help myself to some of the ham.”

There is no knowing what one eats, thought I to myself, at the tables of these people of the province. I will have none of their rabbit *au-chat*﻿—and, for the matter of that, none of their *cat-au-rabbit* either.

“And then,” said a cadaverous looking personage, near the foot of the table, taking up the thread of the conversation where it had been broken off﻿—“and then, among other oddities, we had a patient, once upon a time, who very pertinaciously maintained himself to be a Cordova cheese, and went about, with a knife in his hand, soliciting his friends to try a small slice from the middle of his leg.”

“He was a great fool, beyond doubt,” interposed someone, “but not to be compared with a certain individual whom we all know, with the exception of this strange gentleman. I mean the man who took himself for a bottle of champagne, and always went off with a pop and a fizz, in this fashion.”

===Chinese===

这时，三个健壮的侍者刚把一只巨大的盘子——或曰食案——平安地架上桌子；盘里装的，我猜想，便是那「*monstrum, horrendum, informe, ingens, cui lumen ademptum*」（可怕的怪物，形陋体巨，被夺去了光明）。可是凑近细看，我放了心：原来只是一只整烤的小牛，跪着架起来，嘴里含着一只苹果——照英国人摆野兔的规矩。

「谢谢，不必了，」我答；「说句实话，我对小牛肉*à la St.*——叫什么来着？——并不特别偏爱，因为我发觉它同我不大相合。不过我要换一下盘子，尝尝那兔子。」

桌上有好几碟小菜，盛着像是寻常的法式兔肉——一种极美的*一口*（morceau），我愿意举荐。

「皮埃尔（Pierre），」主人喊，「给这位先生换盘子，给他来一碟这兔肉*au-chat*（猫烧兔）。」

「这什么？」我说。

「这兔肉*au-chat*（猫烧兔）。」

「呃，谢谢——转念一想，不必了。我就自己夹点火腿吧。」

这些省里人的桌上，谁知道吃下的是什么，我心里想。他们的猫烧兔我不沾——说实在的，他们的*cat-au-rabbit*（兔烧猫）我也不沾。

「还有呢，」桌子下首一个形容枯槁的人物说，把话头从断了的地方拾起来——「还有呢，在别的怪人之外，我们从前有过一个病人，死心塌地咬定自己是科尔多瓦（Cordova）奶酪，手里拿着刀到处走，恳求他的朋友们从他小腿中间切一小片尝尝。」

「他无疑是个大傻瓜，」有人插进来，「可是比不上我们人人皆知的一位——除了这位奇怪的先生。我是说那位把自己当作一瓶香槟的人，总是『噗』的一声带着嘶嘶的响走掉，这样的架势。」

===Original===

Here the speaker, very rudely, as I thought, put his right thumb in his left cheek, withdrew it with a sound resembling the popping of a cork, and then, by a dexterous movement of the tongue upon the teeth, created a sharp hissing and fizzing, which lasted for several minutes, in imitation of the frothing of champagne. This behavior, I saw plainly, was not very pleasing to Monsieur Maillard; but that gentleman said nothing, and the conversation was resumed by a very lean little man in a big wig.

“And then there was an ignoramus,” said he, “who mistook himself for a frog, which, by the way, he resembled in no little degree. I wish you could have seen him, sir,”﻿—here the speaker addressed myself﻿—“it would have done your heart good to see the natural airs that he put on. Sir, if that man was *not* a frog, I can only observe that it is a pity he was not. His croak thus﻿—o-o-o-o-gh﻿—o-o-o-o-gh! was the finest note in the world﻿—B flat; and when he put his elbows upon the table thus﻿—after taking a glass or two of wine﻿—and distended his mouth, thus, and rolled up his eyes, thus, and winked them with excessive rapidity, thus, why then, sir, I take it upon myself to say, positively, that you would have been lost in admiration of the genius of the man.”

“I have no doubt of it,” I said.

“And then,” said somebody else, “then there was Petit Gaillard, who thought himself a pinch of snuff, and was truly distressed because he could not take himself between his own finger and thumb.”

“And then there was Jules Desoulières, who was a very singular genius, indeed, and went mad with the idea that he was a pumpkin. He persecuted the cook to make him up into pies﻿—a thing which the cook indignantly refused to do. For my part, I am by no means sure that a pumpkin pie à la Desoulières would not have been very capital eating indeed!”

“You astonish me!” said I; and I looked inquisitively at Monsieur Maillard.

“Ha! ha! ha!” said that gentleman﻿—“he! he! he!﻿—hi! hi! hi!﻿—ho! ho! ho!﻿—hu! hu! hu!﻿—very good indeed! You must not be astonished, *mon ami*; our friend here is a wit﻿—a *drôle*﻿—you must not understand him to the letter.”

===Chinese===

这里，说话的人，照我看，极没有礼貌，把右手大拇指塞进左腮，抽出来时带着一声像拔瓶塞的「噗」，随后舌头朝牙齿上一番灵巧的动作，造出一种尖利的嘶嘶气声，持续了好几分钟，摹仿香槟的起沫。这举止，我看得分明，叫马亚尔先生不大痛快；可是那位大人什么也没说，谈话便由一个瘦长的小个子续起，他戴着一顶大假发。

「还有呢，有一个蠢货，」他说，「把自己错当作一只青蛙；顺带说一句，他像青蛙像得着实不少。我倒恨不得您见过他，先生，」——这里说话的人朝向我——「看见他摆出的那些天生的架子，会叫您心里舒服。先生，倘若那人不*是*青蛙，我只能说他没当成青蛙真是可惜。他那样地呱——喔喔喔喔——呱！——喔喔喔喔——呱！是世上顶好的一条嗓子——降B调；他喝下一两杯酒之后，把两肘架到桌上，这样，嘴张到这样，眼睛翻成这样，眼皮又眨得这样飞快，为什么，先生，我斗胆断然说，您一定会对那人的天才叹赏到忘形。」

「这个我不疑心，」我说。

「还有呢，」另外有人说，「还有小加亚尔（Petit Gaillard），他把自己想成一小撮鼻烟，苦恼极了，因为他不能拿自己的手指和拇指把自己捏起来。」

「还有朱尔·德苏利埃（Jules Desoulières），他是顶特别的一个天才，当真，发了疯，认定自己是一只南瓜。他缠着厨子把他做成馅饼——那厨子气冲冲地拒绝。至于我，我远不敢断定一只德苏利埃式的南瓜馅饼会不是顶好吃的东西！」

「您叫我吃惊！」我说；我探询似地朝马亚尔先生望过去。

「哈！哈！哈！」那位大人说——「嘻！嘻！嘻！——嗨！嗨！嗨！——嚯！嚯！嚯！——呼！呼！呼！——妙极了！您可别吃惊，*我的朋友*（mon ami）；我们这位朋友是位妙人——一个*滑稽家*（drôle）——您可别把他的话句句当真。

===Original===

“And then,” said some other one of the party﻿—“then there was Bouffon Le Grand﻿—another extraordinary personage in his way. He grew deranged through love, and fancied himself possessed of two heads. One of these he maintained to be the head of Cicero; the other he imagined a composite one, being Demosthenes’ from the top of the forehead to the mouth, and Lord Brougham’s from the mouth to the chin. It is not impossible that he was wrong; but he would have convinced you of his being in the right; for he was a man of great eloquence. He had an absolute passion for oratory, and could not refrain from display. For example, he used to leap upon the dinner-table thus, and﻿—and﻿—”

Here a friend, at the side of the speaker, put a hand upon his shoulder and whispered a few words in his ear; upon which he ceased talking with great suddenness, and sank back within his chair.

“And then,” said the friend who had whispered, “there was Boullard, the teetotum. I call him the teetotum because, in fact, he was seized with the droll, but not altogether irrational, crotchet, that he had been converted into a teetotum. You would have roared with laughter to see him spin. He would turn round upon one heel by the hour, in this manner﻿—so﻿—”

Here the friend whom he had just interrupted by a whisper, performed an exactly similar office for himself.

“But then,” cried the old lady, at the top of her voice, “your Monsieur Boullard was a madman, and a very silly madman at best; for who, allow me to ask you, ever heard of a human teetotum? The thing is absurd. Madame Joyeuse was a more sensible person, as you know. She had a crotchet, but it was instinct with common sense, and gave pleasure to all who had the honor of her acquaintance. She found, upon mature deliberation, that, by some accident, she had been turned into a chicken-cock; but, as such, she behaved with propriety. She flapped her wings with prodigious effect﻿—so﻿—so﻿—so﻿—and, as for her crow, it was delicious! Cock-a-doodle-doo!﻿—cock-a-doodle-doo!﻿—cock-a-doodle-de-doo dooo-do-o-o-o-o-o-o!”

“Madame Joyeuse, I will thank you to behave yourself!” here interrupted our host, very angrily. “You can either conduct yourself as a lady should do, or you can quit the table forthwith﻿—take your choice.”

===Chinese===

「还有呢，」席间另外哪一位说——「还有大布丰（Bouffon Le Grand）——他那一行的又一位非常人物。他为爱情疯了，认定自己有两个脑袋。一个他坚称是西塞罗的脑袋；另一个他设想是一个合成的，从额头到嘴是德摩斯梯尼的，从嘴到下巴是布劳姆勋爵的。说他错了，并非不可能；可他原能叫您信他不错；因为他是个大雄辩家。他对演说有一种绝对的热爱，忍不住要卖弄。比方说，他惯常这样跳上餐桌，然后——然后——」

这里，说话人旁边一位朋友把手按上他的肩，朝他耳语了几句；他便猛然收了话，瘫回椅子里。

「还有呢，」那位耳语的朋友说，「还有布拉尔（Boullard），陀螺。我唤他陀螺，因为，实情是，他给一个非常滑稽、却未必全不合理性的怪念头攫住了：他认定自己变成了陀螺。您看见他转，准会笑破肚皮。他能一只脚跟转上几个钟头，这样——这样——」

这里，方才被他耳语打断的那位朋友，给自己也来了一套一模一样的动作。

「可是，」老太太扯着嗓子喊，「你们那位布拉尔先生是个疯子，而且顶多是个顶无聊的疯子；因为容我问问您，谁听说过人做的陀螺？这东西荒谬。儒瓦丝夫人（Madame Joyeuse）可是个明白得多的人，您知道。她有一个怪念头，可那念头浸透了常识，给一切有幸认识她的人以快乐。她经过深思熟虑，发觉自己由于什么意外，变成了一只公鸡；可是公鸡也罢，她举止得体。她扇起翅膀来效果惊人——这样——这样——这样——至于她的啼鸣，那真是妙极！喔——喔——喔！——喔——喔——喔！——喔——喔——哒——哒——喔——喔——喔——喔——喔！」

「儒瓦丝夫人，劳您驾放规矩些！」这里我们的主人插进来，怒冲冲的。「您要么拿出夫人该有的样子，要么立刻离席——请选择。」

===Original===

The lady (whom I was much astonished to hear addressed as Madame Joyeuse, after the description of Madame Joyeuse she had just given) blushed up to the eyebrows, and seemed exceedingly abashed at the reproof. She hung down her head, and said not a syllable in reply. But another and younger lady resumed the theme. It was my beautiful girl of the little parlor.

“Oh, Madame Joyeuse *was* a fool!” she exclaimed, “but there was really much sound sense, after all, in the opinion of Eugénie Salsafette. She was a very beautiful and painfully modest young lady, who thought the ordinary mode of habiliment indecent, and wished to dress herself, always, by getting outside instead of inside of her clothes. It is a thing very easily done, after all. You have only to do so﻿—and then so﻿—so﻿—so﻿—and then so﻿—so﻿—so﻿—and then﻿—”

“*Mon dieu!* Ma’m’selle Salsafette!” here cried a dozen voices at once. “What *are* you about?﻿—forbear!﻿—that is sufficient!﻿—we see, very plainly, how it is done!﻿—hold! hold!” and several persons were already leaping from their seats to withhold Ma’m’selle Salsafette from putting herself upon a par with the Medicean Venus, when the point was very effectually and suddenly accomplished by a series of loud screams, or yells, from some portion of the main body of the château.

My nerves were very much affected, indeed, by these yells; but the rest of the company I really pitied. I never saw any set of reasonable people so thoroughly frightened in my life. They all grew as pale as so many corpses, and, shrinking within their seats, sat quivering and gibbering with terror, and listening for a repetition of the sound. It came again﻿—louder and seemingly nearer﻿—and then a third time *very* loud, and then a fourth time with a vigor evidently diminished. At this apparent dying away of the noise, the spirits of the company were immediately regained, and all was life and anecdote as before. I now ventured to inquire the cause of the disturbance.

===Chinese===

那位夫人（方才她还那样描绘儒瓦丝夫人，此刻听见有人这样称呼她，我着实吃了一惊）红到眉毛，受着申斥似乎羞惭极了。她垂下头，半个字也不答。可是另一位年轻些的夫人接上了话头。正是我在小客厅里的美人儿。

「哦，儒瓦丝夫人*是*个傻瓜！」她喊，「可是说到底，欧仁妮·萨尔萨菲特（Eugénie Salsafette）的见解里实在有好多健全的常识。她是一位极美而羞怯到痛苦地步的小姐，她认为寻常的穿衣法子不成体统，情愿总在衣裳外头穿，不在里头穿。这原是极容易办的事。您只消这样——再这样——这样——这样——再这样——这样——这样——再——」

「*我的天*（Mon dieu）！萨尔萨菲特小姐！」这里十几个人同时喊。「您在干什么？——住手！——够了！——我们清清楚楚看见是怎么穿的了！——住手！住手！」好几个人已经从座位上跳起来，要拦住萨尔萨菲特小姐，不叫她把自己摆到美第奇的维纳斯（Medicean Venus）那样的高度上；这时，那一点却叫一阵响亮的尖叫或喊嚎极其有效而突然地办成了，喊声出自城堡正楼的某处。

这些喊嚎确实大大震动了我的神经；可是满座其余的人我倒实在可怜。平生我不曾见过一伙通情理的人这样被吓个透。他们全给吓得像一具具死尸似的白，缩进椅子里，吓得发抖、口里咕哝着恐怖，等那声音再来一遍。它又来了——更响，似乎更近——然后第三回*非常*响，然后第四回，力气分明小了。声音这样仿佛低下去，满座的精神立刻回转，一切又同先前一样，有生气，有谈笑。此刻我壮起胆子探问骚乱的缘由。

===Original===

“A mere bagatelle,” said Monsieur Maillard. “We are used to these things, and care really very little about them. The lunatics, every now and then, get up a howl in concert; one starting another, as is sometimes the case with a bevy of dogs at night. It occasionally happens, however, that the concerto yells are succeeded by a simultaneous effort at breaking loose; when, of course, some little danger is to be apprehended.”

“And how many have you in charge?”

“At present we have not more than ten, altogether.”

“Principally females, I presume?”

“Oh, no﻿—every one of them men, and stout fellows, too, I can tell you.”

“Indeed! I have always understood that the majority of lunatics were of the gentler sex.”

“It is generally so, but not always. Some time ago, there were about twenty-seven patients here; and, of that number, no less than eighteen were women; but, lately, matters have changed very much, as you see.”

“Yes﻿—have changed very much, as you see,” here interrupted the gentleman who had broken the shins of Ma’m’selle Laplace.

“Yes﻿—have changed very much, as you see!” chimed in the whole company at once.

“Hold your tongues, every one of you!” said my host, in a great rage. Whereupon the whole company maintained a dead silence for nearly a minute. As for one lady, she obeyed Monsieur Maillard to the letter, and thrusting out her tongue, which was an excessively long one, held it very resignedly, with both hands, until the end of the entertainment.

“And this gentlewoman,” said I, to Monsieur Maillard, bending over and addressing him in a whisper﻿—“this good lady who has just spoken, and who gives us the cock-a-doodle-de-doo﻿—she, I presume, is harmless﻿—quite harmless, eh?”

“Harmless!” ejaculated he, in unfeigned surprise, “why﻿—why, what *can* you mean?”

“Only slightly touched?” said I, touching my head. “I take it for granted that she is not particularly not dangerously affected, eh?”

“*Mon Dieu!* what *is* it you imagine? This lady, my particular old friend Madame Joyeuse, is as absolutely sane as myself. She has her little eccentricities, to be sure﻿—but then, you know, all old women﻿—all *very* old women﻿—are more or less eccentric!”

“To be sure,” said I﻿—“to be sure﻿—and then the rest of these ladies and gentlemen﻿—”

===Chinese===

「一件小事罢了，」马亚尔先生说。「这类事情我们惯了，实在不大放在心上。疯人们隔一阵子便齐声嚎一回；这个带动那个，如同有时夜里的一群狗。可是偶尔，协奏的喊嚎之后，跟着一个一齐挣脱的举动；那时候，自然，多少危险是要提防的。」

「你们照管着多少位？」

「眼下总共不过十位。」

「想必多半是女病人？」

「哦，不——个个都是男人，而且，我告诉您，都是壮实的家伙。」

「真的！我一向听说，疯人多半是温柔的女性。」

「一般是那样，可不总是。前一阵子，这里有二十七位病人上下；那数目里，不下十八位是女人；可是近来，事情变得多了，您也看见了。」

「是呀——变得多了，您也看见了，」这里插进来那位踢破拉普拉斯小姐小腿骨的先生。

「是呀——变得多了，您也看见了！」满座一齐应和。

「你们个个都闭上嘴！」我的主人怒冲冲地说。于是满座死一般寂静，将近一分钟。至于有一位夫人，她字字句句遵了马亚尔先生的吩咐——伸出舌头（那是一条长得过分的舌头），双手捧着它，十分驯顺地捧到席终。

「这位夫人，」我对马亚尔先生说，俯身朝他耳语——「这位方才开口的、给我们来咯咯哒的好夫人——她，想必，是无害的——全然无害，呃？」

「无害！」他叫出来，是真惊讶，「呃——呃，您*究竟*是什么意思？」

「只是轻症？」我说，指指自己的脑袋。「我想当然以为她不重——不危险，呃？」

「*我的上帝*（Mon Dieu）！您*到底*疑心什么？这位夫人，我的老交情儒瓦丝夫人，同我自己一样十足健全。她自然有小节上的怪僻——可是您知道，所有老妇人——所有*很*老的老妇人——或多或少都有点怪僻！」

「自然，」我说——「自然——那么这些女士先生们其余的诸位——」

===Original===

“Are my friends and keepers,” interupted Monsieur Maillard, drawing himself up with hauteur﻿—“my very good friends and assistants.”

“What! all of them?” I asked﻿—“the women and all?”

“Assuredly,” he said﻿—“we could not do at all without the women; they are the best lunatic nurses in the world; they have a way of their own, you know; their bright eyes have a marvellous effect﻿—something like the fascination of the snake, you know.”

“To be sure,” said I﻿—“to be sure! They behave a little odd, eh?﻿—they are a little *queer*, eh?﻿—don’t you think so?”

“Odd!﻿—queer!﻿—why, do you *really* think so? We are not very prudish, to be sure, here in the South﻿—do pretty much as we please﻿—enjoy life, and all that sort of thing, you know﻿—”

“To be sure,” said I﻿—“to be sure.”

“And then, perhaps, this Clos de Vougeôt is a little heady, you know﻿—a little *strong*﻿—you understand, eh?”

“To be sure,” said I﻿—“to be sure. By the by, Monsieur, did I understand you to say that the system you have adopted, in place of the celebrated soothing system, was one of very rigorous severity?”

“By no means. Our confinement is necessarily close; but the treatment﻿—the medical treatment, I mean﻿—is rather agreeable to the patients than otherwise.”

“And the new system is one of your own invention?”

“Not altogether. Some portions of it are referable to Professor Tarr, of whom you have, necessarily, heard; and, again, there are modifications in my plan which I am happy to acknowledge as belonging of right to the celebrated Fether, with whom, if I mistake not, you have the honor of an intimate acquaintance.”

“I am quite ashamed to confess,” I replied, “that I have never even heard the names of either gentleman before.”

“Good heavens!” ejaculated my host, drawing back his chair abruptly, and uplifting his hands. “I surely do not hear you aright! You did not intend to say, eh? that you had never *heard* either of the learned Doctor Tarr, or of the celebrated Professor Fether?”

“I am forced to acknowledge my ignorance,” I replied; “but the truth should be held inviolate above all things. Nevertheless, I feel humbled to the dust, not to be acquainted with the works of these, no doubt, extraordinary men. I will seek out their writings forthwith, and peruse them with deliberate care. Monsieur Maillard, you have really﻿—I must confess it﻿—you have *really*﻿—made me ashamed of myself!”

===Chinese===

「是我的朋友和看守，」马亚尔先生插进来，昂然挺直了身子——「我顶好的朋友和帮手。」

「什么！他们全都是？」我问——「连女人们都在内？」

「一定，」他说——「我们缺了女人根本不行；她们是世上最好的疯人看护；她们有她们的一套法子，您知道；她们亮亮的眼睛有奇效——有点像蛇的迷魂，您知道。」

「自然，」我说——「自然！她们举止有点怪，呃？——有点*古怪*，呃？——您不这样想么？」

「怪！——古怪！——咦，您*当真*这样想？我们南方人自然不十分拘礼——随心所欲——享乐人生，诸如此类，您知道——」

「自然，」我说——「自然。」

「再说，也许，这伏旧园酒有点上头，您知道——有点*烈*——您明白，呃？」

「自然，」我说——「自然。对了，先生，我听您说过，您用来代替那套大名鼎鼎的安抚体系的体系，是一种极严厉的东西，我没有听错吧？」

「全然不是。我们的拘禁自然严密；可是治法——我是说医学上的治法——病人反而受用得很。」

「而这新体系是您自己的发明？」

「不全是。有些部分可归于塔尔教授（Professor Tarr），您必然听说过他；再者，我方案里还有些改动，我乐于承认它们正当地属于大名鼎鼎的费瑟（Fether），倘若我没有记错，您同他还有知交之雅。」

「我很惭愧地招认，」我答，「我从前连这两位先生的名字也没有听说过。」

「老天！」我的主人叫起来，猛地把椅子往后一拉，举起了双手。「我总不至于听错了您的话！您不是想说，呃？说您连博学的塔尔医生（Doctor Tarr）、或大名鼎鼎的费瑟教授（Professor Fether），连*听说*也没有听说过？」

「我不得不承认我的无知，」我答；「可是真应当被奉为神圣，凌驾一切。尽管如此，竟不认识这些无疑非同凡响的人物的著作，我自觉羞到尘埃里。我立刻去寻他们的著作，用心细读。马亚尔先生，您实在——我必须招认——您*实在*叫我自己羞愧了！」

===Original===

And this was the fact.

“Say no more, my good young friend,” he said kindly, pressing my hand﻿—“join me now in a glass of Sauterne.”

We drank. The company followed our example without stint. They chatted﻿—they jested﻿—they laughed﻿—they perpetrated a thousand absurdities﻿—the fiddles shrieked﻿—the drum row-de-dowed﻿—the trombones bellowed like so many brazen bulls of Phalaris﻿—and the whole scene, growing gradually worse and worse, as the wines gained the ascendancy, became at length a sort of pandemonium in petto. In the meantime, Monsieur Maillard and myself, with some bottles of Sauterne and Vougeôt between us, continued our conversation at the top of the voice. A word spoken in an ordinary key stood no more chance of being heard than the voice of a fish from the bottom of Niagara Falls.

“And, sir,” said I, screaming in his ear, “you mentioned something before dinner about the danger incurred in the old system of soothing. How is that?”

“Yes,” he replied, “there was, occasionally, very great danger indeed. There is no accounting for the caprices of madmen; and, in my opinion as well as in that of Dr. Tarr and Professor Fether, it is *never* safe to permit them to run at large unattended. A lunatic may be ‘soothed,’ as it is called, for a time, but, in the end, he is very apt to become obstreperous. His cunning, too, is proverbial and great. If he has a project in view, he conceals his design with a marvellous wisdom; and the dexterity with which he counterfeits sanity, presents, to the metaphysician, one of the most singular problems in the study of mind. When a madman appears *thoroughly* sane, indeed, it is high time to put him in a straitjacket.”

“But the *danger*, my dear sir, of which you were speaking, in your own experience﻿—during your control of this house﻿—have you had practical reason to think liberty hazardous in the case of a lunatic?”

===Chinese===

事实也确乎如此。

「不必再说了，我年青的好朋友，」他和气地说，握住我的手——「现在同我共一杯苏玳（Sauterne）酒吧。」

我们喝了。满座毫无节制地照样喝了。他们闲谈——他们说笑——他们大笑——他们干出千百种荒唐事——提琴尖啸——鼓声咚咚——长号像法拉里斯的铜牛一样吼叫——整个场面，随着酒力占了上风，愈来愈糟，末了成了一座袖珍的群魔殿（pandemonium in petto）。这中间，马亚尔先生和我，中间摆着几瓶苏玳和伏旧园，扯着嗓子继续我们的谈话。以寻常调门说出的话，被人听见的指望，同从尼亚加拉瀑布底下发出的鱼声一般无二。

「可是，先生，」我朝他耳朵里喊，「饭前您提起过旧安抚体系招致的危险。那是怎么回事？」

「是的，」他答，「偶尔，危险实在非常大。疯人的脾气无从算计；照我的意见，也照塔尔医生（Dr. Tarr）和费瑟教授（Professor Fether）的意见，听凭他们无人看管地四散乱跑，*从来*不安全。一个疯人可以被所谓「安抚」一时，可是到头来，他极易变得难制。他的狡黠又是出了名的大。倘若他心里有一个图谋，他会以惊人的智慧藏起他的设计；他摹仿健全时那份熟练，向形而上学家呈出心智研究里最奇异的问题之一。说真的，当一个疯子显得*十足*健全时，正是把他塞进约束衣的高峰时刻。」

「可是您方才说的那个*危险*，亲爱的先生——照您自己的经历——在您掌管这座宅子期间——您可有实际的缘由，认为对疯子放任自由有险？」

===Original===

“Here?﻿—in my own experience?﻿—why, I may say, yes. For example:﻿—no *very* long while ago, a singular circumstance occurred in this very house. The ‘soothing system,’ you know, was then in operation, and the patients were at large. They behaved remarkably well﻿—especially so﻿—anyone of sense might have known that some devilish scheme was brewing from that particular fact, that the fellows behaved so *remarkably* well. And, sure enough, one fine morning the keepers found themselves pinioned hand and foot, and thrown into the cells, where they were attended, as if *they* were the lunatics, by the lunatics themselves, who had usurped the offices of the keepers.”

“You don’t tell me so! I never heard of anything so absurd in my life!”

“Fact﻿—it all came to pass by means of a stupid fellow﻿—a lunatic﻿—who, by some means, had taken it into his head that he had invented a better system of government than any ever heard of before﻿—of lunatic government, I mean. He wished to give his invention a trial, I suppose, and so he persuaded the rest of the patients to join him in a conspiracy for the overthrow of the reigning powers.”

“And he really succeeded?”

“No doubt of it. The keepers and kept were soon made to exchange places. Not that exactly either﻿—for the madmen had been free, but the keepers were shut up in cells forthwith, and treated, I am sorry to say, in a very cavalier manner.”

“But I presume a counterrevolution was soon effected. This condition of things could not have long existed. The country people in the neighborhood﻿—visitors coming to see the establishment﻿—would have given the alarm.”

“There you are out. The head rebel was too cunning for that. He admitted no visitors at all﻿—with the exception, one day, of a very stupid-looking young gentleman of whom he had no reason to be afraid. He let him in to see the place﻿—just by way of variety﻿—to have a little fun with him. As soon as he had gammoned him sufficiently, he let him out, and sent him about his business.”

“And *how* long, then, did the madmen reign?”

===Chinese===

「这里么？——照我自己的经历么？——呃，我可以说，有的。比方说：——不算*很*久之前，这座宅子里出过一桩奇事。『安抚体系』您知道，那时正行用着，病人四散自由。他们的举止好得出奇——特别得出奇——但凡有点头脑的人，单凭这个事实——那伙人举止得*这样*出奇——本该早知道某种恶魔的图谋正在酝酿。果真，一个好天气的早上，看守们发觉自己手脚都给捆住，扔进了斗室；在那里，仿佛*他们*才是疯人，由疯人们亲自照管——那些疯人已篡了看守的职分。」

「您不是当真这样说吧！平生我没听说过这样荒唐的事！」

「事实——这一切是靠一个愚蠢的家伙办成的——一个疯子——他不知怎么认定自己发明了一套比从来听说过的都好的施政制度——疯人施政，我是说。我想，他要给自己的发明试一试，于是他劝说其余病人同他结成密谋，推翻当权的势力。」

「毫无可疑。看守与被看守者很快换了位置。也不全然是这样——因为疯人们原是自由的，可是看守们随即被关进斗室，对不起，还受到非常轻慢的待遇。」

「可是我想，一场反革命不久便办成了。这样的局面决不会久存。近乡的乡下人——来参观机构的客人——总会报警的。」

「这里您错了。造反的头目太精明，不至于那样。他一概不放进访客——只除一天，放进来一个相貌蠢极的年轻绅士，他对他没有害怕的理由。他放他进来看看这地方——权当换换花样——拿他找点乐子。等把他哄够了，他就放他出去，打发他忙自己的营生去了。」

「那么疯人们*究竟*统治了多久？」

===Original===

“Oh, a very long time, indeed﻿—a month certainly﻿—how much longer I can’t precisely say. In the meantime, the lunatics had a jolly season of it﻿—that you may swear. They doffed their own shabby clothes, and made free with the family wardrobe and jewels. The cellars of the château were well stocked with wine; and these madmen are just the devils that know how to drink it. They lived well, I can tell you.”

“And the treatment﻿—what was the particular species of treatment which the leader of the rebels put into operation?”

“Why, as for that, a madman is not necessarily a fool, as I have already observed; and it is my honest opinion that his treatment was a much better treatment than that which it superseded. It was a very capital system indeed﻿—simple﻿—neat﻿—no trouble at all﻿—in fact it was delicious﻿—it was﻿—”

Here my host’s observations were cut short by another series of yells, of the same character as those which had previously disconcerted us. This time, however, they seemed to proceed from persons rapidly approaching.

“Gracious heavens!” I ejaculated﻿—“the lunatics have most undoubtedly broken loose.”

“I very much fear it is so,” replied Monsieur Maillard, now becoming excessively pale. He had scarcely finished the sentence, before loud shouts and imprecations were heard beneath the windows; and, immediately afterward, it became evident that some persons outside were endeavoring to gain entrance into the room. The door was beaten with what appeared to be a sledgehammer, and the shutters were wrenched and shaken with prodigious violence.

A scene of the most terrible confusion ensued. Monsieur Maillard, to my excessive astonishment threw himself under the sideboard. I had expected more resolution at his hands. The members of the orchestra, who, for the last fifteen minutes, had been seemingly too much intoxicated to do duty, now sprang all at once to their feet and to their instruments, and, scrambling upon their table, broke out, with one accord, into, “Yankee Doodle,” which they performed, if not exactly in tune, at least with an energy superhuman, during the whole of the uproar.

===Chinese===

「哦，实在很久——一个月是准有的——更长多少，我不能确切说。这中间，疯人们过了一段快活的日子——这您可以赌咒。他们脱下自己那身寒碜衣裳，放开手脚拿府上的衣橱和珠宝随便用。城堡的地窖里葡萄酒存得很足；这些疯人正是会喝酒的那路魔鬼。他们过得很好，我告诉您。」

「那治法呢——造反的头目施行的是哪一种特别的治法？」

「呃，至于那个，疯人未必是傻瓜，我方才已经说过；照我老实的意见，他的治法比它取代的那一套，好得多。那真是一套顶好的体系——简单——利落——毫无麻烦——实在说，妙不可言——它是——」

这里，主人的议论被另一阵喊嚎截断了，同先前搅扰我们的那些一个性质。可是这一回，它们似乎出自几个迅速走近的人。

「老天！」我叫出来——「疯人们无疑破笼而出了。」

「我很怕正是这样，」马亚尔先生答，此刻脸白得厉害。他这句话还没说完，窗户底下便传来大声的喊叫与咒骂；紧接着，分明有人在外面想法子冲进屋里来。门给一件像大锤的东西捶着，窗板给拧着、摇着，摇得极凶。

一幕最可怕的混乱随之而起。马亚尔先生叫我惊愕到极处，一头钻进了餐具柜底下。我原指望他更有胆量的。乐队的那班人，末一刻钟分明醉得不能当差，这时一齐跳起，抓起乐器，连滚带爬登上他们的桌子，异口同声地奏起《扬基歌》（Yankee Doodle）来；那调子奏得，纵说不上合调，至少带着一种超人的气力，奏满了整个这场大乱。

===Original===

Meantime, upon the main dining-table, among the bottles and glasses, leaped the gentleman who, with such difficulty, had been restrained from leaping there before. As soon as he fairly settled himself, he commenced an oration, which, no doubt, was a very capital one, if it could only have been heard. At the same moment, the man with the teetotum predilection, set himself to spinning around the apartment, with immense energy, and with arms outstretched at right angles with his body; so that he had all the air of a teetotum in fact, and knocked everybody down that happened to get in his way. And now, too, hearing an incredible popping and fizzing of champagne, I discovered at length, that it proceeded from the person who performed the bottle of that delicate drink during dinner. And then, again, the frog-man croaked away as if the salvation of his soul depended upon every note that he uttered. And, in the midst of all this, the continuous braying of a donkey arose over all. As for my old friend, Madame Joyeuse, I really could have wept for the poor lady, she appeared so terribly perplexed. All she did, however, was to stand up in a corner, by the fireplace, and sing out incessantly at the top of her voice, “Cock-a-doodle-de-dooooooh!”

And now came the climax﻿—the catastrophe of the drama. As no resistance, beyond whooping and yelling and cock-a-doodling, was offered to the encroachments of the party without, the ten windows were very speedily, and almost simultaneously, broken in. But I shall never forget the emotions of wonder and horror with which I gazed, when, leaping through these windows, and down among us pêle-mêle, fighting, stamping, scratching, and howling, there rushed a perfect army of what I took to be chimpanzees, orangutans, or big black baboons of the Cape of Good Hope.

===Chinese===

这工夫，那位先前给好不容易拦住、没能跳上桌面的先生，翻过瓶瓶罐罐，跳上了主餐桌。他一坐定，便开始演说；那演说无疑妙极，只要能听得见就是了。同一时刻，那位偏爱陀螺的人动手绕着屋子旋转，力气大得惊人，两臂伸直，同身子摆成直角；所以他整个人十足是一副陀螺的样子，凡挡在他路上的，都被他撞倒。此刻又听见难以置信的一片噗噗与嘶嘶的香槟声，我终于发觉那声音出自从前在席间扮演那种美酒的瓶子扮演者的身上。随后，青蛙人呱个不停，仿佛他灵魂的得救全系在他吐出的每一个音上。而在这一切中间，一头驴的连续的嘶鸣升到一切之上。至于我的老朋友儒瓦丝夫人，我真要为那可怜的夫人哭出来，她显得那样狼狈。可是她所做的一切，只是站到壁炉旁一个角落里，扯着嗓子不停地唱：「喔——喔——哒——喔喔喔——喔！」

高潮来了——这出戏的终局。由于外面那伙人的进逼，除了呐喊、嚎叫和喔喔喔之外，屋里不曾作任何抵抗，十扇窗便非常迅速地、几乎同时地被砸开了。可是我永远忘不了我当时惊愕与恐怖交并的情感：隔着这些窗跳进来、乱哄哄（pêle-mêle）落到我们中间的，是打着的、跺着的、抓挠着的、嚎叫着的整整一支军队，我以为是黑猩猩、猩猩，或好望角的大黑狒狒。

===Original===

I received a terrible beating﻿—after which I rolled under a sofa and lay still. After lying there some fifteen minutes, during which time I listened with all my ears to what was going on in the room, I came to same satisfactory denouement of this tragedy. Monsieur Maillard, it appeared, in giving me the account of the lunatic who had excited his fellows to rebellion, had been merely relating his own exploits. This gentleman had, indeed, some two or three years before, been the superintendent of the establishment, but grew crazy himself, and so became a patient. This fact was unknown to the travelling companion who introduced me. The keepers, ten in number, having been suddenly overpowered, were first well tarred, then carefully feathered, and then shut up in underground cells. They had been so imprisoned for more than a month, during which period Monsieur Maillard had generously allowed them not only the tar and feathers (which constituted his “system”), but some bread and abundance of water. The latter was pumped on them daily. At length, one escaping through a sewer, gave freedom to all the rest.

The “soothing system,” with important modifications, has been resumed at the château; yet I cannot help agreeing with Monsieur Maillard, that his own “treatment” was a very capital one of its kind. As he justly observed, it was “simple﻿—neat﻿—and gave no trouble at all﻿—not the least.”

I have only to add that, although I have searched every library in Europe for the works of Doctor *Tarr* and Professor *Fether*, I have, up to the present day, utterly failed in my endeavors at procuring an edition.

===Chinese===

我挨了一顿好打——之后我滚到一张沙发底下，躺下不动。在那里躺了十五分钟光景，其间我竖起耳朵听着屋里进行的一切，我对这出悲剧得出了一个差强人意的结局。原来，马亚尔先生给我讲那个煽动同伴造反的疯人的故事时，讲的不过是自己的功业。这位先生，实在说，两三年前原是这机构的主持人，可是自己也疯了，于是成了病人。这个事实，那位引我前来的旅伴并不知道。看守们一共十位，突然被制服，先给涂足了焦油，再仔细粘上羽毛，然后关进地下的斗室。他们被这样囚了一个多月；囚禁期间，马亚尔先生慷慨地不但许给他们焦油和羽毛（那构成了他的「体系」），还给他们一些面包和大量的水。后者是每天用泵抽上去浇的。终于，有一个从阴沟里逃出去，放出了其余全体。

「安抚体系」——经重要的改动——如今在城堡里恢复了；可是我不由得赞同马亚尔先生：他自己的那套「治法」，就它那一类而言，实在是一套顶好的。正如他公道地说的，它「简单——利落——毫无麻烦——丝毫不麻烦」。

我只需再添一句：虽然我搜遍了欧洲的每一座图书馆，寻找塔尔（*Tarr*）医生与费瑟（*Fether*）教授的著作，我直到今天，在弄到一版书这件事上，全然失败了。

## The Facts in the Case of M. Valdemar / 瓦尔德马先生病例的真相
===Original===

Of course I shall not pretend to consider it any matter for wonder, that the extraordinary case of M. Valdemar has excited discussion. It would have been a miracle had it not﻿—especially under the circumstances. Through the desire of all parties concerned, to keep the affair from the public, at least for the present, or until we had farther opportunities for investigation﻿—through our endeavors to effect this﻿—a garbled or exaggerated account made its way into society, and became the source of many unpleasant misrepresentations; and, very naturally, of a great deal of disbelief.

It is now rendered necessary that I give the *facts*﻿—as far as I comprehend them myself. They are, succinctly, these:

My attention, for the last three years, had been repeatedly drawn to the subject of Mesmerism; and, about nine months ago it occurred to me, quite suddenly, that in the series of experiments made hitherto, there had been a very remarkable and most unaccountable omission:﻿—no person had as yet been mesmerized in articulo mortis. It remained to be seen, first, whether, in such condition, there existed in the patient any susceptibility to the magnetic influence; secondly, whether, if any existed, it was impaired or increased by the condition; thirdly, to what extent, or for how long a period, the encroachments of Death might be arrested by the process. There were other points to be ascertained, but these most excited my curiosity﻿—the last in especial, from the immensely important character of its consequences.

===Chinese===

当然，我不会假装认为瓦尔德马先生这桩奇案引起议论有什么可怪。它若不引起议论，才是奇迹——尤其在这样的情形下。由于有关各方都愿此事暂不外传——至少眼下，等我们有进一步调查的机会——由于我们为此所作的种种努力，一份走样或夸大的说法流进了社会，成了许多不快的误传、也很自然地成了许多不信的源头。

现在有必要由我来说明*事实*——就我自己所领会的。扼要说来是这样：

三年来，我的注意一再被引向催眠术这个题目；约莫九个月前，我忽然想到：在迄今做过的一系列实验里，有一处极堪注意、也最难解释的疏漏——还不曾有人在死关头上被催眠。有待查明的是：第一，处在这种状态，病人身上还有没有对磁力影响的易感；第二，若有，这状态是削弱还是增强了它；第三，死的进迫，能被这手段止住到什么程度、止住多久。还有别的几点待查，但最鼓动我好奇的是这几条——尤其末一条，因为它后果的性质重到了极点。

===Original===

In looking around me for some subject by whose means I might test these particulars, I was brought to think of my friend, M. Ernest Valdemar, the well-known compiler of the “Bibliotheca Forensica,” and author (under the nom de plume of Issachar Marx) of the Polish versions of *Wallenstein* and *Gargantua*. M. Valdemar, who has resided principally at Harlem, NY, since the year 1839, is (or was) particularly noticeable for the extreme spareness of his person﻿—his lower limbs much resembling those of John Randolph; and, also, for the whiteness of his whiskers, in violent contrast to the blackness of his hair﻿—the latter, in consequence, being very generally mistaken for a wig. His temperament was markedly nervous, and rendered him a good subject for mesmeric experiment. On two or three occasions I had put him to sleep with little difficulty, but was disappointed in other results which his peculiar constitution had naturally led me to anticipate. His will was at no period positively, or thoroughly, under my control, and in regard to clairvoyance, I could accomplish with him nothing to be relied upon. I always attributed my failure at these points to the disordered state of his health. For some months previous to my becoming acquainted with him, his physicians had declared him in a confirmed phthisis. It was his custom, indeed, to speak calmly of his approaching dissolution, as of a matter neither to be avoided nor regretted.

When the ideas to which I have alluded first occurred to me, it was of course very natural that I should think of M. Valdemar. I knew the steady philosophy of the man too well to apprehend any scruples from *him*; and he had no relatives in America who would be likely to interfere. I spoke to him frankly upon the subject; and, to my surprise, his interest seemed vividly excited. I say to my surprise, for, although he had always yielded his person freely to my experiments, he had never before given me any tokens of sympathy with what I did. His disease was of that character which would admit of exact calculation in respect to the epoch of its termination in death; and it was finally arranged between us that he would send for me about twenty-four hours before the period announced by his physicians as that of his decease.

It is now rather more than seven months since I received, from M. Valdemar himself, the subjoined note:

My dear P﻿—﻿—﻿,

===Chinese===

环顾四周，寻一个可供验证这几点的对象，我想到了我的朋友埃内斯特·瓦尔德马先生——《法学书库》那位著名的编纂者，又（以伊萨卡·马克思的笔名）是《华伦斯坦》与《巨人传》波兰译本的作者。瓦尔德马先生自 1839 年起主要寓居纽约哈莱姆，他（或说曾经）特别引人注目的，是他极度清瘦的身形——两条下肢很像约翰·伦道夫的；还有他颊须的白，同头发的黑形成猛烈的对照——以至于那头发极普遍地被误认作假发。他的气质显著地神经质，使他成为催眠实验的好对象。有两三回，我毫不费力就使他入睡；但他那特殊的体质使我自然期待的其他效果，却令我失望。他的意志从不曾确实地、彻底地受我掌控；至于透视，我在他身上一无所成。我一向把这些失败归咎于他健康的失调。在我结识他之前几个月，医生们已宣告他患了确诊的瘭病。他也实在惯于平静地谈他临近的终局，像谈一件既不必避免、也不必惋惜的事。

我提到的那些念头初起时，我自然想到瓦尔德马先生，是最顺理成章的。这人的坚定哲学我知道得太清楚，不担心*他*有什么顾忌；他在美洲又没有可能出面干预的亲属。我同他坦白谈了这题目；出乎我的意料，他的兴味像被强烈地燃起来了。我所以说出乎意料，是因为他虽然一向慨然以身供我实验，却从不曾对我所做的事露出过一点同情。他的病，其性质恰容许对死期作精确的计算；我们终于约定：他会在医生们宣告的死期前约二十四小时差人来叫我。

此刻距我收到瓦尔德马先生亲笔的下面这封短简，已有七个多月：

亲爱的 P——：

===Original===

You may as well come *now*. D﻿—﻿— and F﻿—﻿— are agreed that I cannot hold out beyond tomorrow midnight; and I think they have hit the time very nearly.

Valdemar.

I received this note within half an hour after it was written, and in fifteen minutes more I was in the dying man’s chamber. I had not seen him for ten days, and was appalled by the fearful alteration which the brief interval had wrought in him. His face wore a leaden hue; the eyes were utterly lustreless; and the emaciation was so extreme that the skin had been broken through by the cheekbones. His expectoration was excessive. The pulse was barely perceptible. He retained, nevertheless, in a very remarkable manner, both his mental power and a certain degree of physical strength. He spoke with distinctness﻿—took some palliative medicines without aid﻿—and, when I entered the room, was occupied in penciling memoranda in a pocketbook. He was propped up in the bed by pillows. Doctors D﻿—﻿— and F﻿—﻿— were in attendance.

After pressing Valdemar’s hand, I took these gentlemen aside, and obtained from them a minute account of the patient’s condition. The left lung had been for eighteen months in a semi-osseous or cartilaginous state, and was, of course, entirely useless for all purposes of vitality. The right, in its upper portion, was also partially, if not thoroughly, ossified, while the lower region was merely a mass of purulent tubercles, running one into another. Several extensive perforations existed; and, at one point, permanent adhesion to the ribs had taken place. These appearances in the right lobe were of comparatively recent date. The ossification had proceeded with very unusual rapidity; no sign of it had been discovered a month before, and the adhesion had only been observed during the three previous days. Independently of the phthisis, the patient was suspected of aneurism of the aorta; but on this point the osseous symptoms rendered an exact diagnosis impossible. It was the opinion of both physicians that M. Valdemar would die about midnight on the morrow (Sunday). It was then seven o’clock on Saturday evening.

On quitting the invalid’s bedside to hold conversation with myself, Doctors D﻿—﻿— and F﻿—﻿— had bidden him a final farewell. It had not been their intention to return; but, at my request, they agreed to look in upon the patient about ten the next night.

===Chinese===

您不妨*现在*就来。D——同 F——都断定我捱不过明天半夜；我想他们掐得八九不高十。

瓦尔德马

短简写就不到半个钟头我便收到；再过一刻钟，我已坐在垂死者的房里。我有十天不曾见他，短短十天在他身上造成的那可怕的变化，叫我骇然。他的脸罩着一层铅色；眼睛全然无光；消瘦到极处，颧骨竟顶破了皮。他的痰咳得凶。脉搏几乎摸不出。然而他以极不寻常的方式，既保着心智的力气，又保着几分体力。他说话清楚——不服人手、自己吞下几剂姑息的药——我进屋时，他正忙着在记事本上用铅笔录备忘。他靠枕头支在床上。D——和 F——两位医生在旁侍疾。

握过瓦尔德马的手，我把两位先生拉到一旁，从他们口中得了病况的细账。左肺十八个月来已成半骨半软骨的状态，对生命的一切目的自然全无用处。右肺上叶也部分、即便不是全部骨化；下叶只是一团脓性结核，彼此串连。有几处大面积穿孔；有一处，同肋骨发生了永久性的粘连。右叶的这些征象，年代较近。骨化进展得异常地快；一个月前还没有发现它的痕迹；粘连也只是三天前才见。除瘭病外，病人还疑似主动脉瘤；但在这一点上，骨质的症状使精确的诊断无从下手。两位医生的意见是：瓦尔德马先生大约明日（星期日）半夜死去。那是星期六晚七点钟。

D——和 F——两位医生离开病榻来同我谈话时，已向他作了最后的道别。本不打算再回来；但应我的请求，他们答应次晚十点左右再来看视。

===Original===

When they had gone, I spoke freely with M. Valdemar on the subject of his approaching dissolution, as well as, more particularly, of the experiment proposed. He still professed himself quite willing and even anxious to have it made, and urged me to commence it at once. A male and a female nurse were in attendance; but I did not feel myself altogether at liberty to engage in a task of this character with no more reliable witnesses than these people, in case of sudden accident, might prove. I therefore postponed operations until about eight the next night, when the arrival of a medical student with whom I had some acquaintance, (Mr. Theodore L﻿—﻿—﻿l,) relieved me from farther embarrassment. It had been my design, originally, to wait for the physicians; but I was induced to proceed, first, by the urgent entreaties of M. Valdemar, and secondly, by my conviction that I had not a moment to lose, as he was evidently sinking fast.

Mr. L﻿—﻿—﻿l was so kind as to accede to my desire that he would take notes of all that occurred, and it is from his memoranda that what I now have to relate is, for the most part, either condensed or copied verbatim.

It wanted about five minutes of eight when, taking the patient’s hand, I begged him to state, as distinctly as he could, to Mr. L﻿—﻿—﻿l, whether he (M. Valdemar) was entirely willing that I should make the experiment of mesmerizing him in his then condition.

He replied feebly, yet quite audibly, “Yes, I wish to be. I fear you have mesmerized”﻿—adding immediately afterwards, “I fear you have deferred it too long.”
