## Hop-Frog / 跳蛙
===Original===

I never knew anyone so keenly alive to a joke as the king was. He seemed to live only for joking. To tell a good story of the joke kind, and to tell it well, was the surest road to his favor. Thus it happened that his seven ministers were all noted for their accomplishments as jokers. They all took after the king, too, in being large, corpulent, oily men, as well as inimitable jokers. Whether people grow fat by joking, or whether there is something in fat itself which predisposes to a joke, I have never been quite able to determine; but certain it is that a lean joker is a *rara avis in terris*.

About the refinements, or, as he called them, the “ghosts” of wit, the king troubled himself very little. He had an especial admiration for *breadth* in a jest, and would often put up with *length*, for the sake of it. Over-niceties wearied him. He would have preferred Rabelais’ *Gargantua* to the *Zadig* of Voltaire: and, upon the whole, practical jokes suited his taste far better than verbal ones.

At the date of my narrative, professing jesters had not altogether gone out of fashion at court. Several of the great continental “powers” still retain their “fools,” who wore motley, with caps and bells, and who were expected to be always ready with sharp witticisms, at a moment’s notice, in consideration of the crumbs that fell from the royal table.

*Our* king, as a matter of course, retained his “fool.” The fact is, he *required* something in the way of folly﻿—if only to counterbalance the heavy wisdom of the seven wise men who were his ministers﻿—not to mention himself.

His fool, or professional jester, was not *only* a fool, however. His value was trebled in the eyes of the king, by the fact of his being also a dwarf and a cripple. Dwarfs were as common at court, in those days, as fools; and many monarchs would have found it difficult to get through their days (days are rather longer at court than elsewhere) without both a jester to laugh *with*, and a dwarf to laugh *at*. But, as I have already observed, your jesters, in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred, are fat, round, and unwieldy﻿—so that it was no small source of self-gratulation with our king that, in Hop-Frog (this was the fool’s name), he possessed a triplicate treasure in one person.

===Chinese===

我从不知道有谁像那位国王那样，对笑话如此热衷。他仿佛专为说笑而活。讲一个上好的笑话，讲得又好，是博取他欢心最稳当的路。于是他的七位大臣，个个以说笑的本领著称。他们也都在体格上学足了国王：又高大、又肥硕、又油光满面，还是无可企及的说笑大家。人究竟是越说笑越肥呢，还是肥肉里本有什么东西叫人爱说笑，我一直断不定；但可以断定的是，瘦个子笑匠是 rara avis in terris（世间的稀有禽鸟）。

至于风趣的精微之处——或者照他的叫法，风趣的「鬼魂」——国王是很不耐烦去费神的。他特别赏鉴的是笑话的「宽度」，为了宽，常常连「长度」也一并忍了。过分精雅的玩意儿叫他疲倦。他宁可要拉伯雷的《巨人传》，不要伏尔泰的《查第格》：而且总的說来，恶作剧比口头戏言对他的口味得多。

在我叙述的那个年代，以说笑为业的小丑，在宫廷里还没有全然过时。大陆上几个大的「强权」仍养着他们的「傻子」，穿彩衣，戴缀铃的帽，随时随刻备着俏皮话，以领受御桌上掉下的残屑。

我们的国王，当然也养着一个「傻子」。实情是，他需要一点愚行——哪怕只为抵销他那七位智者大臣沉重的智慧——更不必说他自己了。

不过他的傻子，职业小丑，还不单是个傻子。他同时又是个侏儒兼残废，这在国王眼里，身价登时涨了三倍。那时节，侏儒同傻子一样，在宫廷里比比皆是；多少君主，若没有一个可供同乐的笑匠、一个可供取笑的侏儒，日子便难过下去（宫廷里的日子，比别处可要长得多）。可是，如我方才所说，笑匠百例里有九十九例是肥肥圆圆、笨手笨脚的——所以在跳蛙（这就是那傻子的名字）身上，我们的国王一人得了三件宝贝，其自得也就非同小可了。

===Original===

I believe the name “Hop-Frog” was *not* that given to the dwarf by his sponsors at baptism, but it was conferred upon him, by general consent of the seven ministers, on account of his inability to walk as other men do. In fact, Hop-Frog could only get along by a sort of interjectional gait﻿—something between a leap and a wriggle﻿—a movement that afforded illimitable amusement, and of course consolation, to the king, for (notwithstanding the protuberance of his stomach and a constitutional swelling of the head) the king, by his whole court, was accounted a capital figure.

But although Hop-Frog, through the distortion of his legs, could move only with great pain and difficulty along a road or floor, the prodigious muscular power which nature seemed to have bestowed upon his arms, by way of compensation for deficiency in the lower limbs, enabled him to perform many feats of wonderful dexterity, where trees or ropes were in question, or anything else to climb. At such exercises he certainly much more resembled a squirrel, or a small monkey, than a frog.

I am not able to say, with precision, from what country Hop-Frog originally came. It was from some barbarous region, however, that no person ever heard of﻿—a vast distance from the court of our king. Hop-Frog, and a young girl very little less dwarfish than himself (although of exquisite proportions, and a marvellous dancer), had been forcibly carried off from their respective homes in adjoining provinces, and sent as presents to the king, by one of his ever-victorious generals.

Under these circumstances, it is not to be wondered at that a close intimacy arose between the two little captives. Indeed, they soon became sworn friends. Hop-Frog, who, although he made a great deal of sport, was by no means popular, had it not in his power to render Trippetta many services; but *she*, on account of her grace and exquisite beauty (although a dwarf), was universally admired and petted; so she possessed much influence; and never failed to use it, whenever she could, for the benefit of Hop-Frog.

===Chinese===

我相信「跳蛙」并不是他教父教母在洗礼上给他起的名字，而是七位大臣一致同意加给他的，因为他不能像常人那样走路。事实上，跳蛙只能靠一种感叹词式的步法行进——介于跳跃与扭动之间的什么东西——这步法给国王供给了无穷的笑料，自然还有安慰，因为（尽管国王腆着肚子，脑袋又天生虚胖）满朝上下还是公认他一表人才。

然而，跳蛙虽然双腿变形，在平路上、地板上走路要忍着大痛大难，造化却仿佛为补偿他下肢的欠缺，把他双臂的筋力给得惊人，凡有树可攀、绳可爬、有什么可登的，他便能干出许多神妙矫捷的活计来。做这类运动，他确实更像一只松鼠，或一只小猴，而不像蛙。

跳蛙原先从哪国来，我说不确切。只知道是某个谁也不曾听说的蛮荒地域——离我们国王的宫廷极远极远。跳蛙同一个只比他矮不了多少的年轻姑娘（身段却极匀称，舞跳得出神入化），是被人从各自家中强行掳走的，两家只在相邻的省份，被我们国王麾下一位无往不胜的将军当作礼物献了进来。

在这样的境遇下，两个小俘虏之间生出亲密的情谊，就毫不足怪了。他们果真很快就成了莫逆。跳蛙虽然尽给人逗乐，人缘却极坏，帮不上特里佩塔什么忙；而她，凭她的优雅和绝色（虽是侏儒），到处受人宠爱娇惯；所以她颇有势力，而凡有机会，从不忘了为跳蛙出力。

===Original===

On some grand state occasion﻿—I forgot what﻿—the king determined to have a masquerade, and whenever a masquerade or anything of that kind, occurred at our court, then the talents, both of Hop-Frog and Trippetta were sure to be called into play. Hop-Frog, in especial, was so inventive in the way of getting up pageants, suggesting novel characters, and arranging costumes, for masked balls, that nothing could be done, it seems, without his assistance.

The night appointed for the fête had arrived. A gorgeous hall had been fitted up, under Trippetta’s eye, with every kind of device which could possibly give éclat to a masquerade. The whole court was in a fever of expectation. As for costumes and characters, it might well be supposed that everybody had come to a decision on such points. Many had made up their minds (as to what roles they should assume) a week, or even a month, in advance; and, in fact, there was not a particle of indecision anywhere﻿—except in the case of the king and his seven minsters. Why *they* hesitated I never could tell, unless they did it by way of a joke. More probably, they found it difficult, on account of being so fat, to make up their minds. At all events, time flew; and, as a last resort they sent for Trippetta and Hop-Frog.

When the two little friends obeyed the summons of the king they found him sitting at his wine with the seven members of his cabinet council; but the monarch appeared to be in a very ill humor. He knew that Hop-Frog was not fond of wine, for it excited the poor cripple almost to madness; and madness is no comfortable feeling. But the king loved his practical jokes, and took pleasure in forcing Hop-Frog to drink and (as the king called it) “to be merry.”

“Come here, Hop-Frog,” said he, as the jester and his friend entered the room; “swallow this bumper to the health of your absent friends, [here Hop-Frog sighed,] and then let us have the benefit of your invention. We want characters﻿—*characters*, man﻿—something novel﻿—out of the way. We are wearied with this everlasting sameness. Come, drink! the wine will brighten your wits.”

===Chinese===

在某一个盛大的节典上——我忘了是什么——国王决意要办一场化装舞会；每逢宫里办化装舞会或那一类的事，跳蛙和特里佩塔的才具便必定要派上用场。尤其是跳蛙，编排盛装游行、设计新奇角色、张罗化装舞会的行头，样样别出心裁，离了他，似乎什么事也办不成。

行乐之夜到了。一座华丽的厅堂，在特里佩塔的监看下布置起来，凡能给化装舞会增光的机关，应有尽有。满朝上下翘首企足。至于行头和角色，可以想见，人人早已拿定了主意。许多人早在一个月甚至一星期之前，就定了自己该扮什么；事实上，处处没有半点犹豫——只除开国王和他的七位大臣。他们为什么犹豫，我说不清，除非他们把这犹豫也当作一个玩笑。多半是因为太肥，连主意也肥得难下。总之，时间飞逝；万般无奈，他们派人去唤特里佩塔和跳蛙。

两个小朋友应召而来，看见国王正同内阁的七位成员饮酒；君王的神色很不痛快。他知道跳蛙不爱喝酒，因为酒会把这可怜的残废人激得几乎发狂；而发狂不是好受的滋味。可国王偏爱恶作剧，乐于强跳蛙喝酒，乐于（照国王的说法）叫他「快活快活」。

「过来，跳蛙，」小丑和他的朋友进屋时他说，「干了这一大杯，祝你不在跟前的好友们健康（跳蛙在这里叹了口气），然后让我们领你的妙想。我们要角色——角色，伙计——要新奇的——别开生面的。这老一套把我们腻死了。来，喝！酒会叫你的脑子亮起来。」

===Original===

Hop-Frog endeavored, as usual, to get up a jest in reply to these advances from the king; but the effort was too much. It happened to be the poor dwarf’s birthday, and the command to drink to his “absent friends” forced the tears to his eyes. Many large, bitter drops fell into the goblet as he took it, humbly, from the hand of the tyrant.

“Ah! ha! ha! ha!” roared the latter, as the dwarf reluctantly drained the beaker. “See what a glass of good wine can do! Why, your eyes are shining already!”

Poor fellow! his large eyes *gleamed*, rather than shone; for the effect of wine on his excitable brain was not more powerful than instantaneous. He placed the goblet nervously on the table, and looked round upon the company with a half-insane stare. They all seemed highly amused at the success of the king’s “*joke*.”

“And now to business,” said the prime minister, a *very* fat man.

“Yes,” said the King; “Come, Hop-Frog, lend us your assistance. Characters, my fine fellow; we stand in need of characters﻿—all of us﻿—ha! ha! ha!” and as this was seriously meant for a joke, his laugh was chorused by the seven.

Hop-Frog also laughed, although feebly and somewhat vacantly.

“Come, come,” said the king, impatiently, “have you nothing to suggest?”

“I am endeavoring to think of something *novel*,” replied the dwarf, abstractedly, for he was quite bewildered by the wine.

“Endeavoring!” cried the tyrant, fiercely; “what do you mean by *that*? Ah, I perceive. You are sulky, and want more wine. Here, drink this!” and he poured out another goblet full and offered it to the cripple, who merely gazed at it, gasping for breath.

“Drink, I say!” shouted the monster, “or by the fiends﻿—”

The dwarf hesitated. The king grew purple with rage. The courtiers smirked. Trippetta, pale as a corpse, advanced to the monarch’s seat, and, falling on her knees before him, implored him to spare her friend.

The tyrant regarded her, for some moments, in evident wonder at her audacity. He seemed quite at a loss what to do or say﻿—how most becomingly to express his indignation. At last, without uttering a syllable, he pushed her violently from him, and threw the contents of the brimming goblet in her face.

The poor girl got up as best she could, and, not daring even to sigh, resumed her position at the foot of the table.

===Chinese===

跳蛙照例想编句笑话回敬国王的这番抬举；可这回力不从心。偏偏这天是可怜侏儒的生日，这一声为他「不在跟前的好友」干杯的命令，逼出了他的眼泪。他从暴君手里谦卑地接过酒杯时，许多大颗大颗的苦泪落进了杯中。

「啊！哈！哈！哈！」侏儒勉强干杯时，暴君吼道。「看，一杯好酒多管用！怎么，你的眼睛已经亮了！」

可怜人！他那双大眼睛是凶光直冒，说不上亮；因为酒在他易激的脑子上的药力，来得比什么都快。他颤着手把酒杯放回桌上，半疯似的环视众人。众人对国王这记「玩笑」的得手，一个个乐不可支。

「现在说正事。」首相说——一个肥得不能再肥的人。

「是，」国王说；「来，跳蛙，帮我们一把。角色，我的好伙计；我们需要角色——我们全都需要——哈！哈！哈！」这话既是当正经玩笑说的，七位便齐声附和着笑。

跳蛙也笑了，只是笑得有气无力，有些发直。

「来，来，」国王不耐烦地说，「你就没有一点建议？」

「我正想法子来点新奇的，」侏儒心不在焉地答，酒把他灌糊涂了。

「正想法子！」暴君恶狠狠地喊；「这是什么话？啊，我明白了。你在闹脾气，想再讨酒喝。来，喝了这杯！」他又满满斟上一杯，递到残废人面前；残废人只瞪着它，喘不上气来。

「喝，我说！」这畜生吼道，「不然凭众恶魔起誓——」

侏儒还在踌躇。国王气得发紫。朝臣们窃笑。特里佩塔面白如尸，抢到君王座前，跪倒在他脚下，哀求他饶了她的朋友。

暴君把她端详了几秒，显然惊于她的胆大。他似乎一时不知如何是好、说什么是好——怎样出口恶气才最得体。末了，他一言不发，一把将她狠命推开，把满杯的酒泼在了她脸上。

可怜的姑娘勉力爬起来，连叹都不敢叹一声，回到桌子下首她的位置上。

===Original===

There was a dead silence for about half a minute, during which the falling of a leaf, or of a feather, might have been heard. It was interrupted by a low, but harsh and protracted *grating* sound which seemed to come at once from every corner of the room.

“What﻿—what﻿—*what* are you making that noise for?” demanded the king, turning furiously to the dwarf.

The latter seemed to have recovered, in great measure, from his intoxication, and looking fixedly but quietly into the tyrant’s face, merely ejaculated:

“I﻿—I? How could it have been me?”

“The sound appeared to come from without,” observed one of the courtiers. “I fancy it was the parrot at the window, whetting his bill upon his cage-wires.”

“True,” replied the monarch, as if much relieved by the suggestion; “but, on the honor of a knight, I could have sworn that it was the gritting of this vagabond’s teeth.”

Hereupon the dwarf laughed (the king was too confirmed a joker to object to anyone’s laughing), and displayed a set of large, powerful, and very repulsive teeth. Moreover, he avowed his perfect willingness to swallow as much wine as desired. The monarch was pacified; and having drained another bumper with no very perceptible ill effect, Hop-Frog entered at once, and with spirit, into the plans for the masquerade.

“I cannot tell what was the association of idea,” observed he, very tranquilly, and as if he had never tasted wine in his life, “but *just after* your majesty, had struck the girl and thrown the wine in her face﻿—*just after* your majesty had done this, and while the parrot was making that odd noise outside the window, there came into my mind a capital diversion﻿—one of my own country frolics﻿—often enacted among us, at our masquerades: but here it will be new altogether. Unfortunately, however, it requires a company of eight persons and﻿—”

“Here we *are*!” cried the king, laughing at his acute discovery of the coincidence; “eight to a fraction﻿—I and my seven ministers. Come! what is the diversion?”

“We call it,” replied the cripple, “the Eight Chained Orangutans, and it really is excellent sport if well enacted.”

“*We* will enact it,” remarked the king, drawing himself up, and lowering his eyelids.

“The beauty of the game,” continued Hop-Frog, “lies in the fright it occasions among the women.”

“Capital!” roared in chorus the monarch and his ministry.

===Chinese===

死一样的寂静约有半分钟，这工夫里，一片叶子、一根羽毛落地都听得见。寂静被一种低而尖利、绵长的锉磨声打断——那声音仿佛同时从屋子四角里发出来。

「你——你——你弄出这声音干什么？」国王狂怒地转向侏儒喝问。

后者仿佛已从醉酒里大半醒转，定定地、却安静地望着暴君的脸，只吐出一句：

「我——我？怎么会是我呢？」

「声音像是外头传来的，」一位朝臣说。「我想是窗上的鹦鹉，在笼丝上磨喙。」

「不错，」君王答，这话仿佛叫他大大松了口气，「但凭骑士的名誉，我本可以发誓，那是这流氓在锉牙。」

侏儒闻言笑了（国王是说笑的行家，从不忌讳别人笑），露出一口又大又结实、非常怕人的牙。他还表示，多少酒他都乐于奉陪。君王的气平了；又干下一大杯，看不出什么坏处，跳蛙便立刻精神抖擞地谈起化装舞会的方案来。

「我说不上是什么念头联的，」他极平静地说，仿佛生平从不曾沾过酒，「可就在陛下打了那姑娘、把酒泼在她脸上之后——就在陛下做完了这一手、窗外的鹦鹉正怪叫的那工夫——我心里起了一个顶好的余兴——我们家乡的一种嬉戏——我们那里化装的时候常演：可在这里，保管全新。只是不幸，它要八个人一伙，而且——」

「我们正好是八个！」国王喊，为自己的敏锐发现这巧合而大笑；「不多不少八个——我和我的七位大臣。快讲！什么余兴？」

「我们叫它，」残废人说，「八只锁链猩猩，演得好，实在是一等一的乐子。」

「我们就来演，」国王说，挺起身子，垂下眼皮。

「这游戏的妙处，」跳蛙接着说，「在它吓着娘儿们。」

「妙极！」君王同他的内阁齐声吼道。

===Original===

“I will equip you as orangutans,” proceeded the dwarf; “leave all that to me. The resemblance shall be so striking, that the company of masqueraders will take you for real beasts﻿—and of course, they will be as much terrified as astonished.”

“Oh, this is exquisite!” exclaimed the king. “Hop-Frog! I will make a man of you.”

“The chains are for the purpose of increasing the confusion by their jangling. You are supposed to have escaped, en masse, from your keepers. Your majesty cannot conceive the *effect* produced, at a masquerade, by eight chained orangutans, imagined to be real ones by most of the company; and rushing in with savage cries, among the crowd of delicately and gorgeously habited men and women. The *contrast* is inimitable.”

“It *must* be,” said the king: and the council arose hurriedly (as it was growing late), to put in execution the scheme of Hop-Frog.

His mode of equipping the party as orangutans was very simple, but effective enough for his purposes. The animals in question had, at the epoch of my story, very rarely been seen in any part of the civilized world; and as the imitations made by the dwarf were sufficiently beast-like and more than sufficiently hideous, their truthfulness to nature was thus thought to be secured.

The king and his ministers were first encased in tight-fitting stockinet shirts and drawers. They were then saturated with tar. At this stage of the process, someone of the party suggested feathers; but the suggestion was at once overruled by the dwarf, who soon convinced the eight, by ocular demonstration, that the hair of such a brute as the orangutan was much more efficiently represented by *flax*. A thick coating of the latter was accordingly plastered upon the coating of tar. A long chain was now procured. First, it was passed about the waist of the king, *and tied*; then about another of the party, and also tied; then about all successively, in the same manner. When this chaining arrangement was complete, and the party stood as far apart from each other as possible, they formed a circle; and to make all things appear natural, Hop-Frog passed the residue of the chain in two diameters, at right angles, across the circle, after the fashion adopted, at the present day, by those who capture chimpanzees, or other large apes, in Borneo.

===Chinese===

「我来把你们装扮成猩猩，」侏儒往下说；「一切都交给我。扮得保管像煞，满场的化装客要把你们当成真野兽——自然，他们又惊又吓，惊吓加倍。」

「哦，妙不可言！」国王喊。「跳蛙！我要抬举你做个上等人。」

「锁链是用来叮当作响、添乱添惊的。你们就算是集体从看管人手里逃出来的。陛下想象不出，化装舞会上八只锁链猩猩——满场宾客多半当了真——嘶叫着冲进衣香鬓影的男女人堆里，是什么效果。那对比，妙不可仿。」

「一定妙，」国王说；内阁慌忙起座（时候不早了），去执行跳蛙的计划。

他把这一伙装扮成猩猩的法子极简单，可对他的目的却足够了。在我故事的年代，猩猩这种动物在文明世界的任何地方都极难见到；侏儒做出的这副扮相又够兽性、更够狰狞，它的逼真自然万无一失。

国王和他的大臣先被套进紧身的针织衫裤，随后浑身浇透沥青。进行到这一步，有人提议粘羽毛；这提议立刻被侏儒驳回，他当场用眼见为实说服了八位：像猩猩这样的畜生，它的毛用亚麻来仿，效力远比羽毛大。于是一厚层亚麻糊上了沥青层。然后取来一条长链。先缠上国王的腰，打结；再缠上另一位，也打结；再依次缠上全体，照此办理。锁链拴停当，一伙人彼此离得越远越好，围成一个圈；为使一切逼真，跳蛙又把余下的链子折成两股，成十字交叉，从两个直径方向横过圆圈——就像如今婆罗洲人捕黑猩猩或别的大猿用的那个办法。

===Original===

The grand saloon in which the masquerade was to take place, was a circular room, very lofty, and receiving the light of the sun only through a single window at top. At night (the season for which the apartment was especially designed) it was illuminated principally by a large chandelier, depending by a chain from the centre of the skylight, and lowered, or elevated, by means of a counterbalance as usual; but (in order not to look unsightly) this latter passed outside the cupola and over the roof.

The arrangements of the room had been left to Trippetta’s superintendence; but, in some particulars, it seems, she had been guided by the calmer judgment of her friend the dwarf. At his suggestion it was that, on this occasion, the chandelier was removed. Its waxen drippings (which, in weather so warm, it was quite impossible to prevent) would have been seriously detrimental to the rich dresses of the guests, who, on account of the crowded state of the saloon, could not *all* be expected to keep from out its centre; that is to say, from under the chandelier. Additional sconces were set in various parts of the hall, out of the war, and a flambeau, emitting sweet odor, was placed in the right hand of each of the Caryatides that stood against the wall﻿—some fifty or sixty altogether.

The eight orangutans, taking Hop-Frog’s advice, waited patiently until midnight (when the room was thoroughly filled with masqueraders) before making their appearance. No sooner had the clock ceased striking, however, than they rushed, or rather rolled in, all together﻿—for the impediments of their chains caused most of the party to fall, and all to stumble as they entered.

The excitement among the masqueraders was prodigious, and filled the heart of the king with glee. As had been anticipated, there were not a few of the guests who supposed the ferocious-looking creatures to be beasts of *some* kind in reality, if not precisely orangutans. Many of the women swooned with affright; and had not the king taken the precaution to exclude all weapons from the saloon, his party might soon have expiated their frolic in their blood. As it was, a general rush was made for the doors; but the king had ordered them to be locked immediately upon his entrance; and, at the dwarf’s suggestion, the keys had been deposited with *him*.

===Chinese===

举行化装舞会的大厅是一间圆厅，极高，只在顶上开一扇天窗采光。入夜（这屋子正是专为夜里用的），照明主要靠一盏大吊灯，吊灯由一根链子挂在天窗正中，照例凭一个平衡锤升降；但（为了观瞻）那平衡锤是穿过穹顶外面、翻过屋顶走的。

厅堂的布置本来全交特里佩塔督办；但有几处，看来她依了她朋友那残废人更冷静的判断。正是依他的主意，这一次吊灯撤去了。蜡烛的滴淌（天气这样热，万难防止）势必要糟蹋宾客们的华服；厅里人那样挤，不能指望人人都躲开厅心——也就是说，躲开吊灯底下。厅内各处又在碍不着人的地方添了壁灯架；靠墙立着的那些女像柱——总共有五六十尊——每尊的右手里都插上一支散发香气的火把。

八只猩猩依了跳蛙的嘱咐，耐心守到午夜（厅里挤满了化装客）才露面。钟声刚落，他们便一齐冲——不如说滚——了进来；因为锁链的拖累，进门的多半跌倒，个个踉跄。

化装客中的轰动非同小可，国王的心里乐开了花。不出所料，宾客中不止几个把那群凶相毕露的家伙当成了真野兽，纵使未必恰是猩猩。许多妇女吓得晕了过去；若不是国王预先防了一手，不准一件兵器进厅，他这一伙怕早已拿血赎了这场嬉闹。虽是这样，人潮还是朝各门狂涌；可国王早已吩咐，他一进厅便把各门落锁；而且依侏儒之计，钥匙都交在了侏儒手里。

===Original===

While the tumult was at its height, and each masquerader attentive only to his own safety (for, in fact, there was much *real* danger from the pressure of the excited crowd), the chain by which the chandelier ordinarily hung, and which had been drawn up on its removal, might have been seen very gradually to descend, until its hooked extremity came within three feet of the floor.

Soon after this, the king and his seven friends having reeled about the hall in all directions, found themselves, at length, in its centre, and, of course, in immediate contact with the chain. While they were thus situated, the dwarf, who had followed noiselessly at their heels, inciting them to keep up the commotion, took hold of their own chain at the intersection of the two portions which crossed the circle diametrically and at right angles. Here, with the rapidity of thought, he inserted the hook from which the chandelier had been wont to depend; and, in an instant, by some unseen agency, the chandelier-chain was drawn so far upward as to take the hook out of reach, and, as an inevitable consequence, to drag the orangutans together in close connection, and face to face.

The masqueraders, by this time, had recovered, in some measure, from their alarm; and, beginning to regard the whole matter as a well-contrived pleasantry, set up a loud shout of laughter at the predicament of the apes.

“Leave them to *me*!” now screamed Hop-Frog, his shrill voice making itself easily heard through all the din. “Leave them to *me*. I fancy *I* know them. If *I* can only get a good look at them, I can soon tell who they are.”

Here, scrambling over the heads of the crowd, he managed to get to the wall; when, seizing a flambeau from one of the Caryatides, he returned, as he went, to the centre of the room﻿—leaped, with the agility of a monkey, upon the kings head, and thence clambered a few feet up the chain; holding down the torch to examine the group of orangutans, and still screaming: “*I* shall soon find out who they are!”

===Chinese===

乱到极处、每个化装客只顾自身安全的时候（实在的，狂乱人潮的挤压大有真危险），那根平日吊吊灯的链子——撤灯时收了上去的——可以被看见，正极缓极缓地降下来，直到带钩的那一头离地不过三英尺。

不多时，国王同他的七位朋友满厅乱晃了一通，终于晃到了厅心，自然同那链子打了个照面。正这时，那悄没声儿缀在他们脚跟后面的侏儒——方才还一直在撩他们闹——一把攥住他们自己那条链子上两股交叉的十字处。说时迟那时快，他把吊灯常用的那只钩子挂了上去；转瞬之间，不知是哪里来的力，吊灯链猛地向上升，升到钩子够不着的高度；随之而来的必然结果，是把那群猩猩拉作紧密的一团，面对面凑在一处。

化装客们到这时也已定下几分神，渐渐把这桩事看作一场布置周妙的玩笑，见猿猴们的狼狈相，便放声大笑起来。

「交给我！」跳蛙尖声喊，那又尖又细的嗓音透出喧嚣，人人听得清楚。「交给我。我看我认得他们。只要让我好好瞧上一眼，我立刻就能说出他们是谁。」

说着，他从人头上爬将过去，挤到墙边；从一尊女像柱手里夺过一支火把，原路回来，到了厅心——猿猴一般敏捷地一跃，跳上国王的头顶，又顺链子攀上几英尺；把火把往下探着，端详那一群猩猩，口中还在尖叫：「我这就看出他们是谁了！」

===Original===

And now, while the whole assembly (the apes included) were convulsed with laughter, the jester suddenly uttered a shrill whistle; when the chain flew violently up for about thirty feet﻿—dragging with it the dismayed and struggling orangutans, and leaving them suspended in midair between the skylight and the floor. Hop-Frog, clinging to the chain as it rose, still maintained his relative position in respect to the eight maskers, and still (as if nothing were the matter) continued to thrust his torch down toward them, as though endeavoring to discover who they were.

So thoroughly astonished was the whole company at this ascent, that a dead silence, of about a minute’s duration, ensued. It was broken by just such a low, harsh, *grating* sound, as had before attracted the attention of the king and his councillors when the former threw the wine in the face of Trippetta. But, on the present occasion, there could be no question as to *whence* the sound issued. It came from the fang-like teeth of the dwarf, who ground them and gnashed them as he foamed at the mouth, and glared, with an expression of maniacal rage, into the upturned countenances of the king and his seven companions.

“Ah, ha!” said at length the infuriated jester. “Ah, ha! I begin to see who these people *are* now!” Here, pretending to scrutinize the king more closely, he held the flambeau to the flaxen coat which enveloped him, and which instantly burst into a sheet of vivid flame. In less than half a minute the whole eight orangutans were blazing fiercely, amid the shrieks of the multitude who gazed at them from below, horror-stricken, and without the power to render them the slightest assistance.

At length the flames, suddenly increasing in virulence, forced the jester to climb higher up the chain, to be out of their reach; and, as he made this movement, the crowd again sank, for a brief instant, into silence. The dwarf seized his opportunity, and once more spoke:

“I now see *distinctly*,” he said, “what manner of people these maskers are. They are a great king and his seven privy-councillors﻿—a king who does not scruple to strike a defenceless girl and his seven councillors who abet him in the outrage. As for myself, I am simply Hop-Frog, the jester﻿—and *this is my last jest*.”

===Chinese===

这时，满场的人（猿猴也在内）正笑得打颤，小丑忽然打了一声唿哨；那链子便猛地向上升了约莫三十英尺——把那群惊慌挣扎的猩猩一并拽起，吊在天窗与地板之间的半空里。跳蛙紧攥着链子随它上升，同八个面具人始终保持着原先的相对位置，还（仿佛没事人一般）把火把一递一递地往下探，像是要辨认出他们是谁。

这一升把满场的人都惊呆了，约有一分钟，死一样的寂静。寂静又被那种低而尖利的锉磨声打破——同先前国王把酒泼在特里佩塔脸上时，引得国王和枢密们侧耳的那种声音一模一样。只是这一回，声音从何处发出，再无半点疑问。它来自侏儒那口獠牙似的牙齿：他咬得它们咯咯作响，口中喷着白沫，满面狂怒，逼视着底下国王和他七位同伴仰起的脸。

「啊，哈！」狂怒的小丑终于开口。「啊，哈！我如今看出这些人是干什么的了！」说着，他装作把国王端详得更细些，把火把凑向裹住国王的那身亚麻衣——衣裳霎时腾起一片明亮的大火。不到半分钟，八只猩猩一齐熊熊燃烧，底下的人群望着他们尖叫，吓瘫了，一丝一毫的救应也无从施。

末了，火势骤然凶猛起来，逼得小丑顺链子再往高爬，躲开火头；他这一动，人群又霎时静了片刻。侏儒抓住时机，再度开口。

「我如今看得分明，」他说，「这些面具人是什么货色了。他们是一位大国王和他的七位枢密——一位殴打无助女子的国王，和七位助纣为虐的枢密。至于我，我不过是跳蛙，一个小丑——这是我的最后一个玩笑。」

===Original===

Owing to the high combustibility of both the flax and the tar to which it adhered, the dwarf had scarcely made an end of his brief speech before the work of vengeance was complete. The eight corpses swung in their chains, a fetid, blackened, hideous, and indistinguishable mass. The cripple hurled his torch at them, clambered leisurely to the ceiling, and disappeared through the skylight.

It is supposed that Trippetta, stationed on the roof of the saloon, had been the accomplice of her friend in his fiery revenge, and that, together, they effected their escape to their own country; for neither was seen again.

===Chinese===

亚麻连同粘着它的沥青都极易燃烧，侏儒这篇短短的话音未落，复仇的工程已告完成。八具尸首吊在链子上，一团焦黑、恶臭、面目难辨的东西。残废人把火把掷向他们，从容攀上屋顶，从天窗里不见了。

据推断，特里佩塔守在厅堂顶上，是她朋友这场火刑复仇的同谋；两人一起逃回了自己的家乡；因为此后谁也没有再见过他们。

## Von Kempelen and His Discovery / 冯·肯佩伦和他的发现
===Original===

After the very minute and elaborate paper by Arago, to say nothing of the summary in *Silliman’s Journal*, with the detailed statement just published by Lieutenant Maury, it will not be supposed, of course, that in offering a few hurried remarks in reference to Von Kempelen’s discovery, I have any design to look at the subject in a *scientific* point of view. My object is simply, in the first place, to say a few words of Von Kempelen himself (with whom, some years ago, I had the honor of a slight personal acquaintance), since everything which concerns him must necessarily, at this moment, be of interest; and, in the second place, to look in a general way, and speculatively, at the *results* of the discovery.

It may be as well, however, to premise the cursory observations which I have to offer, by denying, very decidedly, what seems to be a general impression (gleaned, as usual in a case of this kind, from the newspapers), viz.: that this discovery, astounding as it unquestionably is, is *unanticipated*.

By reference to the *Diary of Sir Humphrey Davy* (Cottle and Munroe, London, pp. 150), it will be seen at pp. 53 and 82, that this illustrious chemist had not only conceived the idea now in question, but had actually made *no inconsiderable progress, experimentally*, in the very *identical analysis* now so triumphantly brought to an issue by Von Kempelen, who although he makes not the slightest allusion to it, is, *without doubt* (I say it unhesitatingly, and can prove it, if required), indebted to the *Diary* for at least the first hint of his own undertaking.

===Chinese===

在阿拉戈（Arago）那篇极细密极详尽的论文之后——不必说《西利曼杂志》（Silliman's Journal）里的摘要，也不必说莫里中尉（Lieutenant Maury）刚刚发表的详细陈述——自然，谁也不会设想：我在这里就冯·肯佩伦（Von Kempelen）的发现匆匆谈上几句，还打算从*科学的*观点看这问题。我的目的只是：第一，就冯·肯佩伦本人说几句话（几年前，我有幸同他有过一点私交），因为此刻凡关涉他的一切必然都引人兴趣；第二，从一般的、思辨的角度，看看这发现的*结果*。

不过，最好还是先把我打算提出的粗浅之见，作一点坚决的否认，用来开头：人们普遍有一个印象（照这类事情的惯例，从报纸上采来的），即这桩发现，无论确实怎样惊人，却是*出人意料*的。

翻翻《汉弗莱·戴维爵士日记》（Sir Humphrey Davy's Diary）（科特尔与门罗出版，伦敦，共150页），在第53页与第82页可以看到：这位杰出的化学家不但设想过如今这个观念，而且*在实验上*已实实在在取得不小进展，做的正是冯·肯佩伦如今如此凯旋地告成的*同一个分析*；冯·肯佩伦虽然对那部日记只字不提，却*毫无疑问*（我毫不犹豫地说，需要时我能证明）至少就他自己这番事业的最初提示而言，得力于那部《日记》。

===Original===

The paragraph from the *Courier and Enquirer*, which is now going the rounds of the press, and which purports to claim the invention for a Mr. Kissam, of Brunswick, Maine, appears to me, I confess, a little apocryphal, for several reasons; although there is nothing either impossible or very improbable in the statement made. I need not go into details. My opinion of the paragraph is founded principally upon its *manner*. It does not *look* true. Persons who are narrating *facts*, are seldom so particular as Mr. Kissam seems to be, about day and date and precise location. Besides, if Mr. Kissam actually *did* come upon the discovery he says he did, at the period designated﻿—nearly eight years ago﻿—how happens it that he took no steps, *on the instant*, to reap the immense benefits which the merest bumpkin must have known would have resulted to him individually, if not to the world at large, from the discovery? It seems to me quite incredible that any man of common understanding could have discovered what Mr. Kissam says he did, and yet have subsequently acted so like a baby﻿—so like an owl﻿—as Mr. Kissam *admits* that he did. By-the-way, who *is* Mr. Kissam? and is not the whole paragraph in the *Courier and Enquirer* a fabrication got up to “make a talk”? It must be confessed that it has an amazingly moon-hoaxy-air. Very little dependence is to be placed upon it, in my humble opinion; and if I were not well aware, from experience, how very easily men of science are *mystified*, on points out of their usual range of inquiry, I should be profoundly astonished at finding so eminent a chemist as Professor Draper, discussing Mr. Kissam’s (or is it Mr. Quizzem’s?) pretensions to the discovery, in so serious a tone.

===Chinese===

《信使与问询报》（Courier and Enquirer）上那一段文字，如今正在各报轮转，声称这发明属于缅因州布伦斯威克（Brunswick）的基萨姆先生（Mr. Kissam）；我承认，那在我看来有点可疑，有几个缘故；虽然所述的话里并没有什么不可能或太不合情理的。细节我不必细说。我对那一段的意见，主要根据它的*腔调*。它*看着*不像真的。叙述*事实*的人，很少像基萨姆先生那样，对日子、日期和确切的地点那样讲究。况且，倘若基萨姆先生当真*确实*在指定的时期——将近八年前——碰上了他说的发现，那他怎么竟没有*立即*采取步骤，去收取那无边的利益？最乡下的庄稼汉也该知道，那发现即便不惠及普世，至少会单单落到他自己头上。在我看来，凡有寻常理解力的人，竟能发现基萨姆先生自称发现的东西，随后又行事像个小娃娃——像只猫头鹰——基萨姆先生*自己承认*他就是那样——这实在叫人难以相信。顺带问一句，基萨姆先生*究竟*是谁？《信使与问询报》整段文字，岂不是一篇编出来「造个话题」的赝品？必须承认，它带着一股惊人的月亮骗局的气味。照我浅见，对它切莫多信；要不是我凭经验深知：在平常考察范围之外的问题上，科学界的先生们何等容易被*蒙骗*，那么看到德雷珀教授（Professor Draper）这样杰出的化学家，用那样正经的腔调讨论基萨姆先生（还是奎兹姆先生？）对这发现的冒领，我本该深为惊叹。

===Original===

But to return to the *Diary* of Sir Humphrey Davy. This pamphlet was *not* designed for the public eye, even upon the decease of the writer, as any person at all conversant with authorship may satisfy himself at once by the slightest inspection of the style. At page 13, for example, near the middle, we read, in reference to his researches about the protoxide of azote: “In less than half a minute the respiration being continued, diminished gradually and *were* succeeded by analogous to gentle pressure on all the muscles.” That the *respiration* was not “diminished,” is not only clear by the subsequent context, but by the use of the plural, “were.” The sentence, no doubt, was thus intended: “In less than half a minute, the respiration [being continued, these feelings] diminished gradually, and were succeeded by [a sensation] analogous to gentle pressure on all the muscles.” A hundred similar instances go to show that the MS. so inconsiderately published, was merely a *rough notebook*, meant only for the writer’s own eye, but an inspection of the pamphlet will convince almost any thinking person of the truth of my suggestion. The fact is, Sir Humphrey Davy was about the last man in the world to *commit himself* on scientific topics. Not only had he a more than ordinary dislike to quackery, but he was morbidly afraid of *appearing* empirical; so that, however fully he might have been convinced that he was on the right track in the matter now in question, he would never have spoken *out*, until he had everything ready for the most practical demonstration. I verily believe that his last moments would have been rendered wretched, could he have suspected that his wishes in regard to burning this *Diary* (full of crude speculations) would have been unattended to; as, it seems, they were. I say “his wishes,” for that he meant to include this notebook among the miscellaneous papers directed “to be burnt,” I think there can be no manner of doubt. Whether it escaped the flames by good fortune or by bad, yet remains to be seen. That the passages quoted above, with the other similar ones referred to, gave Von Kempelen *the hint*, I do not in the slightest degree question; but I repeat, it yet remains to be seen whether this momentous discovery itself (*momentous* under any circumstances) will be of service or disservice to mankind at large.

===Chinese===

可是回到汉弗莱·戴维爵士的《日记》。这本小册子*并不是*预备给公众看的，甚至作者身故之后也不是；凡是稍通写作的人，只须把那文体略略一过目，立刻可以自证。比方第13页近中段，我们读到一句关于他研究笑气——亚氮的初级氧化物——的话：「不到半分钟，呼吸继续着，逐渐减小，*并且*被类似一切肌肉上轻轻压按的东西接着。」那*呼吸*并没有「减小」，这不但由后文看得分明，也由复数的「并且（were）」看得分明。那句子的本意，无疑是这样：「不到半分钟，呼吸〔继续着，这些感觉〕逐渐减小，并被〔一种感觉〕接着——类似一切肌肉上轻轻压按。」一百个类似的例子，可以证明：那部不经意付印的手稿，不过是一本*草率的笔记簿*，只预备给作者自己的眼睛看；可是把那小册子翻一翻，几乎任何肯想的人都会信服我这个提示的真。实情是，汉弗莱·戴维爵士在科学的题目上，原是世上顶不肯*轻易表态*的人之一。他不但对江湖骗术有一种超乎寻常的厌恶，而且病态地怕*显得*只凭经验说话；所以，无论他多么信服自己在眼下这问题上走上了正道，他也决不肯*说出来*，直到一切都备齐，可以作最实际的演示为止。我实在相信，倘若他能疑心到：他焚毁这部《日记》（满是粗糙的玄想）的遗愿竟没有被执行——像看光景它没有被执行那样——他临终的时刻都会被搅得凄凉。我说「他的遗愿」，因为他原打算把这本笔记簿列入那些吩咐「付之一炬」的杂件之中，我想断无可疑。它逃出火里，是好运还是歹运，尚待分晓。上面引的几段，连同引到的其他类似的几段，给了冯·肯佩伦*提示*，这一点我半点也不怀疑；可是我再说一遍：这桩重大发现本身（无论在任何情势下都*重大*）究竟将有益还是有害于人类全体，尚待分晓。

===Original===

That Von Kempelen and his immediate friends will reap a rich harvest, it would be folly to doubt for a moment. They will scarcely be so weak as not to “*realize*,” in time, by large purchases of houses and land, with other property of *intrinsic* value.

In the brief account of Von Kempelen which appeared in the *Home Journal*, and has since been extensively copied, several misapprehensions of the German original seem to have been made by the translator, who professes to have taken the passage from a late number of the Presburg *Schnellpost*. “*Viele*” has evidently been misconceived (as it often is), and what the translator renders by “sorrows,” is probably “*lieden*,” which, in its true version, “sufferings,” would give a totally different complexion to the whole account; but, of course, much of this is merely guess, on my part.

Von Kempelen, however, is by no means “a misanthrope,” in appearance, at least, whatever he may be in fact. My acquaintance with him was casual altogether; and I am scarcely warranted in saying that I know him at all; but to have seen and conversed with a man of so *prodigious* a notoriety as he has attained, or *will* attain in a few days, is not a small matter, as times go.

===Chinese===

冯·肯佩伦和他的近亲密友将收割一场丰饶的收获，这连片刻怀疑也是愚蠢的。他们不致懦弱到不及时去「*变现*（realize）」，大购房屋田地，连同其他有*内在*价值的产业。

《家庭杂志》（Home Journal）上那篇冯·肯佩伦小传——随后被广泛转载——的译者，似乎对德文原文有几处误解；那位译者自称译文采自普雷斯堡（Presburg）晚近一期的《快邮报》（Schnellpost）。「*Viele*」分明被误会了（这是常事），译者译作「愁绪」的那个字，恐怕本是「*lieden*」；那字本义是「苦楚」，照它真实的译法译出，会给整篇记载一种全然不同的面色；不过，当然，这一切多半只是我的揣测。

然而冯·肯佩伦决不是什么「厌世者」，至少就外貌而言，无论实际如何。我同他的相识全然是偶然的；我说我认识他，几乎说不过去；可是见过、同这样一位得了——或*将要*在几天之内得到——*惊人*声名的人交谈过，照时下的风气，总不算小事。

===Original===

*The Literary World* speaks of him, confidently, as a *native* of Presburg (misled, perhaps, by the account in *The Home Journal*) but I am pleased in being able to state *positively*, since I have it from his own lips, that he was born in Utica, in the State of New York, although both his parents, I believe, are of Presburg descent. The family is connected, in some way, with Mäelzel, of Automaton-chess-player memory. In person, he is short and stout, with large, *fat*, blue eyes, sandy hair and whiskers, a wide but pleasing mouth, fine teeth, and I think a Roman nose. There is some defect in one of his feet. His address is frank, and his whole manner noticeable for bonhomie. Altogether, he looks, speaks, and acts as little like “a misanthrope” as any man I ever saw. We were fellow-sojourners for a week about six years ago, at Earl’s Hotel, in Providence, Rhode Island; and I presume that I conversed with him, at various times, for some three or four hours altogether. His principal topics were those of the day; and nothing that fell from him led me to suspect his scientific attainments. He left the hotel before me, intending to go to New York, and thence to Bremen; it was in the latter city that his great discovery was first made public; or, rather, it was there that he was first suspected of having made it. This is about all that I personally know of the now immortal Von Kempelen; but I have thought that even these few details would have interest for the public.

There can be little question that most of the marvellous rumors afloat about this affair are pure inventions, entitled to about as much credit as the story of Aladdin’s lamp; and yet, in a case of this kind, as in the case of the discoveries in California, it is clear that the truth *may be* stranger than fiction. The following anecdote, at least, is so well authenticated, that we may receive it implicitly.

===Chinese===

《文学世界》（The Literary World）满有把握地称他为普雷斯堡*土生*（也许给《家庭杂志》的记载引岔了）；可是我能*确凿*地声明——这话是我从他亲口听来的——他生在纽约州的尤蒂卡（Utica），虽然他的双亲，我相信，都是普雷斯堡血统。这一家，不知怎的，同那位造自动下棋机器而留名的梅尔策尔（Mäelzel）沾着亲。论人，他矮而壮，蓝眼睛大而*浮肿*，头发连鬓须是沙色，嘴阔而可喜，牙齿齐整，鼻子，我想，是罗马式的。他一只脚上有些缺陷。他谈吐坦直，整个人风度以淳厚见称。总之，他的相貌、言语、举止，像「厌世者」的程度，比我所见过的任何人都少。大约六年前，我们在罗得岛州普罗维登斯的厄尔旅馆（Earl's Hotel）同住了一星期；我想我同他前后谈过三四个钟头的话。他谈的多是当日的话题；他吐出的没有一句话，叫我疑心他的科学造诣。他比我先离旅馆，打算去纽约，再从不来梅（Bremen）；正是在后者那座城里，他伟大的发现头一次公布于众；或者不如说，在那里他头一次被疑心已经做出了它。这就是我个人知道的、如今已不朽的冯·肯佩伦的全部；可是我想，连这几条细节，对公众也不无兴趣。

关于这件事传布的绝大多数奇迹式的谣言，很少有问题纯粹是编造，配得上的信誉同阿拉丁神灯的故事相仿；可是，在这一类事情上，同加利福尼亚的种种发现一样，分明*可能*真比虚构更离奇。下面这段轶事，至少，取证这样确凿，我们可以全盘领受。

===Original===

Von Kempelen had never been even tolerably well off during his residence at Bremen; and often, it was well known, he had been put to extreme shifts in order to raise trifling sums. When the great excitement occurred about the forgery on the house of Gutsmuth & Co., suspicion was directed toward Von Kempelen, on account of his having purchased a considerable property in Gasperitch Lane, and his refusing, when questioned, to explain how he became possessed of the purchase money. He was at length arrested, but nothing decisive appearing against him, was in the end set at liberty. The police, however, kept a strict watch upon his movements, and thus discovered that he left home frequently, taking always the same road, and invariably giving his watchers the slip in the neighborhood of that labyrinth of narrow and crooked passages known by the flash name of the “Dondergat.” Finally, by dint of great perseverance, they traced him to a garret in an old house of seven stories, in an alley called Flatzplatz; and, coming upon him suddenly, found him, as they imagined, in the midst of his counterfeiting operations. His agitation is represented as so excessive that the officers had not the slightest doubt of his guilt. After handcuffing him, they searched his room, or rather rooms, for it appears he occupied all the *mansarde*.

===Chinese===

冯·肯佩伦住在不来梅的时候，从来没有宽裕过；人人知道，他常常为凑几文小钱，被逼到极窘的境地。古茨穆特公司（Gutsmuth & Co.）伪造案闹得沸沸扬扬的时候，疑心便指向冯·肯佩伦，因为他在加斯佩里奇巷（Gasperitch Lane）置下了一宗可观的产业，而被质问时又拒绝说明置产的钱从何而来。他终于被捕；可是不利于他的事一点也没有显出，末了释放了。可是警察紧紧盯住他的行踪，于是发觉他时常出门，走的总是一条路，而且总在那一带迷宫似的窄巷弯弄里甩掉盯梢的人——那片迷宫，黑话里叫作「堂德加特」（Dondergat）。终于，凭着极大的锲而不舍，他们把他追到弗拉茨普拉茨（Flatzplatz）巷一座七层旧楼的一间顶楼里；冷不防撞见他，如他们所想，正在伪造的营生当中。他的惊慌据说到了过分的程度，警官们对他的罪行便半点也不疑心了。给他上了手铐之后，他们搜查他的屋子——不如说几间屋子，因为他占着整个*复折屋顶层*（mansarde）。

===Original===

Opening into the garret where they caught him, was a closet, ten feet by eight, fitted up with some chemical apparatus, of which the object has not yet been ascertained. In one corner of the closet was a very small furnace, with a glowing fire in it, and on the fire a kind of duplicate crucible﻿—two crucibles connected by a tube. One of these crucibles was nearly full of *lead* in a state of fusion, but not reaching up to the aperture of the tube, which was close to the brim. The other crucible had some liquid in it, which, as the officers entered, seemed to be furiously dissipating in vapor. They relate that, on finding himself taken, Kempelen seized the crucibles with both hands (which were encased in gloves that afterwards turned out to be asbestic), and threw the contents on the tiled floor. It was now that they handcuffed him; and before proceeding to ransack the premises they searched his person, but nothing unusual was found about him, excepting a paper parcel, in his coat-pocket, containing what was afterward ascertained to be a mixture of antimony and some *unknown substance*, in nearly, but not quite, equal proportions. All attempts at analyzing the unknown substance have, so far, failed, but that it will ultimately be analyzed, is not to be doubted.

Passing out of the closet with their prisoner, the officers went through a sort of antechamber, in which nothing material was found, to the chemist’s sleeping-room. They here rummaged some drawers and boxes, but discovered only a few papers, of no importance, and some good coin, silver and gold. At length, looking under the bed, they saw *a large, common hair trunk, without hinges, hasp, or lock*, and with the top lying carelessly *across* the bottom portion. Upon attempting to draw this trunk out from under the bed, they found that, with their united strength (there were three of them, all powerful men), they “could not stir it one inch.” Much astonished at this, one of them crawled under the bed, and looking into the trunk, said:

“No wonder we couldn’t move it﻿—why it’s full to the brim of old bits of brass!”

===Chinese===

同他们逮住他的那间顶楼相通的，是一间小储藏室，十英尺乘八英尺，安着一些化学仪器，那些仪器的用途至今没有查明。储藏室一角有一座极小的炉子，炉火烧得通红，火上是一副孪生坩埚似的东西——两只坩埚由一根管子连着。一只坩埚几乎盛满*熔化状态的铅*，却没有满到管子的开口，那开口紧挨埚沿。另一只坩埚里有些液体；警官们进去时，那液体仿佛正狂怒地在蒸汽里消散。他们说，一发觉自己被擒，肯佩伦便双手抓起两只坩埚（那双手后来证明裹着石棉手套），把内容物泼在铺砖的地板上。就在这时他们给他上了手铐；在动手搜查这宅子之前，先搜了他人身，可是除了一件东西，没有找到什么异常：他外套口袋里一只纸包，里面装的后来查明是锑和某种*未知物质*的混合物，两种几乎、但并不全然等量。分析那未知物质的一切尝试，至今都失败了；可是它终究会被分析出来，这是无可怀疑的。

带着犯人走出储藏室，警官们穿过一间前厅——那里没有发现什么要紧的东西——来到化学家的卧室。他们在这里翻了几只抽屉几只箱子，可是只发现几页无足轻重的纸，和几枚好钱币，银的金子都有。末了，朝床底下一望，他们看见*一只大的、寻常的毛发皮箱，没有铰链、没有搭扣、没有锁*，箱盖马马虎虎地*横*在下截箱身上。他们想把这只皮箱从床底拖出来，却发现凭着齐心合力（他们共三人，个个都是壮汉），那箱子「一寸也挪不动」。大为诧异之下，其中一个爬到床底，朝箱里望了一眼，说：

「难怪我们挪它不动——嘿，它满得齐边都是旧铜块！」

===Original===

Putting his feet, now, against the wall so as to get a good purchase, and pushing with all his force, while his companions pulled with all theirs, the trunk, with much difficulty, was slid out from under the bed, and its contents examined. The supposed brass with which it was filled was all in small, smooth pieces, varying from the size of a pea to that of a dollar; but the pieces were irregular in shape, although more or less flat-looking, upon the whole, “very much as lead looks when thrown upon the ground in a molten state, and there suffered to grow cool.” Now, not one of these officers for a moment suspected this metal to be anything *but* brass. The idea of its being *gold* never entered their brains, of course; how *could* such a wild fancy have entered it? And their astonishment may be well conceived, when the next day it became known, all over Bremen, that the “lot of brass” which they had carted so contemptuously to the police office, without putting themselves to the trouble of pocketing the smallest scrap, was not only gold﻿—real gold﻿—but gold far finer than any employed in coinage﻿—gold, in fact, absolutely pure, virgin, without the slightest appreciable alloy!

I need not go over the details of Von Kempelen’s confession (as far as it went) and release, for these are familiar to the public. That he has actually realized, in spirit and in effect, if not to the letter, the old chimera of the philosopher’s stone, no sane person is at liberty to doubt. The opinions of Arago are, of course, entitled to the greatest consideration; but he is by no means infallible; and what he says of *bismuth*, in his report to the Academy, must be taken cum grano salis. The simple truth is, that up to this period *all* analysis has failed; and until Von Kempelen chooses to let us have the key to his own published enigma, it is more than probable that the matter will remain, for years, *in statu quo*. All that as yet can fairly be said to be known is, that “*pure gold can be made at will, and very readily from lead in connection with certain other substances, in kind and in proportions, unknown*.”

===Chinese===

此刻他把双脚蹬住墙，好取得一个用力的支点，全力去推，同伴们全力去拉，皮箱费了很大的劲才从床底滑出来，内容物接受了检查。那满箱的所谓铜，全是小块的、光滑的，从豌豆大小到一元银币大小不等；块的形状不规则，虽然总的看来或多或少发扁，「同铅在熔态下泼在地上、任它冷却的模样非常相像」。可是这些警官没有一个一时疑心这金属*不是*铜。它是*金子*的念头自然从不曾钻进他们的脑子；这样狂野的念头*怎么能*钻进去？第二天，全不来梅都知道了：他们满不在乎地用车拉到警察局、连最小一片也不屑装进自己腰包的那「一堆铜」，不但是金子——真金——而且比铸币所用的任何金子都纯——金子，实在说，绝对纯净、原生、没有一丝可觉的合金！——他们的惊愕便可以想见了。

冯·肯佩伦的供词（就它所及的限度而言）与释放，我不必复述其细节，公众对这些已经很熟。他已经实际上——在精神与效果上，纵使不在字面上——实现了哲人之石那个古老的幻想，任何神志健全的人都无权怀疑。阿拉戈的见解自然应当受最高的尊重；可是他决不是不会错的；他在呈学院的报告里关于*铋*的话，必须加着一把盐（cum grano salis）来领受。简简单单的真，是直到此刻*一切*分析都告失败；而且，直到冯·肯佩伦肯把他自己发表的那个谜的钥匙交给我们，这事多半要*维持原状*（in statu quo），一过几年。到此为止还可以公道地算作已知的，只有这一句：「*纯金可以随意制造，极易，从铅出发，连同某些别的物质，其种类与分量，未知。*」

===Original===

Speculation, of course, is busy as to the immediate and ultimate results of this discovery﻿—a discovery which few thinking persons will hesitate in referring to an increased interest in the matter of gold generally, by the late developments in California; and this reflection brings us inevitably to another﻿—the exceeding *inopportuneness* of Von Kempelen’s analysis. If many were prevented from adventuring to California, by the mere apprehension that gold would so materially diminish in value, on account of its plentifulness in the mines there, as to render the speculation of going so far in search of it a doubtful one﻿—what impression will be wrought *now*, upon the minds of those about to emigrate, and especially upon the minds of those actually in the mineral region, by the announcement of this astounding discovery of Von Kempelen? a discovery which declares, in so many words, that beyond its intrinsic worth for manufacturing purposes (whatever that worth may be), gold now is, or at least soon will be (for it cannot be supposed that Von Kempelen can *long* retain his secret), of no greater *value* than lead, and of far inferior value to silver. It is, indeed, exceedingly difficult to speculate prospectively upon the consequences of the discovery, but one thing may be positively maintained﻿—that the announcement of the discovery six months ago would have had material influence in regard to the settlement of California.

In Europe, as yet, the most noticeable results have been a rise of two hundred percent in the price of lead, and nearly twenty-five percent that of silver.

===Chinese===

猜想，自然忙得很，忙在这发现眼前与终极的结果上——这发现，凡肯想的人都会毫不犹豫地把它归到近来加利福尼亚的种种进展所引起的、对黄金一事普遍增长的兴味上去；而这层反思又把我们不由分说地带到另一层——冯·肯佩伦那个分析的*不合时宜*。倘若过去有许多人不敢到加利福尼亚去闯，仅仅因为怕金子在那里矿藏丰盛，价值便要大减，把跑到那么远去寻金的投机变成一桩没把握的事——那么*如今*，这冯·肯佩伦惊人的发现的公布，将在那些准备移民的心里，尤其将在那些实际在矿区的人的心里，造成什么印象呢？这发现分明用直白的话宣告：除了它在制造上的内在价值（无论那价值是什么），金子如今是——或者至少很快将是（因为不能设想冯·肯佩伦能*长久*守住他的秘密）——不再比铅有更大的*价值*，而远逊于银子了。要预先推究这发现的后果，实在极其困难；可是有一点可以断然维持——倘若六个月之前公布这发现，它本会对加利福尼亚的拓居产生实质的影响。

在欧洲，到此刻为止，最惹眼的结果，是铅价上涨了百分之二百，银价将近百分之二十五。

## X-ing a Paragrab / 给段落打叉
===Original===

As it is well known that the “wise men” came “from the East,” and as Mr. Touch-and-go Bullet-head came from the East, it follows that Mr. Bullet-head was a wise man; and if collateral proof of the matter be needed, here we have it﻿—Mr. B. was an editor. Irascibility was his sole foible, for in fact the obstinacy of which men accused him was anything but his *foible*, since he justly considered it his *forte*. It was his strong point﻿—his virtue; and it would have required all the logic of a Brownson to convince him that it was “anything else.”

I have shown that Touch-and-go Bullet-head was a wise man; and the only occasion on which he did not prove infallible, was when, abandoning that legitimate home for all wise men, the East, he migrated to the city of Alexander-the-Great-o-nopolis, or some place of a similar title, out West.

I must do him the justice to say, however, that when he made up his mind finally to settle in that town, it was under the impression that no newspaper, and consequently no editor, existed in that particular section of the country. In establishing *The Teapot* he expected to have the field all to himself. I feel confident he never would have dreamed of taking up his residence in Alexander-the-Great-o-nopolis had he been aware that, in Alexander-the-Great-o-nopolis, there lived a gentleman named John Smith (if I rightly remember), who for many years had there quietly grown fat in editing and publishing the *Alexander-the-Great-o-nopolis Gazette*. It was solely, therefore, on account of having been misinformed, that Mr. Bullet-head found himself in Alex﻿—suppose we call it Nopolis, “for short”﻿—but, as he *did* find himself there, he determined to keep up his character for obst﻿—for firmness, and remain. So remain he did; and he did more; he unpacked his press, type, etc., etc., rented an office exactly opposite to that of the *Gazette*, and, on the third morning after his arrival, issued the first number of *The Alexan*﻿—that is to say, of *The Nopolis Teapot*:﻿—as nearly as I can recollect, this was the name of the new paper.

===Chinese===

众所周知，「智者」来自「东方」；一触即发·弹头先生（Touch-and-go Bullet-head）来自东方；由此推得：弹头先生是位智者。这桩事若还需要旁证，这里便有——弹头先生是位编辑。暴躁是他唯一的弱点；因为人们指责他的那份固执，实在算不得他的*弱点*，他公道地把它看作自己的*强项*。那是他的长处——他的美德；要说服他相信那是「别的东西」，恐怕得用上布朗森（Brownson）的全部逻辑。

我已表明一触即发·弹头先生是位智者；他唯一一次没有证明自己不会犯错，是当他抛开一切智者的合法故乡——东方——迁往西边的亚历山大大帝诺波利斯城（Alexander-the-Great-o-nopolis），或某个题目相仿的地方的时候。

可是我必须公道地替他说一句：他终于拿定主意在那座城里住下的时候，心里以为这个国家的那一角没有报纸，因而也没有编辑。办《茶壶报》（The Teapot）的时候，他指望独占那片园地。我确信，倘若他知道亚历山大大帝诺波利斯城里住着一位名叫约翰·史密斯（John Smith）（若我记得不错）的绅士，多年在那里安安稳稳地把《亚历山大大帝诺波利斯公报》（Alexander-the-Great-o-nopolis Gazette）编辑出版、养得肥肥的，他做梦也不会想住到亚历山大大帝诺波利斯去。因此，仅仅由于消息不确，弹头先生才发现自己身在亚历山大——我们姑且简称「诺波利斯」（Nopolis）——可是，他*既然*发现自己在那里，便决意维持他那倔——不如说坚韧——的声名，留下来。他也就留下来了；而且做得更多：他拆开他的印刷机、铅字等等等等，租下一间正对着《公报》的办公室，在到达后的第三个早上，出了《亚历山……》创刊号——就是说，《诺波利斯茶壶报》的第一期：——凭我的记忆，这就是新报纸的名字。

The leading article, I must admit, was brilliant﻿—not to say severe. It was especially bitter about things in general﻿—and as for the editor of *The Gazette*, he was torn all to pieces in particular. Some of Bullet-head’s remarks were really so fiery that I have always, since that time, been forced to look upon John Smith, who is still alive, in the light of a salamander. I cannot pretend to give *all* the *Teapot*’s paragraphs *verbatim*, but one of them runs thus:

“Oh, yes!﻿—Oh, we perceive! Oh, no doubt! The editor over the way is a genius﻿—O, my! Oh, goodness, gracious!﻿—what is this world coming to? *Oh, tempora! Oh, Moses!*”

A philippic at once so caustic and so classical, alighted like a bombshell among the hitherto peaceful citizens of Nopolis. Groups of excited individuals gathered at the corners of the streets. Everyone awaited, with heartfelt anxiety, the reply of the dignified Smith. Next morning it appeared as follows:

“We quote from *The Teapot* of yesterday the subjoined paragraph: ‘*Oh*, yes! *Oh*, we perceive! *Oh*, no doubt! *Oh*, my! *Oh*, goodness! *Oh*, tempora! *Oh*, Moses!’ Why, the fellow is all *O*! That accounts for his reasoning in a circle, and explains why there is neither beginning nor end to him, nor to anything he says. We really do not believe the vagabond can write a word that hasn’t an *O* in it. Wonder if this *O*-ing is a habit of his? By the by, he came away from Down-East in a great hurry. Wonder if he *O*’s as much there as he does here? ‘*O!* it is pitiful.’ ”

===Chinese===

社论，我必须承认，是辉煌的——不说严厉的话。它对万事万物尤其苦毒——至于《公报》的编辑，更被单独撕成了碎片。弹头先生的一些话实在火辣，从那时起，我不得不把至今活着的约翰·史密斯看作一只火蜥蜴。我不敢自命能把《茶壶报》的段落*逐字*奉告，可其中一段是这样的：

「哦，是的！——哦，我们明白！哦，毫无疑问！街对面的编辑是位天才——哦，天！哦，老天爷，发发慈悲！——这个世界要变成什么样了？*哦，时代哦！哦，摩西哦！*」

一篇这么辛辣又这么古典的痛骂，像一枚炸弹落在诺波利斯到此为止安分的市民中间。激动的人群聚到街角。人人怀着由衷的焦灼，等待威严的史密斯的答复。第二天早晨，答复如下：

「我们从昨天《茶壶报》引出下面一段：『*哦*，是的！*哦*，我们明白！*哦*，毫无疑问！*哦*，天！*哦*，老天爷！*哦*，时代哦！*哦*，摩西哦！』呃，这家伙浑身都是*哦*！这就说明他为什么绕着圈子推理，也解释了为什么他和他说的一切都无始无终。我们实在不信这流浪汉写得出一个不含*哦*的字。不知这*哦*是不是他的习惯？顺带说一句，他从东北部走的时候匆匆忙忙。不知他在那边*哦*不*哦*得像这边一样厉害？『*哦！*真是可怜。』」

===Original===

The indignation of Mr. Bullet-head at these scandalous insinuations, I shall not attempt to describe. On the eel-skinning principle, however, he did not seem to be so much incensed at the attack upon his integrity as one might have imagined. It was the sneer at his *style* that drove him to desperation. What!﻿—*he* Touch-and-go Bullet-head!﻿—not able to write a word without an *O* in it! He would soon let the jackanapes see that he was mistaken. Yes! he would let him see how *much* he was mistaken, the puppy! He, Touch-and-go Bullet-head, of Frogpondium, would let Mr. John Smith perceive that he, Bullet-head, could indite, if it so pleased him, a whole paragraph﻿—aye! a whole article﻿—in which that contemptible vowel should not *once*﻿—not even *once*﻿—make its appearance. But no;﻿—that would be yielding a point to the said John Smith. *He*, Bullet-head, would make *no* alteration in his style, to suit the caprices of any Mr. Smith in Christendom. Perish so vile a thought! The *O* forever; He would persist in the *O*. He would be as *O*-wy as *O*-wy could be.

Burning with the chivalry of this determination, the great Touch-and-go, in the next *Teapot*, came out merely with this simple but resolute paragraph, in reference to this unhappy affair:

“The editor of the *Teapot* has the honor of advising the editor of the *Gazette* that he (the *Teapot*) will take an opportunity in tomorrow morning’s paper, of convincing him (the *Gazette*) that he (the *Teapot*) both can and will be *his own master*, as regards style;﻿—he (the *Teapot*) intending to show him (the *Gazette*) the supreme, and indeed the withering contempt with which the criticism of him (the *Gazette*) inspires the independent bosom of him (the *Teapot*) by composing for the especial gratification (?) of him (the *Gazette*) a leading article, of some extent, in which the beautiful vowel﻿—the emblem of Eternity﻿—yet so offensive to the hyper-exquisite delicacy of him (the *Gazette*) shall most certainly *not be avoided* by his (the *Gazette*’s) most obedient, humble servant, the *Teapot*. ‘So much for Buckingham!’ ”

弹头先生对这可耻的影射的义愤，我不想描写。可是照剥鳝鱼皮的原理，他对于攻击他的人品，倒不像人们想象的那么怒。把他逼到绝望的，是对他*文体*的讥嘲。什么！——*他*，一触即发·弹头先生！——写不出一个不含*哦*的字！他不久就要叫那猴崽子看看他错了。不错！他要叫他看看他错得*多么*厉害，那小狗！他，蛙塘镇（Frogpondium）的一触即发·弹头先生，要叫约翰·史密斯先生明白：他，弹头先生，只要高兴，能写出整段——哼！整篇文章——其中那个可鄙的元音一次也不——连一次也不——露面。可是不；——那等于向这位约翰·史密斯让步。*他*，弹头先生，决不为了迎合基督教世界任何一位史密斯先生的怪想，改动自己的文体。让这样卑劣的念头死掉吧！*哦*，永远；他要坚持*哦*。他要*哦*味十足，十足到*哦*味的极限。

怀着这个决心的骑士之火，伟大的「一触即发」在下一期《茶壶报》里，只拿出这样一段朴素而坚决的文句，谈这桩不幸的事情：

「《茶壶报》编辑荣幸地告知《公报》编辑：他（《茶壶报》）将趁明天早晨的报纸，使他（《公报》）信服：他（《茶壶报》）在文体上*既能也愿意*自作主宰；——他（《茶壶报》）有意向他（《公报》）表明，他（《公报》）的批评在独立的心胸里——他（《茶壶报》）的——激起的无比的、甚至枯萎一切的轻蔑，办法是：特为他（《公报》）的消遣（？）撰写一篇有一定篇幅的社论，其中那个美丽的元音——永恒的徽记——却叫他（《公报》）过分精致的敏感如此反感——保证*不*被他（《公报》）最恭顺的谦卑仆人——《茶壶报》——所回避。『关于白金汉，就说这些！』」

In fulfilment of the awful threat thus darkly intimated rather than decidedly enunciated, the great Bullet-head, turning a deaf ear to all entreaties for “copy,” and simply requesting his foreman to “go to the d﻿—﻿—﻿l,” when he (the foreman) assured him (the *Teapot*!) that it was high time to “go to press”: turning a deaf ear to everything, I say, the great Bullet-head sat up until daybreak, consuming the midnight oil, and absorbed in the composition of the really unparalleled paragraph, which follows:﻿—

“So ho, John! how now? Told you so, you know. Don’t crow, another time, before you’re out of the woods! Does your mother *know* you’re out? Oh, no, no!﻿—so go home at once, now, John, to your odious old woods of Concord! Go home to your woods, old owl﻿—go! You won’t! Oh, poh, poh, John, don’t do so! You’ve *got* to go, you know! So go at once, and don’t go slow, for nobody owns you here, you know! Oh! John, John, if you *don’t* go you’re no *homo*﻿—no! You’re only a fowl, an owl; a cow, a sow; a doll, a poll; a poor, old, good-for-nothing-to-nobody, log, dog, hog, or frog, come out of a Concord bog. Cool, now﻿—cool! *Do* be cool, you fool! None of your crowing, old cock! Don’t frown so﻿—don’t! Don’t hollo, nor howl nor growl, nor bow-wow-wow! Good Lord, John, how you *do* look! Told you so, you know﻿—but stop rolling your goose of an old poll about so, and go and drown your sorrows in a bowl!”

Exhausted, very naturally, by so stupendous an effort, the great Touch-and-go could attend to nothing farther that night. Firmly, composedly, yet with an air of conscious power, he handed his MS. to the devil in waiting, and then, walking leisurely home, retired, with ineffable dignity to bed.

Meantime the devil, to whom the copy was entrusted, ran upstairs to his “case,” in an unutterable hurry, and forthwith made a commencement at “setting” the MS. “up.”

为了履行这桩凶险的恫吓——它暗示得幽暗，却没说得干脆——伟大的弹头先生对一切催「稿子」的哀求充耳不闻；当工头向他（《茶壶报》！）担保上机的时候到了，他只请工头「去见——鬼」；我说，对一切都充耳不闻，伟大的弹头先生坐到天亮，烧着午夜的灯油，专心炮制那真正无与伦比的段落，如下：——

被如此惊人的努力弄得筋疲力尽——自然如此——伟大的「一触即发」那晚再不能照管任何别的事。他坚决、沉着、却带着一种自觉的威力的神气，把手稿交给当值的小鬼（排字学徒），然后悠然步行回家，以无可言状的尊严就寝。

这工夫，那受托的小鬼，说不出的匆忙，跑上楼去到他的「字盘」跟前，立刻动手把稿子「排」「起来」。

The exigency here described is by no means of rare occurrence in printing-offices; and I cannot tell how to account for it, but the fact is indisputable, that when the exigency *does* occur, it almost always happens that *x* is adopted as a substitute for the letter deficient. The true reason, perhaps, is that *x* is rather the most superabundant letter in the cases, or at least *was* so in the old times long enough to render the substitution in question an habitual thing with printers. As for Bob, he would have considered it heretical to employ any other character, in a case of this kind, than the *x* to which he had been accustomed.
