Txld yxu sx, yxu knxw﻿—but stxp rxlling yxur gxxse xf an xld pxll abxut sx, and gx and drxwn yxur sxrrxws in a bxwl!”

===Chinese===

「*非常*好，」鲍勃答，「这就去干！」他急忙奔回他的字盘，一面走一面咕哝：「说得*相当*好，那几句粗话，出在一个不骂人的人嘴里。这么说，我是要去抠走他们全部的眼睛了，呃？还要咒他们全部的砂囊！好！干这个，正有我这号人。」实情是，鲍勃虽然只有十二岁、四英尺高，打起小架来，多大的阵仗他也对付得了。

这里描绘的窘境，在印刷所里绝非罕见；我无法说明其故，可是事实无可争辩：这窘境*果真*出现的时候，几乎总是拿*x*来顶替所缺的字母。真正的缘故，也许是*x*在字盘里算是最富余的字母，或者至少在旧时代如此，久到上述的顶替竟成了排字工的习惯。至于鲍勃，这类事情上，若不用他惯用的*x*，倒去用别的字符，他会看作异端。

「*我*只好把这段段落*叉*了，」他自言自语，惊愕地把稿子读了一遍，「可是这真是我*平生*见过的最*哦*味十足的一段段落。」于是他毫不退缩地把它*叉*了；它*叉*着上了机。

第二天早上，诺波利斯的居民翻开《茶壶报》，读到下面这篇奇文社论，全都吓了一跳：

「叉叉，叉翰！叉样叉样？跟你说过叉，你知道叉。别叉叉啼了叉，在你出林子之前叉！你妈*知道*你出门了叉？叉，不，不叉！——就回家去叉，马上叉，现在叉，叉翰，回你那可恶的康科德老林子去叉！回你的林子去叉，老猫头鹰——去叉！你不肯叉！叉，叉，叉，叉翰，别这样叉！你*非*走不可叉，你知道叉！那就马上走叉，别磨蹭叉，因为这里没人拥有你叉，你知道叉！叉！叉翰，叉翰叉，你*不*走叉，你就不是*人*——不是叉！你不过是只家禽叉，一只猫头鹰；一头牛叉，一头母猪；一个木偶叉，一只鹦鹉；一根穷苦叉、老迈、于人无用的木头叉、一条狗叉、一头猪叉或一只青蛙叉，从康科德泥塘里爬出来。冷静点叉——冷静叉！*千万*冷静叉，你这傻瓜叉！别叉叉啼了叉，老公鸡叉！别这样皱眉叉——别叉！别嚎叫叉，也别嗥叉，也别咆哮叉，也别汪汪汪叉！老天叉，叉翰，你*这副*模样叉！跟你说过叉，你知道叉——可是别再把你这鹅一样的老脑袋摇来晃去了叉，去把你的愁苦淹死在一大碗里叉！」

===Original===

The uproar occasioned by this mystical and cabalistical article, is not to be conceived. The first definite idea entertained by the populace was, that some diabolical treason lay concealed in the hieroglyphics; and there was a general rush to Bullet-head’s residence, for the purpose of riding him on a rail; but that gentleman was nowhere to be found. He had vanished, no one could tell how; and not even the ghost of him has ever been seen since.

Unable to discover its legitimate object, the popular fury at length subsided; leaving behind it, by way of sediment, quite a medley of opinion about this unhappy affair.

One gentleman thought the whole an X-ellent joke.

Another said that, indeed, Bullet-head had shown much X-uberance of fancy.

A third admitted him X-entric, but no more.

A fourth could only suppose it the Yankee’s design to X-press, in a general way, his X-asperation.

“Say, rather, to set an X-ample to posterity,” suggested a fifth.

That Bullet-head had been driven to an extremity, was clear to all; and in fact, since *that* editor could not be found, there was some talk about lynching the other one.

The more common conclusion, however, was that the affair was, simply, X-traordinary and in-X-plicable. Even the town mathematician confessed that he could make nothing of so dark a problem. X, everybody knew, was an unknown quantity; but in this case (as he properly observed), there was an unknown quantity of X.

The opinion of Bob, the devil (who kept dark about his having “X-ed the paragrab”), did not meet with so much attention as I think it deserved, although it was very openly and very fearlessly expressed. He said that, for his part, he had no doubt about the matter at all, that it was a clear case, that Mr. Bullet-head “never *could* be persuaded fur to drink like other folks, but vas *con*tinually a-svigging o’ that ere blessed XXX ale, and as a naiteral consekvence, it just puffed him up savage, and made him X (cross) in the X-treme.”

===Chinese===

这篇神秘兮兮、符咒一般的文章掀起的骚动，无法想象。民众形成的第一个明确的念头，是那些象形文字里藏着某种恶魔式的叛逆；人群一齐涌向弹头先生的寓所，预备把他捆上木杠抬起来游街；可是那位先生哪里也找不到。他消失了，谁也说不清怎么消失的；从那以后，连他的鬼影也再没有人见过。

合法的靶子找不到，民愤终于平息了；沉淀下来的，是对这桩不幸事情的五花八门的意见。

有一位先生觉得，整件事是一个*叉妙*（X-ellent）的笑话。

另一位说，弹头先生确实显出了想象的极大*叉逸*（X-uberance）。

第三位承认他*叉怪*（X-entric），仅此而已。

第四位只能猜：那是北方佬有意笼统地*叉泄*（X-press）他的*叉忿*（X-asperation）。

「不如说，给后世立一个*叉范*（X-ample），」第五位提议。

弹头先生是被逼到了绝境，这人人明白；实在说，既然那一位编辑找不到，有人便议论着要把另一位私刑处治。

然而更通行的结论是：这桩事情，简直，*叉奇*（X-traordinary）而且*叉不可解*（in-X-plicable）。连城里的数学家也招认，这样幽暗的题目他做不出来。*叉*，人人都知道，是一个未知量；可是在这桩案子里（他中肯地指出），有未知量的*叉*。

鲍勃——那个小鬼——的意见（他对自己「把段落*叉*了」一事讳莫如深），虽有他毫无保留、毫无畏惧的表白，所得的注意却不如我以为它应得的那样多。他说，就他而言，这事他全无怀疑，案情清楚：弹头先生「从来不肯像别人那样喝淡酒，偏没完没了地灌那受祝福的XXX麦酒（XXX ale），照自然的后果，那酒把他发起野蛮来，弄成一副*叉*（cross，凶横）相，*叉*到了*叉*（X-treme）点」。

## Landor’s Cottage / 兰多的小屋
===Original===

A Pendant to “The Domain of Arnheim”

===Chinese===

——《阿恩海姆庄园》的姊妹篇

===Original===

During a pedestrian trip last summer, through one or two of the river counties of New York, I found myself, as the day declined, somewhat embarrassed about the road I was pursuing. The land undulated very remarkably; and my path, for the last hour, had wound about and about so confusedly, in its effort to keep in the valleys, that I no longer knew in what direction lay the sweet village of B﻿—﻿—, where I had determined to stop for the night. The sun had scarcely *shone*﻿—strictly speaking﻿—during the day, which nevertheless, had been unpleasantly warm. A smoky mist, resembling that of the Indian summer, enveloped all things, and of course, added to my uncertainty. Not that I cared much about the matter. If I did not hit upon the village before sunset, or even before dark, it was more than possible that a little Dutch farmhouse, or something of that kind, would soon make its appearance﻿—although, in fact, the neighborhood (perhaps on account of being more picturesque than fertile) was very sparsely inhabited. At all events, with my knapsack for a pillow, and my hound as a sentry, a bivouac in the open air was just the thing which would have amused me. I sauntered on, therefore, quite at ease﻿—Ponto taking charge of my gun﻿—until at length, just as I had begun to consider whether the numerous little glades that led hither and thither, were intended to be paths at all, I was conducted by one of them into an unquestionable carriage track. There could be no mistaking it. The traces of light wheels were evident; and although the tall shrubberies and overgrown undergrowth met overhead, there was no obstruction whatever below, even to the passage of a Virginian mountain wagon﻿—the most aspiring vehicle, I take it, of its kind. The road, however, except in being open through the wood﻿—if wood be not too weighty a name for such an assemblage of light trees﻿—and except in the particulars of evident wheel-tracks﻿—bore no resemblance to any road I had before seen. The tracks of which I speak were but faintly perceptible﻿—having been impressed upon the firm, yet pleasantly moist surface of﻿—what looked more like green Genoese velvet than anything else. It was grass, clearly﻿—but grass such as we seldom see out of England﻿—so short, so thick, so even, and so vivid in color. Not a single impediment lay in the wheel-route﻿—not even a chip or dead twig.

===Chinese===

去年夏天，我徒步游历纽约州一两个依河的县，天色向晚时，对自己走的这条路竟犯了踌躇。这一带地势起伏得厉害；近一个钟头来，我的小路为了贴着谷地走，绕来绕去绕得昏天黑地，以致我已辨不清那个宜人的 B——村在哪个方向——我原打算到那里过夜的。严格说，太阳这一天几乎不曾「照」过，天却热得难受。一层烟霭，类似印第安夏的那种，裹住了万物，自然又添了我的迷惘。倒不是我很把这事故在心上。日落前、甚至天黑前若撞不上村子，那么一座荷兰式的小农舍之类，多半很快就会现出来——虽然，事实上左近（也许因为它如画有余、肥沃不足）人烟极稀。无论如何，背包作枕头，猎犬作哨兵，来一场露天的野宿，正是我求之不得的乐事。于是我逍遥自在地照旧走——庞托替我衔着枪——直走到末了，正当我开始纳闷，那些通向四面八方的小空地究竟算不算路，其中一条已把我引上一条确凿无疑的马车道。这错不了。轻车的辙印分明；虽然高高的灌木和蔓生的野树在头顶合了拢，下半截却毫无阻隔，连弗吉尼亚的山地大货车也过得去——我想那是同类车辆里气魄最大的一种了。只是这条路，除了穿林而过（若「林」字不算太重，叫它一片疏林也可）——除了明显的轮辙这一节——同我平生见过的任何路都不像。我说的辙印只隐约可辨——印在一片坚实而温润宜人的地面上，那地面看去与其像别的，不如像绿色的热那亚丝绒。是草，明明白白——可这样的草，出了英国我们难得见到——这样短，这样密，这样匀，颜色又这样鲜活。轮辙路上没有一样碍事的东西——连一片木屑、一根枯枝也没有。

===Original===

The stones that once obstructed the way had been carefully *placed*﻿—not thrown﻿—along the sides of the lane, so as to define its boundaries at bottom with a kind of half-precise, half-negligent, and wholly picturesque definition. Clumps of wild flowers grew everywhere, luxuriantly, in the interspaces.

What to make of all this, of course I knew not. Here was *art* undoubtedly﻿—*that* did not surprise me﻿—all roads, in the ordinary sense, are works of art; nor can I say that there was much to wonder at in the mere *excess* of art manifested; all that seemed to have been done, might have been done *here*﻿—with such natural “capabilities” (as they have it in the books on Landscape Gardening)﻿—with very little labor and expense. No; it was not the amount but the *character* of the art which caused me to take a seat on one of the blossomy stones and gaze up and down this fairy-like avenue for half an hour or more in bewildered admiration. One thing became more and more evident the longer I gazed: an artist, and one with a most scrupulous eye for form, had superintended all these arrangements. The greatest care had been taken to preserve a due medium between the neat and graceful on the one hand, and the *pittoresque*, in the true sense of the Italian term, on the other. There were few straight, and no long uninterrupted lines. The same effect of curvature or of color appeared twice, usually, but not oftener, at any one point of view. Everywhere was variety in uniformity. It was a piece of “composition,” in which the most fastidiously critical taste could scarcely have suggested an emendation.

I had turned to the right as I entered this road, and now, arising, I continued in the same direction. The path was so serpentine, that at no moment could I trace its course for more than two or three paces in advance. Its character did not undergo any material change.

===Chinese===

原先挡路的石头，都被仔仔细细地「安放」——而不是抛掷——在巷道两侧，给它的底界立了一种半是工整、半是疏放、全然入画的界石。空当里，一丛丛野花到处恣意地开着。

这一切该作何解，我自然不知道。这里有「人工」是无疑的——这不叫我惊奇——寻常意义上的路，都是人工之物；单是人工的「过甚」，也没有多少可怪；这一切若出在此地——凭这样天然的「资质」（造园书上的话）——费不了多少工本也办得到。不；不是分量，是这人工的「品格」，叫我拣一块开花的石头坐下，对这条仙境似的林荫道上下打量了半个钟头还多，赞叹得出神。我越看越明白的一件事是：有一位艺术家，一位对形式一丝不苟到极处的艺术家，督办了这一切布置。这里下过最大的功夫，在整洁风雅与 pittoresque（意大利文真正意义上的「如画」）之间保住恰当的中道。直线很少，绵长不断的直线一条没有。同一道弧、同一色，在同一视点通常出现两回，绝不多于两回。处处是整齐中的变化。这是一篇「构图」，最挑剔的眼光也几乎无处可以下笔修改。

进这条路时我是朝右拐的，如今站起来，我照旧朝右走。小路曲曲折折，任一时刻，往前望去我都只能看清两三步的走向。路的样子没有起什么大变化。

===Original===

Presently the murmur of water fell gently upon my ear﻿—and in a few moments afterward, as I turned with the road somewhat more abruptly than hitherto, I became aware that a building of some kind lay at the foot of a gentle declivity just before me. I could see nothing distinctly on account of the mist which occupied all the little valley below. A gentle breeze, however, now arose, as the sun was about descending; and while I remained standing on the brow of the slope, the fog gradually became dissipated into wreaths, and so floated over the scene.

As it came fully into view﻿—thus *gradually* as I describe it﻿—piece by piece, here a tree, there a glimpse of water, and here again the summit of a chimney, I could scarcely help fancying that the whole was one of the ingenious illusions sometimes exhibited under the name of “vanishing pictures.”

By the time, however, that the fog had thoroughly disappeared, the sun had made its way down behind the gentle hills, and thence, as if with a slight chassez to the south, had come again fully into sight, glaring with a purplish lustre through a chasm that entered the valley from the west. Suddenly, therefore﻿—and as if by the hand of magic﻿—this whole valley and everything in it became brilliantly visible.

The first coup d’oeil, as the sun slid into the position described, impressed me very much as I have been impressed, when a boy, by the concluding scene of some well-arranged theatrical spectacle or melodrama. Not even the monstrosity of color was wanting; for the sunlight came out through the chasm, tinted all orange and purple; while the vivid green of the grass in the valley was reflected more or less upon all objects from the curtain of vapor that still hung overhead, as if loth to take its total departure from a scene so enchantingly beautiful.

===Chinese===

不多时，潺潺水声轻轻落进我耳中——又过片刻，随着道路比先前更陡地一转，我发觉前方一道缓坡脚下卧着什么建筑。因为小雾谷里弥漫着雾，我什么都看不真切。好在太阳将落，一阵微风起来；我立在坡顶当儿，雾渐渐散作一绺一绺，浮在这片景色上空。

它这样——如我所描述的这般「渐渐」地——一块一块地整个呈现出来：这里一株树，那里一闪水光，这里又是一截烟囱顶，我几乎不能不信，整个儿是一幅巧夺天工的幻景，就是有时以「渐隐画」之名展出的那一种。

可等雾散尽，太阳已落到温柔的山丘背后，随即仿佛朝南轻轻一错步，又整个儿露了出来，带着紫红的光焰，从西面切入山谷的一道石罅间逼射过来。于是，仿佛有魔法一挥手——整条山谷连同谷中的一切，霎时灿然可见。

太阳滑入上述位置的那第一眼（coup d’oeil），给我的印象，正如我幼年看一场布置精妙的舞台奇观或传奇剧的收场时所得的印象。连色彩的浓艳也不曾缺席：日光从石罅里透出，染得一片橙紫；谷中草色的鲜绿，又或多或少映在万物上，映自那片还悬在头顶、仿佛不忍全然离开这片奇美的 vapor 帷幕上。

===Original===

The little vale into which I thus peered down from under the fog canopy could not have been more than four hundred yards long; while in breadth it varied from fifty to one hundred and fifty or perhaps two hundred. It was most narrow at its northern extremity, opening out as it tended southwardly, but with no very precise regularity. The widest portion was within eighty yards of the southern extreme. The slopes which encompassed the vale could not fairly be called hills, unless at their northern face. Here a precipitous ledge of granite arose to a height of some ninety feet; and, as I have mentioned, the valley at this point was not more than fifty feet wide; but as the visitor proceeded southwardly from the cliff, he found on his right hand and on his left, declivities at once less high, less precipitous, and less rocky. All, in a word, sloped and softened to the south; and yet the whole vale was engirdled by eminences, more or less high, except at two points. One of these I have already spoken of. It lay considerably to the north of west, and was where the setting sun made its way, as I have before described, into the amphitheatre, through a cleanly cut natural cleft in the granite embankment; this fissure might have been ten yards wide at its widest point, so far as the eye could trace it. It seemed to lead up, up like a natural causeway, into the recesses of unexplored mountains and forests. The other opening was directly at the southern end of the vale. Here, generally, the slopes were nothing more than gentle inclinations, extending from east to west about one hundred and fifty yards. In the middle of this extent was a depression, level with the ordinary floor of the valley. As regards vegetation, as well as in respect to everything else, the scene *softened and sloped* to the south. To the north﻿—on the craggy precipice﻿—a few paces from the verge﻿—up sprang the magnificent trunks of numerous hickories, black walnuts, and chestnuts, interspersed with occasional oak; and the strong lateral branches thrown out by the walnuts especially, spread far over the edge of the cliff.

===Chinese===

我从雾幕底下这样窥望的这条小谷，长不过四百码；宽度则从五十到一百五十、也许二百码不等。北端最窄，往南渐开，却并无精确的规则。最宽处在南端八十码之内。环抱小谷的坡，除非在北面，实在当不得「山」字。北面一道花岗岩绝壁拔起九十来英尺；如我方才所说，谷在此处宽不过五十英尺；可来访者从崖下往南走，便觉左右的坡，一齐矮了、缓了、也少了石头。一言以蔽之，万物向南倾斜、向南柔化；然而整条谷，只除两处，仍被高高低低的峰峦环束着。一处我已说过，在西偏北，正是落日如前所述、循着花岗石堤上一道天生的净切石罅照进这圆形剧场的地方；那道罅在最宽处约有十码宽，目力所及而已。它仿佛一道天然的堤道，向上、向上，通进未经勘探的深山老林。另一处开口正在谷的南端。这里两坡一般不过是缓缓的斜面，东西延展约一百五十码。正中有一处洼落，与谷底相平。至于草木，同其余一切一样，景物也是「向南柔化、向南倾斜」的。北面——在那嶙峋的绝壁上——离崖缘几步——拔起一株株山核桃、黑胡桃和栗树的雄干，间杂几株橡树；胡桃树尤其横出的强枝，远远探出崖沿。

===Original===

Proceeding southwardly, the explorer saw, at first, the same class of trees, but less and less lofty and Salvatorish in character; then he saw the gentler elm, succeeded by the sassafras and locust﻿—these again by the softer linden, redbud, catalpa, and maple﻿—these yet again by still more graceful and more modest varieties. The whole face of the southern declivity was covered with wild shrubbery alone﻿—an occasional silver willow or white poplar excepted. In the bottom of the valley itself﻿—(for it must be borne in mind that the vegetation hitherto mentioned grew only on the cliffs or hillsides)﻿—were to be seen three insulated trees. One was an elm of fine size and exquisite form: it stood guard over the southern gate of the vale. Another was a hickory, much larger than the elm, and altogether a much finer tree, although both were exceedingly beautiful: it seemed to have taken charge of the northwestern entrance, springing from a group of rocks in the very jaws of the ravine, and throwing its graceful body, at an angle of nearly forty-five degrees, far out into the sunshine of the amphitheatre. About thirty yards east of this tree stood, however, the pride of the valley, and beyond all question the most magnificent tree I have ever seen, unless, perhaps, among the cypresses of the Itchiatuckanee. It was a triple-stemmed tulip-tree﻿—the *Liriodendron Tulipiferum*﻿—one of the natural order of magnolias. Its three trunks separated from the parent at about three feet from the soil, and diverging very slightly and gradually, were not more than four feet apart at the point where the largest stem shot out into foliage: this was at an elevation of about eighty feet. The whole height of the principal division was one hundred and twenty feet. Nothing can surpass in beauty the form, or the glossy, vivid green of the leaves of the tulip-tree. In the present instance they were fully eight inches wide; but their glory was altogether eclipsed by the gorgeous splendor of the profuse blossoms. Conceive, closely congregated, a million of the largest and most resplendent tulips! Only thus can the reader get any idea of the picture I would convey. And then the stately grace of the clean, delicately-granulated columnar stems, the largest four feet in diameter, at twenty from the ground.

===Chinese===

往南走，探访的人先看见同一类树，只是越来越矮、越来越少萨尔瓦托式的野气；随后是较温柔的榆，接以檫木和皂荚——再接以更软的椴树、紫荆、梓树和枫——再往后，是更秀气、更谦和的品种。南坡的全副面目只覆着野灌木——偶尔一株银柳或白杨除外。谷底本身——（须知方才讲的草木都只长在崖上坡上）——可见三株离立的树。一株是榆，身量好，姿态绝美：守着谷的南门。另一株是山核桃，比榆大得多，整体也更出色，虽然两株都美到极处：它似把守着西北的入口，从峡谷咽喉的一丛乱石里拔起，把婀娜的身子以将近四十五度的斜角，远远探进这圆形剧场的日光里。而在这株树以东约三十码，立着这山谷的骄傲——毫无疑问是我平生所见最壮丽的一株树，或许只有伊奇亚图卡尼的柏树林里的可与之相比。那是一株三干的鹅掌楸（Liriodendron Tulipiferum）——木兰的天然一属。三干自母本离地约三英尺处分出，微微地、渐渐地岔开，到最大一干抽叶成荫处相距不过四英尺：那已在约八十英尺的高处。主干全高一百二十英尺。鹅掌楸叶子的形态、光亮鲜活的绿，其美无可逾越。眼前这几株，叶宽足有八英寸；可叶的荣华，全教繁花的富丽盖了下去。请想象：百万朵最大、最辉煌的郁金香紧紧簇拥在一处！读者唯有这样，才能约略领会我要传达的画面。还有那洁净、细粒的圆柱形树干——最大者离地二十英尺处围径四英尺——那样端庄的雍容。

===Original===

The innumerable blossoms, mingling with those of other trees scarcely less beautiful, although infinitely less majestic, filled the valley with more than Arabian perfumes.

The general floor of the amphitheatre was *grass* of the same character as that I had found in the road; if anything, more deliciously soft, thick, velvety, and miraculously green. It was hard to conceive how all this beauty had been attained.

===Chinese===

数不清的花，同旁的树的花交融——那些树虽远不及它雄伟，美丽却也不相上下——用胜过阿拉伯的芬芳，注满了山谷。

圆形剧场的整片地面，是同我在路上见过的一色草；若说有什么不同，是更受用地柔软、更厚、更如丝绒、更绿得神奇。这一切美如何养成，叫人难以想象。

===Original===

I have spoken of two openings into the vale. From the one to the northwest issued a rivulet, which came, gently murmuring and slightly foaming, down the ravine, until it dashed against the group of rocks out of which sprang the insulated hickory. Here, after encircling the tree, it passed on a little to the north of east, leaving the tulip tree some twenty feet to the south, and making no decided alteration in its course until it came near the midway between the eastern and western boundaries of the valley. At this point, after a series of sweeps, it turned off at right angles and pursued a generally southern direction meandering as it went﻿—until it became lost in a small lake of irregular figure (although roughly oval), that lay gleaming near the lower extremity of the vale. This lakelet was, perhaps, a hundred yards in diameter at its widest part. No crystal could be clearer than its waters. Its bottom, which could be distinctly seen, consisted altogether, of pebbles brilliantly white. Its banks, of the emerald grass already described, rounded, rather than sloped, off into the clear heaven below; and so clear was this heaven, so perfectly, at times, did it reflect all objects above it, that where the true bank ended and where the mimic one commenced, it was a point of no little difficulty to determine. The trout, and some other varieties of fish, with which this pond seemed to be almost inconveniently crowded, had all the appearance of veritable flying-fish. It was almost impossible to believe that they were not absolutely suspended in the air. A light birch canoe that lay placidly on the water, was reflected in its minutest fibres with a fidelity unsurpassed by the most exquisitely polished mirror. A small island, fairly laughing with flowers in full bloom, and affording little more space than just enough for a picturesque little building, seemingly a fowl-house﻿—arose from the lake not far from its northern shore﻿—to which it was connected by means of an inconceivably light-looking and yet very primitive bridge. It was formed of a single, broad and thick plank of the tulip wood. This was forty feet long, and spanned the interval between shore and shore with a slight but very perceptible arch, preventing all oscillation.

===Chinese===

我讲过谷的两处开口。从西北那处淌出一道小溪，轻轻絮语、微微泛沫，顺峡谷而下，直撞在离立山核桃所自的那丛乱石上。它绕树一匝，再往东偏北行去，把鹅掌楸留在南面二十英尺，一路不见大的改向，直行到谷的东西两界的中途附近。在那里，它拐了几个大弯，成直角折向南去，一路蜿蜒——最后没入一个小湖。湖形不规则（大体是椭圆），在谷的下端附近莹莹发亮。这小湖最宽处约莫一百码。没有什么水晶比它的水更清。湖底看得分明，全是莹白的卵石。湖岸是方才描写过的翡翠般的草，与其说是坡入、不如说是圆入下面那片清澈的天；而这天那样清，时时把上界的万物照得毫发不爽，以致真岸止于何处、映影的岸又起于何处，竟是个不小的难题。鳟鱼和别几种鱼——这池塘里的鱼挤得几乎不便——个个都像真的飞鱼。要说它们不是凌空悬着，几乎叫人不能信。静浮水面的一只轻巧桦皮独木舟，连同它最细的木纹，映在水里，其忠实胜过最精致的磨面镜子。一座小岛，正开着满岛的花，笑盈盈的，只比一座入画的小屋——看去是座禽舍——大出不多一点——从近北岸的湖心里隆起——同湖岸相连的，是一座看着轻得叫人不敢信、却又极原始的桥。桥由一块宽厚的鹅掌楸木板独木而成，长四十英尺，微弓而觉察得到的弧，跨在两岸之间，杜绝了一切晃动。

===Original===

From the southern extreme of the lake issued a continuation of the rivulet, which, after meandering for, perhaps, thirty yards, finally passed through the “depression” (already described) in the middle of the southern declivity, and tumbling down a sheer precipice of a hundred feet, made its devious and unnoticed way to the Hudson.

The lake was deep﻿—at some points thirty feet﻿—but the rivulet seldom exceeded three, while its greatest width was about eight. Its bottom and banks were as those of the pond﻿—if a defect could have been attributed, in point of picturesqueness, it was that of excessive *neatness*.

The expanse of the green turf was relieved, here and there, by an occasional showy shrub, such as the hydrangea, or the common snowball, or the aromatic seringa; or, more frequently, by a clump of geraniums blossoming gorgeously in great varieties. These latter grew in pots which were carefully buried in the soil, so as to give the plants the appearance of being indigenous. Besides all this, the lawn’s velvet was exquisitely spotted with sheep﻿—a considerable flock of which roamed about the vale, in company with three tamed deer, and a vast number of brilliantly-plumed ducks. A very large mastiff seemed to be in vigilant attendance upon these animals, each and all.

Along the eastern and western cliffs﻿—where, toward the upper portion of the amphitheatre, the boundaries were more or less precipitous﻿—grew ivy in great profusion﻿—so that only here and there could even a glimpse of the naked rock be obtained. The northern precipice, in like manner, was almost entirely clothed by grapevines of rare luxuriance; some springing from the soil at the base of the cliff, and others from ledges on its face.

===Chinese===

从湖的南端又续出一道溪，蜿蜒约三十码，穿过南坡正中那处「洼落」（已述），从百来英尺的直壁上跌落，曲曲折折、悄没声息地一路投奔哈德孙河去了。

湖是深的——深处有三十英尺——溪却很少超过三英尺深，最宽约八英尺。溪底溪岸同池塘一个样——若说入画上还能挑一样毛病，那就是「太整洁」。

绿茵的旷处，这里一丛、那里一丛地点缀着醒目的灌木，绣球、寻常的雪球花、香喷喷的塞林迦；或更常见的，是一丛丛天竺葵，开得斑斓万状。这些花都栽在盆里，盆又小心地理进土中，叫花木俨然土生。此外，草坪的绒毯上还精巧地点着羊——相当大的一群，同三头驯鹿、一大群彩羽的鸭子一起在谷中游荡。一条很大的獒犬，仿佛在警惕地照应着这些牲灵，一头也不漏。

沿东西两崖——近圆形剧场上端处，两界多少有些陡削——遍生着藤藤蔓蔓的长春藤——只有这里那里才露得出一线裸岩。北面的绝壁，也几乎全叫繁茂罕见的葡萄藤裹住了；有的从崖脚的土里发出来，有的从崖面的石台上垂下来。

===Original===

The slight elevation which formed the lower boundary of this little domain, was crowned by a neat stone wall, of sufficient height to prevent the escape of the deer. Nothing of the fence kind was observable elsewhere; for nowhere else was an artificial enclosure needed:﻿—any stray sheep, for example, which should attempt to make its way out of the vale by means of the ravine, would find its progress arrested, after a few yards’ advance, by the precipitous ledge of rock over which tumbled the cascade that had arrested my attention as I first drew near the domain. In short, the only ingress or egress was through a gate occupying a rocky pass in the road, a few paces below the point at which I stopped to reconnoitre the scene.

I have described the brook as meandering very irregularly through the whole of its course. Its two *general* directions, as I have said, were first from west to east, and then from north to south. At the *turn*, the stream, sweeping backward, made an almost circular *loop*, so as to form a peninsula which was *very* nearly an island, and which included about the sixteenth of an acre. On this peninsula stood a dwelling-house﻿—and when I say that this house, like the infernal terrace seen by Vathek, “*était d’une architecture inconnue dans les annales de la terre*,” I mean, merely, that its tout ensemble struck me with the keenest sense of combined novelty and propriety﻿—in a word, of *poetry*﻿—(for, than in the words just employed, I could scarcely give, of poetry in the abstract, a more rigorous definition)﻿—and I do *not* mean that merely outré was perceptible in any respect.

In fact nothing could well be more simple﻿—more utterly unpretending than this cottage. Its marvellous *effect* lay altogether in its artistic arrangement *as a picture*. I could have fancied, while I looked at it, that some eminent landscape-painter had built it with his brush.

The point of view from which I first saw the valley, was not *altogether*, although it was nearly, the best point from which to survey the house. I will therefore describe it as I afterwards saw it﻿—from a position on the stone wall at the southern extreme of the amphitheatre.

===Chinese===

作为这片小领地南界的那道微微的高垄，顶上是一道齐整的石墙，高度恰好拦得住鹿。别处再看不见什么栅栏；因为再无别处需要人工的围圈：——比如哪只迷路的羊，若想顺着峡谷逃出谷去，走不了几码，就会叫一道岩石绝壁拦住去路，从那壁上跌落的，正是我初近这片领地时便攝住我注意的那挂小瀑。总之，唯一的进出通道，是路上一处石隘间的一扇门，离我驻足眺望的地点只有几步。

我说过，这小溪一路曲折得毫无规则。它的两段「大方向」，如前所述，先是自西而东，后是自北而南。在「转折」处，溪水向后一兜，绕出一个近乎圆环的套，围成一个小半岛——离岛只差一点点——约占地十六分之一英亩。半岛上立着一所住房——当我说这房子同《瓦泰克》里所见的地狱平台一样，「était d’une architecture inconnue dans les annales de la terre」（属于尘世史册所不载的一种建筑）」时，我的意思仅仅是：它的整体给我以一种新异与妥帖交织的至锐之感——一句话，一种「诗」——（因为我几乎不能给出比这几个字更严格的、关于抽象的「诗」的定义）——我并不是说它哪里显出一点单纯的怪诞。

事实上，再没有什么比这座小屋更简单——更全然不事张扬的了。它奇妙的「效果」，全在它作为一幅画的艺术安排。我望着它，几乎要想象，是哪位高明的风景画家，用画笔把它搭起来的。

我初见山谷的那一点，虽已近乎最好，却不是「完全」最好地打量这座房子的地点。因此我按后来所见的样子来描写它——从圆形剧场南端那道石墙上的位置望去。

===Original===

The main building was about twenty-four feet long and sixteen broad﻿—certainly not more. Its total height, from the ground to the apex of the roof, could not have exceeded eighteen feet. To the west end of this structure was attached one about a third smaller in all its proportions:﻿—the line of its front standing back about two yards from that of the larger house, and the line of its roof, of course, being considerably depressed below that of the roof adjoining. At right angles to these buildings, and from the rear of the main one﻿—not exactly in the middle﻿—extended a third compartment, very small﻿—being, in general, one-third less than the western wing. The roofs of the two larger were very steep﻿—sweeping down from the ridge-beam with a long concave curve, and extending at least four feet beyond the walls in front, so as to form the roofs of two piazzas. These latter roofs, of course, needed no support; but as they had the *air* of needing it, slight and perfectly plain pillars were inserted at the corners alone. The roof of the northern wing was merely an extension of a portion of the main roof. Between the chief building and western wing arose a very tall and rather slender square chimney of hard Dutch bricks, alternately black and red:﻿—a slight cornice of projecting bricks at the top. Over the gables the roofs also projected very much:﻿—in the main building about four feet to the east and two to the west. The principal door was not exactly in the main division, being a little to the east﻿—while the two windows were to the west. These latter did not extend to the floor, but were much longer and narrower than usual﻿—they had single shutters like doors﻿—the panes were of lozenge form, but quite large. The door itself had its upper half of glass, also in lozenge panes﻿—a movable shutter secured it at night. The door to the west wing was in its gable, and quite simple﻿—a single window looked out to the south. There was no external door to the north wing, and it also had only one window to the east.

===Chinese===

正屋约长二十四英尺、宽十六——决计不多。从地面到屋脊，总高不超过十八英尺。正屋西头接建着一间，各边都约小三分之一：——正面比大屋缩进两码上下，屋脊自然也大大低于邻屋的屋脊。与这两座屋成直角、自正屋后部——不正在中间——伸出第三隔，很小——大体比西厢又小三分之一。两大间的屋顶极陡——从脊梁以一道长长的凹弧扫下来，在正面至少探出墙外四英尺，正好给两道游廊作顶。这后两片屋顶，自然无须支撑；可它们既有着「须支撑」的仪表，便只在四角立了细而素净的柱子。北厢的屋顶只是主顶一片的延伸。正屋同西厢之间，升起一根很高而颇细的方烟囱，硬邦邦的荷兰砖，黑红相间：——顶上一道砖砌的浅浅挑檐。两个山头上，屋顶也探出极多：——正屋东侧约四英尺，西侧约两英尺。正门不正在正间上，略偏东——两扇窗则偏西。窗不落地，却比寻常的长而窄得多——各配一扇门式的独扇窗板——窗玻璃呈菱形，块头颇大。门本身的上半也是玻璃，也是菱形块——夜里有一扇活动窗板关护。西厢的门开在山墙上，极简单——一扇窗朝南。北厢没有外门，也只有一扇朝东的窗。

===Original===

The blank wall of the eastern gable was relieved by stairs (with a balustrade) running diagonally across it﻿—the ascent being from the south. Under cover of the widely projecting eave these steps gave access to a door leading to the garret, or rather loft﻿—for it was lighted only by a single window to the north, and seemed to have been intended as a storeroom.

The piazzas of the main building and western wing had no floors, as is usual; but at the doors and at each window, large, flat irregular slabs of granite lay imbedded in the delicious turf, affording comfortable footing in all weather. Excellent paths of the same material﻿—not *nicely* adapted, but with the velvety sod filling frequent intervals between the stones, led hither and thither from the house, to a crystal spring about five paces off, to the road, or to one or two outhouses that lay to the north, beyond the brook, and were thoroughly concealed by a few locusts and catalpas.

Not more than six steps from the main door of the cottage stood the dead trunk of a fantastic pear-tree, so clothed from head to foot in the gorgeous bignonia blossoms that one required no little scrutiny to determine what manner of sweet thing it could be. From various arms of this tree hung cages of different kinds. In one, a large wicker cylinder with a ring at top, revelled a mocking bird; in another an oriole; in a third the impudent bobolink﻿—while three or four more delicate prisons were loudly vocal with canaries.

The pillars of the piazza were enwreathed in jasmine and sweet honeysuckle; while from the angle formed by the main structure and its west wing, in front, sprang a grapevine of unexampled luxuriance. Scorning all restraint, it had clambered first to the lower roof﻿—then to the higher; and along the ridge of this latter it continued to writhe on, throwing out tendrils to the right and left, until at length it fairly attained the east gable, and fell trailing over the stairs.

===Chinese===

东山墙那面光墙，由一道斜跨墙面的石级（带栏杆）破了寂——从南面拾级而上。趁着大展的屋檐，这几级台阶通向一扇阁楼门——或者说顶楼——因为它只靠北面一扇窗取光，看着本是作储物间用的。

正屋和西厢的游廊不像通常那样铺地；只是在门口和每扇窗下，大块扁平的不规则花岗石板嵌在柔软可爱的草皮里，无论什么天气都落脚稳当。同样石料的好路径——并不细细切磋，石与石之间常由绒毯似的草皮填缝——从屋前四通八达：通到五步开外一泓水晶泉，通到那条路，或通到北面溪外的一两间杂屋——那儿叫几株皂荚和梓树遮得严严实实。

离小屋正门不出六步，立着一株枯死的怪形梨树，从头到脚裹满了华丽的紫葳花，不细看，真辨不出这甜美的东西究竟是何物。树上各枝挂着形形色色的鸟笼。一只带顶环的大柳条圆笼里，一只反舌鸟正恣情欢跃；另一只是黄鹂；第三只是那没皮没脸的食米鸟——另有三四只更精巧的牢笼，金丝雀正唱得喧天。

游廊的柱子缠满素馨和香甜的忍冬；而正屋同西厢前墙的夹角里，迸出一株繁茂无比的葡萄藤。它不屑受一点约束，先攀上低屋顶——再攀上高的；又沿着这后一道屋脊蜿蜒向前，左右抛出卷须，末了竟爬到了东山墙，垂垂地淌下石级。

===Original===

The whole house, with its wings, was constructed of the old-fashioned Dutch shingles﻿—broad, and with unrounded corners. It is a peculiarity of this material to give houses built of it the appearance of being wider at bottom than at top﻿—after the manner of Egyptian architecture; and in the present instance, this exceedingly picturesque effect was aided by numerous pots of gorgeous flowers that almost encompassed the base of the buildings.

The shingles were painted a dull gray; and the happiness with which this neutral tint melted into the vivid green of the tulip tree leaves that partially overshadowed the cottage, can readily be conceived by an artist.

From the position near the stone wall, as described, the buildings were seen at great advantage﻿—for the southeastern angle was thrown forward﻿—so that the eye took in at once the whole of the two fronts, with the picturesque eastern gable, and at the same time obtained just a sufficient glimpse of the northern wing, with parts of a pretty roof to the spring-house, and nearly half of a light bridge that spanned the brook in the near vicinity of the main buildings.

I did not remain very long on the brow of the hill, although long enough to make a thorough survey of the scene at my feet. It was clear that I had wandered from the road to the village, and I had thus good traveller’s excuse to open the gate before me, and inquire my way, at all events; so, without more ado, I proceeded.

The road, after passing the gate, seemed to lie upon a natural ledge, sloping gradually down along the face of the northeastern cliffs. It led me on to the foot of the northern precipice, and thence over the bridge, round by the eastern gable to the front door. In this progress, I took notice that no sight of the outhouses could be obtained.

As I turned the corner of the gable, the mastiff bounded towards me in stern silence, but with the eye and the whole air of a tiger. I held him out my hand, however, in token of amity﻿—and I never yet knew the dog who was proof against such an appeal to his courtesy. He not only shut his mouth and wagged his tail, but absolutely offered me his paw﻿—afterward extending his civilities to Ponto.

===Chinese===

整座房子，连同两厢，都用老式荷兰木瓦盖的——瓦宽，角不圆。这种材料有个特性：用它盖的房子，看着下宽上窄——埃及建筑的路数；在眼前这一座，这一极入画的效果，又由几乎绕屋一周的一盆盆华丽的花给成全了。

木瓦漆着暗灰色；这中性色调怎样幸福地化进鹅掌楸叶子的鲜绿里——那树半笼着小屋——艺术家一想便知。

从靠近石墙的那个位置望去，如所述，这几座屋看正得势——因为东南角向前一挑——一眼便把两个正面连同入画的东山墙尽收眼底，同时又不多不少，瞥见北厢一角、泉屋的一角秀气的屋顶，和横跨在大屋近旁溪上那道轻桥的将近一半。

我在坡顶待得不久，却足以把脚下景色做一番周详的勘察。显然，我已偏离了去村里的路；这样，我便有了旅行者再好不过的借口，去推开面前的门，至少问一问路；于是我不必多礼，径自前行。

路过了门，像是落在一片天然的石台上，沿东北崖的崖面缓缓向下。它把我引到北崖脚下，再过桥，绕过东山墙，直到正门前。这一路，我留意到，那几间杂屋是望不见的。

我刚拐过山墙角，那条獒犬便一声不吭、凛然地朝我扑来，眼睛和满身气派却是一头虎。我把手向它递过去——以示修好——而我还不曾见过哪条狗抗得住这一礼。它不但闭了嘴、摇了尾，竟还把爪子递给我——随后又把它的殷勤扩及庞托。

===Original===

As no bell was discernible, I rapped with my stick against the door, which stood half open. Instantly a figure advanced to the threshold﻿—that of a young woman about twenty-eight years of age﻿—slender, or rather slight, and somewhat above the medium height. As she approached, with a certain *modest decision* of step altogether indescribable. I said to myself, “Surely here I have found the perfection of natural, in contradistinction from artificial *grace*.” The second impression which she made on me, but by far the more vivid of the two, was that of *enthusiasm*. So intense an expression of *romance*, perhaps I should call it, or of unworldliness, as that which gleamed from her deep-set eyes, had never so sunk into my heart of hearts before. I know not how it is, but this peculiar expression of the eye, wreathing itself occasionally into the lips, is the most powerful, if not absolutely the *sole* spell, which rivets my interest in woman. “*Romance*,” provided my readers fully comprehended what I would here imply by the word﻿—“romance” and “womanliness” seem to me convertible terms: and, after all, what man truly *loves* in woman, is simply her *womanhood*. The eyes of Annie (I heard someone from the interior call her “Annie, darling!”) were “spiritual grey;” her hair, a light chestnut: this is all I had time to observe of her.

At her most courteous of invitations, I entered﻿—passing first into a tolerably wide vestibule. Having come mainly to *observe*, I took notice that to my right as I stepped in, was a window, such as those in front of the house; to the left, a door leading into the principal room; while, opposite me, an *open* door enabled me to see a small apartment, just the size of the vestibule, arranged as a study, and having a large *bow* window looking out to the north.

Passing into the parlor, I found myself with *Mr. Landor*﻿—for this, I afterwards found, was his name. He was civil, even cordial in his manner, but just then, I was more intent on observing the arrangements of the dwelling which had so much interested me, than the personal appearance of the tenant.

The north wing, I now saw, was a bedchamber, its door opened into the parlor. West of this door was a single window, looking toward the brook. At the west end of the parlor, were a fireplace, and a door leading into the west wing﻿—probably a kitchen.

===Chinese===

看不见门铃，我便用手杖叩了叩那扇半开着的门。立时一个身影迎到门限——是一位二十八岁上下的少妇——苗条，不如说纤瘦，比中等身量略高。她走近时，步子里有一种全然难以描述的「羞怯的决断」，我对自己说：「这无疑就是天然——与人工相拗的——风致的极境了。」她给我的第二个印象——也是两者中鲜明得多的一个——是「热忱」。她深陷的双眼里闪出的那种「罗曼」——也许我该这样叫它——或出尘之气的强烈神采，从不曾这样沁进我的心灵深处。不知怎么，这种特有的眼神，偶或又漾上唇边，是把我的兴味钉在女人身上的最强大的——若非唯一的——咒语。「罗曼」——只要读者完全领会我在这里用这字所指的东西——「罗曼」与「女性」，在我看来是可互换的词；说到底，男人真正爱慕于女人的，无非是她的女性本身。安妮（我听见屋里有人唤她「安妮，亲爱的！」）的眼睛是「性灵的灰」；头发是浅栗色：这是我来得及观察到的全部。

承她至为客气地相邀，我进了门——先过一道颇宽的前厅。我此来主要是为了「观察」，便留意到进门右手是一扇窗，同屋前的那种相仿；左手一扇门通正屋；正对面一扇敞开的门，让我望见一间小室，恰与前厅等大，布置成一间书房，一扇凸窗朝北。

走进客厅，我便同兰多先生——因为这是他后来的姓名——到了一处。他客气，甚至热络，只是那时我更专心于观察这座深深引起我兴味的居所的布置，而不大留意主人的仪表。

北厢我此刻看出是一间卧房，门开在客厅里。这门以西是一扇独窗，向着小溪。客厅西头，是一处壁炉和一扇通往西厢的门——想必是厨房。

===Original===

Nothing could be more rigorously simple than the furniture of the parlor. On the floor was an ingrain carpet, of excellent texture﻿—a white ground, spotted with small circular green figures. At the windows were curtains of snowy white jaconet muslin: they were tolerably full, and hung *decisively*, perhaps rather formally in sharp, parallel plaits to the floor﻿—*just* to the floor. The walls were prepared with a French paper of great delicacy, a silver ground, with a faint green cord running zigzag throughout. Its expanse was relieved merely by three of Julien’s exquisite lithographs *a trois crayons*, fastened to the wall without frames. One of these drawings was a scene of Oriental luxury, or rather voluptuousness; another was a “carnival piece,” spirited beyond compare; the third was a Greek female head﻿—a face so divinely beautiful, and yet of an expression so provokingly indeterminate, never before arrested my attention.

The more substantial furniture consisted of a round table, a few chairs (including a large rocking-chair), and a sofa, or rather “settee;” its material was plain maple painted a creamy white, slightly interstriped with green; the seat of cane. The chairs and table were “to match,” but the *forms* of all had evidently been designed by the same brain which planned “the grounds;” it is impossible to conceive anything more graceful.

On the table were a few books; a large, square, crystal bottle of some novel perfume, a plain ground glass *astral* (not solar) lamp with an Italian shade; and a large vase of resplendently-blooming flowers. Flowers, indeed, of gorgeous colours and delicate odour formed the sole mere *decoration* of the apartment. The fireplace was nearly filled with a vase of brilliant geranium. On a triangular shelf in each angle of the room stood also a similar vase, varied only as to its lovely contents. One or two smaller bouquets adorned the mantel, and late violets clustered about the open windows.

It is not the purpose of this work to do more than give, in detail, a picture of Mr. Landor’s residence﻿—*as I found it*.

===Chinese===

再没有比这客厅的陈设更严格地简单的了。地板上铺一条织工极好的提花地毯——白地，缀小小的圆形绿纹。窗上是雪白的贾科内特细布窗帘：帘子相当宽大，「决然」地——也许有些拘板地——以平行挺括的褶直垂到地——「恰好」到地。墙上糊着一种极雅致的法国壁纸，银地，一道淡绿的细纹通体曲折而行。整面墙上，只以三幅朱利安精美的三色粉笔石版画破寂，都不装框，直接贴在墙上。其中一幅画的是东方的奢华——不如说靡曼；另一幅是一幅「狂欢图」，气韵无与伦比；第三幅是一颗希腊女子的头——那样天仙般美丽、神情却又那样恼人地无定的脸，从不曾这样攝住过我。

较为结实的家具，是一张圆桌、几把椅子（包括一把大摇椅）、一张沙发——或者说「长榻」；木料是素枫木，漆乳白，微间绿条；坐面为藤。椅和桌都「成套」，可所有这些「形」，显然出自设计「庭园」的那同一颗头脑；再想象不出更优雅的东西了。

桌上有几本书；一只大方形水晶瓶，盛着某一种新奇的香水；一盏素净的毛玻璃「星」灯（不是「日」灯），配一只意大利灯罩；还有一大瓶开得煌煌的鲜花。的确，颜色艳丽、气味芬芳的花，是这间屋子里唯一的「装饰」。壁炉里几乎插满一瓶灿烂的天竺葵。屋里每个角落一张三角小架上，也各立着这样一瓶，只瓶中的可爱内容不同。壁炉台上缀着一两束小花，迟开的紫罗兰簇在敞开的窗边。

本篇的目的，仅在于细绘一幅兰多先生居所的图画——照「我所见」的样子。
